en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the *Subodhālaṅkāra*:
The Introduction to the Work.
He who, by means of the three worlds— beginning with the one worshipped at the soles of his stainless feet—
which are unimpaired and undisturbed, made known his own incomparability.
I pay homage to the Lord of Sages, the one worthy of worship,
by whose favor he who has conquered his enemies attained the state of King of the True Dharma at the foot of the Bodhi tree of victory.
Homage be to him, whose excellent qualities are vast, stainless,
and praised by the virtuous; he who has attained the state of being a worthy vessel for that jewel which is the essence of the True Dhamma.
I honor with my head that supreme assembly,
which honors this most precious jewel of the Dhamma with their heads bowed in reverence.
Those who have obtained the essence known as the "Mātās" through the churning of the ocean of infinite scriptures by means of the supreme wisdom arising from the Mount Mandara of their minds—
being themselves happy, they bring happiness to others.
These my teachers are most venerable because of their virtues.
1. Chapter One: Comprehension of Faults; Commentary on the Homage to the Triple Gem.
May the speech of the Sage, beautiful as it was born from the lotus-like interior of the Lord of Sages and a refuge for all living beings, gladden my mind. Now,
at the commencement of this work, the author [offers salutations] to those endowed with the qualities of a poet, which are established by nature through the continuity of previous efforts.

Having perceived that hundreds of calamities had befallen young merchants who were devoid of other means, and with a heart whose essence was born of compassion, the author—desiring to compose the *Bandhalakkhaṇa* (The Characteristics of Knots) as a means to remedy them—first spoke the verse beginning with “*Muninde*,” etc., in order to demonstrate his own recollection of the True Dhamma and the deities, which serves as a sign for the attainment of his desired goal.
Now, it was stated: “desiring to compose the *Bandhalakkhaṇa*. [Is this not so?]
"What is the use of defining the characteristics here, when even those who have not seen the characteristics are seen binding [the verses]? True;

nevertheless, it should be understood that they might either be like the letters carved by woodworms appearing spontaneously, or follow the practice of those skilled in such matters, or perhaps result from prior familiarity with the treatises.
"My speech delights my mind" is the connection [of the sentence]. Or, "vāṇī" is another name for the goddess Sarasvatī.
There is a certain deity who, being entirely white, sits within the calyx of a white lotus that accomplishes every desired purpose; such is the popular saying.
But "Vāṇī" (Speech) refers to the True Dhamma spoken by the Fully Enlightened One, which is the sole refuge for the accomplishment of one's cherished goals through the absence of contradiction.
It is for this very reason that this deity is affected [by it]. In this regard, just as there is a gladdening of the mind from the arising of a voice (*sarassati*) among sentient beings...

The world [is delighted] by the True Dharma deity; indeed, it is the gladdening of the mind. For that [deity], who is entirely free from all defects, utterly stainless, and whose continuous activity provides manifold protection, there is the complete gladdening of the mind.
Through that, there is tranquility (*passaddhi*); through that, happiness (*sukha*); and through that, concentration (*samādhi*).

Because of the arising of the realization of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtāvabodha*) from the occurrence of concentration, various and manifold distinctions of meanings and words manifest effortlessly. From that—
And because the accomplishment of one's desired success [depends on him], he hopes for his favor through crooked conduct.
To specify what kind [of person he is], he says "the Lord of Sages" (*muninda*), and so forth. He is a *muni* because he knows (*munāti*) both worlds;

he is an *inda* because he exercises supreme sovereignty (*indati*) everywhere. Thus, he is a *muninda* as a sage who is a lord, or the lord (*inda*) of sages (*munīnaṃ*); that is, the Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddho*).

Thus, this is his perception based on a sign (*nimittakasaññā*). Even though there are other synonymous words, this term *muninda* is particularly appropriate for expressing the meaning desired by the poet as a singular designation;

for it is indeed fitting that the word *muni-inda* (Lord of Sages) nourishes the highest excellence, since he who exercises supreme sovereignty even over those sages who possess sovereignty through knowledge of both worlds causes others to rejoice by being their cause. This applies likewise to other words as well.
It nourishes elegance. For indeed, Sundarī was born within the interior of the lotus-face of such a one;
for that very reason she is her refuge, and therefore she delights the mind. His face is like the face of the Lord of Sages; it is a lotus (*ambhoja*).

Or rather, by virtue of shared characteristics such as being endowed with fortune (*lakṣī*), that very face is a lotus, a *paduma*. It is its interior (*gabbha*). By being born there—that is, by existing therein—...
Or, she is a faultless deity by virtue of her very origin. Furthermore, her speech is indeed faultless, as it is untouched by even a trace of defect;
thus he will say: "Endowed with the ornaments of excellence" (Subodhālaṅkāra 14), and so forth.
Therefore, she is a deity who serves as a refuge for living beings—those possessed of breath—merely by bringing about specific qualities such as eloquence and the like.
But by means of speech, she is the ultimate refuge through the warding off of all calamities and the accomplishment of all welfare and happiness.
And here, because the word *sabhāva* is inherently neuter, there is no change of gender. The word *mayhaṃ* (mine) is used in the singular to express one’s own lack of conceit;
this conveys the conduct of the virtuous. Furthermore, this is an instance of *silesa* (paronomasia), because the word *āvīkata* is employed in every sense. This is *silesa*.
And this [poetic ornament] nourishes glory everywhere through its crooked mode of expression. As it will be said in the *Subodhālaṅkāra*, verse 172:
"It nourishes [glory] among those of crooked conduct, but the *sileso* [straightforward ornament] [nourishes] glory in others. This is the commentary on the meaning here by way of summary.
However, by way of detailed exposition, the meaning can be explained in various ways; if that were done, there would also be the burden of excessive length.
The word "siyā" (it may be) is accepted as precisely this mode [of expression].

This venerable teacher Saṅgharakkhita Mahāsāmi, the author of most wonderful treatises whose range of intellect was perfectly pure, having crossed over to the further shore of all the scriptures including the Three Piṭakas, experienced abundant joy and happiness through his realization of the two teachings: practice (*paṭipatti*) and penetration (*paṭivedha*).

Since it is rooted in the scriptures (*pariyatti*), thinking, "Perhaps by means of some method or other, through the understanding of the meaning of those scriptures, I might indeed satisfy the virtuous," he who is undertaking this treatise—which serves as a means for attaining that [understanding]—performs a salutation to the chosen deity at the beginning of the work for the purpose of protecting his own conduct (*satācārānurakkhaṇatthaṃ*). (Variant: for the purpose of protecting good conduct.)
Recollection of the chosen deity (*iṭṭhadevatā*) is the cause for the completion of the desired work without obstruction;

thus, demonstrating the subject matter (*abhidheyya*), the means (*karaṇa*), the manner (*pakāra*), and the purpose (*payojana*)—which precede the removal of obstacles to the commencement of the book and the warding off of people who would oppose it—he uttered these three stanzas beginning with:
"The lotus-like face of the Lord of Sages... Herein, regarding the first stanza:
The homage to the Three Jewels, known as the "Wish-Fulfilling Deity," has been shown; in the second verse, those who would obstruct the undertaking have been repelled;

and in the third verse, the title and so forth have been presented. For thus, by way of expressing a desire for mental satisfaction regarding the "All-Knowing One’s Speech"—which is the scriptural tradition based on the supramundane Dhamma—his own confidence in the treasure of the Dhamma that is beneficial in its entirety is made manifest. And that confidence in the Dhamma...

Because it is inseparable from that [the Buddha], it is established that the homage directed toward the Triple Gem is also accomplished; thus, he demonstrates through a figurative mode of expression (*vaṅkavutti*) the homage whose object is the Three Jewels.
For in its actual meaning (*atthato*), it is a wholesome volition (*kusalacetanā*) that brings about the performance of the act of homage. Here, the result has already been stated above.
Furthermore, those who say that this composition of ornaments is like grinding flour when the ornaments of *rūpaka*, *samāsokti*, and so forth are already present, [are mistaken].
Having raised the objection that there is no existence for those who hold opposing views, such as Rāmasamma and others, and having accepted [the point], they are prohibited by the statement:
"Those from Suddhamāgadha do not employ [them]. For the fruit of refuting [objections] is indeed the faultlessness of the text.

Furthermore, by means of the word *alaṅkāra*—which illuminates both verbal ornaments (*saddālaṅkāra*) and semantic ornaments (*atthālaṅkāra*)—there is both the designation known as the "body of the text" (*ganthasarīra*) and the designation known as the "definition" (*saññā*).
Having stated that the word *alaṅkāra* refers to sound-ornaments (*saddālaṅkāra*) and so forth, and that it possesses the quality of being pure Māgadhī,
and having employed the word *anurūpa* as an adjective for the word *alaṅkāra*, it is understood that the Buddha’s word (*buddhavacana*) becomes useful through the usage of the Māgadhī language;
furthermore, by this [statement], the instrumental mode is established because the activity of the *alaṅkāra* treatise is dependent upon the ornamentation of meaning (*atthālaṅkāra*) and so forth.
By the word "ornament" (*alaṅkāra*), he demonstrates both the ornament itself and its purpose, which is known as the "construction of ornaments.

Furthermore, the relationship between the treatise and its purpose—characterized by the nature of the means and the end—is also implicitly stated simply by showing the treatise and purpose that serve as the basis for that relationship, because it depends upon them. For it has been said:
"The treatise and the purpose, both are the support and the dependent of the relationship."
"By the very statement of that [subject] and its function, that which depends upon them is also stated.
The meaning of this is as follows: both the subject (*sattha*) and the purpose (*payojana*), being the basis for the relationship and the support for it, have been stated;
by the very mention of those two—namely, by the speaking of their function—that relationship which arises depending upon them is also thereby stated.
In this context, it should be understood that the statement regarding the designations is for the sake of ease of conventional usage,

whereas the statement regarding the subject matter and so forth is for the purpose of demonstrating that only those texts endowed with these qualities— such as those preceded by wise understanding— are worthy of acceptance, while those contrary to them,
such as the words of a madman, are not worthy of acceptance. For it has been said:

“[A statement] that possesses a means consistent with the connection, a means consistent with the related entities, which expresses the purpose of man, which is attained through investigation, which is governed by investigation, and which is not [merely] based on the authority of another. This is its meaning:
[it is] one that possesses a means consistent with the connection—that is, the relationship characterized as the goal and the means, which serves as the basis for the signified and the signifier.
It is a collection of sentences endowed with the characteristics stated in the 106th verse of the *Abhidhānappadīpikā*—
“A group of words having a single verb may be a sentence, provided it possesses a factor of action”—

which serves as the cause for thoroughly understanding the mutually corresponding qualities of related things, and which expresses the aims of man, namely the fourfold aims of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.

The treatise that conforms to the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*) is what has been attained through investigation; it is attained through the examination of the characteristics of the range of knowledge (*ñāṇagati*), and it is intended.
Beyond this, any other treatise not attained from the stated characteristics is not intended. This, then, is the purpose for the placement of these verses here:
[of] her named Sarasvatī, who dwells within the lotus-heart in the world, who is white in all her limbs, and who accomplishes whatever desired aim.

Having applied this meaning to the deity by way of the conventional designation "speech," the meaning of the words should be understood as follows—since it is stated by means of the ornament of *abhinnapada-sileśa* (the poetic figure of unbroken-word-riddle):

she is beautiful because of her birth, occurrence, or arising within the womb—the interior—of the lotus known as the mouth of the Lord of Sages (*muninda*), which is like a mouth due to its possession of qualities such as splendor and fragrance; yet she is not [beautiful] through the birth of the lotus that is the mouth itself.
The goddess Sarasvatī— whose speech is stainless and beautiful, and who is therefore the refuge for living beings,
serving as a shelter for all creatures by the power of removing harm and bringing about welfare, and who is endowed with the aforementioned qualities—
is not the "speech of the Omniscient One," that jewel of the True Dhamma; yet, while I am occupied in composing this book, it gladdens my mind.
"May he satisfy [us] by accomplishing our desired aims.

He is a *muni* because of his knowledge of both worlds, and an *Inda* because of his exercise of lordship; thus, by a *kammadhāraya* compound, he is *muninda*. Alternatively, by being the fifth among the four types of *muni*—the householder *muni*, the non-householder *muni*, the trainee *muni*, and the non-trainee *muni*—he is *Inda*;
thus, by a *chaṭṭhītappurisa* compound, he is *muninda*. This is like the word "speaking" (*vadana*) when applied to a deity.

"Face" (*vadana*) is [used] for "lotus" (*ambhoja*); when both the face and the lotus are understood through metaphorical application (*upacāra*) as being like a lotus on the side of the True Dhamma (*saddhamma*), there is a *kammadhāraya* compound.

Thus, the sentences are: "The lotus-face of the Lord of Sages" (*munindassa vadanambhojam*), "the womb of that [face]" (*tassa gabbho*), "the arising within that [womb]" (*tasmiṃ sambhavo*), and "beautiful by means of that [arising]" (*tena sundarī*).
Even though the word "merchant woman" (*vāṇiyā*) functions as a qualifier, because the word "refuge" (*saraṇa*) is exclusively neuter...
There is no change of gender. The short vowel in *pāṇinaṃ* [is used] because of the deviation of the long vowel.
By the singular form *mayhaṃ*, he illuminates his own lack of pride, which is the cause for the arising of virtuous qualities.

Even though there are other epithets for the Victor (*jina*), the word *muninda* (Lord of Sages) possesses other meanings characterized as being desirable, pleasing to the mind, resembling a lotus, beautiful, and a refuge.
It is appropriate because it nourishes propriety (*ocitya*). For indeed, the face of such a person is like a lotus;
the beautiful woman born within that mouth is therefore a refuge for living beings. Precisely for that reason, her proficiency in gladdening the mind is well-established, and thus there is propriety.
This propriety, which is widespread in the world, is worthy of respect; for in this regard, only the supreme poets [possess it].
"Teachers. For it is said in the *Subodhālaṅkāra*, verse 104:
"That which is known as 'propriety' (ocitya) is to be understood as that which is renowned in the world with great respect;
therein, the virtuous ones, the preeminent among poets, are those whose origin is instruction (upadesa)."
The ancient sages,
adorned with the ornaments of the Rāmāyaṇa and Mahābhārata, exist;
nevertheless, those pure Māgadha [grammarians] do not employ them.

2. Having thus demonstrated the worship of the chosen deity (*iṭṭhadevatā-pūjā*) by way of the direct manifestation of the Jewel of the True Dharma (*saddhamma-ratana*), which has been personified by various skillful deities who have attained the perfection of immeasurable success, [the author] first refutes those people who object to the commencement of another characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) by asking, "Is not the previous [characteristic] already possessed of the defining mark of being existent?
Therefore, what is the use of this grinding of flour? [He then states] the subject matter (*abhidheyya*) and the purpose (*payojana*).

In order to show the relationship [between the author and the work], he says: “Rāmasamma,” and so forth. This refers to the ancient teachers beginning with Rāmasamma; or else, it refers to those works related to them.
For indeed, by virtue of such a relationship, a designation for one thing may be applied to another, just as some medical treatise is called “Bimbisāra.
*Alaṅkāras* are specific types of ornaments; they are designated as “ornaments” (*alaṅkāra*) in the sense that they establish the ornaments of composition.

Or, they are specific compositions (*ganthavisesā*). "Santo" means beautiful. Both are ancient (*purātanā*), having existed in former times (*pubbakāle*); they are archaic (*porāṇikā*). Both exist (*santi*).
Even though they are found (*saṃvijjanti*), nevertheless, this collection of particles beginning with *tu* is used to introduce a distinction.
The meaning is: "even though this is so. "Suddhamāgadhikā" means those existing in Magadha, or those known there as Magadha.
*Sad-dā*: these are their [sounds], or they are fixed (*niyutta*) within them; thus, they are *Māgadhikā*.

And they are *suddhā*—pure by virtue of being free from the impurities of the speech of the Sakkaṭas and others, or unmixed because they have not been familiarized with it—and since they are *Māgadhikā*, they are *Suddha-Māgadhikā*, i.e., the *Yatipotā*.
They do not employ the aforementioned ornaments (*alaṅkāra*), which are specific types of jewelry, nor do they experience the specific modes of adornment (*pasādhana*).
Regarding the specific types of compositions (*ganthavisesa*), the literal meaning (*saddattha*) here is as follows:

because of the capacity for grasping, retaining, and so forth, they constitute one's own *suddhamāgadhika* (pure Māgadhī) [speech], while Rāmasamma and others constitute the *sakkaṭa* (Sanskrit) and other [languages]. Furthermore, the sense of "state" (*bhāvattha*) is fulfilled here through the application of such a conception (*patīti*).
Those ornaments, which were previously beautiful due to their own state of purity (*suddhamāgadhikā*), have now reached a state of being seized by impurity (*malaggahita*).
Thinking, "What use have we, who are pure beings, for those things that are defiled?
they do not employ them. However, there is indeed some matter that is being understood in the compositions of the great poets.
As it has been said: "That which exceeds the well-known constituent parts shines forth like the loveliness in women."
2. Because they are praised by the wise, these ornaments are beautiful (*sobhana*). They are ancient (*purātana*), having arisen in former times.
They are called the *rāmasamma* and other ornaments because they were composed by teachers such as Rāmasamma;
or, due to their connection with them, they bear names similar to those [teachers], just as the medical treatise known as the *Bimbisāra* is so designated. These are the ornaments (*alaṅkāra*).
Although there exist specific types of ornaments— either particular adornments or specific literary works so named because they establish the nature of ornamentation—
nevertheless, even though such things exist, those who speak only the Māgadhī language do not employ these ornaments, such as the *rāmasamma* and others, as a means of embellishment,
due to their lack of familiarity with other languages such as Sakkata, Pākaṭa, and so forth, whether by way of learning, memorizing, or otherwise.
They do not frequent [them]. "Māgadha" refers to sounds existing in Magadha or known among them.
They possess these [sounds], or they are connected with them, thus they are called *māgadhikā*. The word *suddha* (pure) is either a qualifier of "Magadha" or a qualifier of "*māgadhika*.
Because such sounds possess a specific mode of cognition (*patīti*), here even the sense of "existence" (*bhāva*) is implied. For thus, the pure Magadhan [speech] [is distinguished] by its own...
Even though they possess purity through their arrangement and beauty, those who despise them as "impure" because the language is archaic do not employ them.

It should be understood that even the "lesser meaning" (bhāvatthalēsa), which serves as a support for the intended meaning desired by the speaker, is found only in the utterances of the great poets. For it has been said:
"But there is indeed some subject matter being perceived in the works of the great poets,
which exceeds the well-known constituent parts— "
“...does not shine forth like beauty in women.

Its meaning is as follows: whatever subject matter—be it even a mere fragment of meaning—that is understood or perceived within the speech, that is, the specific expressions, of the *mahākavis*, the honored poets, truly exists; that very subject matter [is present] in women (*aṅganāsu*), in wives.

It shines and glows, being more than the well-known constituent parts—exceeding the visible members of the body such as hands and feet—just as beauty (*lāvaṇya*) exceeds [the sum of] its parts, or as loveliness becomes an object of the mind;
thus, it appears as something exceeding the well-known constituent parts, being more than the constituent parts of the word *pakāsa*.
This concludes the commentary on the term *abhidhāna*.
"Even with that, one might satisfy them when they are devoid of ornaments;
yet this exertion is disproportionate to suitable ornaments.
(3) "By that," and so forth. By which reason they do not employ ornaments—that is, by way of being devoid of ornaments, meaning [devoid] of jewelry—[they are satisfied].
Or, being devoid of specific poetic ornaments (*gantha-viseṣa*), or even if they are [present] but lacking those ornaments already mentioned—

may I, by means of an ornament or adornment appropriate to these young elephants of ascetics (*yatipotaka*), because they are now being composed in a novel manner and because they consist of speech dwelling within the lotus-face of the One Possessing Ten Powers (*dasabala*), satisfy them according to their desire for the fulfillment of their wishes.
Or, by way of [the practice of] listening and retention, when one is satisfied with mere usage, the thought "I shall do so; perhaps indeed, what if..."—this is the exertion.

This is our application of the equipment for ornaments that produces such satisfaction. It is called an *alaṅkāra* because "by means of this, they adorn the personal existence (*attabhāva*)," namely, an ornament such as a necklace, an armlet, and so forth. Or, it is because "by means of this, they adorn the bound body."

However, by the word "alaṅkāra" (ornament), the master Alaṅkāratissa has included various kinds of verbal ornaments, such as *pasāda* (clarity) and so forth, as well as objective ornaments, such as *sabhāva-vutti* (natural expression) and so forth; by means of these, the body of the composition—consisting of both word and meaning—is made beautiful.
For just as ornaments such as necklaces and armlets are placed upon the body of a man so that it shines, so too is it with the body of the composition.
Both verbal ornaments (*saddālaṅkāra*) and semantic ornaments (*atthālaṅkāra*) are set forth, by means of which [the composition] shines. For this very reason, he will say:

“But ornaments lead to that [beauty], because they are more easily found,” which is Subodhālaṅkāra verse 9; and also “In that which is endowed with semantic ornaments,” etc., which is Subodhālaṅkāra verse 164.
However, by virtue of its function as the provision of ornament (*alaṅkāravidhānabhāva*), the body of the composition itself is an ornament because it serves that purpose;
likewise, the treatise named *Subodhālaṅkāra*, which explains that [ornament], is like the *Maṅgalasutta* because it provides an explanation of what is ornamented. For he will say:
"The book too is an expositor of the ornaments of the poet's speech" (*Subodhālaṅkāra*, verse 12), and so forth. To this, it is said:
“This word ‘mukhyo-laṅkāra-saddo’ (the primary ornament-word) is based on the ornamenting of the meaning of words;
however, by implication, it applies likewise to the subject matter and to the treatise as well.
By this, its denotable objects and other characteristics are stated. That which is denoted is the *abhidheyya* (denotable); [this refers to] the entire treatise taken together.
This is the meaning of "to be spoken" (*vacanīyattha*). And that consists in the presentation of those [ornaments] through the arrangement of bodily ornaments.
For they are presented by means of the *Subodhālaṅkāra*. Furthermore, since that by which something is presented has this as its meaning, it is also the subject matter (*abhidheyya-sattha*).
The purpose (*payojana*), however, is clearly shown to be the preparation of the bodily ornaments, because the *Subodhālaṅkāra* proceeds based upon that.

For that which exists for the sake of something is its purpose (*payojana*); and that [purpose] is characterized by poetry, fame, renown, and so forth, because the composition of the *Subodhālaṅkāra* is intended for that end through tradition.
As for the relationship between the teacher and the purpose, characterized as the means and the goal, it has indeed been shown by the author himself. As he said:
“The word, the purpose, both the connection and the support;
[these are] stated for the sake of what has been said and what is yet to be said, and that which depends on them is also stated.

And the mention of the denotation and so forth is because they are taken up by those possessing a particular kind of investigation, whereas for others it is something to be abandoned, like the speech of a madman. For this has been said:

“[That] which possesses a means [of practice] consistent with its connection, which expresses the welfare of persons, and which is attained through investigation—such is the Word; that which is other than this is not the Word.

And here, by the term “Word,” it is precisely the Teacher’s teaching itself that is intended—a collection of intermediate sentences endowed with the characteristics of a sentence and having the nature of a great sentence.
3. By reason of the ornaments they employ, [the verses] are devoid of specific ornaments or specific poetic figures;

being free from these, they are pure Māgadhī. This purity of the Māgadhī is due to their being fresh and conforming to the nature of the Māgadhī language, as well as because they were composed according to the words spoken by the One of Ten Powers (the Buddha).
"Or perhaps I might satisfy her with a suitable ornament or a particular kind of jewelry, or with a special perfume;
or by causing her to wear ornaments, or by making her master and retain a particular treatise or subject of study—I might indeed make her content, thinking, 'Oh, how wonderful!
This is my exertion, this is my application of ornaments and requisites. 'Apināma' means 'perhaps'."
Here, the word *iti* is understood [as an ellipsis].
"Devoid of ornaments" means either "those by whom ornaments are avoided" or "devoid of those which are ornaments. "Anurūpa" means conforming to form (*rūpa*), or form that has followed after form;
[the phrase] means "by that which is conforming" (*anurūpena*). That by which one adorns the personal body (*attabhāva*) is an "ornament" (*alaṅkāra*), such as necklaces, armlets, and so forth.

Regarding the category of ornaments (*ābharaṇa-pakkha*), as for the category of composition (*gantha-pakkha*), it is called "ornament" (*alaṅkāra*) because one adorns the body of the composition with it.

By virtue of this primary sense, both the ornaments of sound—such as alliteration (*pasāda*) and so forth—and the ornaments of meaning—such as natural description (*sabhāva-vutti*) and so forth—are spoken of.

However, in a secondary sense, even the body of the composition itself, which serves as the basis for these two types of ornament, is designated by such terms as *maṅgala-sutta* (Auspicious Discourse) or *ratana-sutta* (Jewel Discourse).

It is also called by the name *Subodhālaṅkāra-vara* (The Excellent Treatise on Clear Understanding of Figures of Speech), because it elucidates figures of speech and is so named in the sense that "by means of this, the two kinds of figures of speech are rightly understood. This very point has been stated:
"This word *alaṅkāra* is primarily used in the sense of 'ornament,' based upon the ornamentation of words and meanings."
"But by way of capacity, there is a determination; likewise, it is possible in the case of the Teacher as well.

Herein, "capacity" (sāmatthiya) means that if, according to the conventional usage of the support and that which establishes it, there were no object supported nor anything to be established by it, what else could it be? It is characterized solely by the impossibility of its being otherwise.
For those whose wisdom is not accumulated—that which is praised in many other treatises—
Overwhelmed by delusion, these do not understand anything at all.
What is the use of listening to the words of those for whom there are no teachers here in this world?
Only those who are strewn with the dust from their [the teachers'] feet are truly virtuous and discerning.

4–5. Having thus shown the subject matter and so forth, preceded by the rejection of the commencement of characteristics and the refutation of those who raise objections, there now follows the discernment of merits and faults by the Teacher himself in all instances. For this very reason it is said:
“The discernment of merits and faults in all cases is done by the Teacher alone;
what greater rashness than this could there be to do it without the Teacher?”

Therefore, the investigation into the distinction between merits and defects belongs only to those who know the science [of poetics], not to those who are ignorant of the treatise or who are mere "beasts among men" (purisapasū). Thus it is said in the *Kāvyādāsā* (1.8):
"How can people who do not know the science [of poetics] distinguish between merits and defects?
What authority does a blind man have for perceiving the differences in forms?"

Since it is thus, he spoke the two verses beginning with "Of those who... (*yesaṃ*) in order to demonstrate through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that this [insight] was attained only by one who possesses the many-hundred-eyed vision of the Buddhas in seeing virtues and faults, and not by anyone else who is the opposite.
Therein, "of those" (*yesaṃ*) is an indefinite designation; the meaning is "by whom.
By whom they were not accumulated, nor gathered into a heap, nor—even though existing in various continuities—perfumed into a single continuity by way of the principle of unity (*ekattanaya*).
"Not cultivated" is what is meant. What is it? It is wisdom, which consists in the discernment of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted. To the question "Of what kind?", he says:

"Accustomed to many treatises. This means that for those by whom this wisdom—which is accustomed to, that is, familiarized through hearing, memorizing, and so forth—with many treatises such as the Tipiṭaka, logic (takkā), grammar (byākaraṇa), and the *alaṅkāra*—has not been accumulated, they are [described as such]. The word "these" (*ete*) is a restrictive term referring to those previously mentioned.

"Overwhelmed by delusion" (*sammohabbhāhatā*) means that, due to the absence of the aforementioned wisdom characterized by excellence, they are overwhelmed—that is, specifically struck down—by delusion which has attained strength;

the intention is that they have become thus afflicted. Since this is so, therefore, regarding anything whatsoever among the things to be abandoned or adopted, such as the lack of application to what is improper, or the failure to obtain seclusion through listening to the venerable teachers' words and relying upon them—the wisdom of seclusion... [text continues]
"They do not understand through their own gain" means they do not know.

For even one who is burdened by the defects of laziness and other such faults may, by virtue of constant practice and service, become devoted to the lotus-like feet of a venerable teacher—even if scattered far away—and after a long time, through the power of familiarity with various other treatises, attain such proficiency in wisdom.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“A person who associates with the inferior declines;
one who associates with equals never falls away;
by approaching the superior, one rises quickly.”
"Therefore, one should associate with one who is superior to oneself" (Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.26). The intended meaning here is this:
only such a wise person is qualified for the discernment of virtues and faults; no other, being the opposite of that, is a true "birth of man.
This is a conventional usage of a specific sense. Therefore he said: "What use have you for those who merely listen to his words?"

“For those who have no teachers here. “Here” means in this world; for those people who have no teachers toward whom they ought to show obedience at their feet and perform service, what is the use of that wisdom, even if it possesses the flavor of discernment, for those who lack direct knowledge?
There is not even a trace of it; the intention is that they have simply not attained it here. Now, [the author explains] by way of contrast:

He said, beginning with "those who," and so forth: those who are endowed with the excellence of merit previously performed and the like, who are covered, overspread, and strewn with the dust of the feet of those teachers;

they alone are the virtuous ones (sādhū), well-known by way of the aforementioned method through the measure of their wisdom, and indeed discerning persons (vivekino) possessed of the perfection of wisdom that determines the distinction between the qualities of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted.
The intention is that those very [qualities and faults] have been understood here through the discrimination of virtues and defects.

Furthermore, since this service to the feet of the teacher must be performed with distinguished devotion, he directs virtuous people toward its practice by means of a crooked course (vaṅkavutti). 4–5.
If those who possess the proficiency of knowledge acquired from the entirety of the scriptures should attribute a fault [to this work], the refutation of that fault [is provided].

He spoke these two verses beginning with “Yesaṃ... pe... kiṃ no” in order to show that those who pride themselves on being learned disregard the words [of the Buddha] merely because they lack a thorough understanding of the specific points (padesāvabodhana), and to demonstrate through that very means his own unique and profound reverence, which must be cultivated by virtuous people with the highest respect, while also illustrating his crooked conduct.
[This refers to] many treatises, such as the Tipiṭaka, the *Tarka*, the *Vyākaraṇa*, and so forth.
The wisdom consisting of hearing (*sutamayā paññā*)— which is cultivated through the means of hearing, grasping, and retaining the inner meaning designated as "reality" among many texts—
is not accumulated by those [who lack it], because even though two [moments of consciousness] do not arise simultaneously,
there is a state of accumulated mass, and because the later wisdom receives the conditions of immediate proximity, repetition, and so forth from the earlier wisdom.
Or, because they occur as a predominance of distinct states, there is no accumulation into a mass even though they are to be accumulated.

These people, devoid of such proficiency in wisdom and struck down by delusion, do not understand anything at all regarding what is to be abandoned or what is to be adopted, for they have been specifically overwhelmed by delusion which has gained strength due to the absence of proficiency in wisdom.
[The terms] "not one" and "not many," and "those who are teachers," and "between them"—[these are the respective meanings].
And there is the analysis [of the compound] as "accustomed to that" and "struck down by delusion. Therefore it was said in the *Kāvyādāsa* (1.8):
"How can people—who do not know what is beneficial or harmful regarding virtues and faults—discriminate?
What authority does a blind man have for perceiving the distinctions of forms?"
The meaning of this is: how can people who do not know the treatises distinguish between virtues and faults?

For instance, in the perception of the various kinds of forms, what role does the act of bringing [an object] before one’s eyes play for a blind person in the discernment of specific forms such as blue or yellow? It plays no role at all.
Therefore, the discrimination between virtues and faults occurs only through the well-clear eye of wisdom that has entered into many different treatises.
In its absence, it simply does not occur. This very point is stated:
"The discernment of virtues and faults is found only where there is a teacher;
what could be more reckless than that which one performs without a teacher?"
The meaning of this is as follows: In all matters, the discernment of virtues and faults comes from the teacher alone.

Apart from the teacher—that is, apart from the wisdom appropriate to a teacher and so forth—whatever act of distinguishing between the beneficial and the harmful one performs is nothing other than recklessness;
such impulsive actions, performed without investigation, do not exist at all.
In this world, for those people who have not performed meritorious deeds,
their teachers are dear, venerable, and worthy of esteem;
they are counselors who are patient with their speech.
“He shall deliver profound discourse, yet he shall not urge [one] toward what is improper.
For teachers who possess the qualities thus specified, there is no need for attending at their feet or service at their feet; what is the use of those?

The purpose [of this work] is as follows: those people who have performed meritorious deeds and are sprinkled with the dust from the feet of their teachers—being thus adorned by the dust from the feet of those venerable ones—become truly virtuous and secluded individuals, having attained distinguished wisdom through seclusion by attending upon spiritual friends and teachers;
it is they alone who understand seclusion, such is the meaning. *Sussūsā* is the desire to hear, and based upon that, there is also the service of attending at the feet which ought to be performed.
That constitutes what is called "eager desire for that purpose. The grammatical analysis (*viggaha*) is: "eager desire for their feet," "their feet," "dust upon them," and "covered by that [dust].

Because disciples are dependent upon the teacher for the attainment of all their own progress, they should serve those who are indeed superior to themselves in virtue. For it was said by the Blessed One:
“A person who associates with the inferior falls away;
one who associates with equals never declines;
by approaching the superior, one rises quickly.”
"Therefore, one should associate with those who are superior to oneself.
(Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.26) Poets whose minds are fixed on the stage of drama compose whatever they may;
this is not at all a cause for wonder to others.
Even while reflecting upon that very [work], it is that same bond which is full of wonder;

by means of it, they satisfy the wise, even though they have not applied themselves there with diligence. (6–7) Having thus demonstrated what is understood through the method of agreement and difference (*anvaya-vyatireka*), [the author now considers]: "What is the use of our lack of familiarity with poetry and drama, or the exhaustion produced by the application to composing special literary works?"
He encourages his audience, who have become despondent, with the words beginning "poets and actors" (*kabbanāṭakā*). Poetry (*kavba*) is that which belongs to a poet (*kavi*);

it is the composition consisting of poetic application. It is of various types: prose (*pajja*), verse (*gajja*), mixed prose and verse (*pajjagajja*), and that called *campū*, which consists of a collection of intermediate sentences endowed with the nature of constituent parts such as the *muttakā* and so forth, and is composed of great sentences. It is distinguished by various classes of meters (*vuttajāti*).

And there is the *mahākavva* (great poem). Now, that *mahākavva* is called a *saggabandha* because it is bound—that is, composed—by means of specific sections named "heavens" (*sagga*). Its characteristics are described in various ways, such as:
"The opening of a *saggabandha* may be a benediction, a salutation, or a statement of the subject matter related to the composition," and so forth. How is that?
“The *Saggabandha* is called the Great Poem (*Mahākavva*); its characteristics are:
salutation, description of the subject matter, and benediction as its opening.
It consists of narratives derived from history or is based upon the peaceful [state].”
Dependent upon the fruit of the four groups, with four noble leaders,
it contains the descriptions of the city, the new moon, Mount Sela, and the rising of the sun;
as well as the sporting in gardens and waters, and the festival of the drinking of honey-wine.
With deceptions and marriages, with the birth and growth of princes,
and also with secret spells, envoys, expeditions, battles, and the exaltation of leaders—
this work is adorned, not abbreviated, and continuous with aesthetic flavors and dramatic sentiments.
“With verses that are not overly prolix, with charming diction and smooth transitions,
and with the boundaries of the sections clearly demarcated in every respect—
such a poem, well-adorned, becomes delightful to the world and endures for the duration of an eon. (Kāvyādāsa 1.14–19)

In this context, "based on traditional narratives" (*itihāsakathubbhūta*) means based on accounts of events from the past. "Based on what is existent" (*santasannissaya*) means based on the conduct of kings and others who possess other forms of excellence or beauty.

"Dependent on the fruit of the four groups" (*catuvaggaphalāyatta*) means dependent on the fruits of the four groups, beginning with the Dhamma. "Dhamma" refers to that which has the arising of prosperity and Nibbāna as its cause.
"Attha" (benefit) refers to the acquisition of knowledge, lands, and so forth, according to what is known, as well as the protection of what has been acquired. "Kāma" (pleasure) refers to...
Hell is the realm; application is the practice. Liberation means the cessation of all suffering of saṃsāra.

"The four noble leaders" refers to that wherein there is a leader who is skillful in the four [tasks], noble and magnanimous through his endowment with the power of energy, the power of courage, and the power of strength, as well as through his excellence in generosity and other virtues;
he is the opposite and the adversary of [the enemy]. Honey is wine. Deception is separation.
The *manta* (counsel) is the deliberation on what ought to be done together with those who know statecraft (*nīti*). The *dūta* (envoy) is a person dispatched for the purpose of establishing peace.

*Payānaṃ* (expeditions) is the setting out for the sake of battle and so forth. *Āji* (battle) is conflict in the absence of a treaty. Regarding the phrase "uncontracted, possessing many flavors, and continuous": "uncontracted" means not abbreviated; "flavors" (*rasa*) refers to the many [emotions] such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), the heroic (*vīra*), and so on;

"states" (*bhāva*) refers to joy, enthusiasm, and so on; it is "continuous" because it is pervaded by these. "By means of pleasant expressions and smooth transitions" (*piyavuttasusandhibhi*): [this refers to the style].
"By those [verses] which are dear, beautiful to hear, and composed in the *indravajra* and other meters;
by those whose junctions (*sandhi*) are lovely due to their mutual connection and association, and whose cadences (*sagga*) are mutually harmonious.

Furthermore, in order to show that—even among the aforementioned components such as the description of the city—whatever is possible, even if devoid of "drinking honey" and the like, delights the minds of those who know it and is indeed grasped by the virtuous, he said:
“Even if a poem lacks some parts of its constituent elements, those who know it will surely find satisfaction if it possesses the excellence of its binding components. (Kāvyādāsā 1.20).
Furthermore—
“Having first spoken of the Leader’s virtues, one should then refute the enemy by means of them;
this is the path that is naturally beautiful.
Even when describing the lineage, heroic sons, and so forth, even of an adversary—”
“...and the narration of the hero’s excellence by Tājja brings us peace,” they say in the verses 1.21–22 of the *Kāvyādās*.

What need is there for the exhaustion produced by mental distress for those noble persons (*sappurisa*) whose hearts have drunk the essence of the nectar of the True Dharma, who turn their backs on the abundant, spreading poison of idle chatter (*samphappalāpa*), and who are constant vessels for the jewels of conduct?
"It was presented in a manner corresponding to that.
*Nāṭaka* refers to a dramatic composition defined in various ways in the dramaturgical treatises (*nāṭya-śāstra*) of Bharata and others;

it consists of the nine types of dramatic works (*rūpaka*), such as the *prakaraṇa*, which possess characteristics that constitute a portion of its defining marks. The *nāṭikā* is also included within this very category. Both *kabba* (poem) and *nāṭaka* (drama)—among these...
The analysis of the compound is: "those by whom the eye and the mind have been cast forth and established. Who are they? They are the poets (*kavino*).

Therein, by the expression "having cast forth and established the eye and the mind," the contemplation of what has been heard is shown by way of reasoning and refutation (*ūhāpoha*) according to the method as it was grasped; the determination of the unerring meaning;

the cultivation of that which has been determined; and uninterrupted application. By the expression "poetry and drama" (*kabba-nāṭaka*), [the stages of] what has been heard and what has been contemplated are indicated.

And that which has been cultivated has also been demonstrated. When the [object of] what is heard (*suta*) has been demonstrated, it follows that the knowledge consisting of what is heard (*sutamaya-ñāṇa*), which is dependent upon it, must also have been demonstrated.

By the phrase "with their eyes and minds fixed on the drama of poetry," he demonstrates the capacity for poetic composition in those who have attained proficiency in wisdom through the successive stages of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
For such persons, that very hearing and so forth serve as the cause for their composition. Indeed, it has been said:
“Natural eloquence,
vast and stainless learning,
and this unwearied application— ”
"Reason is the bond here," says the verse from the *Kāvyādāsā* (1.103).
"Whatever" refers to any kind of composition that has entered one's own mind. By this indefinite expression, however, he demonstrates his lack of particular regard for it.
They "compose" means they create. This "composition" created by them is [for] another...

The intention is that it is not at all astonishing, because for one who possesses such excellence of means (*upāya*), the presence of excellence in the goal (*upeyya*) is entirely natural and thus not surprising.
In this context, regarding those specific compositions of drama and dance which are exclusively means,
even those wise and virtuous persons who have not bestowed their attention upon them— meaning they have not paid heed to them through hearing and so forth— by whatever particular literary form...
The wise—those who know virtues and faults, who are learned in the scriptures, and who are sagacious—delight and satisfy such people.
For even though they lack innate eloquence, when striving in such matters through the means of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, they indeed delight them.
As it is said: "Even if there is no prior latent impression..."
"Marvelous eloquence follows upon virtue;
speech attended by learning and patience certainly bestows some kind of favor. This is the verse from the *Kāvyādāsā*, 1.104.

Those who possess discernment (*paññā*) characterized by the discrimination between what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted are called "wise," and they alone are true persons of integrity (*sappurisa*).
Even while being accompanied by wonder—thinking, "What kind of bond is this?
How could such a binding occur even for those devoid of such means?"—that very bond, due to the absence of such means and the presence of undesirable conditions, [binds] that very fetter itself.
"Because it is real, it is not otherwise.

Now, in order to encourage those who might shrink back, wondering, "How can there be any understanding of the nature of our own literary composition for those unacquainted with plays and dramas?", he inspires them with the two verses beginning with "Kabbanāṭaka": "Those whose minds are fixed on the plots of plays and dramas..."
When poets and authors of poetry— whose minds are fixed on the eye [of composition] by way of reflection upon and cultivation of what they have heard in poetic dramas—
compose or produce whatever they themselves desire, this bondage is not exceedingly wonderful or marvelous;
for it is the construction of a work that serves as the means [to an end], achieved through constant application and the perfection of wisdom rooted in established methods.
The intended meaning is that it indeed exists. The analysis of the compound is as follows: "kabba" refers to poetry; "nāṭaka" refers to drama, such as dance, song, and so forth.
However, in this context, a "nāṭaka" is a treatise that elucidates discourse on those [arts]. Furthermore, the analysis is:
"those by whom the mind is directed toward both poetry (*kabba*) and drama (*nāṭaka*)," and "among those people who are therein, in those poems and dramas."

Even without formal training, those wise ones who—by means of such things as the retention of the *savana* (listening/learning)—are free from agitation, satisfy and gladden others through a particular composition of texts;
they alone become possessed of the wisdom termed *paṭibhāna* (readiness of wit), being "possessors of *paṭibhā*.

That very composition (*bandha*) is "wondrous" (*savimhaya*), accompanied by the wonder that arises in others. Furthermore, it is so called because "they possess *paṭibhā*" and because it is "with wonder" (*saha vimhayena*).
The analysis of the compound is: "it proceeds" (*vattati*) and "those by whom respect has not been established" (*avihita-ādara*).

What is meant is this: even in the absence of application to external teachers and even in the absence of prior latent tendencies (*pubba-vāsanā*), one who applies himself here without interruption achieves such a capacity. For it is said:
"Even if there is no prior latent tendency..."
"Wondrous eloquence that follows upon virtue;
speech attended by learning and patience surely brings about some kind of benefit"— this is the verse from the *Kāvyādāsā*, 1.104.
The meaning of this is as follows: even if such a marvelous eloquence (*paṭibhāna*)— which would otherwise be accompanied by the continuity of the qualities of past impressions (*pubbavāsanā*),
being linked through the reinforcement of the impressions from familiarity in previous births— does not exist, nevertheless,

speech provides some assistance to one who has attended upon [the teacher] through hearing (*suta*), listening (*savana*), and exertion (*ussahana*), or through the exertion of speech in making [the teachings] proficient, or who has performed service to the guru.
It certainly and invariably produces some degree of proficiency in wisdom.

Herein, "poetry" (*kabba*) refers to that which is complete through sentences such as *muttaka* and *kulaka*, and through the collection of intermediate sentence-components possessing their own intrinsic characteristics;

it is distinguished by the specific qualities of what has been expressed, and consists either purely of prose (*pajja*), or purely of verse (*gajja*), or is known as *campū*, consisting of both prose and verse.

And it exists by way of the nature of great sayings (*mahāvākya*). What is called a *nāṭaka* (drama) is that which displays various types of characteristics found in the treatises on acting by Bharata and others.

And a *kabba* (poem), according to the characteristics shown right here, includes the nine types of dramatic forms (*rūpaka*) such as the *prakaraṇa*, which are composed in part, as well as the *nāṭikā*.
The characteristics of a *kabba*, however, should be understood as follows:
“The *Saggabandha* is called the Great Poem (*Mahākavva*); its characteristics are stated as follows:
salutation, description of the subject matter, and a benediction are its opening.
Furthermore, it consists of narratives derived from history or is based upon a sacred tradition.”
Dependent upon the fruits of the four groups, with four noble leaders,
it contains descriptions of the city, the new moon, Mount Sela, and the rising sun;
as well as sporting in gardens and waters, and the festival of the drinking of honey-wine.
With deceptions and marriages, with the birth and growth of princes, with secret spells, messengers,
expeditions, battles, and the exaltation of leaders— thus it is adorned,
concise yet continuous in its development of aesthetic flavor (rasa) and emotional states (bhāva).
“With verses that are not overly prolix, with pleasant diction and smooth transitions,
and with rhymes that do not break apart anywhere—
such a poem, well-adorned, becomes pleasing to the world and endures for the duration of an eon. (Kāvyādāsa 1.14–19)
Its meaning is as follows: the "Great Poem" (*mahākāvya*) is so called because it is bound by specific structural divisions known as "heavens" (*sagga*).

Its characteristic is now stated; this is the connection [of the sentence], according to the maxim of the crow’s eye (*kākakkhigola-kanaya*), which refers to its beginning—that is, the opening of that poem—which consists of either a salutation (*paṇāma*) or the invocation of deities (*devatānamassana*), and the description of the subject matter (*vatthuniddesa*).
“In the northern direction there is a divine being,
the sovereign of mountains named Himālaya;
having plunged into the eastern and western oceans, [he stands]— ”
"Is he standing? Like a measuring rod for the path," as in *Kumārasambhava* 1.1.
Thus, there is the presentation of some subject connected to a beginning such as this, or there may be a benediction (*āsīsā*) such as "May it delight my mind," which is a desired wish.
Or it may be based on historical narratives (*itihāsa*), or dependent on ancient accounts, or even dependent on existing things, whether they be beautiful or otherwise.
The Dhamma is that which depends on royal conduct and so forth, which is contingent upon the fruits of the fourfold assembly, and which is the cause of mundane and supramundane happiness;
the accumulation of the planes of knowledge (*vijjābhūmi*) and so forth is *attha* (the goal), as is the preservation of what has been accumulated;

*kāma* (sensual pleasure) is defined as the five strands of sensual desire that lead to the states of misery; and *mokkha* (liberation) is the cause for turning away from all suffering—thus [this treatise] is dependent on the fruits of the fourfold assembly and has the four noble leaders as its guides.

Wherein there is a leader who is endowed with the power of energy (*ussāha*), abundant in the strength of his weapons, skilled in the four [stratagems], noble and sublime through his possession of extraordinary generosity and other virtues, and who has either a favorable faction or an opposing faction;

that aforementioned city—described by the metaphors of the ocean, the seasons, the mountain, and the rising of the moon and sun—is the "city" (*pura*); the "ocean" (*aṇṇava*) is the sea; the "seasons" (*utu*) are the winter, spring, and so forth; the "mountain" (*sela*) is the peak; and the "rising of the moon and sun" (*indusavitūdaya*) is the appearance of the moon and the sun.
That [text] wherein there is the description of the rising of the moon and sun; "Savitā" here ends with the *tu*-suffix.

That wherein there is a festival consisting of garden sports, water-sports, drinking honey-wine, and joyful celebrations—namely, festivals characterized by garden games, drinking wine, and amorous play—and which [deals] with deceits and marriages, with the separation from wives and the taking of wives, and with the birth and growth of princes, and the arising and development of youths.

And by means of counsel, envoys, military expeditions, battles, and the prosperity of one’s own leader—wherein "counsel" (*manta*) is the wisdom that understands policy, the "envoy" (*dūta*) is the maker of alliances, the "expedition" (*payāna*) is the marching forth for war, the "battle" (*āji*) is what is known as combat, and the "prosperity" (*abhyūdaya*) is the increase of one’s own side’s leader—it was thus adorned and prepared;
it was not abbreviated... [etc. ...the interval was not abbreviated, but extensive.
The eight aesthetic flavors (rasas), such as the erotic (siṅgāra) and so forth; the emotional states (bhāvas), such as love (rati), exertion (ussāha), and so forth— by these [qualities],

which are spoken of in the Indravajra and other meters that are beautiful to hear and possess well-knit joints, those heavens whose joints are beautiful due to the discernment of the connection between what precedes and what follows,
and which have distinct divisions in every section throughout their entirety, are "bhinnasagga" (having distinct divisions).

That poem which is endowed with and joined by endings that are not overly prolix—meaning those defined as "not excessively expansive"—and which is well-adorned, possessing beautiful ornaments, is delightful to the world;

being such, it arises as something that lasts for an eon (*kappa*), remaining continuously for an eon, or at least remaining for the duration of an eon. Herein, even descriptions of cities devoid of honey-drinking and the like [contribute to this].
If it pleases those who know, then that too is not faulty. For it has been said:
“Even if a poem lacks some of its constituent parts, If those who know it should find it pleasing through the excellence of its composition, Then, indeed, it is not considered defective.”

The meaning of this is as follows: here, even if among these poetic components there is a deficiency—meaning a lack—in some parts or some members (*aṅga*), the word *ni-* being used in the sense of "not" (*natthi*), the poem does not fail.
Furthermore, that non-failure consists in the perfection of the components of composition, such as the arrangement of the introductory praise and other elements;
if these satisfy the people who know poetry—that is, those skilled in poetry—according to their desires, [then the poem is successful].

This being so, it occurs as follows: Furthermore, in the descriptions of a leader, after describing the leader of one's own side, it is also appropriate to describe how he effects a refutation [of the opponent].
If not, then after describing the adversary, it is likewise fitting to describe how one's own leader overcomes him. For it is said:
"Having first spoken of the Leader according to his virtues, [one should speak] of his enemies by means of him..."
This path of refutation is naturally beautiful.
Even when describing the lineage, heroic sons, and so forth of an enemy,
our joy arises from the narration of the Leader’s triumph over him.
8. Furthermore, "composition" (*bandha*) refers to the meanings of words;
when combined and free from defects, it becomes threefold through the distinction between *padya*, *gadya*, and *miśra*.
Having thus shown the encouragement of the audience by means of these [definitions], he now states "composition" (*bandha*) because he intends to compose [the work].
He begins to define the characteristics with the words "And the bond," and so forth. "Free from faults" means devoid of contradictions based on words and based on meanings;
or, those by whom such faults have been abandoned. "Accompanied by word and meaning" means they are joined and unified.

Those who possess the aforementioned characteristics are said to be "accompanied" by the ancient teachers. The state of being accompanied is the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*), which is the cause for delighting the heart.

"Sāhiccaṃ" (poetry). Thus, having restated that which is well-established—namely, that "composition" (*bandha*) consists of three types according to its mode of expression as natural (*sabhāva*), crooked (*vaṅka*), or ornamental (*alaṅkāra*)—within the context of words and meanings that are free from faults and endowed with excellence, the body of composition, which is not yet established, is prescribed, just as in the statement:
"He who has earrings is Devadatta. The word "ca" (*and*) is a conjunction of other things to be mentioned; the sense is "furthermore."
In this context, the primary meaning (*mukhya*) of words is fourfold, characterized by genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), and substance (*dravya*).

Because the primary meaning is fourfold, the word that denotes it is likewise fourfold among the three types of words: the genus-word (*jātiśabda*), the quality-word (*guṇaśabda*), the action-word (*kriyāśabda*), and the substance-word (*dravyaśabda*).

For the word is threefold according to its functional distinction (*vyāpāra*): the denotative (*vācaka*), the indicative (*lākṣaṇika*), and the manifestive (*vyañjaka*). As for the function (*vyāpāra*)...
And indeed, the function of a word consists solely in causing the comprehension of its meaning. For that [function] is threefold:

primary (*mukhya*), indicative (*lakkhaṇa*), and suggestive (*byañjana*). Among these, the operation of a word whose object is a continuous referent such as a genus (*jāti*) and so forth is the primary one. That very [operation] is called "denotation" (*abhidhā*).
A word such as "cow" (*go*) and so forth, which expresses that meaning through its own unmediated genus and so forth by means of that operation, is [the primary word].

The *vācaka* (denotative function) is that which expresses the primary meaning of a word. The *lakkhaṇa* (indicative function) is the operation of a word pointed out as having another word’s meaning as its object. This [lakkhaṇa] is twofold: pure (*suddhā*) and mixed with metaphorical usage (*upacāramissā*).
Among these, the pure is, for example: “Let the cow be released,” “The beds cry out,” and “A roar on the Ganges.
Here, by the word “cow,” only the commonality of the lineage (*gotta-sāmañña*)—the specific quality—is expressed, and not the individual cow (*gobyatti*). For it has been said:

"This is the principle found in the second chapter (*ullāsa*) of the *Kāvyappakāsa*: 'The denotation [of a word] does not proceed to the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) when its power has been exhausted in the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).
Because the universal (*sāmānya*) is all-pervasive and lacks a physical body, binding and releasing are not possible therein;

therefore, the manifestation of the cow (*go*), which serves as its own substratum, is drawn along. Likewise, since shouting is not possible for cots (*mañca*), [the word 'cots' draws along] their own..."
In order to accomplish the act of proclamation, men who possess beds are dragged [along].

Likewise, since it is impossible for the flow of water—which is denoted by the word "Ganges"—to be the source of the sound, the word "Ganges" indicates the bank, which is proximate to its own expressed meaning, the flow of water.
Because metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) is of many kinds, figurative indication (*lakkhaṇā*) mixed with metaphor is also manifold.

It may be so. Just as in some cases the cause is metaphorically designated by the name of the effect, as in "a jar of life" (*āyu-ghata*); in some cases there is no distinction between cause and effect, as in "the life-span itself is longevity" (*āyu-yeva āyusmim*);
in some cases the object of comparison is metaphorically designated by the name of the standard of comparison, as in "a cowherd" (*go-bāhika*);
in some cases there is identity between them, as in "this is a cow indeed" (*go-yevāyam*); and in some cases [it is due to] being the locus of that or having the meaning of that.
That designation [is applied] in the following ways: first, by way of identity, as in “the lamp-stand is a lamp.
In some cases, it is a designation based on a connection with that action, as in “this carpenter is also a carpenter.

In some cases, it is based on a connection with its master, as in “a man connected with a king is a king. In some cases, there is a designation of the whole for a part, as in “the word ‘cloth’ [is used] for a portion of a cloth,” and so forth.

The word that is the basis for the indicative [meaning] is the indicative word (*lakkhaṇika*). However, the word whose nature is the phoneme (*byañjana*) is the third function of the word, which is the indirect expression (*parapariyāya*);
the word that is the basis for that is the phonemic word (*byañjanaka*). Thus, by way of these three types of words, the meaning (*attha*) is also threefold:

the expressible (*vācya*), the indicative (*lakkhaṇiya*), and the implied (*byaṅgya*). Among these, it is the implied meaning alone that is called the "subject matter of composition" (*bandhasattha*). For this very reason...

The masters of old have maintained that a composition (bandha) where the *vyaṅgya* (the suggested meaning) is predominant is the highest; where it is not predominant, it is middling; and where there is no *vyaṅgya* at all, it is inferior.

They further held that a composition devoid of *vyaṅgya* would be lifeless (*nijjīva*). However, one should not suspect that even a composition consisting of a mere description of natural state (*sabhāvavutti*) is lifeless.

For such a description leads to the poets' mastery of worldly convention (*lokavohārakosalla*). Indeed, [it is through this] that the entire order of the world— *Note: The provided text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*
He does not know; he is not truly a poet.
Now, in order to clarify this threefold meaning for the sake of awakening those of similar disposition, we shall cite the verse beginning with “munindavadanambhoje.
Herein, the word *vāṇī* (speech) has as its expressed meaning the True Dhamma (*saddhamma*). For speech is volition (*cetanā*), and within that—
As long as the sense of "deity" is not superimposed [upon the lotus], it does not coincide with the satisfaction of one's own mind or the expectation [of the speaker];
thus, by the very power of the sentence, the superimposed meaning of the word *devatā* (deity) is indicated according to the specific fitness of the context.
Likewise, for the word *vadana*, the mouth is the expressed meaning (*vācyattha*), while the superimposed meaning of the word *ambhoja* (lotus) is the indicated meaning (*lakkhaṇyattha*).

However, because a mental unification (*manosampīṇana*) cannot otherwise arise, there occurs—by way of the sequence beginning with tranquility (*passaddhi*)—the possibility of awakening to reality as it is (*yathābhūtāvabodha*).

Consequently, through the effortless manifestation of various and manifold meanings of words, the accomplishment of the desired purpose, which is termed the completion of the composition, indeed takes place; this is the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyattha*).
Since the words expressing that [meaning] possess the characteristic of being expressive (*vācakalakkhaṇika*), they are manifestors (*byañjaka*); thus it is in all cases.
The investigation of the meaning of the words should be pursued.
To the question, "In how many ways does that very body of the bond (bandhasarīra) as described above exist? he says: "Pajja," and so forth.
This aforementioned bond, this body of the bond, may be threefold—it may be of three kinds; it is neither more nor less. How so? Of *pajja*, *gajja*, and *vimissa*...
It is established that [the *vutti*] is threefold according to the specific distinctions of *pajja*, *sabhāva*, and so forth.
Among these, *pajja* refers to the various types of *vuttajāti* (verse-genres) consisting of four lines, which have been defined by us ourselves in the prosody titled *Vuttodaya*;

it is precisely a type of *vuttajāti* such as *muttaka* and others that has been defined there. For that very reason, they are not shown here. Among those [three], one verse (*gāthā*) completes its meaning.

*Muttaka* (isolated verse) consists of verses with their own independent purpose that do not depend on other verses. *Kulaka* consists of verses whose meaning is completed individually, yet which are mutually dependent through a single syntactical action. *Kosa* (treasury) refers to verses with their own independent purpose and distinct syntactical actions, arranged like a treasury within various walls.
*Sammodanīya-gāthā* (verses of greeting) function as a collective whole to describe a single subject, such as the transgression against a wall, even though they possess distinct syntactical actions.

It should be understood that *gāthā* (verse) is a collection [of words], and it too is of four kinds, including the types of prose (*pajjappakāra*) and the aforementioned types of verse-bound compositions (*saggabandha*).
What is called *gajja* (prose) is a composition consisting of forms ending in *si* (nominative) or *ti* (third person verb), lacking the conclusion of a metrical foot. It has two varieties:

the narrative (*ākhyāyikā*) and the story (*kathā*). That which consists of a mixture of verse and prose includes dramatic works (*nāṭaka*) and the like, as well as the *campū* and the *Jātakamālā* and similar texts.

8. Now, for those who desire to understand [the meaning], he speaks the words beginning with "bond" (bandha), demonstrating—just as in the well-known statement, "He who has earrings is Devadatta"—the prescription of the less well-known status of being Devadatta by way of restating the well-known possession of earrings, while taking the body of the composition based on ornamentation as the primary subject, saying, "That very thing is the bond.
In that context, "bond" (bandha) means binding; however, [it refers to] those excluding hatred (dosa).
"Free from defects based on word and meaning" means either abandoned by those [defects], or devoid of them; "suchlike" refers to these.
"Conjoined" means having attained coexistence (*sahabhāva*) in the sense of mutual suitability. "Word and meaning" refers to the word (*sadda*) and the meaning (*attha*).

They say it is called "literature" (*sāhicca*) in the sense of the verbal definition: "the state (*bhāva*) of such words and meanings—conjoined with mutually suitable qualities—that produce satisfaction in the wise."
Regarding the phrase "the meanings of words" (*saddatthā*): what is the distinction between these meanings of words? The word (*sadda*), however, is threefold according to its different functions:
its primary function (*mukhyabyāpāra*), its indicative function (*lakkhaṇabyāpāra*), and its expressive function (*byañjanasabhāvabyāpāra*).

In sequence, it is threefold as the denotative (*vācaka*), the indicative (*lakkhaṇika*), and the expressive (*byañjanaka*). Likewise, the meaning (*attha*) is also threefold: the denoted (*vāccā*), the indicated (*lakkhaṇiyā*), and...

The denotative word (*vācaka-sadda*) is threefold. However, because the primary object (*mukhyattha*) to be illuminated by it is fourfold—divided into genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), and substance (*davva*)—the denotative word itself is also fourfold, according to its divisions as words for genus, quality, action, and substance.
The primary function of the denotative word is conventionally termed "denotation" (*abhidhā*). That primary function operates upon an object that is not mediated by genus and so forth. Likewise...

For in expressions such as “the cow,” “the blue,” “the cook,” and “the horned one,” the primary function of words like “cow” and so forth operates only upon the universal (jāti), quality (guṇa), action (kriyā), and substance (davva) that serve as qualifiers—namely, the class of cows, the color blue, the cloth, the agent who cooks, and the horn—and not upon the individual cow and so forth which serve as the substrata for those universals and the rest.
Indeed, this is the principle found in the second chapter of the *Kāvyappakāsa*, where it is stated: “The denotation does not reach the qualified when its power is exhausted in the qualifier.”

The meaning of this is as follows: when the denotation— which has its power exhausted and its function ceased with respect to the qualifiers such as genus (*jāti*)— does not reach or attain the qualified substance (*dabbam*),
then if the denotation does not express the support (*nissaya*) of the genus and so forth, such as the body of the cow, this being the case,

[the fault applies] to expressions such as "the cow goes," "he wears blue," "the cook comes," or "the horned one runs," where the words *go* and so forth [denote] the bodies of cows and so forth as qualified by genus and the like.

How is it that [a word] possesses denotative function (*vācakatta*)? When terms such as substance (*dabba*), genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), and so forth are mentioned, [the word] functions as a denoter by way of figurative usage (*pariyāya*) with respect to the specific substance characterized by those [attributes].

However, in its non-figurative sense (*nippariyāya*), it is the domain of the operation of the pure definition (*suddhalakkhaṇabyāpāra*) alone. Furthermore, the operation of the definition is twofold:
pure (*suddha*) and mixed with figurative usage (*upacāramissa*). Among these, the pure operation of the definition has as its object an entity devoid of genus and the like.
For instance, in such cases as “the cow goes,” “he wears blue,” “the cook comes,” “the horned one runs,” “the beds cry out,” and “there is a sound in the Ganges,” since it is impossible for genus,
quality, action, the horned [animal], substance, the bed, or the Ganges to be directly connected with going and so forth,
one must go beyond genus, quality, and the rest to [the substrata] of going, wearing, coming, running, crying out, and sounding, respectively.
One grasps such things as a lump of clay that serves as a support for a living being.
However, the "mixed" [metaphorical application] is manifold due to the various types of figurative usage (*upacāra*).

For instance, in some cases, the effect is metaphorically applied to the cause, as in the expression "a jar of life" (*āyughata*); here, the designation of the effect—life—is superimposed upon the jar, which is the cause for the increase of life.

It exists. The application of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) should also be applied above according to what is appropriate. For metaphorical designation consists in the attribution of a certain nature to that which lacks that nature.

In some cases, there is no distinction between cause and effect, as in "the life-span itself is the jar. In some cases, there is the metaphorical designation of the object of comparison (*upameyya*) as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), as in "a cowherd is a bull.
In some cases, there is no distinction between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison, as in "this cowherd is indeed a bull."
In some cases, there is a metaphorical designation based on being the locus of that [quality], as in: "The oil-lamp bowl is a lamp.

In some cases, there is a designation by that [name] due to a connection with the action, as in: "Even though he is not a carpenter, he is a carpenter. In some cases, there is a designation by that [name] due to a connection with a patron, as in:
"Even though he is a king’s favorite, he is a king. In some cases, there is a designation of the whole by means of a part.
As in the expression, “the cloth is burnt. Through this gateway, the various types of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) are to be understood.
That which is the very function of the literal sense (*byañjana-sabhāva-vyāpāra*) is called “wealth,” and it should be understood that the object of that third function is precisely such a sentence.

In this regard, they say: a composition whose life is the suggested meaning (*byaṅgyattha*) is the best; a composition in which the suggested meaning is predominant is middling; and a composition devoid of the predominance of the suggested meaning is inferior. And on this point, there are these [verses]:
In the attainment of meaning, the function of sound (sadda-byāpāra) may be threefold:
primary (mukhya), indicative (lakkhaṇa), and suggestive (vyañjana).
Herein, the first function is synonymous with denotation (abhidhā).
Furthermore, the third [type of] function (*byāpāra*) is that which has "immediacy" (*dhananta*) as its synonym;
it is primary when the meanings are contiguous, whereas indication (*lakkhaṇā*) occurs when the meaning is concealed.
However, another [function], namely syntactic connection (*vākya*), operates only upon the meaning itself.
According to the distinction of function, the expressive word (*vācaka*) is also threefold:
the denotative (*lakkhaṇika*), the indicative (*byañjaka*), and so too its meaning is considered threefold:
the denoted (*vācya*), the indicated (*lakkhaṇiya*), and the suggested (*byaṅgya*). Thus is the expressive word categorized among words.
It is fourfold according to the divisions of genus (jāti),
quality (guṇa), action (kriyā), and substance (davva). Because the denoted meaning is divided into four categories starting with genus,
it is likewise considered to be characterized by the distinctions of genus and the rest.
