This is a single-form *yāmaka* (chiasmus) beginning with a four-line verse, which is both *avyapeta* (unseparated) and *vyapeta* (separated).

If a person were to give their own mind—their consciousness—to the Teacher, the Conqueror, for even a single moment, the mind and consciousness of that Teacher, the Lord of Sages, would gladden and thoroughly satisfy the mind and consciousness of that person. Therefore, one should give mind to mind and consciousness to consciousness;
if one does not so give, the mind and consciousness of that person [will not be satisfied].
Even for a moment, even for a brief instant, one who is worthy of praise by the virtuous should not be honored by them.
[For it is said: “When you are thus uplifted in mind, how could those things not be yours?”
"Since they are neither bent nor unbent here,
those bends would not be beautiful. This four-line verse is a central yamaka (majjhayamaka), consisting of a single form, both separated and unseparated.

Since, by that reason—that is, by that beautiful, lofty, and perfectly elevated cause of yours—those various beauties and those various splendors would not fail to exist even when bent or inclined, nor when unbent or uninclined, but would indeed come to be;
therefore, for that reason, how could those beauties and splendors not exist when bent or inclined? They would surely come to be.
I bow to the Jina, who inclines virtuous people toward him,
establishes non-virtuous people in virtue,
and makes those worthy of training vessels for excellence.

"Truly, let this person be called a virtuous person (*sajjana*). This four-line verse is a *yamaka* (rhyme/pun) of a single form consisting of four feet; it is a difficult construction involving both contiguous (*avyapeta*) and non-contiguous (*vyapeta*) *yamakas*. [The meaning is:
"I bow to the virtuous person (*sajjana*); I bow to the person who possesses good people (*sādhujana*)—that is, the person to be trained (*veneyyajana*)—without being negligent."

I bow down to that Jina who, by this very reason, makes himself his own— meaning he identifies with him— who is like collyrium for the eyes of those to be trained (*vineyya*), who establishes and directs them toward virtues such as moral discipline (*sīla*), who is a vessel for virtues, the very foundation of virtues,
and who is the collyrium of the virtuous; indeed, I pay homage to that Conqueror who regards the virtuous people as his own.
“In this world, the splendor of the Conqueror shines forth in every assembly;
by that very splendor it always speaks.
If it did not shine by that splendor, how could it not [speak]?”
“His own radiance shines surpassing all other radiances. This [verse] consists of a set of four quarters, etc., characterized by the repetition of the same form (*ekarūpa*).

In the world (*bhuvane*), that is, in the realm of sentient beings (*sattaloke*), the Victor’s radiance (*sābhā*)—a beautiful light (*sobhanā ābhā*) existing amidst other existing radiances (*sābhāsu vijjamānābhāsu*)—shines forth by means of its own existing radiance (*sābhāya vijjamānāya*).
Or, because it shines with beautiful radiance, it always speaks—that is, it truly blazes and shines.
If that radiance of the Victor (jinābhā) does not shine—that is, if it does not speak—having become superior to the existing radiance of other beings;
then how could the radiance of those such as Brahmā, whose radiance is accompanied by existing beautiful splendor, not shine, transcending (*aticca*) their beautiful radiances? It certainly shines.
“Even those gods, though adorned, were not radiant;
likewise, the Asuras, though numerous and unconquered by liquor, were not so;
and even the king, though well-conquered in the assemblies, was not thus.”
"Just as those who have emerged from intoxication shine brightly. This four-line verse is devoid of repetition (*ekarūpa*) within the *Majjhima-yamaka*.
Just as people who have emerged from intoxication—that is, those who have departed from drinking liquor—shine brightly, so too do they shine when adorned and especially decorated.

Even those gods, those *surā*, were not radiant or beautiful; likewise, even the many *asura*s such as Vepacitti and others, who had been defeated because of drinking *surā*—the "vanquished by liquor"—were not radiant and did not shine.
Similarly, even a king who is well-adorned and victorious (*surājita*) does not appear radiant in assemblies.
“Those who, out of hope for their own welfare, place their trust in the command of the Conqueror,
will certainly find that their hopes are fulfilled and their fears dispelled. Therefore,
one should always have confidence in all evils as being truly fearsome.”
"Remaining tranquil, they have abandoned the craving for existence.
This is a four-line verse with a *yamaka* (chiasmus) structure where the form is displaced by one syllable.
Those true persons who have laid down their craving regarding the Victor’s instruction—the instruction known as the Buddha’s formulation of the Vinaya—by way of non-transgression...
Their hopes are firmly established, their hopes are grounded, and their hopes are purified. These virtuous ones have destroyed their [worldly] hopes;
gradually, with craving destroyed, they inevitably and absolutely become free from hope and devoid of fear.

Therefore, because of that, among all evils and all unwholesome states—which are indeed full of hope and accompanied by fear—the virtuous people, possessing the desire for faultless conduct, remain established in peace, dependent on peace, and they surely fulfill their hopes for mastery and their aspirations for lordship.
"Yamakas and riddles (*paheḷī*) are not exclusively sweet"—thus, out of fear of exhausting my students, I have remained indifferent toward all of them.
Is it not true that what is called a *yamaka* (a rhyming palindrome) indicates a particular excellence in the skill of poets, and thus it is useful in that regard? As for riddles...
And such play and amusement are useful for the purpose of diversion, for creating confusion in others, and for causing extreme bewilderment (as stated in *Kāvyādāsā* 3.97).
Therefore, as to how equanimity (*upekkhā*) can exist therein, he says "the yamaka" and so forth. That aforementioned *yamaka* is divided into the easy and the difficult;
as for the riddles (*paheḷikā*), sixteen types have been pointed out by the ancient masters, beginning with the *samāgata*, the *avañcita*, and others.
In this regard, the characteristic is as follows:
There may be what is called "conjoined" (samāgata), where the meaning is hidden by the connection of words;
and there is "deceived," where there is deception by means of a word that has become conventionalized in another sense.
A sequence of words that is obscured by elision or excessive separation may cause delusion;
it may also be forgotten if its meaning is difficult to grasp. A phrase may consist of words that, while having similar forms, impose a non-primary meaning upon them.
That which arises from harsh conditions and so forth, even if it is somehow produced as sound,
is called "reckoned" (*saṅkhyāta*) when it is a reckoning that serves as a cause for confusion;
where the meaning of the sentence appears otherwise than it is, that is "fabricated" (*pakappita*).
That [term] is a "name" (nāma) for which there is no conceptualization of multiple meanings;
it is established as having a single meaning because it arises from a cause that conveys a uniform sense.
It is a word with identical phonemes, established through a synonym of the desired term.
Those that are confused, even when their meanings have been clearly indicated, are due to sheer delusion.
That which possesses a multiplicity of connections is called *pārihārikī* (circumlocutory).
*Ekacchannā* (single-concealed) consists of *byañjanādheyya* (phonetic insertion), *nissaya* (support), and *gopanā* (concealment).
She is "covered on both sides" (*ubhayacchannā*) for one who guards both [the body and speech];
she is called "mixed" (*saṃkiṇṇā*) for one who has a confusion of various characteristics.

Furthermore, this [term] should not be applied as a fault to any of these [persons] in cases such as being "cut off" (*ukkantādi*), even when there is a state of fault. For this [term] refers to the mind (*manaso*). (ka.)
The verse from the *Subodhālaṅkāra* numbered 44, beginning with “*bahuguṇe paṇamati*,” was not stated under the name *vākyasaṃkiṇṇa*,

but was rather designated by the verse from the *Subodhālaṅkāra* numbered 112, beginning with “*yā te dutiyaṃ nilayan*,” as an example of *pakappita* due to its avoidance of the fault of ambiguity (*saṃsayadosa*).
“O Great One, your power is vast, your conduct is free from pride, and your mindfulness is great.”
“May you be victorious for a long time, O Lord, you who bring about abundant fruit.
This is the *Samāgatā*.
“One should indeed attend upon the auspicious one, whose intoxication and evil have been shaken off;”
"He shall reach the secure city, he who is self-controlled and devoted to himself.
This is the "deceived" (vañcitā).
As for the "forgotten" (pamussitā) and the others, they should be understood according to their characteristics and according to the examples given therein.
Thus, these riddles devised by former teachers are all, by necessity and rule, not sweet;
because they cannot be relished due to the absence of any flavor of meaning or flavor of sound, the very weariness that arises in the students is itself the "fear.
Therefore, it should be connected as follows: "I remained indifferent toward them because of that weariness, or rather, because of the fear arising from that weariness."

33. Having thus stated the twofold nature [of *yamaka*] by way of being easy or difficult to compose, he points out the reason for not mentioning riddles (*paheḷika*) that have a purpose—such as those used to demonstrate the capacity of poets, for amusement, to clear a crowded place, or to bewilder others—in the passage beginning with "the *yamaka*," etc.
That *yamaka*, as previously described, is divided into categories such as easy and difficult.
The *Yamakajāta* and the riddles (*paheḷi*)—such as the riddles concerning *samāga* and so forth, which were pointed out by former teachers—all these are not exclusively sweet;
because there is an absence of the flavor of meaning (*attharasa*) or the flavor of sound (*saddarasa*) that ought to be relished, they are not exclusively sweet.
For this reason, and out of fear of exhausting the students—that is, due to the students' inability to endure them—[they have been omitted].

I maintain equanimity toward the fear born of intolerance and toward fear itself. The analysis of the compound is: "fear arising from the exhaustion of students" (*sissakheda*) or "fear produced by the exhaustion of students.
Here, the riddle (*paheḷikā*) should be understood in this way:
The "Collected" (samāgatā), the "Desirous of Deceiving" (vañcitu-kkantā), and the "Forgotten" (pamussitā);
the "Similar in Form" (samānarūpā), the "Harsh" (pharusā), the "Enumerated" (saṅkhyātā), and the "Constructed" (pakappitā).
Furthermore, the "Interval of Names" (nāmantarikā), the "Hidden" (nibhūtā), and the "Enigmatic" (paheḷikā).
Furthermore, there are those with a common reputation, the confused, the one who causes loss,
the one with one side covered, the one with both sides covered, and the one who is promiscuous—
these are the sixteen. Herein, this is their definition:
There may be what is called "conjoined" (samāgata), where the meaning is hidden by the connection of words;
there is "deceived," where there is deception by means of a word that has become conventionalized for another sense;
and there is "over-cut" (ukkanta), which causes confusion through the application of excessive separation.
There may be a sequence of words whose meaning is difficult to understand and which has been forgotten;
there may be words that, while having a similar form, impose a primary meaning upon them;
or there may be words produced by grammatical suffixes and the like, which are harsh in some way.
"Enumeration" (saṅkhyātā) means counting, wherein there is a cause for confusion;
that wherein the meaning of a statement appears otherwise is "constructed" (pakappitā).
That is "naming" (nāmantarikā), wherein there is the construction of various meanings within a name.
Those whose knowledge of other meanings is unmanifested [are so called] because their hearing of the meaning is equal to the cause.
That [term] is established through a synonym for the word *iṭṭha* (desired) using identical sounds;
it is "confused" precisely due to its confusion, even though the meaning has been clearly demonstrated.
That which has a multiplicity of connections is called *pārihārikī*;
that which is covered on one side involves the concealment of the genitals and the protection of the support.
That which is covered on both sides is that which involves the protection of both.
"Confused" (*saṃkiṇṇā*) means that there is a mixture of various characteristics.

Here, however, is the meaning: because the words are joined together by means of word-connections (*padasandhi*), they may be "combined" (*samāgatā*)—that is, having a hidden meaning (*guḷhatthā*), their sense is not manifest.
"Having a hidden meaning" means that, by way of restating what is already established, something unestablished is being enjoined as combined. Furthermore, beyond this...
The relationship between the explanatory term (*anuvāda*) and the term to be explained (*anuvaḍdhabhāva*) should be understood in this way:
where, in a riddle (*paheḷikā*), there might be deception by means of a conventional term (*ruḷhisadda*)—a word well-established in another sense—it is called "deception.
Because it involves an excessively remote application—that is, being joined with words whose connection is greatly interrupted—it is therefore delusive and causes confusion.

The "interwoven" (*paheḷikā*) is called "extracted" (*ukkantā*). That interweaving for which the sequence of words and the arrangement of phrases has a meaning that is difficult to understand and a subject matter that is hard to comprehend is said to be "forgotten" (*pamussitā*).

Because words placed there by the imposition of a non-primary meaning are joined with words that manifest the primary meaning by relying on some common property (*sadhamma*), they may be considered "identical in form" (*samānarūpā*) when their word-connections are established.
[This occurs] through conditions (*paccaya*) and so forth, such as the substitution of conditions (*paccayādesa*) and the like.
In whatever way or by whatever means sounds are produced or articulated, they are called "harsh" [or "rough"].
A riddle (*paheḷikā*) is said to be "numerical" (*saṅkhyātā*) when even the mention of a number or a calculation within it serves as a cause for confusion.
A riddle is said to be "verbal" (*vākyatthā*) or "collective" (*samudāyatthā*) when its meaning or its composite sense is otherwise [than literal].
That which appears and is cognized in a particular manner is called "constructed" (*pakappitā*).

That riddle (*paheḷikā*) in which the construction of various meanings and the construction of diverse designations occur within the names and the applied terminology is called a "riddle of internal names" (*nāmantarikā*).
This is due to the occurrence of synonymous words based on the cause of similarity in meaning.
When the meaning is fixed yet the phrasing is established differently, it is called "obscure" (*nibhūtā*).
That which is enigmatic, accomplished through synonyms for the desired sound, and produced by substitutes for the word expressing the intended meaning, is called "homophonous" (*samānasaddā*).
Even when the meaning is clearly indicated and the expressed meaning is appropriate, that which results in confusion due to sheer delusion serves the purpose of causing bewilderment.
That which occurs thus is called "confused" (*sammuḷhā*).
That riddle for which a name is given when its composition is being shown—because of the abundance of connections, that is, the multiplicity of relations—is called "circumstantial" (*pārihārikī*).
That [riddle] whose contained meaning is manifested by making the indicator manifest...
Protection by means of support is protection of the container; this is called "single-covering.
That in whose application there is protection of both—the protection of both the container and the contained—is called "double-covering.
That in which there is a confusion of various characteristics—a confusion of various kinds of characteristics such as those that have come together—is called "mixed."
Now, the characteristics of *samāgata* and the others should be known in their proper order as follows:
"O Lord, may your great mindfulness— which is the source, which has transcended the states of existence,
and which is free from decay— be victorious for a long time, accomplishing abundant fruits."
This [body] has come together.
O Protector, from the time it originated from you, it has been spread out by way of bowing down, having abandoned the state of being upright; being thus, it appears like a river.
Its origin is manifest and possessed of beauty. O Lord, yours is great mindfulness—vast indeed.

May this equal command—extended to those who have crossed over the flood (vittiṇṇa) and to the people who are not bowed down (anate)—be victorious for a long time, accomplishing abundant fruit and producing manifold benefits through its excellence.
Here, the meaning is concealed by the connection between *pabhava* (origin), *āṇata* (commanded), and *iti* (thus).
“One should indeed associate with the fortunate, who have shaken off intoxication and evil.”
"May he, who has tamed himself, reach the secure city that he has cultivated.
This is the "deceived" [verse].

[The verse] beginning with "Having shaken off intoxication and impurity, having destroyed pride and hatred, the auspicious one, even if fond of little food... [refers to those] among those of auspicious nature.
It appears as if it were said: "Among elephants, one should associate only with an elephant of noble breed.

The meaning is: "One should associate only with the noble, that is, with a supreme person. If one asks, "For what purpose is this association?"—in the case of the elephant, that elephant, being tamed and trained, brings the person who associates with him, who frequents him, to safety and fearlessness in the city or town. But in the case of a human being...
The tamed noble person, having tamed himself, leads both himself and the people he has served to the secure city,
the city free from suffering— the city of Nibbāna. In this context, "deception" refers to using a conventional term, such as "elephant," for something other than its intended,
supreme meaning desired by the poet.
“This person bows even to the wicked who possess many virtues;
always joyfully recollecting the Well-Gone One, they remember what is beneficial.
This is the *Ukkantā* [verse]. Its meaning will follow further on.

Although it contains a mixture of faults, this [verse] is desirable because it has ascended to the level of a *paheḷikā* (a riddle). For it is said: “When it has ascended to the level of a *paheḷikā*, it is not indeed faulty due to its being defiled. Here, there is an intervention caused by the non-establishment of the relevant words in their proper place:
“The face-blossom, the *giṅgamaka* [necklace], the *niyu* [earring], the uplifted and depressed [breasts];
the rag-robe is excellent for the man who wears them while his beloved is timid.”
This is what has been forgotten.
"Facial ornaments" refers to tilaka and the like; "adornment" refers to such items as *giṅgamaka*. "Niyyūra" means a bracelet; "uggatthana" means a breast-cloth;
"unnata" refers to a forehead-ornament and so forth; and "mukhato unnata" refers to an ornament raised above the face.
For a timid woman who wears a tattered garment of rags, a man is better—indeed, most excellent.
Here, because it is composed of sounds devoid of much utility, the meaning is difficult to comprehend:
"In this mine of jewels, the nine supreme gems are seen..."
"Of these eight men, there is another who is not common to the eight"—this is the one of similar form.
In this mine of jewels, nine supreme jewels are seen; herein, among these jewels, eight jewels...
The qualities of the eight types of persons are uncommon, while another jewel is common.
These nine supramundane states are called "jewels" in the sense of being honored and so forth; and the Fully Enlightened One, who is their source, is designated as the "mine.
Thus, there is an application of the terms "jewel" and so on to these secondary meanings.
“The gods and gandhabbas find seven sap-filled reeds on the great floor of the Himālaya,
yet even the nāgas do not observe the Uposatha.
This is the harsh [speech].
On the great floor of the Himalayas, upon the summit of the Himālaya, the gods and gandhabbas enjoy and frequent seven lakes of delicious water, such as Anotatta and others;
even the nāgas do not find [the opportunity to frequent] them on their Uposatha days. This is another meaning.

On the great floor of the Himalayas, on the terrace of the Great Palace joined with the rays of the moon, the gandhabbas sport; [there are] seven [lakes] of delicious water endowed with sweet qualities...
All [beings]—whether *vīṇās*, *chañjās*, and so forth—experience the seven notes; even *nāgas*, *ariyas*, and those who have observed the *uposatha* do not experience or perceive them.
Here, they "shine" (*dibbanti*), thus they are called *devas*. The analysis of the term is: "those for whom the *uposatha* exists" (*uposatho etesamatthīti uposathā*).
According to the sequence of characteristics, because of their established and common usage, [the word *aññadatthā* refers to] requisites and so forth by whatever slight pretext.
The existence of sound that has been produced:
"In the sound of song there are two vowels each for [the notes] except for *cha* and *jja*;
there are six vowels. Just as the eye is five-colored, so too is the nose six-colored."
This is the enumeration.
In the sound of song there are two types of scales (*sara*): the hexatonic (*chañja*) and the pentatonic (*aññatra chañjato*), the latter being that which excludes the sixth note (*chañja*).

Excluding the sixth note, [the notes are] *usabha*, *gandhāra*, *majjhima*, *pañcama*, *dheva*, and *nisāda*. Here, from the pair, there are two each; thus there are six scales and six scale-possessors.

Just as the eye has five colors, so too the nose has six colors. It is stated thus because of the presence of the two vowels *ī* and *ā* in the sound of the song, because of the threefold nature of the vowels among the musical scales such as *usabha* when setting aside the sixth (*chañja*), because of the presence of the five colors by way of vowels and consonants in the term "eye" (*cakkhu*), and because of the presence of the six [colors] in the term "nose" (*nāsikā*).
Herein, the determination of the sounds such as the song and the numbers mentioned leads to confusion.
“May the risen king protect you— he who is glorious, with his orb of darkness dispelled,
joined by a host of auspicious planets and constellations, and endowed with excellent marks.
This is the *pakappitā* (the composed).

May the King, the lord of men—possessed of glory, himself glorious, with a circle of ministers devoted to him as the moon has its circle of stars, and surrounded by a circle of subjects who are loyal to him;
joined with his own retinue of kṣatriyas who are dense and numerous like the host of stars in the thick of the sky;
endowed with auspicious marks, praised for the characteristics of a noble man, risen and renowned—may he protect you.
"May he protect"—this is not the intended meaning here. Because it is stated that "Sirimā is so called because she is the dwelling place of Lakṣmī," [the moon] is possessed of splendor (sirīmanta).
At its rising, it possesses a red orb; it is joined with a multitude of radiant constellations and stars, being endowed with a host of radiant constellations and stars.
It is well-marked (sulakkhaṇa), meaning it is clearly characterized by auspicious marks; it has risen, having ascended—the King, the Moon.

By including the word *guṇī* (possessor of qualities) as a common attribute for both sides in the phrase "may you protect us," the meaning of the sentence here appears differently [than it would otherwise]. "One should say:
'From this, one who is exceedingly great in his assistance...'"
"And Sanātana is neither a seer (isi), nor a friend, nor Sanātana.
This is the section on names.
At first, one was previously called "a seer" (isi); he was one who provides great assistance, endowed with exceedingly great assistance, and eternal (sanātana).
He is both eternal (*sassata*) and yet not a non-seer (*isi*); he is not a friend (*sakhā*) nor even a companion (*mitta*);

he is not the ancient (*sanātana*) nor even the eternal (*sassata*). This is the meaning of what is being traversed. He is "sumahā," exceedingly great; he is called "Āda" because of his beginning (*ādi*), for he is the Seer (*isi*) at the start;
he is "anta" in the middle, being endowed with the letter *pa* (*pakāravā*); and he is both the ancient (*sanātana*) and the eternal (*sassata*).
There is no such thing as "isi," nor is there "nāma," nor is there "mitta"; yet he is not devoid of the two syllables *nā* and *ta*, for he is his own kinsman (*nātana*).
Since the beginning and the middle have been stated, the end is understood; thus it should be taken as "Isipatana-vihāra.
In that regard, because the meaning of "going" (*gamyamāna*) is implied by the name Isipatana, there is the conceptualization of various meanings (*nānatthakappanā*).
“Rushing from the rising to the setting [mountain], it does not turn back for even a moment;
this is neither the lunar orb nor the solar orb.
This is the *nibhūtā* (the vanished).
From its rising until its setting, as it rushes and speeds toward its setting, it does not turn back nor does it return for even a moment—a brief interval of time.
This is neither the lunar disk nor the solar disk. From its arising at rebirth until its passing away at death:
"rushing" refers to the function of life-span, [the rushing] of the moon and other luminaries toward their setting.
Because the words expressing those [meanings] are identical, there is the possibility here of other meanings such as "moon" established therein:

"Having abandoned the goddess named Kittimahī and the city called Kaḷāra, that wise man did not remember her even while performing his duties, though she was called 'Uyyamā'"; thus, "even while performing" means "even while releasing" (according to the Ka commentary).
This is a compound of identical sounds.
Having abandoned and renounced both the queen named Kittimahī— so called because she possessed the two names "Kitti" and "Mahī"—
and the city named Kaḷāra, so called because it possessed the two names "Kaḷāra" and "Attha," that wise man departed.
While making himself possessed of the name "Uyyama" (Exertion) through the practice of exertion, the Great Being did not recall his prosperity nor did he look back upon it;
and while abandoning Queen Yasodharā and the city of Kapilavatthu to apply himself to the effort known as *vīriya*, he did not remember his former success.
Herein, the desired words such as "Yasodharā" and so forth have been composed by means of synonyms such as "kitti" (fame), "mahī" (earth), and so on.
“Bound with faces turned toward the four directions,
the four Sindhava horses themselves enjoy the grass laid out before them in the middle, according to their pleasure.
This is the confused [verse].
Just as four horses from Sindh, tied so that they face the four directions,
eat the grass placed in their midst at their own pleasure, appearing as if they were tied with their backs to one another,
yet in fact they are tied facing one another— in this context, the phrase is “tied facing the four directions.”
Because it has already been explained, to bind it by making it the back [of the argument] leads to confusion.
As it is said: "A person who honors the words of one who binds with the joy of living attains [merit], even while remaining within the range of the exhaustion of merit."
This is the protective [verse].

Honoring and worshipping the speech— the words— of the Perfectly Enlightened One, the kinsman of the sun who brings joy to the lotuses born from life and water, people [dwell] in the sphere where merit is not exhausted.
Because it is the opposite of demerits— those unwholesome states designated as "enemies of merit"—
one attains and reaches the path and fruit that arise by taking Nibbāna as their object, which serves as the sign for the destruction of those enemies of merit.

Here, by the phrases "the kinsman who brings joy to those who know him while living" and "he causes [the mind] to proceed by taking as its object the sign for the destruction of the enemies of merit," the Buddha [is shown] through the path and fruit.
And because they are stated through a continuous succession of connections, there is an abundance of such connections.
[As it is said: “He does not grasp even a loud sound, nor does he seek adornment;
this ear of no four-footed creature whatsoever is not fruitless.”
This is "one-sided.
Even for a four-footed animal, the ear does not perceive even a great sound; it does not take it as an object, nor does it grasp its manifestation.
Nevertheless, it is said that this ear is not fruitless; rather, it is said that from being fruitful, it does not become fruitless. This is the "horse-ear" (assakaṇṇa).
A tree. Here, by making "ear" (*kaṇṇo*) the object to be supported (*ādheyya*), there is a "protection through dependence" (*nissayagutti*) because the support itself is not explicitly mentioned:
"Adorning the world, together with its gods, and possessing splendor—where was he born and raised, and who is not smeared by him?"* *Note:
This verse is a riddle (pāḷi-pañha) where the answer is "the sun" (*sūriyo*). The "ear" refers to the "horizon" or "direction," which is the support for the sun's rising.*
This [lotus] is covered on both sides.
Because it adorns the world together with its gods, it appears like the Buddha.
Adorning the world—that is, the water known as *bhuvana*—constantly, it is "splendid" (*sassirika*), meaning endowed with beauty; in what water was it born and raised?
Which one is which, and by what water does it not become soiled, does not get stained? "The lotus" (*paduma*) is the answer.
For *paduma* is a term that functions as both masculine and neuter. Here, because both types—the water-born and the land-born—are covered, they are called "covered on both sides" (*ubhayacchanna*).
"That which is the beginning is itself the end, and the beginning of the middle is the middle."
"I declare the unconditioned state (asaṅkhata-pada) as it exists in the Siddhānta and other [treatises].
This is the miscellaneous section.
That which occurs at the end or the conclusion is the same as that at the beginning; that which constitutes the beginning of the middle is the middle itself.
"Siddham" means accomplished (*nipphanna*); "speak" (*vada*) means tell of the unconditioned state (*asaṅkhata-pada*) as it exists among those Noble Ones (*ariya*).
This is another meaning. At the beginning (*ādi*), that very letter *sa*; at the end (*anta*), that very letter *ya*;

the middle (*majjhima*) refers to the middle vowel, which is the letter *ma*, the beginning of the word "middle. It exists, by way of being expressive, within the established conclusions (*siddhanta*), etc., and within the systems of tenets (*mata-samaya*), time (*kāla*), and so forth.
"Speak—explain—the designation (paññatti) that is the unconditioned state (asaṅkhatapada), which, because it is other than the conditioned, is itself unconditioned.

For the word *samaya* here refers to a name-designation (*nāmapaññatti*). In this context, since the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) is included by the word "tenet" (*siddhanta*), the sense of "such" (*tādi*) is obtained;
thus, due to the profundity of the meaning and by the characteristic of being brought together, [the terms] "that" (*so*), "which" (*yo*), and "unconditioned state" (*asaṅkhatapada*) [are used].
Because it is deceived by a word that has been applied to another meaning, it possesses the characteristic of being deceptive;
and because the word *samaya* is conceived as having various meanings, it possesses the characteristic of having a different name. Thus, it is mixed with all three characteristics.

In the remaining cases as well, the state of being "mixed" (*saṃkiṇṇa*) should be understood in exactly this way. Following the characteristics stated in each respective instance, the etymological nature of terms such as *samāgata* and so forth should be understood.
Whatever contradicts place, time, art, the world, logic, or scripture—that is a contradictory statement;
this is made clear by the following examples. (34) "Place," and so forth: "place" refers to land, water, and the like;
"time" refers to day and night; "art" refers to dance, song, and the like; "the world" [refers to common consensus].

The occurrence of moving and non-moving beings. *Ñāya* means logic or reasoning. *Āgama* here refers to the word of the Buddha; elsewhere, however, it refers to the *suti-dhamma-saṃhitā* (the tradition of heard doctrine), and those [texts] as well.
That which has contradiction with these is *desa-virodhi* (contrary to place) … [and so on] … *virodhi*.

Having restated "that which" (*yaṃ*), "that contradictory term" (*taṃ virodhipadaṃ*) is predicated. And this term is clear and evident from both examples and definitions, because [there is a contradiction] when lotuses and the like are found on dry land and the like.
Furthermore, there is the contradiction regarding manifestation and so forth; the occurrence of flowers and the like—which arise from passion and so on—in the days and so forth;

the violation of the definitions stated in the treatises on the arts (*kalāśāstra*), such as: "The seven musical notes (*svara*) are called *bhinnachaḍja* and so on among the sixty-four arts including dance, song, and the rest";
the transgression of worldly conventions, such as saying "fire is cold" or "the *khadira* tree is sapless"; and [the contradiction] with the arising of what has been stated as impossible.

Furthermore, the contradiction with the method [of establishing] the transformation of *middha* (torpor) into material form (*rūpa*), as well as the contradiction with its respective scriptural authority (*āgama*), can easily be understood because they are evident;
therefore, the intention is that none of this has been stated here. 34.

Having thus explained the reason for not showing the "Yamaka-pahelikā" (the pairs of riddles), he now addresses the fault of contradiction that has arrived according to the order of the summary (*uddesa*).
He speaks by means of the phrase beginning with "place and time" (*desakāli*). "Place" (*deso*) refers to locations such as dry land, water, mountains, and so forth.

"Time" (*kālo*) is threefold by way of night and day, and winter and so on; it is sixfold by way of spring and so on. "Arts" (*kalā*) refers to the sixty-four arts, such as dance, song, and the rest. "World" (*loko*) is defined as the occurrence of beings, both stationary and moving. "Logic" (*ñāyo*) is reasoning.

"Tradition" (*āgamo*) here refers to the word of the Buddha, whereas elsewhere it includes what is associated with the heard doctrine (*suti-dhamma*). Contradiction with these [is what is being addressed].

"It has this" refers to a place... [and so on] ...up to "contradictory. That is called a contradictory term (*virodhipada*). This contradictory term is clear and well-understood through examples and characteristics:
namely, the state of being water-born and so forth in the case of *vassika*, jasmine, and the like; the state of being land-born and so forth in the case of lotuses, water-lilies, and the like;

the occurrence during the day and so forth of water-lilies and the like which are found at night and so forth; and [the contradiction] regarding the sixty-four arts such as dancing, singing, and so forth.

Regarding the musical arts (*kalā*), the Teacher’s attainment [of mastery] is demonstrated by the fact that he designated the *chañja*—which is one part of the seven notes shown as "the six-sound, the bull, the Gandhāra, the middle, the fifth, the Dhevatā, and the Nisāda"—by the name "Broken Seven-Sound *Chañja*" through such means as conventional usage based on the whole; and his transcendence of characteristics is shown by such statements as:
"Fire is cold, sandalwood is hot, the Khadira tree is pithless, and the castor-oil plant has pith."

The intention is as follows: since the contradiction of nature is evident in all these cases—such as the transgression of worldly conventions by [statements] beginning with "thus," the statement that contradicts the reasoning for establishing the existence of form (rūpa) despite the fact that the arising in the formless realm (arūpabhava) has already been mentioned regarding torpor (middha), and the statement that transgresses one's own respective scripture—we shall not provide further examples.
Regarding these very instances of contradiction with place and so forth, their non-contradiction is established within this very section on the avoidance of the fault of contradictory words.

It is seen [in the texts] by such expressions as “by the power of the Bodhisatta. One who has opposition to a country (*desa*), and so forth, or to a village (*gama*) is called *desavirodhi* (one opposed to a country), and so forth.
Here, the sense of possession (*atthi*) is intended in the sense of censure (*nindā*).
That which is brought from the past and is to be spoken of, they call *neyya* (to be inferred).
"Just as all directions shine white during the night. (35) "That which... and so forth.
It is not disagreeable either in sound or in meaning; nor is there any other understanding [of it] because of the absence of any other text.
For he will say: "The difficult-to-attain comprehension transcends the power of the words' literal capacity. Having brought together whatever verse [is appropriate]...
Having brought it forward, it should be stated: that is what they call *neyya* (that which requires further interpretation). He provides an illustration with the word "yathā" (as for example).

When it is stated that "all directions"—meaning all ten directions, beginning with the eastern direction—shine and blaze white and bright during the night (*rajanya*), to this extent the rays of the moon are indicated as being of the *neyya* type.
35. Now he illustrates the fault of *neyya* with the words beginning with "yaṃ": "That word which is not understood by means of another word, [and] by the meaning expressed by that..."
Or, when the meaning has not been understood, one must bring it forward and state, "This is its meaning";
from that very point, another word must be brought forward and stated. This they call "neyya" (to be inferred); the ancients called it "the fault of being neyya.
An example of this is as follows: "All directions shine white during the night. Here, "all directions" refers to the ten directions, beginning with the east and south, which are white.

"Setā" means they shine and illuminate during the night. Here, because it is not intended to ask from where the quality of whiteness—the qualifier of the direction—has arisen (such as from the peak of Mount Kailāsa, a plastered wall, the rays of the moon, etc.), the word "dhavala" (white) is faulty due to the defect of *neyya* (being too obscure).

This is because, in order to exclude other [colors], one must bring in a term denoting the moon's rays or similar things, such that it would have to be said, "whiteness by this [moonlight]. "Patītaṃ" means understood or known.
"Not fallen, not un-fallen. Here, the negative particle *a-* functions as an absolute negation (*pasajjapaṭisedha*).
The wise everywhere consider such [a usage] to be rare;
for it is difficult to find a comprehension that transcends the conventional power of words.
36. To show that the wise do not desire what is unconvincing, he says "ne" (not) and so forth.

All wise ones—those who know what is to be known—do not highly regard, do not esteem, and do not employ such a subject matter (*neyya*) as was described in the preceding passage, whether it be the "roaring" [of a teacher] or otherwise.
If one asks why they do not highly regard it, he says "dullabhā" (rare) and so forth. For indeed, *avagati* is the comprehension of the meaning.

Because it transgresses and abandons both the expressive word (*sadda*) and the method of its semantic capacity (*sāmatthiya-ñāya*) by not providing a corresponding illustration, it is "transgressing the word and its capacity" (*saddasāmatthiyavilaṅghinī*);
such [an expression] is rare and not found. It is that whose meaning is neither supported by the method (*ñāya*) nor supported by the word (*sadda*).
The meaning is: it cannot be understood merely by the fact of its being fixed in the mind. Therefore, it must be understood from either the word or the meaning.
The opposite of that is to be understood as *neyya*. 36.
Showing that this term *appatīta* is not favored by the wise, he says "not such" (*nedisaṃ*) and so forth.
All wise people do not highly esteem such a *neyya*—of the kind already described—in all cases, such as the *gajjapajja* and others.
They do not conceive [the meaning] nor do they apply [it]. "Understanding" (*avagati*) is the comprehension of the meaning that transcends the capacity of words;
it proceeds by overstepping both the word known as the signifier and the knowledge known as the capacity [of that signifier], and it is difficult to obtain because such application is rare.
Whatever meaning has been conveyed by the word, even if it does not conform to the [logical] method (*ñāya*), it becomes established in the mind of the speaker merely by being present there.
The intention is that all poets avoid the phrase *patīto na hoti* because it contains the fault of being ambiguous (*neyyadosa*).

In the sentence "they show great respect," the verbal root is *maññati* (to honor), meaning they hold [it] in high esteem. That which by its nature transgresses the conventional power of words is called *saddasāmatthiyavilaṅghinī*.
It may require a qualification,
but once that qualification has been reached,
it is meaningful, just as in the case of "he."
“He sees even more with his eye. (37) “*Siyā*” and so forth:
that word which, having received a qualifier (*visesana*), functions together with its meaning is *sātthaka* (meaningful).
But that which is without a qualifier has only the stated meaning; it may require a qualifier. He illustrates this with “*taṃ yathā*” and so on. “He sees.”
When it is stated, the term "by the eye" (*cakkhunā*) is indeed obtained. 37.

Regarding "it may be" (*siyā*) and so forth: that word which, upon reaching a qualifier, becomes meaningful—that is, possessed of meaning—and which would otherwise be meaningless in its absence, is called "dependent on a qualifier" (*visesanāpekkha*).
It may be, as for example, [the word] *taṃ* (that), just as in the illustration of that very [word], [one says] "he [saw] that even more."
“He sees with the eye. That man sees that other man for the most part with the eye. Here, when it is said simply “he sees,” it is understood that it is “with the eye.
The word *cakkhunā* (with the eye) becomes meaningful only by receiving a qualifier (*visesana*).
It is a compound (*samāsa*) because it has a dependence upon a qualifier (*visesane apekkhā assā*), and because it is expressed together with its meaning (*saha atthena vattamānam sātthakam*).
Whatever qualifying term makes the thing qualified inferior—that becomes a term with the sense of inferiority (*hīnattha*), as for example:
“The sun rises, having rendered the firefly lusterless.
(38) “‘Inferior,’ etc.: Whatever qualifying word (*visesanapada*) should make the thing qualified (*visesya*), that which is to be distinguished, inferior (*hīna*) or base, [that is a *hīnattha*].”
That qualifying word has a low meaning; that which has a low meaning is called "low-meaning" (*hīnattha*). He illustrates this with the words beginning with "yathā. [The phrase means:
"The sun, the maker of light, by whom the glow-worm is rendered lusterless, rises—that is, approaches.
In this context, there is no praise of the sun in the act of taking away the glow-worm's light.
38. “*Hīnaṃ kare*,” etc. That word which makes the qualificand inferior (*hīna*) becomes a term with the sense of inferiority (*hīnattha*).

For example, as there is that very illustration: “The sun rises, having rendered the fireflies lusterless (*nippabhīkatakhajjoto*),” meaning the sun, the maker of light, rises or ascends, by whom the fireflies have been deprived of their radiance. By this phrase, “having rendered the fireflies lusterless,” [the inferiority of the fireflies is shown].
The illumination that overcomes the firefly—which has obtained its existence in a lowly place—is actually a censure of the thousand-rayed sun, not a praise;
thus, the qualifying term has a base meaning. The analysis (*viggaha*) is as follows:

"that which has a base meaning" (*hīno attho yassa*), "those which have no radiance" (*natthi pabhā etesaṃ*), "made devoid of radiance" (*nippabhā katā*), and "by whom the fireflies were made devoid of radiance" (*nippabhīkatā khajjotā yena*).
Whatever serves merely to fill out the meter is considered to be "meaningless" (anattha).
For example: *vande buddhassa pādapaṅkeruhampica* (I worship the lotus-feet of the Buddha).
Here, because the particles *hi*, *api*, and *ca* serve merely to fill out the meter, they are meaningless. This is the fault of the qualifying and qualified terms.

39. “*Pādapūraṇī*,” and so forth. That word which is a mere filler—meaning it serves only to complete the fourth part (the *pāda*)—is considered and known to be meaningless (*anattha*). The word *yathā* has the meaning already stated. One pays homage to the Buddha’s lotus-foot, his lotus-like foot.
For here, since [the particle] *api ca* does not function in the sense of completion and so forth, [it is understood as a mere filler].
It serves merely to fill out the verse and is therefore devoid of purpose. The word *matta* is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). This is a fault of the qualifying and qualified terms.
The commentary on the description of faults of words is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the description of faults of sentences.

"That which is stated by way of word and by way of meaning, where it is further stated again—this is called 'repetition' (ekattha), just as the term *vārida* and *vārido* shine forth with the same sense.

(40) Regarding the phrase "by way of word" (*saddato*) and so forth: "By way of word" means because of the repeated application of that very same word for that very same meaning by means of its denotative function.

Because it restates—without distinction—the very same basis (*vatthu*) that was previously presented by its meaning (*abhidheyya*), it is called "connected" (*payutta*). Having referred to that form of word-meaning which is stated again—that is, employed once more—in a particular sentence, as "that is one in meaning" (*ekattha*), it is then prescribed by the phrase beginning with "just as" (*yathā*).
One who gives water is a "water-giver" (*vārida*). This is a water-giver.
"The cloud shines, it blazes. This is identical in meaning from the perspective of the word alone, considering merely the act of giving water.
40. Now, he explains the defects of a sentence according to the order in which they were listed, beginning with "from the perspective of the word" (*saddato*).

Wherein, in whatever sentence, that form of a word-meaning (*padattharūpa*) which is expressed—that is, employed—both from the perspective of the word (*saddato*), by means of the signifier (*vācakena*), and from the perspective of the meaning (*atthato*), by means of the signified (*abhidheyyena*), [is found] even more...
Furthermore, it is said that when a statement is redundant—that is, when it expresses the same meaning—it is called the fault of *ekattha* (redundancy).
An example is the verse beginning with "yathī" and so forth: "The rain-giver (*vārida*), the water-bestower (*jaladāyaka*), this rain-giving cloud (*megha*) shines (*ābhāti*).

Because the mere act of giving water is already expressed by the word "rain-giver," the addition of the qualifying epithets "water-bestower" and so forth is redundant from the perspective of the sound-meaning; thus, it is called *ekattha*.
Just as he abandons the seeds that are the sprouts of the heretics' views here,
this Great Sage inspires confidence in the people who already possess it.

41. Abandoning and distancing the sixty-two views—the speculative positions that serve as the seeds and causes for the arising of the sprouts known as the *titthiya* (heretics)—that Great Sage, the Fully Enlightened One, inspires confidence in the great multitude of people in this world who are already confident and full of faith;
this is another illustration. Regarding the meaning of "confidence" (*pasāda*), [it is said]: "In those who are confident..."
Because it is stated [in the text], “he inspires confidence,” this has the same meaning in substance. 41.

Regarding the passage beginning with “titthiyi”: that Great Sage, abandoning (*jaham*) the seeds of the sprouts of the sectarians (*titthiya*), namely the sixty-two views divided into categories such as eternalism and so forth, which constitute the causes for the arising of those sprouts known as “sectarian views.”
Taking [faith] away from those who are confident here in this world, he inspires confidence in the great masses of people who are confident in himself.

Because the meaning expressed by the word *pasanna*—namely, that which is designated as "confidence"—is also expressed by the verb *pasādeti*, even though the words differ, they are identical in meaning; thus, this is an example of "identity in meaning.
Only the sectarians are the sprouts; their seeds have gone into [their] views; [they are] the views.
Or the analysis [of the compound] is "thus gone" (*evaṃ-gatāni*).
Just as there may be a certain wisdom, a certain virtue, or even a certain nature in one whose progress has begun but not been interrupted, and whose composure is broken— oh, such is yours!

42. *Āraddho* means one who has begun or is about to proceed; *kamo* means the sequence of speech. Its interruption is *bhaṅgo* (break). [The author] illustrates this with the words beginning with "yathā" (just as).
Even though it was not explicitly stated, it is supplied by implication through the influence of the [author's] approval (*pasāda*). O Great Sage, your wisdom is indeed something extraordinary;
because of its excellence, its specific nature (*sabhāvavisesa*) is not fully determined. Aho! This is because, even while it is functioning, its essential character remains undetermined.
The meaning is "wonderful. Here, in the phrase *kāpi kopīti sabbanāmapadakkamassa pakatīti*, because of the interruption [of the sequence], there is a breach of the rhythmic flow (*bhaggarīti*).

42. Regarding the phrase beginning with *āraddhakkama*: when there is an interruption in the sequence that has been commenced, the rhythmic flow of the words initiated for the subject matter is broken;
thus, there occurs the syntactic fault known as *bhaggarīti*. He provides an example beginning with *yathī* and so forth: "O Great Sage, of yours..."

Your wisdom is preeminent; it is truly beyond compare because it transcends the scope of words. Your virtues—the collection of extraordinary qualities such as morality, concentration, and so forth—are likewise beyond compare, for they cannot be grasped by any measure even with the slightest degree of error. Your very nature is inconceivable;
your nature is just like that. Oh, how difficult it is to realize the true essence of these existing qualities, such as wisdom and the rest—how truly marvelous!
In the phrase *kāpi kopīti*, there is a breach of the established mode (*rītibhaṅga*) because of the voidness (*suññattā*) of the term "natural" (*pakati*). The analysis (*viggaha*) here is:
"the sequence (*kama*) has indeed been commenced, but its continuity is broken; its mode is shattered; or [it is so] in this case.
Where there is a difficult placement of words, confusion arises.
That should be understood as "confused" (*byākiṇṇa*), according to its illustration.

43. Regarding the phrase "of words" (*padānaṃ*) and so forth: in whatever sentence there arises or occurs a delusion—a state of being bewildered—due to the difficulty of properly placing the words, namely those ending in case-suffixes (*syādyanta*) and verbs (*ākhyātika*), that sentence should be understood as "confused."

This is to be understood. The author demonstrates the example of that "confused" (*byākiṇṇa*) [fault] by means of the word "just as" (*yathā*). The meaning is: "Just as this is, so too is another. 43.

Regarding the passage beginning with "words" (*padāni*): because words—namely, words ending in case-suffixes (*syādyanta*) or personal endings (*tyādyanta*)—are difficult to arrange due to their improper placement, that sentence in which confusion or delusion arises is to be known as the fault of being "confused" (*byākiṇṇadosa*). An example of that fault of being confused is as follows:
It should be understood according to the method that will be explained hereafter:
"This person bows to those of many virtues, even though they be wicked people;
always joyful, he constantly recollects the Sugata for his own welfare."
44. Because of the manifoldness and abundance of his virtues such as morality (*sīla*) and the rest, this entire world of people— recollecting those virtues correctly, rising up again and again,
and recollecting them while establishing mindfulness directed toward those qualities— is for that very reason joyful, delighted, and overjoyed, [thinking] that even wicked people,
such as Devadatta and others who are the opposite of virtuous men, will always have their welfare [ensured].
"He bows down to and pays homage to the Sugata, the Perfectly Enlightened One"—this is the meaning intended by the poet.

In this regard, because the application of the words "bahuguṇe paṇamati" and so forth involves a separation of terms (*byavahitapadappayoga*), confusion arises; thus it is considered *byākiṇṇa* (disordered).

44. "Bahuguṇe," etc. While recollecting the manifold qualities—such as virtue (*sīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and so forth—which are "many" (*bahuguṇe*) in the sense of being vast due to their infinity.
Recalling [the Buddha] especially, this people—the multitude of beings—rejoices and, for that very reason, is uplifted;
they bow down to and worship the Sugata, the Omniscient One, who is the constant and perpetual benefactor and friend even to the wicked and the unvirtuous.
Here, the disorderly arrangement of the words due to their shifting positions is understood simply by following the sequence of their meanings.
"O maiden, why is it that you do not desire me, who am desiring you? This [speech] is devoid of any statement regarding a distinguished matter, being considered merely vulgar.
(45) It is "devoid of" (*apeta*)—that is, abandoned by—the speaking or stating of any distinguished matter. "O maiden" (*kaññe*) is a form of address.
“I desire you; why do you reject me who am such as I am?”—this is called *gāmaka* (rustic) because it consists of the speech of village folk, beginning with the word “maiden” (*kaññī*).
45. Regarding “distinguished” (*visiṭṭha*) and so forth:
that which is to be distinguished by a particular expression used by one who is dear is [called] *visiṭṭhavacanāpetam*.
Speech that has fallen away from proper expression is considered by poets to be a "village fault" (*gāmmadosa*).
He provides an example beginning with "yathā," etc.: "O maiden! O maiden! You do not desire me, who desires you;
you do not wish for me—what indeed is this? When such an obstruction of desire is being expressed, thus—
“My request for your sake comes to naught day after day;
you are always skillful at shattering the pride of proud women.”
"Has that Manmatha gone elsewhere?"—it is as if [she thinks this].
Because there is no speaking of what is dear, the words beginning with "O maiden" (*kaññe*) are *gāmmya* (vulgar) because they are the speech of barbarians (*milakkhuka*).
Here, there is no fixed rule that the word *kaññā* applies only to a ten-year-old girl. A sentence is [called] *apeta* (deviant) because it departs from the expression of a distinguished meaning.
46. "From the joining of words, something might become difficult to believe;
yet even that is considered vulgar, as in the case of Yābhava’s beloved.
[The commentary on] "In words," etc., begins: From the joining of words—that is, by way of the connection between preceding and following words—whatever sentence [might arise],...
That which produces a perception of beauty where there is actually foulness and lack of charm is called *karaṃ*; that too is considered a vulgar ending as previously described.
For example, he cites: *Bhavato yā kāci vanitā piyā hoti*—this is one meaning. [In the root] *yabh*, [the sense is] sexual intercourse (*methuna*).
The act of sexual intercourse is *yābho*. He in whom that exists is *yābhavā*. Of him, the wife (*piyā*) is also called *yābhavatī*.

46. “*Padasandhāni*,” etc. A certain sentence, due to the joining of words—that is, the connection of preceding and following words—may become difficult to comprehend and reveal an improper or corrupt meaning;

such a sentence is also considered *gāmma*, meaning it is defiled by the aforementioned vulgar fault (*gāmmadosa*), and is thus known as *duppasita* (unpleasant) by all poets. To illustrate this, he provides an example from the *Bhavatō*.
"Whatever woman is dear to you"—this is the meaning intended by the poet. Alternatively, the meaning is "she who is dear to you, who possess sexual intercourse.
For the verbal root is *yabh* (to copulate). *Yābha* is the act of copulating; he who possesses that is *yābhavā*.

When *yābhavataḥ* is taken [as the reading], because it is not something that should be heard [in this context], it causes a lack of conviction. It is indeed a corrupted understanding (*duṣṭā eva pratītiḥ*).
The analysis [of the compound] is: "it makes that" (*taṃ karoti*).
In the cases mentioned and indicated, the division of words is called *yati*;
however, when a word is deficient because of that [division], it is said to be "deficient in *yati*" (*yatihīna*).

47. “In those that have been stated,” and so forth. In those [metres] such as *anuṣṭubh* and others, which have been described in the treatises on prosody (*chandas*) and indicated in their respective places—meaning in the sections of the *Chandoviciti* where it is explained, “herein [the pause] occurs”—the division (*chedo*), the arrangement (*vicchiti*), or the distinction (*vibhāgo*) of words ending in case-suffixes (*syādyanta*) is the restatement (*anuvādo*) of what the pause (*yati*) shall be;
this is what is prescribed. A sentence that is deficient (*hīna*), lacking (*parihīna*), or contrary (*viruddha*) to that pause—
That is called "deficient in pause" (*yati-hīna*), because it is understood as: "The act of restraining (*yamana*) is the pause (*yati*); that [pause] is deficient here.
The word *pana* (but/however) indicates a distinction;

the connection is "but that pause. 47. Regarding the phrase "In those stated," etc.: in the places indicated among the stated prosodic treatises—namely, the *anuṣṭubh* and so forth—it is shown that "this [is the rule] here..."
In the context where it is declared, “yatī,” *yati* refers to the division or pause (*viccheda*) between words such as those ending in *syat*, *tyat*, and so forth.
A sentence that is deficient because of this *yati*—meaning it lacks the proper division of syllables at the intended place—is called "deficient in *yati*" (*yatihīna*).
Such a sentence is said by the wise to be corrupted by the fault of being deficient in *yati*.
The pause (*yati*) occurs at the end of every quarter-verse (*pāda*), especially in those [verses] where half [the syllables] have been specified;
it also occurs in some cases in the middle of a word consisting of multiple syllables, both before and after [the break]. 48.
Regarding the phrase beginning with "pause" (*yati*): "everywhere at the end of the quarter-verse" means at the conclusion of all quarters of a verse, which are reckoned as fourth parts.

"At the beginning" and "at the end" mean specifically, particularly, and exclusively at the half-verse—that is, at the half consisting of two quarters (pādas) that has been stated—and at its conclusion;
this is the intended meaning. The word "might be" (*siyā*) is to be supplied as the remainder. If it is asked:

"Since it was stated that 'there is a word-break' (*padacchedo*), does this not mean that there can never be a pause (*yati*) in the middle of a word? he says "the preceding," etc. [This occurs] in some places—in certain instances—not everywhere.
The connection is that there is a pause (*yati*) even in the middle of words consisting of many syllables (*anekavaṇṇa*) both before and after.

"Before and after" means *pubbāpare*. "Many syllables" means *anekavaṇṇā*. That which has many syllables both before and after is so described. And that is the word; [the pause occurs] even in the middle of that. 48.
Now, with the words beginning "pause," he shows the entire scope of where a pause may occur. Furthermore, that pause applies everywhere.

"At the end of the foot" means specifically and necessarily at the end of a verse-quarter (pāda) counted as a fourth part, and also at the end of a half-verse (aḍḍha)—that is, at the end of the two quarters that constitute a half-verse;

this is the intended meaning. "In some places" means in certain instances, even in the middle of several syllables and words in the preceding or following parts, and also in the middle of words endowed with several preceding or following syllables. This refers to the "pause" (yati) for the division of words.

Because it has been stated [that a pause does not occur] in the middle of a word (*padamajjhe*), the phrase "in the middle of a word consisting of multiple preceding and following syllables" (*pubbāparānekavaṇṇapadamajjhe*) is stated in order to avoid that doubt.
Here, the end of a line (*pādanta*), the half-verse already mentioned, and the middle of a word (*padamajjha*) are the places for the pause (*yati*).
The pause, which is found only in the middle of a word, occurs in certain instances, but it does not occur in the middle of a word consisting of two or three syllables.
In this regard, the examples and counter-examples are as follows:
"I bow my head to that Tathāgata, who has the color of refined gold;
it seems as if he were sprinkling all the quarters with streams of liquid gold."
49. It is called an *udāharaṇa* (example) because it is cited (*udāharīyati*). A counter-example (*paccudāharaṇa*) is an example given as an opposite case.
I bow my head to that Tathāgata whose complexion is like that of refined gold (*cāmīkara*), like fine gold itself. Of what sort is he?
That Tathāgata who, as if with liquid gold—because of his golden hue—douses all ten directions, every single direction, as if with streams of molten gold.

"He sprinkles," so it is thought; one regards that as the Tathāgata. Here, the pause (*yati*) is fixed at the end of the first line and after the syllable *ḍḍha*. Furthermore, the word *cāmīkara* here consists of four syllables;
therein, *cāmī* is the prior portion and *kara* is the subsequent. Here, the pause occurs in the middle of a word consisting of multiple letters, both preceding and following.
However, in the case of *siñcati*, because there is no such state of being in the middle of a word consisting of multiple letters, both preceding and following, [the pause does not occur there].
In the phrase *siñca ittha*, there is a faulty pause (*yati*). This is a counter-example (*paccudāharaṇa*).

49. Among those [cases] where the pauses occur at the end of a quarter-verse or in its middle, because the pauses are evident at the end of a quarter-verse, the examples and counter-examples for the pause in the middle of that word are as follows:
the desired example and its opposite, such as *taṃ name* and so forth; and *yo tathāgato sakalāpi disā*.
"With golden juices"—with streams of liquid gold—it sprinkles, as it were; one might imagine it sprinkling. The word "iva" (as if) expresses a conjecture (*vitakka*).
"Cāmīkaravaṇṇaṃ"—one whose skin-color resembles the color of refined gold; bow your head to that Tathāgata.

Here, in the phrase "cāmīkaravaṇṇaṃ," because the two syllables "cāmī" stand beyond the caesura (*yati*), and because it is not deficient by the two syllables "kara" at the end, [the meter remains correct].
The example for the rule is that there is multiplicity of vowels in the preceding and following parts of a word-division (*padaccheda*).

In the word *siñcati*, even though a pause (*yati*) is observed after the two vowels *si* and *ñca*, there is an absence of multiplicity of vowels because the subsequent part, *ti*, consists of a single vowel;
this is a counter-example (*paccudāharaṇa*). Here, the state of having multiple vowels is to be understood only by way of the word (*pada*). It is like the color of gold.
The analysis of the compound is "he whose complexion is such.
In a compound, the vowel at the end of the preceding member remains as it was even when the case-ending is elided;
otherwise, in that context, [the vowel] may be changed, or there may be substitution by *y*, or it may appear as if it were the beginning of the following member.

50. “*Saro*,” etc. When there is elision of a case ending (*vibhatti*), once the euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) has been effected in the *saṃhitā*, a vowel that constitutes the beginning of the following word becomes like a vowel at the end of the preceding word.

Even though it lacks the quality of having multiple phonemes (*anekavaṇṇatta*), there is no breaking of the rule for the suffix (*ti*) prescribed after it; this is the intended meaning. Otherwise, however, when there is no elision of the case ending...

When a vowel forming the end of the preceding word (*pubbapada*) has been joined in *saṃhitā*, if it becomes otherwise—that is, in a different manner—it becomes as if it were a similar vowel of the following word (*parapada*);
this is the meaning. The intention is that there is no violation of the metrical pause (*yati*) when that [vowel] is excluded along with its case-ending (*vibhatti*).

In that regard, within that metrical pause, just as in the case of the substitution of *y* for *i* and so forth, the substitution of *y* for *i*-vowels and others should be made as if they were the initial part of the subsequent word.

It is like the initial vowel (*ādisara*). The intention is that there is no violation of the caesura (*yatibhaṅga*) when one sets aside the consonant accompanied by the elided case-ending and so forth, provided the caesura is correctly placed.
(50) Now, demonstrating that even when there is a contradiction as stated below, there is still no violation of the caesura, he says: "The vowel," and so forth.

When a case-ending is elided and a sandhi occurs, the "vowel" (*saro*)—referring to the *sandhisara*—is like the final syllable of the preceding word (*pubbanto*), just as it was at the end of the prior member of the compound.
Otherwise, when the case-ending (*vibhatti*) is not elided and the *saṃhitā* (euphonic combination) has been performed, it becomes otherwise:

the vowel belonging to the end of the preceding word (*pubbapada*) becomes as if it were the initial vowel of the following word (*parapada*). In that regard, just as in the case of *yādesa* and so forth, the substitution of *ya* and other sounds for *i*-vowels and so forth—whether by way of being the final element of the preceding word or the initial element of the following word—occurs by resorting to a sound similar to the initial vowel of the following word, even after bypassing a vowel similar to the final [vowel] of the preceding word.

The intention is that even when there is no absence of multiple syllables (*anekavaṇṇatta*), there is no violation of the pause (*yatibhaṅga*) provided that the pause is employed after not overstepping that [preceding word], or after overstepping the final vowel (*sara*) of another word and so forth, as well as its substitute (*ādesa*) and so forth. The phrases are: "the end of the preceding" (*pubbassa anto*);

"that which is the substitute (*ādesa*), and that which has 'm' and so forth as its initial [element]" (*yo ca so ādeso ca, so ādi yassa makārādinoti*); and "the beginning of the following" (*parassa ādi*).
The particles beginning with *ca* (such as *ca*, *vā*, *eva*) are always dependent upon the preceding word;
likewise, those beginning with *pā* (such as *pāda*) are always connected [to the preceding word], whereas those beginning with *para* (such as *para*, *parā*) are connected with the following word.
51. Always (*niccam*), that is, incessantly (*anavaratam*), the particles beginning with *ca*—namely, the particles starting with the letter *c*—are dependent upon, or rely upon, the preceding word.
The meaning is that the final parts [of the preceding words] act as if they were syllables; having made those the end, the pause (*yati*) should be placed.
Because they are constantly connected with the subsequent word, they are "ever-yoked" (*satatayogino*). The particle *tu* is used out of place.

However, the initial parts of the subsequent words, such as *para*, act like the constituent parts of the subsequent word itself; the meaning is that, omitting that [particle], the pause should be placed at the end of the preceding word.
51. “*Cādi*,” etc. Constantly and continuously, the *cādis*—the particles beginning with the letter *ca*—occur in dependence upon the preceding word (*pubbapada*).
Thus, they are like parts at the end of the preceding word, as if belonging to its conclusion.

However, the prefixes (*pādi-upasaggā*) such as *pa-* and others, which are always connected with a following word (*parapada*) and are inseparably joined with it, are like parts at the beginning of the following word, as if belonging to its commencement.

[The words] *honti*. The intended meaning is that a pause (*virāma*) occurring when preceded by *ca* and so forth—even if those [words] are placed outside—or when preceded by *pa* and so forth—even if those [words] are placed inside—constitutes a breach of the *yati* (metrical pause).
The analysis (*viggaha*) is as follows: "those which have *ca* and so forth" (*coādi yesam*), and "the preceding word is *sita*" (*pubbapadam sitā*);

and "those which have *pa* and so forth" (*po ādi yesam*), and "they are always connected" (*niccam sambandhā*). Here, because of the recognition of their respective qualities (*tagguṇasaṃviññāṇattā*), there is also the inclusion of the letter *ca*, the letter *pa*, and so on.
Examples for all cases are as follows:
"I bow my head to that Tathāgata who has transcended all comparison;
for he who has attained the highest state in the world, no simile is indeed appropriate."
I always pay homage to that Muninda, of infinite and supreme wisdom, whose insight and loving-kindness expand without limit.
(52–53) The term *sabbattha* means "in all cases," such as in the beginningless past and so forth. In the two verses beginning with "nametaṃ," the meaning of the words is evident.

The intended meaning, however, is as follows: because he has reached the summit of the world, he is beyond all comparison; because wisdom and loving-kindness flow continuously throughout the world, he possesses infinite intelligence and is supreme.

Here, having formed the compound "sabbā upamā" (all comparisons) and applied the elision of case-endings (*vibhattilopa*) and *saṃhitā*, the initial *u*-vowel of the following word becomes like the letter *a* that represents the final *bb*-vowel of the preceding word. Thus, [the form] becomes "sabba."

In this case, one forms *pādantayati* from *patta*. Here, just as in the case of the substitution of *y* there is a similarity to the beginning of the following word, so too when the case ending (*vibhatti*) is not elided and *saṃhitā* is applied, the letter *a* belonging to the form with its case ending becomes like the letter *u* which is the beginning of the following word;
thus, setting aside what is established for that specific case ending, one forms *pādantayati* from *patta*. Likewise, in the case of *vandāmyananta*.

Since the status of being like what follows (*parādisabhāva*) has been prescribed for that which begins with the letter *ya*, the *yati* occurs after the word *pāda* in the phrase *vandāmi c’ eva*, excluding the word *mya*.
Since it is stated that particles (*ca*-words) situated in the prior member of a compound are like the end of the prior member, the *yati* occurs after the particle *ca* in the phrase *mettā ca*.

Because words connected with a subsequent member are like the beginning of the subsequent member, the *yati* occurs at the beginning [of the second member] in the phrase *nissīmā*, omitting the word *ni*.
52–53. In all cases, regarding the five examples such as vowels that resemble those previously mentioned, the illustrations are as follows:
“I bow my head to him”—and so forth. For that Buddha who has reached the pinnacle of the world, no comparison is fitting;
indeed, it is not fitting because he stands transcending every category of referent. I bow with my head—that is, I pay homage—to that Tathāgata who is beyond all comparisons.

Regarding the word *sabbo*: here, because the vowel *o* at the end of the first member of the compound resembles a preceding *sa*-sound, it serves as an example for a pause (*yati*) that does not exceed the phoneme similar to the beginning of the following member, according to the rule "and *ssopama*. An example of such a pause is "Muninde" and so forth.
Of that Fully Awakened One (*Sambuddha*), wisdom and loving-kindness are his boundaries, because they take as their objects the infinite sentient beings and the infinite knowable things.
It expands boundlessly, free from limits. Because the knowable is infinite, even though there is the arising and passing away [of phenomena], he possesses infinite wisdom;
by applying the designation of the object to the subject, I always pay homage to that supreme and most excellent Lord of Sages.
Since *yā* is similar to *parā*, the *yati* (caesura) occurs without resorting to *tam*. Regarding the phrase *mettācanissīmā*: here—

Because the words beginning with *ca* resemble the preceding members of a compound, and because the words beginning with *pā* resemble the first members of the subsequent members, the metrical pause (*yati*) occurs even in these two cases: *ca* and *nī*.
Examples of counter-examples regarding the words beginning with *ca* and *pā* are as follows:
*Mahāmettā mahāpaññā, ca yattha paramodayā;* (Where there is great loving-kindness and great wisdom, and where there is supreme excellence...)
I pay homage to that Jina, the most excellent, the abode of supreme qualities.
(54) “Mahā,” etc. “Yattha” means in which Jina. “Paramodayā” refers to the great increases of supreme states such as loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) and so forth.

For that very reason, he is the abode of supreme qualities; for that same reason, he is the most excellent and sublime Jina—this is the connection. Here, [the quality] dependent on the preceding word...
The *ca*-consonant is made the initial element of the following word, and the pause (*yati*) is placed before it;

likewise, the *pa*-consonant is made the final element of the preceding word, and the pause is placed after the *pa*-consonant—these two cases are contradictory, and thus both serve as counter-examples (*paccudāharaṇa*). 54.
As for the counter-examples when particles such as *ca* function as the governing scope (*visaya*), they are as follows: "Mahāmetti," etc. In which case... where.
In the Victor, great loving-kindness and great wisdom—these are the supreme, most exalted increases.
I bow down to that Victor, who is the abode of excellent qualities, a mine of supreme virtues, and for that very reason, most eminent.

Here, because the pause (*yati*) occurs by making the letter *ca* the beginning of the subsequent word and the letter *pa* the end of the preceding word, both "ca yattha" and "taṃ pā" serve as counter-examples.
"This [work] is called *kamaccuta* because it is released from the sequence of words and has fallen away from the order [of composition].
'Give me a beautiful field, or a village, or a province' (v.

55). Regarding the phrase beginning with 'pada': it is established that this is *kamaccuta* because it is released—that is, fallen away—from the sequence of the meanings of the words (*padānam atthakkamato muttam gaḷitam*)."
By the phrase "or a field," etc., this sequence of requests indicates a lack of interest on the part of the speaker, which leads to the understanding that he is ignorant of the matter.
For how could one who is unwilling even to give a field ever give a village or the like? 55.
"The meaning of the words," etc. This sentence is "loose" (mutta) and "slipped away" (gaḷita) from the sequence of the meanings of the words according to the order of those words.
This is called *kamaccaya* (the sequence of order). He illustrates it with the passage beginning with "yathā" and so forth: "Give me a beautiful field, or a village, or a district, or a province.
Herein, the sequence of requesting—beginning with "a field"—does not indicate the natural order of the objects of speech except by the speaker's lack of intelligence;
for how could one who does not wish to give even a field ever give a village, town, province, and so forth? Thus, there is a loss of sequence.
“Exceeding the worldly meaning,” as in the expression *ativuttaṃ mataṃ* (“the thought is expressed beyond [the norm]”);
and “excessively narrow,” as in *atisambādhaṃ ākāsaṃ etissā thanajambhane thanajumbhane* (“the space is too cramped for her expanding, swelling breasts”). 56.
“In the world,” etc. That which is known in the world is *lokiya* (worldly); that *lokiyatthaṃ* (worldly meaning) has been *atikkantaṃ* (transcended), i.e., not followed.
That which is stated as "excessive" (ativutta) is defined as such. He illustrates this with the words beginning with "yathā" (as for example).
Regarding the swelling—that is, the expansion—of the breasts (payodhara) of this woman, the sky (gagana) is *atisambādha*, meaning extremely narrow.
56. “*Lokiyatthi*,” etc. That which transcends the worldly sense—the meaning well-known in the world—in its manner of expression...

A statement that has been exceeded is considered "over-stated" (*ativutta*). He illustrates this with the verse beginning with "yathī" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "at the bursting of her breasts":
when her breasts burst open, the space becomes excessively cramped, meaning there is no room. Here, [the poet] says, "I shall describe the greatness of the breasts.
