Because even the sky—which is renowned in the world as "great"—has been surpassed, the statement is marred by the fault of being over-stated.
This [term] is devoid of the meaning of the aggregate (samudāyattha), just as that which is devoid of such meaning is exemplified by:
"The bull, the son of a cowherd, eats grass and drinks water. (57) "Aggregate," and so forth.
The meaning of an aggregate—whether derived from the context of a treatise or from the syntactical connection of words—is its denotation (abhidheyya).
The conventional [meaning] is characterized by the specific relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākāraka*) in the form of principal and subordinate elements (*aṅga-aṅgibhūta*).

That which is devoid of, or departed from, that [conventional meaning] is "empty" (*suñña*). It is not [empty] of the mere referent of the word (*padatthamatta*), because there is no deviation [of the word] from that [referent] anywhere;

such is the injunction: "that which has the sense of being devoid [of the conventional]. For indeed, in cases such as "son of a cow" (*gāviputta*), a collective meaning (*samudāyattha*) is not possible.

57. “*Samudāyi*,” etc. Because it is a word that relates to a collection—a collection of words termed a sentence which is connected with the relationship between the action and its factors (*kāraka*) acting as qualifier and qualified—it has departed from, or is removed from, the meaning corresponding to conventional usage (*vohāra*).

Alternatively, because the meaning of the individual parts (*avayava*) is found everywhere, it is empty of the meaning of the collection; such a sentence is called “one whose meaning has departed. He illustrates this with the words beginning with “*Yathā*.”
“A bull, the son of a cow, ate grass and drank water.
Here, because there is no specific meaning understood apart from the mere collection of its constituent parts, it is said to be "devoid of the collective sense.
That in which harshness resides in the composition is "harsh composition," as for example:
"The harsh stumps have been completely destroyed; what is sown in the field yields abundantly.

(58) Regarding the verse beginning with "bandhe": because they lack pleasantness to the ear, the harsh and rough stumps, such as tree stumps and the like, have been completely destroyed—that is, brought to an end.
Therefore, what is sown in the field—the furrowed plot—[yields its fruit].
*Alam* means it bears fruit or comes to fulfillment. This is a fault of speech (vākyadosa). 58.

Regarding the verse beginning with *bandhe*: where there is harshness (*pharusatā*)—that is, a state of roughness—in a composition (*bandha*), namely in the body of the composition, due to the absence of pleasantness to the ear, that speech is called "harsh in composition" (*bandhapharusa*). To illustrate this, he provides an example: *kharā*.
Since the harshness, barrenness, stumps, and so forth have been completely destroyed—because they have been exhausted—the seed sown and planted in the field bears fruit abundantly;
it comes to fruition. The commentary on the description of defects in speech is finished.
The Explanation of the Description of Faults in the Meaning of Sentences:
The characteristic of "to be known" (ñeyya) is according to its etymological meaning (*anvattha-vasena*) in cases such as "apakkamādi.
Now, I shall demonstrate examples of these.
59. “Ñeyya,” etc. A *lakkhaṇa* (characteristic) is so called in the sense that by means of it an example (*udāharaṇa*) is characterized, as has been indicated for [the faults] such as *apakkama*.

By way of literal meaning (*anvatthavasena*), that in which the sequence (*kama*) has departed is [to be understood]; thus, according to the following of the meanings, it is to be known (*ñeyya*) and understood through [the analysis of] *apakkamanti*, and so forth.
Having now demonstrated the defects of sentences (*vākyadosa*), at this present time when the opportunity has arrived, of these...
I shall now demonstrate and explain the illustration of *apakkama* (departure) and the others. 59.
Now, following the order in which they were enumerated, he clarifies the faults of meaning such as *apakkama* and so forth, beginning with the word "to be known" (*ñeyya*).

The characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) of *apakkama*, *ocitya*, *hīna*, and the rest, is that which serves as the cause for the occurrence of a non-erroneous function of the intellect regarding the objects of *apakkama* and the others.
"According to its meaning" (*anvattha*) means that desire has departed; it is to be known—that is, understood—by means of knowledge following the sense of words such as "where there is," etc.

What is meant is: "I do not state a separate characteristic. Now, I shall demonstrate the illustrative examples of these [terms] such as "departure" (*apakkama*), etc., by way of their characteristics.
The analysis of the compound is: "according to its meaning" (*anvattha*) is that which follows the meaning, by way of the knowledge of what is according to its meaning (*anvattha*).
In this regard, the sequence is as follows:
when cultivation, generosity, and virtue are properly accomplished here,
they are undoubtedly the means for achieving wealth, the heavenly realms, and so forth, up to Nibbāna.

60. “*Bhāvanā*,” etc. [The virtues] have been properly accomplished and brought to completion through the perfect attainment of their causes, such as non-greed (*alobha*). Here, generosity (*dāna*), virtue (*sīla*), and meditation (*bhāvanā*) are, respectively, the causes for wealth, heavenly rebirth, and *nibbāna*; it is not that meditation, generosity, and virtue are themselves the results. 60.
Among those [faults], such as lack of effort (*apakkama*) and so forth, “lack of effort” is to be understood in the same way as the example given for lack of effort.
Just as in the case of “improper” (*ocityahīna*) and the others, the meaning should be understood accordingly. “*Bhāvani*,” etc. Here, in this present existence, they have been properly accomplished.

The virtues of meditation, generosity, and morality—when properly accomplished through the perfection of causes such as non-greed and gathered together—are the means for achieving enjoyments, celestial realms, and Nibbāna;
they are the actualizers of these things, including the arising in heavenly worlds, long life, health, and so forth, as well as Nibbāna itself.
There is no doubt regarding this: there is indeed no doubt concerning their yielding of similar or dissimilar results. Herein, [regarding] enjoyments, celestial realms, and Nibbāna...
However, since giving, virtue, and meditation occur in the order of their causes, the sequence of the causes contradicts the sequence of the fruits;
thus, this is called "contrary order" (kāmāpetam).
An example of what lacks propriety is as follows:
61. "I alone am most worthy of worship in the world, without interruption, because all virtues have arisen together within me alone. [Verse 61 begins with] "Pūjanīya," etc.
Because—*yato*, meaning for which reason—all virtues such as moral discipline (*sīla*) and so forth have arisen together within me alone, who am solitary.

They were gathered together and formed a mass; for that reason, in this world of beings, I alone am the one who is entirely, continuously, and perpetually more worthy of worship, most pre-eminently venerable.
Such self-praise is not pleasing to a true person. 61. Regarding the phrase "more worthy of worship" and so forth:
because all virtues, such as moral discipline and the rest, reside in me alone, in me who am without a second.

Thus, having been gathered together into a mass, I alone have been—therefore, in the world, that is, in the world of beings, I alone am peerless, without a second, and am most worthy of worship, exceedingly worthy of honor at all times and continuously.
Because of such self-praise, there is a falling away from what is appropriate; this is called "loss of propriety" (*ocityahīna*).
And as follows:
“How could I, when asked, not give even my life?
Nevertheless, at the thought of giving away my son, my heart trembles.

(62) Regarding the verse beginning with “When asked”: Here, although Vessantara had demonstrated such magnanimity as to say, “If they should ask, I would give even my life to those who beg,” it was only natural that he spoke thus regarding the trembling of his heart at the prospect of giving away his son.
62. And just as [in the previous example], so too should this illustration of one who lacks propriety be understood, beginning with the words “When entreated,” and so forth.

“When entreated”—that is, when I was entreated by supplicants—how indeed could I not give even my very life? Nevertheless, even though such a disposition toward giving exists, my heart throbs and trembles at the thought of giving away my children.
In this context, Vessantara’s [thought was]: “If they should ask, I would give even my life to the supplicants.”

Having given his promise, saying, "I shall give [him]," to speak of the trembling of his heart due to the gift of his son is inconsistent with the noble quality known as the possession of an excellence of generosity;
thus, it is lacking in propriety (*ocitya*). As for the term *bhaggarīti*: [it refers to] how...
Trust in women and in the wicked does not arise— Not in poison, nor in a rhinoceros, nor in a river, Nor in disease, nor in the royal court. (63) “‘In women,’ etc.:
‘Does not arise’ means it is not appropriate. Here, by the relinquishment of the genitive case in its connection [with the verb], [the meaning is established].”
By means of *viseicca* and so forth, there is a breach of the semantic rule (*attharīti*) due to the use of the locative case for the substratum (*ādhāra*).

By the omission of the letter *ca* at the beginning and in the middle, there is a breach of the linguistic rule (*saddarīti*). Since stylistic rules (*rītis*) are infinite, breaches (*bhaṅgas*) are also infinite.
However, the examples provided are merely illustrative. 63. “*Itthīnaṃ*,” etc. Trust in women and in wicked people—trust through cohabitation and the like—is not appropriate.
It is not logical [to speak of] trust because it is a cause for not turning away from the suspicion of harm.
Trust does not arise toward poison (*visa*), toward a horned beast (*siṅgi*), nor toward the earth inhabited by horned beasts; nor toward a river; nor toward a growing disease;
nor toward a royal family that inflicts execution, imprisonment, and so forth. Here, having begun with the genitive case in the sense of connection at the beginning, and having abandoned that—

Because it is stated in the seventh [chapter], there is the *attharīti*; and because the word "and" (*ca*) is omitted from the beginning, middle, and end, there is the *saddarīti*. These two are distinct.
When employing the word "and," it must be joined either at the very beginning, or at the very end, or with each individual term.

Such usage is called a breach of style (*rītibhaṅga*). Since styles are manifold, the faults of breaching style are also of many kinds; this, however, is merely a demonstration of the general principle.
With eyes longing for the taste of the moonlight of the Moon-Lord of Sages, people were filled with doubt,
like travelers who have set out on a path and are delighted at seeing a cow’s footprint.
64. “The Lord of Sages,” and so forth. Like the moon, he is *candimā*; the Lord of Sages himself is the moon (*munindacandimā*). His *ālokana* is his looking upon [beings], which is seeing;

or it is light, or illumination. The *rasa* in that is passion (*anurāga*). One whose eyes (*locanāni*)—that is, the eyes—are *lolāni*, meaning restless or fickle, because of that passion, such a person has *avakkanta*—meaning descended, entered, or gone down—the path (*pantha*), the way (*magga*), by which he is thus one whose path has been entered (*avakkantapantha*). This refers to the rays (*raṃsī*) of the cows (the sun).

In the phrase "delighted by joy" (*muditoti*), there is a doubt as to whether it refers to the sight of the footprint of the cow, in the sense of indicating the accomplishment of a desired object, or to the sight of the footprint of the *muninda* (the Moon-like Lord).
Here, it is also understood that the sight of the footprint of the *gorūpa* (the cow) is intended. 64.

Regarding the verse beginning with "The Moon-like Lord" (*munindi*): his eyes are greedy for the essence of the light of the Moon-like Lord, who is designated as the *muninda*. Of this Moon-like Lord...

In the light, in seeing, or in manifestation, people with restless eyes, through their craving and attachment, are like those who have descended onto a path—that is, they have entered upon the way for the sake of seeing the Buddha;

this is the intended meaning. "Delighted by the sight of a cow’s footprint" means he is satisfied by seeing the footprints of the rays known as "cows," or by seeing the cow’s footprint regarded as an auspicious omen.
Here, the phrase "by the sight of a cow’s footprint" refers to the sense of the matter.
Because it is currently being traversed, doubt arises as to whether it has been crossed; thus, it is called "doubtful. The grammatical analysis (*viggaha*) is:
"that by which a path has been entered," or "the seeing of the tracks of cattle or rays," or "delighted by the sight of a cow's footprint.
It is considered "obscure" (*gāmma*) because its meaning is difficult to comprehend from the structure of the sentence, just as in the following example:
“This person, possessing energy, having slain the enemy, rests at ease. (Verse 65) Regarding the words beginning with “vākya”:
Having slain—that is, having struck—the enemy, that hero who possesses energy (*vīriyavā*) is this person;
he rests (*vissami*), meaning he is at ease (*vissattho*). This meaning is not difficult to understand. [The alternative interpretation is: “Having utterly destroyed the enemy, the energetic one...”
"This person, whose birth is appropriate, seeks rest"—this meaning is difficult to understand.

(65) Because the characteristic is not evident through its literal sense (*anvattha*), he illustrates the characterized (*lakkhiya*) by means of its own characteristic (*salakkhaṇa*) with the words "from the meaning of the sentence" (*vākyatthato*) and so forth.
It is considered a *gāmī* [fallacy] because it makes the meaning difficult to understand and reveals a contradiction. He provides an illustration with the word "as follows" (*yathā*).
Having slain and killed another, this energetic hero—this person—rested, free from distress;

this is the intended meaning (*iṭṭha*). Having excessively slain another—that is, having committed a transgression—the energetic one, whose strength was accumulated and whose merit was accumulated, this man rested through his exertion, being free from exertion. Of this meaning...
It is "village-like" because it possesses what is not noble. The analysis of the compound is: "that which has energy, exertion, or origin.
That is a "corrupt ornament," wherein there is a defilement of the ornament;
this will become clear in the exposition of ornaments for form.
66. “*Duṭṭhā*,” etc. Wherever—in whatever sentence—there is a corruption or deformity of the ornaments, that is called *duṭṭhālaṅkaraṇa* (corrupt ornament).
The nature (*rūpa*) or form of that corrupt ornament will be revealed and explained in the section titled *Alaṅkāraniddesa*;
the intention is that we shall demonstrate it right there.

66. “*Duṭṭhālaṅkari*,” etc. In whatever sentence there is a corruption of ornament—that is, a contradiction among the ornaments—this sentence, being dependent on the meaning of that [corruption], is called *duṭṭhālaṅkāra* (a faulty ornament).

The form (*rūpa*), nature (*sarūpa*), and characteristic (*lakkhiya*) of such a sentence, which is characterized by the fault of a faulty ornament, is to be found in the section on ornaments (*alaṅkāraniddesa*) within the chapter that serves as the locus for the illustration of ornaments.
It will become manifest. The intention is that although this has already been stated here, it need not be stated again there [in the previous section], and therefore it was not said.

Having stated "ornamented by the wicked" (*duṭṭhālaṅkatī*) in the summary (*uddesa*), the subsequent statement "the ornamenting by the wicked" (*duṭṭhālaṅkaraṇaṃ*) is not contradictory, because the words *alaṅkati*, *alaṅkaraṇa*, and *alaṅkāra* have the same meaning.
This is the preeminent classification of these faults according to my brief summary here;
this alone is sufficient to enlighten poets.
And there is even something more that causes weariness.
Thus ends the chapter titled "The Comprehension of Faults" in the *Subodhālaṅkāra* composed by the great master Saṅgharakkhita.
The First Chapter.

67. Having thus acted in accordance with his promise, "I shall now explain their characteristics along with examples," he now summarizes the method of laying down [the rules] with the words beginning "When three have been performed. Herein, in this section or chapter:

Or rather, this is the most excellent, supreme classification—that is, the analysis—of these aforementioned faults, such as word-faults and so forth, presented by way of summary, that is, by way of a concise method and not in detail;
for since they are innumerable, there is no end to them, yet I have completed and brought this to a conclusion.
Is it not the case that because it was stated "by way of summary," [these faults] have been elucidated by the ancients and those even more ancient than them? (ka.)
"Are many faults to be abandoned? To this it is replied:
because the detailed sequence is not intended here, it is said "by way of summary," but not by way of total abandonment.
For instance, [in such verses as]: "Let this moth destroy the blazing fire of the enemy," and so forth.

"Unbearable," "a different meaning," and so forth, as well as "followed by a contradictory different meaning. For here, by the word *pataṅga* (moth), a different meaning—namely, a firefly—is intended, yet it is incapable [of that sense];
furthermore, phrases such as "they speak of swellings" (*vacanti gaṇḍā*) and the like, which consist of inauspicious or ill-used words, are included within the "defiled" (*kiliṭṭha*).

That which is corrupted by connection, such as "elephant's neighing" (*gajahesādi*), is contrary to worldly convention; whereas that which is established in the Sogata-Āgamas and other texts, such as the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*), is otherwise [acceptable].

It is called "unintelligible" (*appatīta*). This is because it contradicts the scriptures (*āgama-virodhi*), and because it falls under the category of contradictions such as those corrupted by faulty connection (*sambandha-dūsita-appatītādi*);
furthermore, because it requires a reason to be supplied (*ānetabba-hetuttā*), it depends on a cause and is not distinct from the "to-be-inferred" (*neyya*).
"May the Lord dispel the affliction; the sun, weary of Rāhu, has risen."

Furthermore, [the fault] beginning with *iccādi*—which denotes incapacity and so forth—is included among those lacking propriety (*ocitya*). And that which indicates disgust or the unwholesome (*asabbha*), being of a different meaning, is included among those that cause lack of confidence (*duppatītikara*).
(What is difficult to pronounce? It is precisely that which is harsh in its phonetic connection (*sabandhapharusa*).

Herein, however, while those lacking propriety and those causing lack of confidence are faults of the sentence-meaning (*vākyatthadosa*), the harshness of phonetic connection is a fault of the sentence itself (*vākyadosa*).
Due to a fault in the word-meaning, the sentence itself may become faulty; and since a sentence is composed of words, if the words are faulty, the meaning of the sentence will also be faulty.

To demonstrate that the absence or presence of various [faults] in the sentence and its meaning arises from a fault in the word—such as lack of capacity (*asāmatthiya*), unexpressed meaning (*abhidheyya*), and so forth—the term "devoid of propriety" (*ocityahīna*) and others have been included among the faults of the sentence-meaning. Likewise:

Indeed, many defective sentences have been shown by [the author] beginning with the words "viruddha" (contradictory) and so forth, such as sentences composed of archaic terms (*purātana*), terms with contradictory meanings (*viruddhattha*), and other such [faults].
In the phrase "harisamānayī," the intended meaning—*hapubbaṃ risamānayī*—is lost, being utterly abandoned.
That which is joined with uncommon or obscure terms is "obscure" (*guḷha*), as in "Sakko sahassagu."
Thus, [faults such as] dropped syllables (*bhaṭṭha*), harshness (*guḷha*), and so forth, are opposed to clarity (*pasāda*) and ornament (*alaṅkāra*).
Furthermore, in the case of a sentence, that which lacks euphonic combination (*visandhi*) is useless here; a sentence that has merged with another sentence is a "sentence-embryo" (*vākyagabbha*);

and that which is mixed with words from another sentence—such as "This man is seen eating unwholesome food, constantly devouring the physician"—is a "sentence-intermingled" (*vākyasaṃkīrṇa*) fault, both of which are included under the category of the "confused" (*byākiṇṇa*).
“I saw in Kācu Garden a creeper with five sprouts;
on every single sprout there is a cluster of flowers, though it is in vain.
This is non-expressive, being based on an intentional concealment (*pamussitāsannissita*) within a riddle (*paheḷikā*); and therein, by means of the word "garden" (*uyyāna*), the poet—

By the word *vallarī*, which denotes a creeper, the woman is intended; by the word *pallava*, the hands, feet, and lips; and by the word *mañjarī*, the beauty of the nails and the luster of the teeth are intended to be expressed.

Even in the case of the sentence-meaning, such things as the blossoming of lotuses at night and so forth—which are contradictory—are not entirely rejected, but rather they are "hidden" (*nilīna*) within the contradiction;
however, this is not by way of total abandonment. This very [principle] is thus...

This concise method has been concluded according to the manner already described. It serves to dispel the weariness of poets and wise men who might otherwise wonder, "How indeed could such a thing be composed when [these flaws] exist?
It identifies: among word-faults (*pada-dosa*), those such as the unskillful use of synonyms, ambiguity, unintelligible meaning, lack of purpose, and difficult comprehension;
and among sentence-faults (*vākya-dosa*), those such as redundancy, deficiency, and the violation of metrical rules (*chanda*).
Regarding defects in the meaning of a sentence, there is also another kind of flaw, such as "inconsistency between the beginning and the conclusion" (*upakkamopasaṃhāravisamaṃ*) and so forth;
if such [defects] should exist, they too are sufficient to be understood and comprehended by the wise, as they can be inferred according to the aforementioned defects.

And the intention of the author of this work in speaking thus is this: those defects which have not been stated in detail have been condensed by me out of fear of making the book too long, but they have been included by way of their defining characteristics (*lakkhaṇato*). For who can reach the end of them?

In this context, that which contradicts the science of grammar (*saddasattha*) is incorrect. That which, having taken up a cause such as an action (*kriyā*), occurs even with a different meaning, is considered doubtful when employed merely as a technical designation (*saññā*);
for example, "ravimhi himahā" (the sun is cold). However, this [usage] is correct in the sense of a qualifier (*visesanatthe*).
A word constructed through a synonym of a well-known technical term (*pasiddhasaññā*) is to be understood as a synonym (*pariyāyañeyya*).
For example, in the phrase "by the mare's mouth," [the meaning] is "by the face of the female horse.
That which expresses a quality of the qualificand through a relationship of absolute non-deviation is "non-remote" (appatītattha), as in "black ink.

That which serves no purpose for a meaning already understood is "non-contributory" (appayojaka), as in "he crossed the ocean, which was exceedingly frothy. "On the foot, pleasing and thick... [and so on]. "Khādayo... [etc.]
“*Kani bhanti te*,” etc., is difficult to understand (*dubbodha*). *Kaṇi*, *kaññe*, *khādayo*, and *gaggharikā* [are examples].
“*Ime lāvaṇyatallā te, gallā lolavilocane*,” etc., is regional (*desiya*); *tallo* is a particular type of reservoir, while *gallo* is the cheek (*kapola*).
“*Saggasevīnaṃ ripūnamitthīnamakaṅkaṇo pāṇi. Nettaṃ anañjanaṃ*,” etc., is redundant (*adhika*). This is shown by the phrase “*akaṅkaṇo pāṇī*,” etc.
Because it is understood that [the word] *vedhabbyassa* is redundant, the term *“saggasevīnaṃ”* is considered an excess (*adhika*).
That which has a deficiency of what ought to be stated is a deficiency (*ūna*), such as in the phrase *“tilokatilakaṃ muniṃ”* and so forth. Here, the word *“vandāmi”* is deficient;

speech accompanied by a breach of meter is known as *bhaggacchanda* (broken meter). That which is uneven in its beginning and end is *upakkamopasaṃhāravisama* (uneven in commencement and conclusion); that—
Furthermore, the setting aside [of the burden] should be understood as occurring through the relinquishing of the sequence already undertaken.
Thus ends the chapter on the Comprehension of Faults in the *Subodhālaṅkāra*,
in the commentary named *Mahāsāmi*.
67. Having thus fulfilled his promise, “I shall explain their characteristics along with examples,” he now summarizes the faults by concluding with the words “Having committed [these],” etc.

Herein, in this section or chapter, there is a preeminent—that is, the most excellent—classification of these faults, such as the aforementioned faults of words, characterized by their non-contradiction with the defining marks (*lakkhaṇa*).
This very method of analysis according to non-confusion, presented by me through a concise approach that expands upon what was previously stated—
this same method of exposition indeed causes weariness for poets composing verses, giving rise to such distress as they wonder,
"How indeed shall I employ such and such a construction within the body of the verse? Furthermore...

If there is any other refutation, such as that which is unwholesome (*asādhu*) or doubtful (*sandiddha*), this [work] is capable—meaning it is able—to clarify all of it. Furthermore, the analysis (*viggaha*) is:
"it indicates (*niyati*) even a meaning not explicitly stated by this," and "it is both concise (*saṅkhepa*) and a method (*naya*).
What has not been shown here...

The verse beginning with “May this moth destroy the blazing enemy-fire” is not cited because it falls under the fault of *viruddhatthantara* (contradictory meaning) and others, such as *akkhamatthantara* (unbearable meaning). Here, although the word *pataṅga* denotes the sun, it also denotes a firefly; thus, it possesses another meaning that is incapable of destroying the intended enemy-fire.

Expressions such as “the gong sounds” (*vacanti gaṇḍi*) are established by grammatical rules alone, as they are not well-known in the traditional scriptures (*āgama*). The fault of using words in inappropriate application (*appayuttapada*) is included within the faults of corrupted words (*kiliṭṭhapada*), and therefore it is not mentioned separately.

And that which is corrupted by associations such as the trumpeting of elephants and the neighing of horses; and that which employs terms like the aggregate of form (rūpa-khandha) well-known in the scriptures of the Jina, yet used in a sense other than their conventional application—these two types, respectively, constitute contradiction with the world and contradiction with scripture, and are thus included among the contradictory positions.
As for that which depends on a reason (*hetvapekkha*), it is not mentioned here because it is included among the "to-be-understood" (*neyya*), since its reason must be supplied.

"Let the sun, distressed by Rāhu, dispel the defilement"—such examples are included under "deficient in propriety" (ocityahīna) because they involve terms like "incompetent" (asamattha) that are inappropriate; this is not explicitly stated [in the definition].
Here, the sun, being himself seized by Rāhu, is incompetent to remove the defilements of others; thus, its lack of competence is expressed through the qualifying attribute.
This is known by the phrase "rāhukhinno.

As for the three—disgust (*jigucchā*), inauspiciousness (*vamaṅgala*), and unseemliness (*asabbhāna*)—any other indicative, expressive, or distinct meaning is not mentioned because, due to their being vulgar or difficult to believe, they are already included within the very faults of vulgarity (*gāmadoṣa*) regarding the meaning of a sentence. [The fault of] the characteristic of being difficult to pronounce is...

It is not stated that *kaṭṭha* is inseparable from harshness of composition. As for the phrase “*harisamānayī*,” although it should have been said as “*harisamānayī*,” because forms such as *hapubbaṃ risamānayi* deviate from the intended meaning, they are considered *bhaṭṭha* (corrupt).
Furthermore, examples such as “*sakko sahassagū*” are *pariyuttaguḷha* (obscure due to being conventional) regarding unestablished objects.

Since these types of obscurity of meaning (*atthaguḷha*) and so forth are contrary to the ornament of clarity (*pasādālaṅkāra*), they are excluded by the very inclusion of the quality of clarity (*pasādaguṇa*).
"Relinquished" (*pariccatta*) is not mentioned here. For in this case, the name of Sakka—*Sahassagu*, meaning "one who has a thousand cows and eyes"—is a hidden name (*guḷhanāma*).

Regarding defects of sentence (*vākyadosa*), the defect of faulty euphonic combination (*visandhivākya*) is not mentioned here because it is of no use [in this context]. Also not mentioned are the "pregnant sentence" (*vākyagabbha*), which contains another sentence within the middle of a sentence, and the "mixed sentence" (*vākyantarapadasammissa*), which is intermingled with words from another sentence.
“‘This person is seen eating what is unwholesome, constantly devouring the physician’—such sentences, being mixed, are included within the ‘mixed’ category, though they were not explicitly mentioned.

Here, ‘this physician’ is seen to say that [the patient] constantly and perpetually eats what is unwholesome (apāthya), meaning harmful to the disease. This patient constantly and perpetually eats what is unwholesome.”
It eats what is harmful. It sees the physician and becomes angry. In this way, even with many sentences, a compound sentence is called "intermingled" (*saṃkiṇṇa*).
“I saw in the Kācu garden a creeper with five shoots;
in every shoot, in vain, there was a cluster of blossoms.”
This [fault of] non-expressiveness (*avācaka*) was not mentioned [among the faults of riddles], because it is dependent upon that which has been forgotten.

But is it not the case here that, since the author himself did not demonstrate the riddle, the inclusion of the non-expressive within the forgotten is a proof of the unproven by means of the unproven?
This is not so; for in the subsequent section on avoiding the fault of corrupt words, it is said: "I overlook all [these faults] out of fear of wearying my students."
And by the statement, “Having ascended the *paheḷikā*, there is no corruption through defilement,” it is established that the sixteen *paheḷikās* indicated by the ancients are also shown;

thus, what is already proven serves to establish what was not yet proven. In this regard, the poet intends to speak of the house by means of the word “garden” (*uyyāna*), of the woman by means of the synonym for creeper, “*vallarī*,” of the hands, feet, and lips by means of the word “sprout” (*pallava*), and of the luster of the nails and teeth by means of the word “bed” (*mañcarī*).

Regarding the faults of the sentence-meaning (*vākyatthadosa*), it is stated, "In what way is this a summary? in order to show that although things such as the lotuses waking at night are contradictory, they are not explicitly mentioned because they are already included within the category of "contradictory words" (*virodhipada*) themselves; it is not, however, because they have been entirely abandoned.

Herein, when two types of faults—the loss of appropriateness (*ocityahīna*) and the production of a disagreeable impression (*duppatītikara*)—constitute faults of the sentence-meaning, while harshness of composition (*bandhapharusa*) constitutes a fault of the sentence itself (*vākyadosa*).

If there is the fault of contradiction (*virodhin*), and if there are the faults of "denoting incapacity" and so forth, the "words that manifest the triad of loathsomeness" and so forth, the "wooden word," and the meaning of the sentence such as "the blooming of lotuses at night" or "their being difficult to sleep upon" (ka.), how are these four faults included within the distinct categories of *ocitya* (appropriateness) and so forth? True; nevertheless, regarding words...
Since there can be no such thing as the non-defectiveness of sentences or sentence-meanings when a word is defective,

it should be understood that word-defects and the like are included within the defects of sentences and sentence-meanings— in order to inform students that these defects are not distinct [from one another].
For this very reason, many [examples] have been cited by the ancients, such as "a sentence is defective" when it contains words with contradictory meanings and so forth.
It should be understood that these sentences have been shown.

In this very verse—namely, in the line “*tamatthi ce khedakaraṃ parampī*”—by the word *para* (other), one should understand the faults of words such as those that are unwholesome (*asādhu*), ambiguous (*sandiddha*), synonymous (*pariyāya*), obscure (*neyya*), beyond the literal meaning (*appatīta*), non-logical (*appayojaka*), difficult to understand (*dubbodha*), and poorly taught (*dusiya*);

as well as the faults of sentences such as having redundant (*adhika*), deficient (*ūna*), or broken (*bhagga*) meters, and so forth; and [the fault] known as the inconsistency between the introduction (*upakkama*) and the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*).
And one examines the defects in the meaning of a sentence. Herein, that which contradicts the science of grammar (*saddasattha*) is called "incorrect" (*asādhu*).

That which functions in a different sense based on the accomplishment of an action, yet is employed in a technical definition (*saññābhājana*) without the sense of a qualifier (*visesanattha*), is called "ambiguous" (*sandiddha*);

for example, "the sun is the destroyer of frost" (*ravimhi himahā*). In this case, there is no fault if the qualifier "destroyer of frost" (*himahā*) were applied to the sun. [However, this is not the case with] a word that is a well-known technical term (*pasiddhasaññā-sadda*).
A word formed by means of a synonym is called "to be understood through a synonym" (*pariyāyaññeyya*), such as "the face of Vaḷavāmukha" [meaning] "the face of a female horse.
A word expressing a quality of the subject that lacks a specific distinction or developed meaning is called "of unestablished meaning" (*appatītāttha*), such as "black ink.
A word that has been acquired but is not useful [in the context] is called "non-contributory" (*appayojaka*), such as "he crossed the ocean which was exceedingly frothy."
The statement of what is not well-established is called "difficult to understand," as in:
“*Manuññaddhanayo pāde, khādayo kani bhanti te*. Here, *kani* means *kaññe*;

thus, “*manuññaddhanayo*”—possessing enchanting sounds—*khādayo* (cymbals) *bhanti* (shine) upon *te pāde* (your feet). A word established only in a particular region is called "local" (*desiya*), as for example: [text omitted].

“O you with tremulous eyes, these cheeks of yours are pools of loveliness. O you with tremulous eyes, these cheeks—your *kapolas*—are pools of loveliness, that is, pools of charm, which are specific types of reservoirs (*jalāsayavisesa*). An expression used by taking up a meaning already indicated by some slight hint is called *adhika*. For example: “When you reign, O Lord of Kings, your enemies resort to heaven; ... [the verse continues] ... In this case, the fact that the enemies have gone to heaven has already been indicated by the word “reigning” (*rājati*), yet the phrase “resort to heaven” (*saggasevinaṃ*) is employed as an additional statement. Thus, it is *adhika*. Furthermore, there is no fault here because it serves to clarify the intended meaning. This is because the word “resort” (*sevinaṃ*) is used in the sense of “having resorted,” and thus the meaning is not redundant. Alternatively, one may interpret it as follows: when you reign, your enemies, being unable to endure your splendor, go to heaven; therefore, they are said to “resort to heaven. In this way, the meaning is not redundant. Or else, the word “reign” (*rājati*) is used in the sense of “shining” (*rājati*); thus, when you shine, your enemies, being unable to endure your splendor, go to heaven. Therefore, the meaning is not redundant. Or again, the word “reign” (*rājati*) is used in the sense of “being victorious” (*jayaṃ karoti*); thus, when you are victorious, your enemies, being unable to endure your splendor, go to heaven. Therefore, the meaning is not redundant. Or finally, the word “reign” (*rājati*) is used in the sense of “protecting” (*pālanaṃ karoti*); thus, when you protect [them], your enemies, being unable to endure your splendor, go to heaven. Therefore, the meaning is not redundant. In this way, there is no fault. However, in the following example, there is a fault: “O King, when you rule, your enemies do not even look upon the sun, much less the moon. In this case, the fact that they do not look upon the sun has already been indicated by the word “do not look upon” (*na pekkhanti*), yet the phrase “much less the moon” (*kiṃ pana candimam*) is employed as an additional statement. Thus, it is *adhika*. Furthermore, there is a fault here because it does not serve to clarify the intended meaning. This is because the word “much less” (*pana*) is used in the sense of “even” (*api*), and thus the meaning is indeed redundant. Or else, the word “much less” (*pana*) is used in the sense of “how much more” (*kiṃ bahunā*); thus, when you rule, your enemies do not look upon the sun, how much more so the moon. Therefore, the meaning is redundant. Or again, the word “much less” (*pana*) is used in the sense of “therefore” (*tasmā*); thus, when you rule, your enemies do not look upon the sun, therefore they do not look upon the moon. Therefore, the meaning is redundant. Or finally, the word “much less” (*pana*) is used in the sense of “but” (*ca*); thus, when you rule, your enemies do not look upon the sun, but they do look upon the moon. "Her hand is without bracelets, her eyes are without collyrium.
Here, by the very phrase "her hand is without bracelets, her eyes are without collyrium," widowhood is already understood;

therefore, the addition of the word "saggasevinam" ("one who dwells in heaven") used for the purpose of clarifying that [fact] is what is called "excessive" (adhika). It is deficient in terms of what ought to be said.

A sentence that is deficient is called *ūna*. In the phrase “The Sage, the ornament of the three worlds,” it is deficient because the word “I revere” (*vandāmi*), which ought to be stated, has not been said.
A verse connected with the loss of desire is called *bhaggacchanda*. This becomes evident through the deficiency or excess of syllables in those respective desires.
That which is uneven from beginning to end is called *upakkamopasaṃhāravisama* (uneven in commencement and conclusion). This...
It should be understood that after abandoning the sequence already undertaken, one is restricted by another sequence.
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Subodhālaṅkāra-nissaya*.
2. Commentary on the Chapter on Understanding the Avoidance of Faults:
Sometimes, through the skill of a poet, even this entire collection of contradictions transcends the enumeration of faults and plunges into the path of excellence.
So that there may be no contradiction with what was stated by him [the opponent],
the understanding of how to avoid those faults is now set forth.
(68–69) Having thus delimited the classification of faults, he now speaks in order to point out the sequence for avoiding the faults as they have been described:
"Sometimes," and so forth. This entire contradiction—arising from contradictory meanings and the like—is not any single fault among the faults;
rather, it sometimes transcends the number, the calculation, and the very nature of faults, and enters, that is, accepts, the path, the track, and the essential nature of virtues.
This occurs only occasionally, not at all times, due to the skill of the poet who employs such expressions.
This is because of the skillful means characterized by the grasping of such objects, and not just in any way whatsoever.

Regarding the phrase "Therefore," etc.: for that reason, in whatever manner and by whatever method the non-contradiction—that is, the faultlessness—of the contradictions such as "opposing meanings" and so forth, which have been stated, might come to be, in that very manner and by that method, there is the avoidance, meaning the removal to a distance, of those faults.

"Avabodha" means that by means of this, one awakens and understands; "tassāvabodho" refers to the delimitation (pariccheda) bearing that name. The meaning is: "Now it is being led forth," "brought forward," or "stated.
68–69. Having thus delimited the classification of faults, he now begins for the purpose of avoiding the aforementioned faults:

He says, "At times," and so forth. This entire contradiction—beginning with defects of words and the like—is a defect in number, or rather, it exceeds the count of defects, the enumeration of defects, or the very nature of being a defect.

For, due to the poet’s skill, and because of the poet's proficiency in wisdom characterized by familiarity with grammar, lexicography, prosody, poetics, and so on, it [the work] enters the path of qualities—that is, the track of qualities—and becomes purely of the nature of quality.

It penetrates and accepts; for that reason, "non-contradiction"—that is, the state of being non-contradictory—of the aforementioned contradictions, such as the faults of words already mentioned, occurs in such a way that it may exist by whatever manner it might be;

and because it is the cause of understanding the sequence of avoidance related to the faults of words already mentioned, the section named after that [is] the "Understanding of the Avoidance of Faults."

Now, having obtained the opportunity, it is introduced and discussed. The intention is this: since the aforementioned defects may attain the state of being defectless through the power (*sāmatthiya*) of the poet, we shall provide instruction on that power.
This concludes the commentary on the avoidance of word-defects (*padadosaparihāravaṇṇanā*).
In this regard, the resolution of the contradiction with another meaning is as follows:
"Seeing the rice that is ripe and delicious brings happiness;
how then can this poison-cloud possibly bring happiness to people?"

70. “Vindantaṃ,” etc. How indeed can this cloud, this rain-bearing mass, bring happiness to that person who finds (*vindantaṃ*) mental ease and joy (*somanassaṃ*) upon seeing the rice—whether it be the *rattasāli* and other varieties of rice, which are pleasant or suitable for consumption through their state of being ripened by cooking?
In this context, the failure to provide happiness to such a person [is the fault].
The contradiction regarding the meaning of "garala" (poison) and "megha" (cloud) has been removed. 70.
In that regard, the resolution of the contradiction regarding the meaning is as follows: "They find," and so forth.
Because of the sight—on account of seeing—the rice that is "pākasālīna," which is fit for ripening, or the "manuñña" (delightful) rice such as *rattasāli* and other varieties, there is happiness.
How indeed could this cloud—poisonous and yet a giver of water—not bring happiness to those people, those farmers, who find and experience mental joy?
It does not bring them happiness at all. Giving suffering to such people is fitting even for a cloud that gives poison;
thus, the contradictory meaning has been removed. The analysis (*viggaha*) is "sāli by means of ripening" (*pākena*). Happiness...
"Karoti" means "to bring happiness"; this is a verbal root (nāmadhātu).
Or, for example:
"Vināyaka was also a Nāga."
O Great-minded One, though you are Gotama,
and though you are refined yet devoid of worldly flavors,
my heart, O Lord, is drawn toward your path.
71. “Vināyako” and so forth. *Vīna* means the leader of birds; *garuḷa*.

One who leads (*vineti*) beings is a *vināyaka*, namely the Buddha and the Blessed One. In that context, when *vināyaka* refers to *garuḷa*, then [the phrase] “the serpent, the snake” (*nāgo pannago*) is contradictory;
however, in the other sense, it is not contradictory because of the absence of passion and the like in the Blessed One. Of these cows, he is the most excellent cow, thus *Gotama*.
The Blessed One is called "Gotama" because he has descended into the lineage of the Gotamas;

you, O Mahāmata, are a "lowly beast" (*hīnapasu*) because of your possession of eighty contradictions and your lack of great wisdom—this is contradictory. However, in another sense, there is no contradiction.

The Sugata is "excellent" (*paṇīta*) and "sweet" (*madhura*) in flavor, and "supreme" (*uttama*). In that regard, it is contradictory for you to be "devoid of" (*apeta*) or "separated from" (*apagata*) that sweet flavor.
But it is appropriate to say that the Blessed One is free from the flavors (*rasa*) such as the erotic (*siṅgāra*) and so forth.

"Me" means "my. "Sāmi" is a form of address. "Te" means "your. Your course, your activity, and your mind are marvelous. Here, the ornament of contradiction (*virodhālaṅkāra*), which consists of a contradictory meaning, is to be praised; therefore, that [objection] has been refuted. 71.
Or, this is how the avoidance of the aforementioned fault is achieved: "The Leader," and so forth. O Lord, you are indeed a leader (*vināyaka*).
Even though you are a *garuḍa*, you are a *nāga* and a serpent. If not, even as a leader (*vināyaka*) who disciplines beings, you are a *nāga* and are free from defilements.

Even though you are a *Gotama* and one who has fallen asleep, O Great-minded One, you are possessed of great wisdom. If not, even by lineage you are indeed a *Gotama*, O Great-minded One, and you are possessed of great wisdom.
Even though you are sublime and sweet, you are devoid of taste, removed from the quality of sweetness. If not—
"Even though it is excellent, it is devoid of flavor," meaning it is free from the flavors such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and so forth.
"Your course of action is wonderful to my mind. Here, the state of being a serpent for Garuḍa and his possession of wisdom for Paṇīta are contradictory;
nevertheless, because they are not contradictory when considered from another perspective, this is the fault of "contradiction in the intended sense" (*viruddhārthāntara-doṣa*).
It is refuted by the ornament of contradiction with what is praised. The leader of birds is Garuḷa; he who disciplines beings is a Vināyaka, the Buddha.
He who has no sin (*āgu*) is a Nāga, the Buddha. By his excellence of qualities (*guṇa*), he is Gotama, the bull (*pasu*).
He who possesses great intelligence is Mahāmata, the Buddha. That which is brought to a state of excellence is *paṇīta*, a sweet flavor.
*Rasāpeto* means "devoid of flavor" (*rasa*); the analysis (*viggaha*) is "one who is devoid of flavor.
As for *ajjhattassa*:
"How, in the absence of such qualities..."
The wicked person pleases the world;
like a firefly that seems to illuminate everything,
what indeed could he be?
72. “How,” and so forth. The qualities of the Tathāgata delight the world; since those qualities do not exist within a wicked person, how could he delight the world—the world of sentient beings?
The meaning is that he would not delight it. He establishes this very point by means of another illustration:
“Could one who illuminates and lights up all directions like a firefly ever be such [as the Tathāgata]? He could not.”

“Because of the absence of such qualities. Here, the fault of [the simile] being deficient because the glow-worm lacks the superior quality of [illuminating] all directions—which was raised by the phrasing of the words beginning with “How, in the absence of such qualities?”—is resolved.
72. Regarding “*ajjhattassa yathā*”: here, *ajjhāhāro* (supplying an ellipsis) is the resolution; it is the same for what follows. “*Kathi*,” etc. A wicked person...

How can a person devoid of virtue satisfy the world—the realm of sentient beings—when such qualities as moral discipline (*sīla*), which are the causes for generating contentment, are absent within him?
He certainly cannot satisfy it; for instance, how could one called a firefly be like that which illuminates all directions?
It simply is not. Herein, the fault lies in the excessive claim that the firefly possesses the illumination of all quarters.

"How is it that, in the absence of such qualities," [this was] refuted by the playful statement beginning with "and so forth. The grammatical analysis (*viggaḥ*) is: "tādī" (such) and "te guṇā" (those qualities).
[The verse says: "Those who have ascended the riddle-puzzle (*paheḷikā*)—for they are neither wicked nor defiled;
beloved and embraced by happiness—who indeed would not embrace them?"
73. “In a riddle,” and so forth. The fault of defilement in words (*kiliṭṭhapadadosa*) is that a female friend who has entered the subject matter of a riddle should not be corrupted.
To the question “Of what kind? he says “to the beloved,” and so forth. “Iti” is used as an illustration.
Does bodily and mental happiness not embrace—that is, does it not join with—what person embraced by a beloved (*piyā*, *vallabhā*)? Indeed, it does. The word “nu” is used for emphasis.
The particle *piyā* here signifies "defiled" (*kiliṭṭha*), meaning it has been brought forth through the imposition of a riddle (*paheḷikā*).

73. Regarding the verse beginning with “In a riddle,” etc.: if defilement—consisting of the faults of defiled words—is present within the domain of a riddle, then even what is faulty does not remain faulty.
What is the example? “Whom does a beloved embrace, and who embraces her? (Piyā sukhāliṅgitaṃ kamāliṅgati nu).
"No" (no): since the word "iti" has the sense of an illustration (*nidassana*), it should be understood that this is a pointer (*upalakkhaṇa*) for other examples.
If not, then because such types of examples would not be encompassed [by the previous definition], the word "iti" has the sense of "manner" (*pakāra*).

"By whom"—that is, by what person—is happiness, both physical and mental, not embraced (*āliṅgati*)? It is indeed embraced by one who is beloved (*piyā*) and dear (*vallabhā*), being embraced (*upaguhita*) or held close. Thus, it is embraced by all.
In this context, the term *piya* (dear) is refuted by applying it as a pun (*paheḷikā*) upon the word *kiliṭṭha* (stained).
One should not employ a *yamaka* (rhyme/pun) when a stained word is intended;
otherwise, every other *yamaka* would be like mere excrement.
74. “In *yamaka*,” etc. “Other than that” means other than the desired *yamaka*. “*Tu*” is a particle indicating a distinction. “As if consisting of this” means as if produced by this defiled word.
74. “In *yamaka*,” etc. One should not employ a defiled word in the desired *yamaka*, nor should one apply it;
however, all other *yamakas* besides that desired *yamaka* are, as it were, “consisting of this” due to the fault of this defiled word.

It is as if it were spoken. Here, the *iṭṭhayamaka* (pair of desirable things) is to be understood according to the method already stated; the analysis (*viggaha*) is: "that which is produced by this, consisting of this. An example of opposition due to place (*desavirodhin*) is as follows:
"By the power of the Bodhisattva, water-born flowers appeared even on dry land."
As if brushing away the long-standing affliction of dwelling there in the water.

75. “In the Bodhisatta,” and so forth. On the day of the birth of the Bodhisatta—the son of Queen Māyā—who was about to be described, by the power of his excellence, that is, by the majesty of his merit, lotus-born flowers (jalajāni) appeared even on dry land; they came to be because of the inconceivability of that power.

Of the power of merit. But what is it that, while performing [meritorious deeds] in such places as ponds and the like, produces an affliction born from dwelling there—that is, residing for a very long time in that water at all times—and which they seem to shake off, as if casting it far away?
Because the power of merit is inconceivable, even such a marvel occurred; thus, there is no contradiction regarding the location.
75. By the power of the Bodhisatta, through the inconceivable majesty of the Bodhisatta,

the water-born flowers— such as the lotus and the kumuda, so called because they resemble water— though established in that water which is well-known for its domain, appeared even on dry land in the ponds and such places,
as if dispelling or casting off the fatigue born from dwelling there for a very long time, having resided there for an exceedingly long duration.

What need for further words? Here, the contradiction regarding location—namely, the statement that lotuses arise on dry land—is refuted by the phrase "by the power of the Bodhisatta," because such wonders manifest through the influence of inconceivable merit. Furthermore, the expression is to be understood as follows:

"one who is intent (satta) upon enlightenment (bodhi)," which is the wisdom of the four paths; "his power" (pabhāva); "having resided there for a very long time"; and "the defilement produced thereby."
An example of that which contradicts the seasons:
The great sage, though possessing such majestic power,
was fanned by a gentle breeze that blew with the qualities of all seasons, scattering flowers alike.

76. “Mahā,” etc. This wind, gentle and mild, gathering together and shaking—scattering—all the blossoms that flower throughout all seasons and at all times, belongs to the Sage (munino) because he is like a sage and because of his future state as a Buddha;
or rather, it belongs to the Sage himself, who possesses great majesty at the moment of attaining perfect enlightenment. It is a messenger (pisuno).

"The wind blows, and it blows forth. Here, although it is impossible for all seasons to occur at once—since various flowers bloom in various seasons—nevertheless, by this [verse], the contradiction regarding time is resolved on the grounds that such a one-worded utterance is possible even from the Blessed One, who possesses great majesty (*mahānubhāva*).
76. "Possessing great majesty," and so forth. This gentle breeze, a non-fierce wind, [blows] throughout all seasons, such as spring and the rest.

Having gathered together the blooming flowers and blossoms, shaking and causing them to tremble, [the wind] blows forth—manifesting the great power of merit of the Sage (muni), who is so called because of his absolute cultivation;
or rather, manifesting the great majesty indicative of the All-Knowing One (sabbaññu) at the time of his attainment of Perfect Enlightenment. Herein, at various times...
Even though there is a contradiction regarding time in the simultaneous arising of flowers that would otherwise arise at different times,

[the author] refutes this chronological inconsistency with the phrase "indicative of great power" (*mahānubhāvapisuno*), showing that the power of the Blessed One’s merit is capable of producing such a marvelous event in a single moment.
The compound may be analyzed as either *mahānubhāvassa pisuno* (the indicator of one who possesses great power) or *mahānubhāvaṃ pisuno* (the indicator of great power).
An example of that which contradicts the context (*kalāvirodhin*) is as follows:

"Even for Pañcaśikha, whose mind was submerged in the virtues of the Buddha, that discord of the strings did not please anyone. In this case, the mention of "the discord of the strings" (*tantissaravirodha*) contradicts the context, for it is impossible for the lute strings to be out of tune while the mind is absorbed in the Buddha’s qualities. Thus, it does not delight anyone.

77. “*Nimugga*,” etc. For Pañcasikha, the son of the Gandhabba deities, whose mind and consciousness (*mano-citta*) were submerged—that is, deeply immersed—in the immeasurable virtues of the Buddha, such as his moral discipline (*sīla*) and so forth, even the sound of his lute strings—divided into the categories of slow, fast, and medium according to the characteristics of the timing and measure of the performance, beginning with the *chaññā* [the sixth note]—did not conflict with whom?
That is to say, it did not fail to delight which person, possessing the grace defined by the science of the arts (*kalā-sattha*)?
It is simply "to gladden. Even the occurrence of distraction in those whose minds are attached to the mundane virtues of the Perfectly Enlightened One gladdens [the mind] in such a manner.
By the phrase "with the mind submerged in the Buddha’s qualities," the contradiction regarding the poetic meter (*kalā*) is resolved. 77.
"Submerged," etc. With the mind submerged in the Buddha’s qualities—that is, in the collection of virtues such as the conduct that produces wonder in the Omniscient One—
Even for Pañcasikha, the son of the Gandhabba deities, whose mind was deeply absorbed, there occurred that discordance of the strings—
a striking against the strings of the lute, the duration of half a *mattikā* or similar measure, and the measurement characterized by the arrangement of the hands and other parts—
possessing these three characteristics, [resulting in] a sound of six or seven notes (*satta-sara*) such as *chañja*, which was broken by being slow, fast, or medium in measure.
What person does the destruction of the sequence of the arts and sciences not afflict? It afflicts them all indeed.
Here, the dissolution of the sequence of the arts and sciences—which is the cause of displeasure—has arisen from an intellect that follows the supramundane qualities of the Buddha;
therefore, because it is said that "the mind is submerged in the Buddha’s qualities," that dissolution is actually a cause for joy, and thus there is no contradiction.
The sentence is: "He has a mind that is submerged," "he hears through the ear-canal," and "there is a contradiction between those two.
An example of a contradiction with worldly convention is:
"He might count the world-system, yet it remains cool even with sandalwood."
*Sambodhisattahṛdayo, padittāṅgārapūritaṃ.* (78) “*Gaṇeyya*,” etc.
He thought: “I would even count [it as] cool with sandalwood. What is that? The world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) filled with blazing coals.
Who is he? One whose heart and mind are intent upon *sambodhi*, which is omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
For one whose intellect is bound to omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), such a binding of the mind does not contradict the world.

78. "Let him count," etc. With the heart of enlightenment (*sambodhisatta*) and a mind attached to omniscience, that Bodhisatta [would not even notice] a world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) filled with burning coals—that is, completely full of blazing embers—even if it were made of sandalwood.
"One should think: 'Having made it even more cool than sandalwood, I shall count it as exceedingly cool.

Because the activity of the mind of one who is greedy for a desired object is of such a nature, the conceptualization of fire as being cooler than sandalwood does not contradict the worldly convention that has arisen—namely, "sandalwood is cool" and "fire is hot.
And [the verse] "In enlightenment, he whose heart is set... and "The burning ones... [are explained].

The graceful display (*vibbhama*) and coquetry (*vilāsa*) of Māra’s women, which was not approved by the Victor, arose as a fire in the heart, a heart-flame, of Māra who wields power.

"By way of figurative usage regarding the cause. "one from whom fault has departed" (*apayāta-apagata-aparādha*), and "become pale-red through anger" (*kodhena pāṭalabhūta*). An example of one with a base meaning (*hīnattha*) is as follows:
A wise person should destroy the power of even small evils,

Khajjoto is the sun (bhāṇumā). 84. “Of the few,” etc.

Even such a firefly is brought to a state of lusterlessness; even one of great power, though it wanders through the hollows of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), does not disregard even a glowworm, thinking, "This one has but a dim light.
Here, by the turn of phrase beginning with "even" (*api*), the fault of inferiority (*hīnatthadosa*) is avoided.

84. “*Appakāni*,” etc. The Wise One, possessed of wisdom, would destroy—even if they be few or very slight—the power of evils, that is, the efficacy of unwholesome states consisting in their capacity to yield karmic results;

He establishes this point through the poetic ornament of *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a similar instance), beginning with “*apicādi*.”
The sun, Bhāṇumā, has brought about the loss of luster even in the firefly; yet, although it is accompanied by glowworms that have been rendered lusterless, its own radiance remains inferior.
The intended meaning is that, having abandoned the glowworm, it no longer produces its own light.
Here, by way of the rhetorical flourish of the expression "even lusterless" (*api nippabha*), even though the inferior side is taken up, it is precisely the majesty of the sun that is [intended].
Because it is a positive term, the qualifying phrase “nippabhatānītakhajjoto” (one by whom the glow-worms have been brought without luster) does not incur the fault of having a base meaning.

The analysis (*viggaha*) is as follows: “those which have no luster” (*natthi pabhā yesam*), “the state of those [things]” (*tesam bhāvo*), and “that by whom the glow-worms have been brought” (*tam ānītā khajjotā yena*).
For example, regarding a negative meaning: [as in *anariyo*].

Fear, anger, praise, and so forth—
If such a distinction is intended to be stated as a fault,

If one wishes to express such a distinction as that which begins with haste and the like—wherein fear and the rest are the beginning—then there is no fault committed therein, in that specific context of fear and the rest, by virtue of their being synonymous (ekatthatāya), that is, by way of having a single meaning.
86. Now, beginning with the words "fear, anger," etc., he undertakes the purpose of avoiding faults in speech.

If such a distinction—one possessed of fear, anger, praise, and so forth, or of mental terror, aversion, flattery, and the like—is desired to be stated, and if it is wished for by the wise, then no fault of speech arises from that distinction of fear and so forth, because it is composed through the state of having a single meaning (*ekatthabhāvena*) due to its unity of sense. The intention is that there is no fault of "redundancy" (*ekattha-dosa*) when a word previously uttered is uttered again in what one wishes to say.

according to the Bhaggarīti:
Any excellence of form whatsoever—

88. “Yo,” etc. Because it is beyond the range of speech and thus cannot be described—even though it is adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man manifested through the secondary characteristics (*anubyañjana*) of form, and graced by the halo of fathom-wide radiance—it is simply “that which is indescribable.

Therefore, "Oh, what a great arising, what a growth for the Buddha! It is truly wonderful! Here, the stylistic mode (*rīti*) initiated by the particle *kiṃ* is not broken anywhere.
