The excellence of the physical body—which is adorned with the eighty minor marks such as the mind-finger (cittaṅguli) and the like, and which is radiant with the garlands of fathom-wide halos—is indescribable (*yo kociyeva*), because it transcends the domain of speech and cannot be grasped by the range of the mind.

Its captivating splendor (*kānti*)—which steals the hearts of the world—is also indescribable (*kāpiyeva*), because it transcends the domain of words. This is the preeminence of its grace (*vilāsātisaya*).
Even the excess of the graceful movements such as walking, which consist of the state of being dear as an object of perception, is indeed anger for the very reason stated above; it is indeed anger.
Therefore, "the great arising of the Buddha" (*buddhamahodayo*)—that is, the arising (*udayo*) consisting of the Buddha’s great growth—is "aho," meaning wonderful.
Here, because the sequence of beginning to speak with the interrogative pronoun *kiṃ* has not been interrupted anywhere, there is no fault of broken rhythm (*bhaggarītidoṣo*).

The masters of poetry praise a composition that is free from confusion, uncluttered, captivating, and characterized by the placement of words that are not too far apart. (89) Regarding the verse beginning with "abyāmoha":
those which do not go far away are called *adūra*; these are the very words (*padāni*), and their arrangement (*vinyāso*) [is what is praised].
That which is established according to reality is such; for that very reason, it is unconfused and unmixed. Because of that very lack of confusion, it is captivating;

thus, it is "unconfused and captivating" (*abyākiṇṇaṃ manoharaṃ*). For that same reason, it does not cause delusion such as "this is the meaning here, or that," and is therefore "non-delusive" (*abyāmohakaro*);
that [is the composition]. It is a composition adorned with clarity and poetic ornaments. The masters of poets are the preeminent ones.
Those who have reached the end of counting even the smallest fingers praise and extol [this work], because it is worthy of supreme praise for its excellence in the quality of such composition.

89. “In non-confusion,” etc. It is possessed of a non-prolix arrangement of words—meaning that at the time of usage, the names and other terms are placed in sequence so that their connection is not remote—and for that very reason, it is free from the interference of words belonging to other connections.

The masters of poetry—meaning the foremost poets who are the preeminent objects of the wise, and who are to be counted on the little finger—are those whose composition is unmixed, captivating, and for that very reason pleasing to the minds of the discerning;
which produces no confusion and does not give rise to doubt as to whether "this is the meaning of this" or "that is the meaning of that";
and whose construction is endowed with clarity and poetic ornamentation. This is the intended meaning.

They praise and extol it. It does not cause delusion; thus, it is "non-delusive" (*abyāmohakara*). It is "crowded" (*byākiṇṇa*) when it is pervaded; "uncrowded" (*abyākiṇṇa*) means not crowded. The analysis (*viggaha*) of the compound is:
that poetic composition (*bandha*) in which there is no distance between those very words—that is, their arrangement or placement.
For example—
His eye has the luster of a blue lotus,
his lower lip is as beautiful as the bandhuka flower,
and his nose is like a golden bit.
This Victor is lovely to behold.

(Verse 90) He utters the words "Just as," beginning with "the luster of a blue lotus" and so forth. The eye—the organ of sight—of this Victor has the luster of a blue lotus (*indīvara*), resembling a pair of blue water-lilies;
his lower lip is as beautiful and charming as the *bandhuka* flower, the *bandhūka* blossom.
The nose is the nostril; the golden hook (*hemakuṃsa*) is indeed a golden hook. For that reason, this Victor is "Piyadassano" (of lovely appearance), because his vision is dear and sweet.
Such [a person] is not possessed of the fault of being "byākiṇṇa" (confused or disordered); rather, he is "abyākiṇṇa," meaning his clarity is undisturbed. 90.
Now, he avoids the fault of being "byākiṇṇa" with the verse beginning "nīluppala... ("blue lotus..."). His eyes are the pair of his two pupils.
His lower lip has the luster of a blue lotus, resembling the petals of a blue lotus; his lower lip is as beautiful as a *bandhuka* flower, radiant like a *bandhuka* blossom;
his nose is like a golden hook, just like a golden goad. For this reason, this Conqueror is lovely to behold and pleasing to look upon.
Here, because it is joined with the ornament of clarity (*pasādālaṅkāra*), there is no fault of incoherence (*byākiṇṇadosa*). [The word] *ābhā*...
The particle *nibha* has the sense of *iva* (like), provided it does not signify "splendor. The analysis [of the compound] is:

"beautiful like a bandhuka flower" (*bandhukamiva rucira*) and "one for whom the sight is dear" (*piyaṃ dassanaṃ yassa*). Here, although the sight is connected to the virtuous people who are its agents, its connection to the Conqueror occurs precisely by way of being its object;
thus, the Tathāgata is understood through the sense of another word (*aññapadatthena*).
91. “That which is composed of speech transcending vulgarity (*gāmmatta*);
because it is for the sake of the essence (*rasa*), it transcends vulgarity.

Regarding the phrase beginning with “transcending” (*samatikkanta*): it is that which has properly (*sammā*) transcended or emerged from. The state of being vulgar is “vulgarity” (*gāmmatta*). Of those [speeches]...

The bond constructed and fashioned by those lovely and sweet words—because it serves as the cause for the sweetness of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*)—exceeds and transcends the vulgarity (*gāmmatta*) previously described.
91. “*Samatikkanta-*,” etc. [It refers to] that which is constructed by lovely speech that has transcended vulgarity, specifically by those [words] that have transcended the state of vulgarity.

The bond composed of lovely words—such as the bond of pearls and so forth—because it is a cause for aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), that is, because it is the cause of the "savor" (*pītirasa*) for the wise, transcends the aforementioned vulgar fault;
it proceeds by going beyond it. The analysis of the compound is as follows:

"those [words] by which the vulgarity has been properly transcended," and "composed by those very same lovely words"; and furthermore, "the cause of the flavor," and "the state of being that [cause]."
Just as—
The fierce outcaste of sensual desire torments me,
being both merciless and pitiless.
"How can you remain indifferent to one who has fallen into such calamity, even though you are happy? (92).
He illustrates this with the word "yathā" (just as): a certain woman, afflicted by passion, cries out to her beloved husband with the words beginning "it pains me," and so forth.
"Compassionate" (*sadayā*) means proceeding together with compassion; it is an affectionate address to one who is dear by way of endearment.

Indeed, such an affectionate address is most appropriate when one desires the welfare of that person. That desire is *kāma* (lust) and is precisely a "Caṇḍāla," because it is not gentle (*akaṇḍo*) and brings about unwanted torment.

And it is entirely fitting to apply the designation "Caṇḍāla" to *kāma*, since those who are unable to endure the unbearable torment inflicted by it—[the torment] being itself intolerable—are [themselves] like Caṇḍālas.
He speaks incoherently while treating him with contempt; he is merciless and pitiless. Even this is fitting for those who cause suffering and lack compassion—such is their destiny.
It pains me excessively and torments me because of his ruthlessness, not you; therefore, you remain at ease.
By this, she indicates his state of being infatuated with another. If you are not infatuated with another, then I am not alone.

"For those who are without companions, there are adversaries. 'Because I am alone and without refuge, I am suffering, I am in pain'—let you be happy as you wish! Such conduct belongs to those who have a protector.
Thus, even though you are happy, why do you remain indifferent toward one who has fallen into such calamity?
In this way, he censures his own crooked conduct while that person experiences its consequences.
And it demonstrates liberation; thus, this is not vulgar. 92.
In order to show the characteristic of avoiding vulgar faults, he says "it torments," and so forth.
Overcome by sensual craving, a woman laments thus, depending on her own beloved: "O compassionate one! O merciful one! That outcaste of lust, that wretch of a love-god!"
“The merciless and pitiless one distresses and oppresses me. Even though you are happy—since, unlike me, you lack the state of being helpless—why do you remain indifferent?
Why are you apathetic toward me, who has fallen into such calamity, having reached this misfortune known as the unbearable torment inflicted by the fierce demon of sensual desire?
For those who are compassionate, the removal of suffering belongs only to those who are themselves afflicted by suffering.

He addresses the objects of sense as "O beloved" out of a tendency toward attachment; yet, in order to nourish his own suffering and distress—which is appropriate for such an address—he speaks of the infliction of cruelty and the mercilessness directed toward those sensual desires that cause oppression, because he maintains equanimity toward himself.
By the word "happy," he admits his transgression due to his lack of attachment to the objects of others. Thus, regarding his own crooked conduct...
It shows that there is passion for the beloved and the absence of such passion toward oneself;
as in the verse, “Why do you not desire me who desires you, O maiden? there is no vulgar fault (*gāmmadosa*) here—this is the avoidance of vulgar faults.
Furthermore, *kāmacaṇḍāla* means that desire itself is a caṇḍāla; [it refers to one] who behaves with compassion, or [to one] for whom there is no compassion.
The analysis of the compound is: "he has happiness" (*sukham assa atthi*).
The particle *api* is used in the sense of "even. This is an avoidance of repetition;
it is not being led [into the present] again, since this was already examined below in the section on the lack of urgency regarding hearing the Dhamma.
93. “*Yati*,” etc. “*Vicāritaṃ*” means it has been explained below by such passages as, “I bow my head to that Tathāgata who is the color of refined gold.

93. “*Yatihī*,” etc. *Yato* (because) means: because there is no capacity for wise people to endure hearing this treatise when they perceive that the sequence for avoiding faults has not been stated according to the sequence for enumerating the faults; therefore...

The avoidance of the fault of deficient restraint (*yati-hīna*) refers to an example occurring by way of avoiding the fault of deficient restraint; it is now not being brought forward again—that is, it is not being cited.
By this, he confirms the very meaning already stated in the section on "Attainment" (*adhigama-māda*).

As for the phrase "this was investigated below," the avoidance of the fault of deficient restraint was investigated below in the immediately preceding chapter [with the words]: "I bow to him with my head..."
It is explained by such passages as, "the Tathāgata, who has the color of refined gold," and so forth.

The intention is that since the method for avoiding the fault of deficient *yati* (caesura) has already been shown in the very beginning, there is no deficiency in the composition even if it is not shown here. The analysis (*viggaha*) is:
"that in which the *yati* is deficient" (*yati-hīna*), "the avoidance thereof" (*tassa parihāro*), and "excitement upon hearing" (*savane ubbegam*).
As for one who has fallen through sensual desire—for example: "You are of noble conduct; therefore, there is satisfaction in you.
Give me land, or a village, or a beautiful field."

94. “Udāra,” etc. The analysis is: he whose conduct (*carita*) is noble (*udāra*), that is, whose practice is an exceedingly virtuous manifestation due to its connection with an excellence of generosity (*cāga*). Here, because the place and other factors are appropriate, there is this avoidance of the sequence of begging being disturbed.
94. “Udārī,” etc. O meritorious one, you are of noble conduct; because of your association with an excellence of generosity, you are endowed with confident manifestation.
For that very reason, my request for your favor (*ārādhanā*) is directed toward you. [I do not ask] for a country or a province. No.

Whether it be a village or a settlement, or whether it be "Give me a beautiful field or a rice-paddy," such a gradual request for inferior objects removes the fault of violating proper sequence, because it is appropriate both to the donor’s act of giving and to the recipient’s attainment of their desired object.
The analysis of the compound is: "one whose conduct is noble" (*udāra-carita*).
As it was said too much:
"Of the rays of the mass of glory produced from the moon of the Lord of Sages..."
“Even this entire space has no room for my stretching out. (95) “O Lord of Sages,” and so forth.
The Lord of Sages himself is the moon; from him arose—that is, became manifest—the mass of glory itself, which is like rays of light.

Of those [rays]. This entire space is indeed the sky itself, not a single portion of it. Because there is no room for expansion or pervasion due to their such nature, it is not an exaggeration to call them "the rays of the mirage.
95. Regarding the verse beginning with “Munindi”:
from the mass of rays of glory produced from the moon that is the Lord of Sages (Munindacanda), from that which is reckoned as the moon of the Lord of Sages...
When the rays consisting of the mass of fame that has become manifest expand—that is, spread—this entire sky becomes without space, without room.

Since even by each individual cause, such as the cause and its fruit, the qualities of the Omniscient One are immeasurable, it is appropriate to speak of the sky—which shares the common nature of being immeasurable—as if it were without space; thus, there is no fault in saying "excessively."
It does not apply here. "Cando iva cando" (like the moon, the moon) means "the Moon-Lord himself is the moon. The analysis (*viggaha*) is:
"a mass of fame arising from him alone, and those rays [of that fame].
The sentence is free from malice, devoid of worldly purpose, and irreproachable.
That [speech] of those who are merely thin and so forth is faulty, except for [the case of] words. 96. "Speech," etc.
Those whose minds are corrupted, ruined, and functioning improperly—of them. Speech is that which possesses the characteristics of speech.
That whose meaning—the referent, the conventional object of expression—is departed, gone, or empty—that [is what is meant].
"Aninditaṃ" means unblamed. "By that reason," as previously stated.
That speech—of one who is insane (ummatta), whose mind is deranged by the disturbance of the elements and so forth;

or of those such as fools (bāla) and others, whose words are incoherent—except in the case of another object where there is no malevolent intent, it becomes "dussati," meaning it arises as corrupted. This is because such speech is appropriate only for those who are insane and the like.

96. “Speech,” and so forth. The speech of those with malevolent minds—those whose minds have reached a state of hostility—consists of a collection of words ending in verbal suffixes (*syādyanta*) or nominal suffixes (*tyādyanta*).

If that speech is devoid of meaning—that is, lacking the collective sense of the composition—and is not censured, meaning it is not condemned by the wise, then for that reason, except in the case of the speech of the insane and so forth (such as those suffering from insanity or delusion), there is no offense in speaking otherwise than [what is normally expected] of one who is not insane.

That speech which is devoid of a collective meaning and connection is "corrupt" (*dussati*), meaning it is defiled by faults. The analysis of the compounds is as follows: *byāpannacittā* means "those whose minds are corrupted";
*atthāpeta* means "that from which the purpose has departed"; and *ummattādī* means "those who are insane, etc.
For example:
"The ocean is being drunk up; today I am afflicted by old age;
these clouds are thundering; Sakkassa’s [elephant] Erāvaṇa is dear.
(97) He cites this with "Just as," beginning with "The ocean" and so forth. For here, there is no [intended meaning] in the collection of words such as "the ocean is being drunk up."
A certain single meaning is grasped, which would be the sense of "binding. However, it is the very state of being a constituent part that appears like a shimmering iron splinter;
such an irreproachable meaning should be understood as intended for those with malevolent minds.
97. “The ocean,” and so forth. This ocean is drunk by whomever drinks it; today I am afflicted by old age.
"Overcome by old age and disease—these clouds (*jīmūtā*) roar and thunder. Sakkassa’s Erāvaṇa is dear.
This is an example of two [types of speech], the censured and the uncensured.

This sentence is called "devoid of meaning" (*apetāttha*) because the intended sense is not understood from the whole in the absence of its constituent parts. Such a sentence, when uttered by the insane and others, is unpleasant.
It is not so; however, what is said by others is as disagreeable to the ear as a pin of iron. "Afflicted by old age" is the phrase.
That [beauty] produced by delicacy, youthfulness, splendor, and radiance would be utterly corrupted by that bond which is harsh with the fault of bondage.
98. “Sukhumāli,” etc. That which does not conflict with virtue is *avirodhī*; its state is *avirodhittaṃ*.
Whose radiant appearance possesses the non-conflict of one who is delicate—that [appearance] is what has been manifested, increased, and connected by it;
the meaning is that it would utterly corrupt and destroy that bond, namely the harsh fault of bondage.

98. “*Sukhumāli*,” etc. That composition is nourished by a state of loveliness (*dittabhāva*)—characterized by the mutual cohesion of phonemes—which is endowed with a non-contradictory nature toward the quality of delicacy (*sukhumālaguṇa*) described by the phrase “abounding in soft syllables,” and which is further augmented by a state of endearment (*piyabhāva*).
Such a composition is free from the fault of harshness in its binding, that is, the fault known as *bandhapharusa*.
"He would corrupt or destroy it"—this is the connection [with the phrase] "the fault of binding and harshness. "Not obstructed by virtue" means *avirodhī*;

[the analysis is: "the state of that," or "one who possesses the non-obstruction of one who is delicate," or "that very thing which is the state of one who is conceited," or "that which is manifested by that"—such is the construction of the sentence.
For example:
Beholding the splendor of forms and hearing sweet voices,
the virtuous wander about during the time of a Fully Enlightened One, their hearts turned away from play.
99. He illustrates with the words “yathā,” “passantā,” and so forth. The connection is: “They wander away from play, devoid of desire for sport.

99. “Passantā,” etc. O virtuous ones, during the time of the Fully Awakened One—while the Buddha was still living—those who were beholding his physical splendor, gazing upon the perfection of his form with satisfied eyes, [and hearing] his sweet voice... his very same...
Hearing the Blessed One’s sweet speech endowed with eight factors, they move, go, and proceed with their faces turned away from play, averse to sport, and devoid of delight in amusement.
This is because [the speech] is possessed of qualities that arise from phonemes easy to pronounce— free from harshness and looseness—
and because it is joined with qualities consisting in the clear manifestation of phonemes that are mutually compatible and non-contradictory with the subtle and delicate virtues [of the meaning].
Herein, there is no fault of harshness in the construction. The analysis [of the compound] is: "those whose faces have been turned away from others for sport.

Here, "time" (kāla) is the action; and in terms of its actual meaning, it is simply the connection consisting in the occurrence of that particular mode [of action]. However, common usage designates "the world" (loka) as a distinct, single referent.
This is the avoidance of the fault of sentence-structure (vākyadosa).
The commentary on the avoidance of faults in phrasing is finished.
The commentary on the avoidance of faults in the meaning of sentences:
For example, regarding its departure—
“Meditative development, generosity, and virtue, when perfectly accomplished here, are the means for attaining Nibbāna, wealth, rebirth in heaven, and so forth—of this there is no doubt.

(100) Regarding the verse beginning with “Meditative development”: having pointed out meditative development and the others here, the fault of omission has been avoided by subsequently pointing out their respective results, such as Nibbāna and the rest, in due order.

100. “In cultivation,” and so forth. Here, in this human world, those acts of cultivation, giving, and virtue that have been properly accomplished—having faith in the fruit of karma—and performed according to rule, set in motion within one’s own continuum, are the means for achieving Nibbāna, wealth, the heavens, and so on;
they are the effectors by way of being the causes for the attainment of the enjoyment and utilization of Nibbāna, the excellence of the heavens, and rebirth therein, respectively.

There is no doubt regarding the proof here. In this case, having first stated the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and so forth, and not deviating from the order of that enumeration, because [the specific details] such as *nibbāna* have not yet been enumerated, there is no room for the fault of "premature departure" (*apakkama*) in the meaning of the statement.
If there were some particular distinction of such a kind within the subject matter already enumerated...
“There is no fault in transgressing the order of sequence when it comes to what has not been specified among those things that have been specified. (101) “Specified,” and so forth.

That particular distinction characterized by the knowledge of the relationship between the specification and the non-specification—wherein the meanings first joined together constitute its domain or range—is such a distinction.
When it comes to those things not specified, [it occurs] by again overstepping the measure of the order of specification.

If there were [an error] among those things misapprehended by way of dependence on another meaning, then there would be no fault in transgressing or skipping the sequence as it was indicated for the *kama*. 101. "In what has been indicated," etc.
There is some such distinction regarding the subject already indicated, concerning the meaning intended by the first application.

Regarding the sequence and non-sequence [of terms], the specific distinction characterized by the thorough knowledge of the relationship—whose characteristic is mutual dependence—is such that one understands: "This is its prior statement;
this is its subsequent statement. This applies when, among those not previously mentioned, something is stated again based on another meaning; [the word] "would be" (*bhaveyya*) is the ellipsis.

As for the transgression of order—that is, the violation of the sequence of the sequence and non-sequence—there is no reason why those learned in the scriptures would find it intolerable upon hearing it.
The phrase *uddiṭṭhā* means "first uttered" or "stated," and *atthā* refers to its meaning, object, or domain. The expression *kamassa vilaṅghanaṃ* (leaping over what? is a rhetorical question.
For example:
among the categories "wholesome," "unwholesome," and "indeterminate," it refers to the last one.
The indeterminate does not yield fruit; the first two [categories] yield fruit.
(102) He illustrates this with the words beginning with "wholesome" (*kusala*). Wholesome [states] are of twenty-one kinds, such as those pertaining to the sense-sphere;
unwholesome [states] are of twelve kinds; and the indeterminate consists of what is termed resultant (*vipāka*) and functional (*kiriya*). Among these three, the latter is the indeterminate.
"Yields ripening" (*pākadam*) means it gives rise to fruition (*vipāka*). "No" (*na*) is a particle. The first two [types of consciousness] yield wholesome and unwholesome fruition;

thus they are called "yielding fruition" (*pākadanti*). Here, the distinction should be understood as follows: the state of not yielding fruition belongs only to the indeterminate (*abyākata*), while the state of yielding fruition belongs to those two [the wholesome and unwholesome].
102. "In the wholesome," etc. The wholesome consists of the twenty-one types of wholesome [consciousness] belonging to the sense-sphere and so forth, and the unwholesome is of twelve kinds.

Regarding the unwholesome (*akusala*) and the indeterminate (*abyākata*), the latter—consisting of fourfold indeterminate states by way of resultant (*vipāka*), functional (*kiriya*), material form (*rūpa*), and Nibbāna—is, according to the order of enumeration, the final indeterminate state;
it does not give a result, nor is it a giver of result.
The first two—the wholesome and the unwholesome—are "givers of results," meaning they each give their own respective result. Thus: "The subsequent [explanation] follows the numerical order."

"Samānaṃ" refers to Pāṇini’s rule 1.3.10. "Anudeso" means that which is subsequently mentioned; the sense is "pronounced afterwards. The genitive case in "samānaṃ" is used in the sense of a relation (*sambandha*).

Because it is stated [in this way], and because it is obtained by applying an equal number to those very items not mentioned that correspond to those already mentioned, there is no exceeding of the number.
Here, however, due to their intrinsic nature as wholesome (*kusala*) and so forth...

Because it proceeds by way of giving and taking its threefold maturation toward the specific distinctions of the two types of objects—wholesome and unwholesome, etc.—there is no fault of "premature departure," as there is no occurrence of support without first being subject to that sequence according to one's desire. [In the verse:
"When such a cause exists, in the non-manifestation of qualities..."
There is no falling away from the absence of haste for one who proclaims the true meaning.

(103) “Of those possessing qualities,” and so forth. When such a cause—the motive—exists, namely, the accomplishment of the listeners’ own welfare and so on, for him (*sassa*) who proclaims (*saṃsino*) the true (*bhūtaṃ*) meaning as it has occurred—that is, his own conduct characterized by [virtue]—of that person (*attano*), [there is no falling away].

In the exposition of those qualities, by virtue of his authority, when speaking such words as “most worthy of worship in the world,” there is no possibility of him incurring an offense due to a deficiency in eloquence (ocikya). 103. “Possessing qualities,” etc.
When such a cause exists—that is, when such a reason is present for listeners regarding the accomplishment of their own welfare and so forth—

When one who speaks of existing realities— speaking on such an occasion with words such as "I alone am the most worthy of honor in the world" regarding the meaning known as the quality characterized by the restraint of the body and so forth that exists within oneself—

there occurs an impropriety in the manifestation or disclosure of one's own virtues (*saguṇānam sassa attano*) or those virtues belonging to oneself (*sānam vā sakānam guṇānam*); this constitutes the fault known as impropriety (*ocityahīna*).

"Natthīti. Because the particle *sa* expresses both the self (*atta*) and what belongs to the self (*attaniya*), the analysis (*viggaha*) may be either "those qualities (*guṇa*) of his own (*se*)" or "those qualities (*te guṇā*) which are his own (*ca te guṇā ca*).
The meaning is simply "one who exists" (*bhūto eva*). The analysis is: "one whose nature it is to speak (*vadati*) that [meaning] (*taṃ*) by way of praising (*saṃsati*).
That which is known as "propriety" (*ocitya*) should be understood as being renowned in the world with great respect.
Therein, the eminent poets among virtuous people, originating from that very instruction, [state]:
“Appropriateness,” and so forth. In the world—that is, in the world of sentient beings—it is renowned and well-established even among children;

because it is understood by children according to their respective capacity, it is called “appropriateness” (*ocitya*), which is the state of being appropriate. Thus, in common usage, it is out of respect (*ādarena*) for this established convention... [that they speak].
Because there is nothing more worthy of respect than zeal (*ussāha*) beyond that; for nothing unaccustomed can be respected by anyone in every respect, as it would be entirely unsatisfying.

The word "by listeners" (*sotūnam*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the compound]. In that regard, "good people" (*sujanā*) refers to excellent persons, the preeminent among poets, who are the source—that is, the place of origin—of the instruction, which occurs by way of causing one to grasp the first utterance of that propriety (*ocitya*).
"Uttama" means the best of poets (*kaviseṭṭha*); this is what is meant by "the supreme poet. 104.

Regarding the passage beginning with "In propriety" (*ocitye*) and so forth: in the world—that is, in the world of sentient beings—what is known as *ocitya* (propriety), which is established even among children, is to be understood through respect and reverence;
it is to be known by the wise. In that regard, concerning the subject of propriety, [it arises] from instruction at the time of the first utterance.

"Excellent persons" (*sujana*) refers to those who are virtuous people; "bulls among poets" (*kavipuṅgava*) refers to supreme poets. Because it is joined with a word whose conventional meaning is well-established (*pasiddha-oññāta-pada*), the word *nāma* here signifies "conventional renown.
Furthermore, there are the phrases: "the source of instruction" (*upadesassa pabhava*), "they are both males and cows" (*pumāno ca te gāvo ca*), and "bulls among poets" (*kavīnaṃ puṅgavā*).
One who understands the distinction between what is appropriate and inappropriate should avoid what is inappropriate; then,
through the cultivation of what is appropriate, [one attains excellence].
The essence may be in the composition.

105. Regarding “Viññāta,” etc.: that by which the aforementioned poetic figures, clarity, propriety, and excellence are understood or realized—that [poet] should avoid or shun the defect known as the lack of propriety (ocityahīna). Therefore, from that avoidance...

When the development of propriety (*ocitya*) from its cause has been thoroughly increased—that is, when its cultivation is accomplished—there may arise, or come to be, a cultivation of *mādhuriya* (sweetness), which is to say, the quality of being relished in the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). 105.

“In what is known,” etc. One who possesses the excellence known as the knowledge of propriety through the favor of such poets is one endowed with the perfection consisting in the knowledge of propriety.
The poet should avoid and eliminate the flaw known as "lack of propriety" (*ocitya-hīna*).

When that fault has been avoided and propriety has been cultivated and nourished, there will be a nourishment of aesthetic flavor (*rasa-poso*), which is to say, a fulfillment of that which is to be relished, characterized by sweetness (*mādhuriya*).

[The compound] *ocityam eva vibhavo* means "propriety itself is the source of wealth," and *viññāta-ocitya-vibhavo* means "one by whom the source of wealth consisting of propriety is known. Regarding *rasassa*...

The phrase "the state of being a nourisher" (*poso puṭṭhabhāvo*) means the state of being grown (*vuddhabhāvo*), or alternatively, the state of being one who must be nourished (*posetabbabhāvo*). As it is said:
"He whose joy in victory is ever closer and closer as he approaches Māra’s army..."
He did not conceive even [the thought] "It is grass"; may that Victor grant you victory.
(106) "He who," and so forth, he utters as an illustration. "Victory" (*vijaya*) means the overcoming of others;

"victory-festival" (*vijayussava*) means a festival of victory itself, an exaltation, a state of proceeding without opposition. Such is he who [overcame] the army of Māra that had approached close to him, near his own presence.
"He did not regard even a blade of grass as a straw; he regarded even a blade of grass as inferior to a straw.
May that Conqueror, the Vanquisher of Māra, grant you victory—may he ordain it. Here, the title "Conqueror" (*jina*) is most appropriately applied to one who has utterly conquered the five murderers.
He is the Conqueror whose sole essence is the overcoming of adversaries; his singular capacity lies in bestowing victory upon others.
"‘Siyā’ means: ‘He did not regard Māra’s army as even worth a blade of grass.

This, however, is most appropriate here, since even when such an army of Māra had approached him so closely, he regarded it as inferior even to a blade of grass; therefore, his singular intent toward granting victory to others is especially fitting.
(106) Here, although the Master desires a concise method throughout this treatise, he has respectfully included what is called "appropriateness" (*ocitya*) along with the other [eight] qualities.

Having thus instructed his disciples in detail, saying, "Having mastered it, it must be applied," he now cites the *Lakkhiya* as an example in order to avoid what is inappropriate, beginning with the words:
"He who, when Māra’s army was near... Here, "near the festival of victory" means the festival consisting of the imminent defeat of the enemy;
or alternatively, it refers to the Victor (*Jina*) who is endowed with the increase characterized by the occurrence of being very close to the absence of adversaries.

He did not even notice or take account of Māra’s army and Māra’s forces, which had approached his vicinity in many terrifying forms, treating them as if they were but blades of grass or a mere scrap of straw.
May that Conqueror (Jina)—he who is called "Conqueror" because he has conquered the five Māras—grant victory to you all.
Herein, he is called "Conqueror" because he has conquered the five Māras; for in the act of overcoming an opponent, there is no need for assistance.

Since he possesses the capacity to grant victory to others, the prayer for victory made with the words “May he grant victory” is most appropriate, for it is precisely the nourisher of the capacity to grant victory [who is addressed].
Thus, there is no need even to mention the thought, “He did not regard Māra’s army as even a blade of grass.
In this way, by means of an utterly appropriate application, the fault of lacking propriety is refuted. Victory.
The analysis is: "one for whom the festival is near, namely the festival of victory.
Regarding the transgression of the sequence [of grammatical operations] such as the commencement of the agent's action and so forth:
this contradiction with the established tradition finds no standing anywhere.

107. “*Āraddha*,” etc. The agent and the object—these being the first among those [factors] such as the instrument (*karaṇa*) for which [the roles of] agent, object, and so forth have been commenced or established;
the sequence of these is their "transgression" (*atikkama*), meaning their abandonment.

When there is a leaping over that [sequence], it is said: "when there is a transgression of the order of the agent, object, and so forth that were begun to be stated. This is the aforementioned contradiction with the broken style (*bhaggarīti*).
Nowhere, in no place whatsoever, does it find a course; it gains no footing.

107. Regarding the phrase "commenced" (*āraddha*) and so forth: in the case of overstepping or transgressing the sequence of the agent, the action, and so on that have been commenced—namely, in the transgression of the order of the agent, the action, and so forth that were begun to be stated—this aforementioned violation of the established stylistic method finds no scope anywhere, in no place whatsoever.

"He finds no footing; he does not obtain it. The analysis (*viggaha*) is: "The transgression (*laṅghana*) of that action, which is the overstepping of those actions such as doing and so forth, for the sake of those [actions] such as making and so forth, even though they have been undertaken.
For example:
Trust in women who know themselves to be virtuous is not appropriate,
just as it is not appropriate to trust poison, a horned beast, disease, a river,
or a royal family. [This applies even] when medicine has been prepared, or toward the Triple Gem consisting of the pure Buddha and the others.
One should always practice faith toward virtuous people and those endowed with good qualities.

(108–109) In this context, regarding the two verses beginning with "sujana" and "bhesajja," there is no violation of the rule of meaning (*attharīti*) due to the non-abandonment of the genitive and locative cases;
nor is there a violation of the rule of sound (*saddarīti*), because the particle *ca* has been employed only once.
Indeed, for the purpose of collecting many points, a single *ca* (and) should be used in a sentence either at the beginning or at the end.
108. Regarding the verse beginning with "In the good person" (*sujane*): association (*vissāsa*)—that is, contact—with the wise, with those other than the virtuous, namely the wicked, and with women;
and with poison, which is capable of taking away life; and with the horned, that is, possessing horns; and with the river of disease and the royal family.

"Nothing arises, because it is contradictory at certain times; therefore, it is not tenable. Herein, there is no violation of the structural integrity (*attharīti*) of the sixth *un-takka* (negative-conditional) formulation that has been commenced, as it is maintained throughout.
Nor is there a violation of the phonetic structure (*saddarīti*), because the particle *ca* is appropriately used in its proper place.
Since the particle *ca* possesses multiple functions, including conjunction (*samuccaya*), as seen in such expressions as "of the wise and of the virtuous" (*sujanaññānañcā*).
Or, it may be applied here according to the stated rule, at the end, or in all instances.
109. In the verse beginning with "In medicine" (*bhesajje*) and so forth, this same method applies; the only difference is the use of the locative case.
When wholesome medicine and remedies have been prepared, and when the Three Jewels—the pure Buddha and the rest—and virtuous people are present, even more so when they possess excellent qualities.

And regarding the virtues that actually exist, a true person (sappurisa) should constantly and perpetually practice confidence—that is, he should cultivate clarity of his own mind; he should act and serve accordingly.
For one who is full of doubt, it is like this: [the light of] the moon-like countenance of the Lord of Sages—
With eyes moist with joy,
the people were like travelers on a road refreshed by the sight of a flash of lightning.
110. “Muninde,” etc. Here, the word *raṃsi* (ray) removes what is accompanied by doubt.
The verse beginning with “muninde,” which serves as an illustration of the removal of what is accompanied by doubt, has its meaning already explained in the immediately preceding chapter.

For it is specifically the word *raṃsi* that constitutes the distinction; here, by means of the word *raṃsi*, the defect of composition known as *sasaṃsaya* (accompanied by doubt)—which arises from the doubt produced in the listeners—is abandoned.

If anything whatsoever is employed for the sake of a wager—even for the purpose of play and so forth—there is no fault at all, provided it is undertaken with a sense of uncertainty. (111) The verse beginning with “In a wager,” etc., explains as follows:

“Play and so forth”—by the word “and so forth” (ādi), activities such as gambling and arranging bets are included. The syntactical connection is: “if anything whatsoever is employed for the sake of a wager even for the purpose of play and so forth.”

111. “*Saṃsayāyeva*,” etc. If, for the sake of sport and so forth—that is, for reasons such as arranging a playful contest—any word whatsoever capable of producing doubt is employed by speakers in that composition solely for the purpose of creating doubt in the listeners, then it is “endowed with doubt,” meaning it is accompanied by the fault of doubt.
"Binding is neither fault nor non-fault"—this is the analysis of the compound *sasaṃsayena samappito*.
For example:
"When you had gone for the second time from your own home to the teacher's abode..."
"May we surely attain happiness through study and so forth.
(112) Regarding the verse beginning with "When you have gone," etc.:

when the teacher, the instructor, has gone from his own home—his primary residence—to a second residence, a second house, [we think] that we shall surely and exclusively attain happiness through study and the like; this is the unintended meaning.
When the teacher—the master of the Veda—is gone from his own home, that is, from his own dwelling place, to a second residence or a second heap [of grain], the intended meaning here is:
"We shall surely attain happiness through the study of the scriptures and other such activities. 112. Regarding the phrase beginning with "gone" (*yāte*):
when the teacher, the master, has departed from his own home—that is, from his own dwelling—toward a second residence or a second...

When he has gone home—this refers to the undesired purpose. When the teacher, the master of the *sura* (wine), has gone from his own house to his second dwelling, that is, to a second heap [of grain], then because of the favorability [of the situation], there will certainly and exclusively be happiness—the mental happiness derived from recitation and so forth, or from learning and so forth.
[The student thinks: "May we reach the completion of the texts, which is the cause of such happiness."
In both cases, when another word follows, the meaning is common [to both].

Here, although the word *guru* used in conjunction with the word *ajjhāyana* expresses the sense of "teacher," it is not faulty because it is employed for the purpose of preserving the intended meaning,
as in such expressions as "this sister is fortunate" (*subhagā bhaginī sā’yam*) and so forth.
The term "village" (*gāma*) has not been specified by any poets whatsoever.
113. “*Subhagā*,” etc.; likewise, “*bhaginī*,” etc. 113. “*Subhage*,” etc.
[This means: “For this man, she—this sister—is *subhagā*, beautiful,” and so forth.
It is indicated that even by all poets this [word] is not considered vulgar (*gāmma*), meaning it is not corrupted by the fault of vulgarity.

*Silesana* (cohesion) is *sileso*, which is the weight of the composition (*bandhagārava*). *Udāratā* (nobility) is loftiness, being endowed with some significant meaning, and being possessed of distinguished qualifications.

117. Now, with the words beginning "Pasādojo," he enumerates those ornaments of sound (*saddālaṅkāra*) in order to analyze them sequentially.

*Pasāda* (clarity) is the ornament of clarity (*pasādālaṅkāra*), consisting of the lucidity of the meaning of sounds, like a string of clear crystal beads upon which a red woolen thread has been strung.
*Oja* (vigour) is the quality (*guṇa*) of both sound and meaning, consisting of an abundance of compound expressions and the mastery of meaning.
And sweetness (*madhuratā*) consists of the mellifluousness of sounds, characterized by their being "tasteful" to the ear;

evenness (*samatā*) is the similarity of the feet when measured line by line, and likewise the similarity of the words within those feet; thus, there is an equality of qualities between the feet and the words;
and delicacy (*sukhumālatā*) is the quality of being well-proportioned and smooth, without being either excessively harsh or excessively loose in its syllables.
*Ślesa* (punning) consists of phonetic similarity arising from place, organ of articulation, and so forth, as well as the quality of being faultless and weighty;
*audāratā* (nobility) is the state of being adorned by some exalted meaning within the composition, as well as being joined with distinguished qualifying words;

*kānti* (loveliness) is the quality of being dear to all; and *arthavyakti* (clarity of meaning) is the state of the intended meaning being well-manifested through its accomplishment or through logical reasoning.

Furthermore, there are these ten qualities of the meaning of the word (*saddattha-guṇa*): [the qualities of] being not surpassed by worldly convention, and not having a non-primary sense through the imposition of other meanings.

For it was by that Conqueror that you were... [the text continues: *uggo*... [the text continues: *vo*.
And that very ocean of *saṃsāra*—terrible, difficult to traverse, and impossible to cross—is the end-point for reaching its limit;
for one to whom the crossing of it has not been ordained, who has not performed it, what indeed is "benefit" or "growth"? It does not exist at all.
Here too, because the compound is so manifest, the quality of *oja* (vitality) is desirable.

Is it not the case that there is a constant connection between the words *ya* and *ta*, such that in expressions like “*tasseveko*” and “*tasmiṃ nu kiṃ kumatayo*,” the word *ya* does not exist in what was stated previously?
True; nevertheless, the word *ta*—when its scope is the sense of "departed," the sense of "well-known," or the sense of "experienced"—does not require the word *ya*. For instance:
"In him, having destroyed all defilements together with their latent tendencies,
he alone— his continuum perfectly purified— was always worthy of honor.

In such passages as these, the demonstrative pronoun "he" (*so*) refers to the object denoted by the past word "Buddha" in the phrase "beginning with the recollection of the Buddha" (*buddhānussati-m-ādito*).
“‘Leap into the fire,’ or ‘Flee from the mountain peak’—if he should say such things, they must be done by those who act for their kinsman; thus is the Victor.
In such passages as these, the word *ta* (that) refers to the well-known referent of the Buddha, because it is something to be performed by those who act for their kinsman.
“I do not grieve for the past, nor do I long for the future;
I maintain myself with the present, and thereby my complexion becomes serene.
In such passages as these, the word *tas* (that) has as its object a meaning already experienced, by way of knowing—namely, non-grieving, non-longing, and maintaining.
Therefore, in all three instances, the word *ta* does not depend upon the word *ya*. Here, however, the word *ta* is intended in the sense of "one who has departed" (*pakkantavisaya*).
Furthermore, the word *ya*, standing in the subsequent sentence, indicates that very same [person] even in the absence of the word *ta* in the preceding sentence. For instance:
"I pay homage to the Bodhi tree, the vessel of victory, which is supreme over death."
To those who have attained the range of the eye, the ear, and mindfulness—
the wise ones whose sole essence is the crushing of the enemy that is the defilements,
and who bring about merit that is the source of well-being for the circle of the world.

I bow to that *bodhi* which has attained and reached the state of being the range and object of the Buddhas—who possess the eye, ear, and mindfulness—and which possesses a single flavor in crushing and trampling the pride of those very enemies of the defilements, namely the arrows of the faults; it is endowed with the function of striving (*padhāna*) and is successful.
This is the connection [of the sentence]. The word *ya*, employed in the preceding clause, refers back to the word *ta* when it is taken up in the subsequent clause.
By causing doubt regarding what is absent, one renders the sentence deficient. An example, however, is well known.
[It concerns] the domain expressed by words, which arises through both compounding and analysis.
Whatever is matured here, that too is like nutritive essence (*ojā*). 123. “*Padi*,” etc.
That which is the expressed meaning of the word *padi* is its object (*visaya*). Wherein the expressed meaning of the word *pacura* [is found]...
The meaning is expressed by concise words; that is *samāsa* (conciseness). Where the intended meaning is expressed by many words instead of few, that is *byāsa* (prolixity).

That which has its origin (*sambhava*) from such *samāsa* and *byāsa*—referring to that state of being matured (*pāriṇatya*) which is the condition of having reached maturity (*pariṇatabhāva*)—is also prescribed here in this treatise as *ojā* (vitality), following the restatement [of the definition]. He illustrates both of these with the words "for example" (*tad-yathā*).

123. “*Pada*,” etc. That which pertains to many or few words, whose objective domain is the meaning of those words, which possesses the scope of both detailed and concise meanings, which arises through both compounding (*samāsa*) and expansion (*byāsa*), and which is produced—or possesses production—through the two modes of summary and detail respectively;

that *saddadhamma* (linguistic phenomenon) and *atthadhamma* (semantic phenomenon) which manifests the transformation of the authors regarding the subject matter of the composition is called *pāriṇati*.

It is said that there is the quality of sound (*saddaguṇa*) and the quality of meaning (*atthaguṇa*); here, in the *Subodhālaṅkāra*, that which is called "vigor" (*oja*) is both the quality of sound and the quality of meaning.

The phrase "how is that? demonstrates two characteristics: namely, that of the maturity (*pāriṇatti*) whose scope is the denoted object of words, and that of the compound (*samāsa*) and the analysis (*byāsa*).
Furthermore, [it refers to] that from which they arise, and that which has its origin therein; [this applies to] the matured (*pariṇata*).

The analysis (*viggaha*) is either "the state of being the agent" or "the state of the treatise itself. In the sense that the agent is the instrument (*pāriṇatti*), the instrumentality of the treatise—which reveals that [agent]—is established for the sake of that [agent].
Having illuminated the True Dharma...
Having delivered the world together with its gods,
he— like a mass of blazing fire—
has attained parinirvāṇa along with his disciples.
124. “Having illuminated,” and so forth. By this, the lineage of Buddhas mentioned previously in detail is stated here in a concise form.

124. “Having illuminated,” and so forth. That Tathāgata, having illuminated the True Dhamma together with its textual exposition—the ninefold supramundane True Dhamma—having made it radiant with the light of his knowledge, having delivered beings including the devas, and having brought them to the further shore of the ocean of *saṃsāra*...

Like a mass of fire, having blazed with great majesty and having flared up with a perfection of physical form unsurpassed by any other, he finally attained final Nibbāna through the Nibbāna of the aggregates together with his disciples—having been extinguished along with his followers.
By this, the meaning expressed in many phrases throughout the entire lineage of Buddhas has been stated in a concise manner. This is the Dhamma of the Noble Ones.
The analysis [of the compound] is: "a phenomenon that exists" (*saṃvijjamāna*) or "is present," and "occurring together with the devas," or "occurring together with the disciples.
May even the skull-bone of one who has died become dust for me, so that by means of my merit they may rest at the two lotus-feet of the Victor. (ka.)
125. “Matthakaṭṭhī,” etc. May the bones on my head—the skull—of me who have met with death, attain the state of dust, that is, reach the condition of powder.

Why? Because, for this reason, by virtue of merit—that is, by means of wholesome karma as the cause—these feet of the Conqueror (Jina) are "jenā" (victorious), and they alone are like lotuses (*ambuja*). Of those [feet]...
They exist and proceed in pairs; whether it be so or not, he speaks solely out of devotion (*paṇa*).
Here, the intention—"How might I always bow my head at the feet of the Blessed One?"—has been stated in detail.
125. Regarding "on the crown of the head" (*matthake*) and so forth: even when I am dead, let the bones on my head—the bones upon my skull—become dust.
"Let the extremely subtle dust reach [the feet]; let it attain [them]. If one asks why he makes this aspiration:

It is because, by means of such merit of mine—that is, by way of that cause consisting of wholesome karma—those dust particles settle upon, or move across, the pair of lotus-feet of the Victor, the two lotuses that are the feet dependent upon the Conqueror.
Although not even a speck of dust or mire ever adheres to the glorious feet of the Buddha, nevertheless...
This was said out of a desire for homage. Herein, the longing—“How may I constantly bow my head at the Blessed One’s glorious feet?”—is expressed in detail.

As for the analysis (*viggaha*): *matthake aṭṭhi* (the bone on the head), *rajaso bhāvo* (the state of being dust), *jinassa ime* (these belong to the Victor), *jenā ca te pādā ca* (and those feet of the Victor), and *teyeva ambujāni* (those very [feet] are lotuses); [the compound is] *tesaṃ dvayaṃ* (the pair of them).
"Thus, here, constant devotion and reverence are seen to be excellent;
this quality arises from the application of those with sharp wisdom.
(126) The phrase "Thus, here," and so forth, explains that his mind is indeed detached. In this way, in this verse, regarding devotion (*paṇati*)—that is, homage (*paṇāma*)—it is shown.
Greed (*gedha*) is an excessive desire; it perceives and recognizes something as "good" or "beautiful.

This aforementioned quality of vitality (*oja*), which is defined as the state of being fully matured, arises and emerges through application—that is, by the power of repeated practice—even though such [qualities] belong only to those of sharp wisdom and preeminent intellect. 126.
Now, he demonstrates the detailed exposition of the summarized meaning with the words beginning "In this regard" (*iccatra*).
Thus, according to the sequence stated in the immediately preceding verse, in this verse here, "niccapaṇatigedho" (constant bending and yielding) refers to the absence of interruption;
"adhikattukāmatākusalacchando" (the wholesome desire to perform more) is clearly manifested (*vibhūta*) or appears as "sādhu" (excellent).
This quality, as previously described, is called *ojas* (vitality), which is the quality of the meaning of words for those of sharp wisdom.
It arises and is accomplished through the application of those with subtle intelligence by means of uninterrupted practice directed toward the subject matter of the texts;
however, it does not arise or succeed for anyone in any way whatsoever merely through the ripening of karma.
"That which constantly occurs," "that which bends," "greed for that," and "those who possess sharp wisdom"—[this is repeated] again and again.
The analysis is: *yoga* and *yuñjanti*. Sweetness (*madhuratta*) is twofold, by way of the proximity of words (*padāsatti*) and the non-arising of harshness (*aranuppāsa*).
In the former case, there may be equal hearing (*samasuti*), as in the subsequent example where there is a change of phonemes (*vaṇṇāvutti*).
127. To explain *mādhuriya* (sweetness), he says "madhuratta" and so forth. *Madhuratta* is the quality of being captivating due to its worthiness to be heard.
That [quality] consists of words or sentence ornaments that are similar in successive stages;

their proximity (*āsatti*)—by way of position and so on—is the closeness of phonemes that are similarly articulated in any manner whatsoever, which is *padāsatti*. It is the subsequent placement or insertion of a syllable after the first one employed.
It is twofold by way of *padāsatti* (the attachment of words) and *anuppāsa* (the following sound). To the question "Of what kind is it?", he says "it may be" (*siyā*), and so forth.
That [verse] whose preceding—that is, the first-mentioned *padāsatti*—is equal to any other subsequent word through mere position, conjunction, and so on, is "it may be.
However, the latter—the subsequent *anuppāsa*—is of the sound characterized by vowels and consonants.

"Repetition" (*āvutti*) means uttering [words] again and again. Thus, in some compositions there is the proximity of identical words (*samānapadāsatti*), in some there is repetition (*anuppāsa*), and in some both;
a composition devoid of these two is considered "flavorless" (*virasa*) by poets. Such sweetness is to be understood as being of two kinds:
it becomes truly delightful only when it is endowed with the quality of *śleṣa* (punning or double entendre) and evenness (*samatā*). This is the defining characteristic.
Having shown [the definition], he illustrates the application of the term "yathā" (as) in both senses by means of the passage beginning with "yadā" and the passage beginning with "munindā. 127.
Now he demonstrates the quality of sweetness (*madhura*) with the verse beginning "madhuri," etc. Sweetness is the state of being pleasant to hear and captivating;
it is the quality of sweetness belonging to words—counted as members of a sentence—such as those ending in case-suffixes (*syādyanta*), which are identical with the following words.
*Āsatti* (proximity) is twofold, distinguished by two factors: proximity to one another in some manner through position (*ṭhāna*), articulation (*karaṇa*), and so forth;
and *anuppāsa*, which is the re-insertion of phonemes previously uttered. Therein, the proximity of preceding words may be "equal hearing" (*samasuti*);
it is the occurrence of phonemes characterized by being heard as proximate due to mere position, articulation, and so forth, between preceding and following phonemes. The latter...
Furthermore, *anuppāsa* (repetition) would be the repeated utterance of the phonemes previously pronounced, which possess the nature of vowels, consonants, and syllables.
The word "such as" (*yathā*) introduces two examples. Thus, in some compositions there is *padāsatti* (enjambement), in some *anuppāsa*, and in some both;
however, a composition devoid of these two is not something that can be appreciated by the wise.
Furthermore, sweetness (*madhuratta*) endowed with the qualities of cohesion (*silesa*) and evenness (*samatā*), which will be explained above, is especially worthy of being relished.

It is called "the state of sweet composition" (*madhurassa bandhassa bhāvo*); it is called "the proximity of words" (*padānam āsatti*); it is called "the subsequent casting of the net" (*anu pacchā pāso pakkhepo*);

it is called "both the proximity of words and the subsequent casting" (*padāsatti ca anuppāso ca*); it is called "the variety of their power" (*tesam vaso bhedo*); and it is [called] "that whose color (*vaṇṇa*) is equal hearing" (*samā sutī vaṇṇo yassā*).
And the analysis [of the compound] is "the recurrence of the color" (vaṇṇassa āvutti).
When this bull among sages attained supreme enlightenment,
From that time forth, a great festival for the Dhamma arose in the world.
(128) When this bull among sages, from whom [it originated], attained and reached full enlightenment and omniscient knowledge—

From that time forth, beginning from that moment, there arose in the world a great festival, a great prosperity, and an unopposed manifestation of the Dhamma— comprising the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, such as the four foundations of mindfulness— in its threefold form. Herein,
in some cases the similarity is due to length, in some cases due to position, in some cases due to combination, and in some cases otherwise.
Therefore he said: "There may have been equal hearing previously.

(128) "If," and so forth. When this bull among sages attained full enlightenment—omniscience—by way of its arising within his own continuum, from that time forward, [he taught] the Dhamma, which is divided into the foundations of mindfulness such as the contemplation of the body, and so on.
A great festival and a great increase of the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment has arisen in the world, that is, in the three worlds beginning with the realm of desire (*kāmaloka*).
Herein, the proximity of the words is as follows: "when this" indicates proximity by way of long duration; "whoever" indicates proximity by way of place;

"having attained full enlightenment" indicates proximity by way of conjunction; and "bhi dhi" indicates proximity by way of phonetic connection (*dhanita*), and so forth. This is the proximity of the words.

[The word *mudusobhagga*] is to be analyzed as follows: it is that by which one fully awakens (*abhisambujjhati*), and it is both masculine (*pumā*) and an object (*go*), and it is the bull among sages (*munīnaṃ puṅgavo*), and it is both great (*mahanto*) and a festival (*ussavo*).
Those gentle smiles of the Lord of Sages possess the splendor of a cluster of *kunda* flowers.
The gentle smiles of the Lord of Sages, which possess the playful charm of a cluster— a mass— of jasmine flowers,
run toward the quarters of the sky as if laughing, mocking the splendor and radiance of the moon. 129.
They follow along. Thus, here there is the recurrence (anuvattana) of the letter *da* together with the letter *na*, and of the letter *ta*.
“The pair of eyes of the Lord of Sages, beautiful as a pair of sapphire petals, the abode of glory, attains the luster of blue lotuses.”
This is another example. 129.

“The Lord of Sages,” and so forth. The playful graces of the Lord of Sages—those gentle smiles of the Buddha that possess the charm of a cluster of *kunda* flowers, resembling a mass of blossoming *kunda* blooms—laugh at the stainless rays of the moon, as if mocking the moonbeams.
They run and scatter, fleeing toward this or that direction, or even running to the very ends of the quarters.
Here, one should understand the recurrence (āvutti) of the letter *da* accompanied by *na*, and the letter *ta* accompanied by *na*. [The compounds are:

"those who have slow laughter" (*mandā ca te hāsā ca*), "the gentle smile of the Lord of Munis" (*munindassa mandahāsā*), "a mass of *kunda* flowers" (*kundānaṃ sandoho*), and "those whose grace is such" (*tassa vibbhamo yesam*).
And the analysis [of the compound] is either "the very end of the directions" (*disāyeva disantaṃ*) or "the limit of the directions" (*disānaṃ vā antaṃ*).
[As in: "The pair of the Lord of Sages' eyes, beautiful as a pair of sapphire petals, attains the luster of blue lotuses."
This is another example of the substitution of the letter *da* for the letter *na* accompanied by *kāra*.
Therein, the pair of eyes of the Lord of Sages (*muninda*), which is as beautiful as a pair of sapphire petals,
enchanting like a pair of sapphire slabs, and thus the very abode of splendor, possesses the luster of an *indīvara*, that is, the radiance of a blue lotus.
One finds and experiences [it]; the intention is that it is like the hue of a blue lotus.
Among all soft colors, no other is as praiseworthy as this garland of jasmine, which is encircled by a swarm of hovering bees.
130. If it is argued that [a composition] is not "unmixed" (*anuppāsa*) because it consists of various [elements], he says "no," beginning with "all" (*sabba*), and so forth.
It is not "unmixed"—meaning it is neither praised nor worthy of commendation—because it contradicts the rules of *śleṣa* (punning/paronomasia).
He illustrates this with the word "just as" (*yathā*). This *mālatīmālā*—a garland of *jāti* flowers—is for those who are languid, afflicted by disease, or fickle...
"Linalolālimālinī" means that she possesses a row of garlands (*mālā-paṅkti*) consisting of bees (*alīna*) that are greedy (*lolupa*) for the nectar of flowers (*kusuma-rasa*).

In order to show that even a *vuttānuppāsa* (a sequence of syllables following a specific meter) is not to be praised if it is composed of entirely soft sounds, he says "sabbakomalavaṇṇehi" and so forth.
A *vuttānuppāsa*, characterized by the arrangement of phonemes, made with all soft (*komala*) syllables—that is, all delicate (*sukumāra*) phonemes—is not to be praised.
Because it is contrary to the *śleṣa* (punning) ornament, it is not praised. The word “yathā” (as for example) provides an illustration of this.

This is a garland of jasmine (*mālatī*), this is a wreath of *jātisumana* flowers; it is a row of bees (*alīnām*)—those that are clinging, those that are active, those that are falling, those that are restless, and those greedy for fragrance—possessing a garland (*mālinī*).
Here, there is a softness of phonemes (*komalavarṇāvṛtti*) due to the repeated use of the letter *l* alone.
The analysis of the compound is as follows: *mālā* and *ati*, and *lolā* and those *alaya*, and *linā* and those *lolālaya*, and *mālā* of them, and "she has that" (*sā assa atthi*).
Or, [it may be analyzed] with only the soft consonants (*mudūhi*).
Whether by pure [colors],
or by mixed ones, there are three ways in which the equality of colors occurs.

131. One perceives evenness by means of the words "soft" (*mudu*) and so forth. By "entirely soft" (*kevalehi mudūhi*) is meant those that are soft in all four feet, being of the same class (*sajātīya*), neither loose nor harsh; or, because looseness and harshness are the opposites of the cohesive quality (*silesa*), it refers to those beginning with the letter *ka*.
By "entirely smooth" (*kevalehi phuṭehi*) is meant those that are exceedingly smooth, beginning with the letter *bha*, [and free from] passion (*rāga*) and the like. (Ka.)
Or, because that which is difficult to speak about is the opposite of that which is easy to speak about, there is a threefold equality— whether in the *gajja* or *pajja* meters—
by means of syllables (*akkhara*) acting as instruments, which are either mixed with subtle variations or associated with soft and medium sounds.
He illustrates this threefold manner with the word "yathā" (just as).
131. Now, in order to clarify the state of evenness (*samatā*), he says "by soft" (*mudūhi*) and so forth.
By means of all soft (*mudu*), relaxed, and delicate phonemes—either the consonants beginning with *ka*, taken either individually or in combination;

or by means of the consonants beginning with *bha*, which are entirely soft, devoid of harsh phonemes, easy to pronounce in their entirety, and exceedingly pleasant to hear, whether taken individually or in combination with the aforementioned soft and harsh mixed [phonemes].
The equality of sounds (*vaṇṇa*), acting as the instruments [of composition], occurs in three ways: in *gajja* (the roaring), *pajja* (the path), or both.

If a composition consisting of soft and gentle sounds belongs to the *silesālaṅkāra* (alliteration), it would contradict the *sukhumālālaṅkāra* (delicacy) which is made with distinct sounds that are difficult to pronounce.
He illustrates these three types by the word "as follows" (*yathā*).
The playful speech of the Lord of Sages is exclusively soft and even,
resembling the warbling of the cuckoo.
It reaches the heart and bestows peace upon the virtuous. 132.
“The cuckoo,” and so forth. The *ālāpa*—the warbling—of the *kokila*, the karavīka bird, accords with and proclaims that [peace].
"By virtue of his voice" means he is like the song of the cuckoo; that is the sense.

The speech of the Lord of Sages—the sound consisting of the eight qualities such as clarity and so forth—its grace and charm reaches the hearts of the wise, the virtuous, following their minds and possessing a sweet quality;
it bestows upon them both tranquility and Nibbāna.
132. “Like the kokila,” and so forth. The meaning is that it is similar to the *ālāpa*—the playful melody of the song—of the *kokila* birds;

that is, it possesses a quality of resonance corresponding to that. Furthermore, the grace (*vibbhamo vilāso*) of the speech of the Lord of Sages, the Omniscient One—the eightfold melody beginning with clarity (*visaṭṭha*)—attains a state that reaches the hearts of the virtuous (*sataṃ sappurisānaṃ*) and satisfies their minds, leading them to *nibbāna*.
Through their connection with the sons, he gives Nibbāna to those very same virtuous ones, and while giving, he is one who gives.

Here, by the phrase "the sound of the cuckoo’s call," grace (*līlā*) is understood through the metaphorical expression of the supported for the support. This is the equality of the mere manifestation (*kevala-phuṭa-samatā*).
To the Blessed One, the destroyer of existence, who is worthy of being honored by those worthy of honor,
[I approach] desiring the means for the transcendence of existence.
Who would not honor the All-pervading One?
(133) “One who is to be honored,” and so forth. “To be honored” means worthy of respect. That whose noble state—that is, its excellent intention—is [present] even in the world with its gods;
that is the Blessed One. He has gone to the state of existence, which is Nibbāna, thus he is the Bhavantagu; him, the All-pervading One, the Blessed One.

"To the Perfectly Enlightened One. "One who desires the accomplishment of existence" (*bhavantasādhanākaṅkhī*) means one who, by means of virtue, desires the attainment and realization of *nibbāna*, which is the end and conclusion of existence and the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*).
Who indeed would be a person caught in the whirlpool of *saṃsāra*? "He would not esteem it"—that is, he would not show respect; the meaning is that he certainly does so.

133. “Worthy of veneration,” and so forth. Who—what person within the cycle of saṃsāra—who desires the means for becoming and longs for the means to nibbāna, would not venerate the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the all-pervading Lord who has gone to the end of existence—that is, to nibbāna—and whose venerable nature is worthy of being honored by the world including the devas, and whose intention is beautiful and respectful? None at all.

The analysis [of the compound] is as follows: "he does indeed show respect" (*karoty eva*); "one who possesses a state that is both peaceful and existent" (*santo ca so bhāvo ca*); "one for whom there is esteem (*sambhāvanīya*) or a state of being (*sambhava*)" (*sambhāvanīyo sambhavo yassa*);

"the end of existence" (*bhavassa anta*); "one who has gone to the state of being" (*bhavantaṃ gata*); "the means of accomplishing that" (*tassa sādhana*); and "one whose nature desires that" (*taṃ ākaṅkhati sīlena*).
The Malaya breeze,
fragrant from contact with sandalwood obtained through various mixtures,
blows gently as if afraid of the wind from the face of the Lord of Sages.
134. “Laddhi,” etc. Having obtained (*laddha*) contact (*saṃsagga*) and familiarity (*paricaya*) with sandalwood trees, it possesses a beautiful fragrance;

thus it is *sugandhī*, fragrant. The Malaya breeze blowing from the south approaches and follows the breath of the Lord of Sages (*muninda*), as if out of fear, because of its own extreme distance from such a state of coolness and excellence of fragrance.
*Manda* is an adverbial modifier of the action of approaching.

134. “Laddhi,” etc. The Malaya breeze, having attained the fragrant contact of sandalwood, and thus endowed with a beautiful scent through its acquisition of the essence of the sandalwood tree, was as if afraid of the wind from the face of the Lord of Munis—the air perfumed by the Buddha’s mouth—because such soft, fragrant, and cool qualities were impossible for it to possess.
"He goes slowly as if afraid" means he approaches gradually. Regarding the analysis (*viggaha*):

"contact with sandalwood" (*candanānaṃ saṃsaggo*), "that which has obtained contact with sandalwood" (*laddho ca so candanasaṃsaggo*), "that which has a beautiful fragrance" (*sobhano gandho yassa*), "fragrant by having obtained contact with sandalwood" (*laddhacandanasaṃsaggena sugandhī*), "the breeze that has come from the Malaya mountains" (*malayato āgato anilo*), and "the wind that has issued from the mouth of the Lord of Sages" (*munindamukhato nikkhanto mārutoti*). [The word] *mandaṃ*...

This is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). Here, in the context of the threefold equality, the similarity between the three types of characteristics—such as "resembling the warbling of a cuckoo"—and the triad of characteristics shown by [the phrases] "either soft" or "purely," etc., is very clearly manifest. [It is characterized by:
having a predominance of non-harsh syllables, being entirely free from all harshness;
The utterance of syllables is difficult due to delicacy (sukhumālatā).
(135) Delicacy is described by the phrase "with non-harsh syllables" and so forth.
That [speech] which has many syllables—meaning phonemes—that are non-harsh and not rough is thus [described]. By the inclusion of the word "many," it is indicated that "the harsh ones are few."

Because it has issued forth and emerged from all exclusively soft, relaxed, and light syllables, and because its consonants are free from and devoid of that which is difficult and painful to pronounce—having thus described it, delicacy (*sukhumālatā*) is established. 135.
Now, he demonstrates delicacy with the words beginning "not harsh" (*aniṭṭhura*): "containing few harsh syllables and abounding in non-grating phonemes."
"Sabba-komala-nissaṭā" means that because it consists mostly of non-harsh syllables, it is entirely devoid of soft consonants;
it is characterized by subtle delicacy (*sukhumālatā*) because it is endowed with syllables that are free from those difficult to pronounce and those that are painful to utter.
Furthermore, it is so called because its harsh syllables are few, while its non-harsh syllables are abundant, and all of these are soft.

The analysis [of the compound] is: "and," "released from those," "pronounced with difficulty," "departed from those," and "that which has these as its phonemes. There is the insertion of a *niggahīta*.
Seeing the splendor of form, hearing the sweet voice;
"Virtuous ones wander during the time of a Fully Enlightened One, turning away from play.
(136) He recites the verse beginning with "seeing," and so forth. The connection is as follows:

seeing the splendor of form—that is, the perfection of form—and hearing the sweet voice or speech, virtuous ones wander, being averse to play, meaning they have no desire for amusement. Where? [The answer follows: "Where?"
He said: "At the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One.
With the words beginning "They see," he provides an example of *lakkhiya*; its meaning has already been explained.
Even when devoid of poetic ornament, [a work] is [considered such] when it is as if before the presence of the virtuous.
It ascends to a pre-eminent degree; it is delightful and radiant.
(137) Even in the absence of any other distinguished quality, this bond alone is to be accepted; thus he says, "In ornamentation," and so forth.
Even when devoid of ornaments, such delicacy [of expression] comes before the presence of the wise—meaning it enters the range of the speech of the learned.
It ascends; it approaches. The word "api" (even) implies: how much more so when it is adorned with the ornament of meaning (*atthālaṅkāra*)!

By means of that ornament—such as its natural disposition (*sabhāvavutti*) and so forth—it is radiant (*ujjalā*), brilliant (*dittā*), and moreover, by way of distinction and excellence, delightful (*ramaṇīyā*) and charming (*manuññā*).

137. Regarding the phrase "alaṅkāre" and so forth: such a state of extreme delicacy (*sukhumālatā*) of this kind, even if devoid of ornaments—that is, even if lacking the ornament of meaning—is [still] thus.

The meaning is that it "ascends" or reaches the presence—that is, the state of being face-to-face—within the range of the speech of the wise who possess wisdom. "Radiant with that" means it shines by means of that ornament of meaning arising from both natural expression and artful expression;
thus, it becomes exceptionally and preeminently delightful and pleasing. The analysis of the compound is: "devoid of ornaments" (*alaṅkārehi vihīnā*) and "radiant with that" (*tena ujjalā*).
These peacocks—the sages—sport, intoxicated by the clouds—the sages, their plumage being the thrill of horripilation, their strength augmented by the shouts of "Well done! (sādhuvāda).

(138) He illustrates this with the verse beginning "romañce" and so forth. "Romance" refers to horripilation (lomahaṃsa), or rather, the thrills themselves are the "romance. These are the "piñcha" (feathers).
Those whose arrangement and construction are in the form of a parasol;
those whose speech or utterance is like the word "Sādhu" (well done); those who have produced a sound known as a *kekā* cry;
and peacocks intoxicated with joy by the water-bearing cloud that resembles a sage, is like a sage, or is reckoned as a sage—these are like virtuous men or are indeed virtuous themselves.
Peacocks sport; they move about endowed with grace, meaning they take delight in one another.
(138) He illustrates the subtlest form of the *atthālaṅkāra* (ornament of meaning) with the verse beginning "On the body" (*rome*) and so forth.

The arrangement of the feathers of the bristling hair—hair resembling swans—or rather, the hair itself as an arrangement of peacock feathers (*piñcha*), expanded out like a parasol, is augmented by the sound of applause.

"Excellent!"—with such words of praise, or with cries like the low, sweet warbling of peacocks, these "peacocks of the virtuous" (sādhu-sikhāvalā)—who are intoxicated by the rain-cloud that resembles a sage (muni-megha-mmada), or who are intoxicated by the cloud known as a sage (muni) resembling a sage—are sporting, being devoid of frivolity;
for they are like noble persons, or indeed, they are like peacocks of the virtuous. This is a condensed metaphor (samāsa-rūpaka) whose scope encompasses all objects.
In the secondary sense, it should be understood as "like horripilation," "like applause," "like a sage," and "like virtuous people";

in the primary sense, it should be understood as "like a fan made of feathers," "like one who has kindled a fire," "like a cloud," and "like a peacock. Furthermore, "horripilation" itself is the "feathers" (*piñcha*);
those for whom there is such a "fan" (*racanā*) of them; the "utterance" (*vāda*) of "well done" (*sādhu*); and that which is "kindled" (*āhita*) and "prosperous" (*dhani*).
The phrase is: *ceti ca*, *sādhuvādo āhitaddhani yesanti ca*, *muni eva meghoti ca*, *tena ummadāti ca*, and *sādhavo eva sikhāvalāti ca*.

In the expression “*munīmegho*,” the lengthening of the vowel is for the sake of preserving the meter (*chanda*). It pertains both to the state of being delicate (*sukhumālatta*) and to the scope of the word-meaning (*padatthavisaya*).
Just as in the case of words such as *mata* (dead) and others, there is the mention of [their] specific qualities like being "killed" (*kitti-sesa*) and so forth;

so too, it is not only the state of being delicate (*sukhumālatā*) that exists, but the meaning (*attha*) also exists—this is what is shown by the statement beginning with “‘Sukhumālattaṃ’” and so on.
