“It exists indeed” (*attheva*) means it is certainly found; however, its occurrence is possible through the avoidance of what is inappropriate, vulgar, and so forth. “As” (*yathā*) provides an illustration of that.
When words such as *mātā* (mother) and others are to be discussed, there is the praising—that is, the speaking—of words such as *kittisa* (fame). 139.
To show that this delicacy (*sukhumālatā*) exists not only in sound but also in meaning, he says: "delicacy" and so forth.
Delicacy exists in meaning alone, and delicacy also exists within the scope of the word-meaning—that is, within the domain denoted by the word.
And that [propriety] is accomplished by avoiding the common faults (*gāmadosa*) that lack fitness (*ocitya*). The word "yathā" (as/how) serves as an illustration of that.
Regarding the words "mata" and so forth which ought to be mentioned, there is the mention—that is, the speaking—of words such as "kitti" and "sesa. As for the analysis (*viggaha*):

"mata" and so forth refers to those such as "jīvitakkhayaṃ patto" (one who has reached the end of life); and "kittisesa" and so forth refers to those such as "devattaṃ gato, saggakāyamalaṅkarī" (gone to the state of a deva, adorning the body of heaven).
This [work], which is a repository of delightful qualities through the association of well-knit words,
is worthy of respect for its structural coherence.
“Sileso” (cohesion) means as follows.
He demonstrates cohesion with the words beginning “siliṭṭhānaṃ. Because they lack looseness in their composition, the words are mutually cohesive;
through their conjunction, there arises a delightful and agreeable quality, which is its abode—that is, its locus of occurrence.

Having restated that "it is called *sabandhagarava* (the weight of the connection) because it exists together with the weight [imposed] by the composition of the connection (*bandha*) and its lack of looseness," it is then prescribed that "this is what is known as *silesa* (punning).
He provides an example with the words "just as that" (*taṃ yathā*).
The meaning of the phrase "just as that" is that just as this is a *silesa*, so too should others of a similar kind be understood; it does not mean that this alone is such.
140. Now he defines *silesa* (alliteration) with the words beginning "siliṭṭha" and so forth. It is the abode of the quality of being delightful through the association of closely joined words;
it is the cause for the arrangement of sounds that are proximate by way of their place of articulation (*ṭhāna*) and effort (*karaṇa*);

it is the locus where the quality of charm arises through the conjunction of words mutually dependent upon one another; and it consists in the non-laxity of the composition known as *bandhagārava* (the gravity of the bond).
That which proceeds together with this is called "bandha" (bond) and "silesa" (cohesion). "Silesa" means the weight of the bond; here, the bond that establishes it is also called "silesa.

It is [called] *siliṭṭhā* (smooth), *te* (those), *padā* (words), *ca* (and), *iti* (thus), *tesaṃ* (of them), *saṃsaggo* (conjunction), *ca* (and), *tena* (by that), *ramaṇīyo* (delightful), *ca* (and), *so* (that), *eva* (itself), *guṇo* (quality), *ca* (and), *tassa* (of that), *ālayo* (abode), *ca* (and), *bandhassa* (of the bond), *guruno* (heavy), *bhāvo* (state), *ca* (and), *tena* (by that), *saha* (together), *pavattatīti* (proceeds).
And there is the sentence (*vākya*). For example: “*Bālindu*,” etc.
May that splendor of the lotus-feet of the Lord of Munis—which cuts through the illusion of the young moon by means of the radiance of the rows of her fingernails—be a protective ornament for you.
141. “*Bālindu*,” etc. *Bālindu*: the fifth [digit] of the fifth moon;
its *vibbhama* is its captivating beauty. That which cuts this by its nature is *bālinduvibbhamacchediyo*.

The rows (*āvaliyo*) of the nails—those claws resembling the digits of the fifth moon—are joined (*valitā*) together with their splendors (*kantibhi*), that is, their beauties. This belongs to the Lord of Sages (*munindassa*).
The feet themselves are the lotuses (*padumāni*); their radiance is what he addresses you with collectively. May he protect you.

141. *Bālindu*... together with the beauty of his rows of nails, which possess a nature that eclipses the splendor of the young moon, that radiance of the lotus-feet of the Lord of Sages—that splendor of the lotus-feet of the Perfectly Enlightened One—may it be with you.
The analysis (*viggaha*) is as follows: "May he protect you" (*avataṃ rakkhatū*); "he who is both a fool and the moon" (*bālo ca so indu ca*); "the confusion of that [moon]" (*tassa vibbhamo*);

"that which cuts through by means of its virtue" (*taṃ chindati sīlena*); "rows of nails" (*nakhānaṃ āvaliyo*); "the beauty of those [rows]" (*tāsaṃ kanti*); "the rows of nail-beauty which cut through the confusion of the fool-moon" (*bālinduvibbhamacchediyo ca tā nakharāvalikantīyo ca*);
"the feet of the Lord of Sages" (*munindassa padāni*); "those very [feet] are lotuses" (*tāniyeva ambhojāni*); and "the beauty of those [lotuses]" (*tesaṃ kanti*). This is the analysis.
If any excellence whatsoever is perceived as being preeminent,
by that it would be considered noble.
The method of binding with support (sanāthā bandhapaddhati).
142. To demonstrate that one must maintain magnanimity (*udāratta*), he says: “*Ukkaṃsavanto*,” etc.

If any quality whatsoever—such as the excellence of generosity (*cāgātisaya*) and so forth—is understood, known, or perceived as being *ukkaṃsavanto*, that is, preeminent or excessive, without the restriction that “this alone [is it],” then it is understood as such.
Because it will be stated [later] as "the method of composition" (*bandhapaddhati*), the rule is: "This shall be sublime. To the question, "Let this be sublime;

what of it?", he says "by that," and so forth. By that quality of excellence (*ukkaṃsavaṃta*), the sequence of composition (*racanakkama*) possesses a protector (*sanāthā*)—that is, it exists together with the sublime qualities of the Lord (*nāthabhūta*). Thus, it is said to be "possessing prosperity" (*sampadāvatī*).
142. Now he indicates loftiness (*udāratta*) with the words beginning "exalted" (*ukkaṃsa*).
If any quality whatsoever—such as the excellence of generosity—that possesses exaltation or pre-eminence, which is to be presented through a series of words, is perceived;

that is, if it is understood within some poetic composition (*bandha*), this aforementioned quality is called "lofty. If one asks what the purpose of this is, [it is] because it binds the composition.

A series of words (*padāvali*) is rendered well-supported and possessed of a foundation when it is endowed with that preeminent quality (*ukkaṃsavatā guṇena*). The grammatical analysis (*viggaha*) is:
"that which has preeminence" (*ukkaṃso assa atthi*), "it exists together with a protector" (*nāthena saha vattati*), and "the path of the bond" (*bandhassa paddhati*).
O Gotama, those whose limbs are anointed with the pollen from your lotus-feet;
"Aho! Those beings go entirely to the state free from dust.
(143) He explains this with the words beginning "pāde" and so forth. "Gotama"—this is an address to the Blessed One by his clan name.

The analysis of the compound is: "those whose limbs (*gattāni*) are smeared (*littāni*), that is, anointed (*upadihitāni*), by the dust (*raja*), the pollen (*reṇu*), of your, the Blessed One’s, lotus-feet (*pādambhojānaṃ*). Those...

People are living beings; because they are unsmeared even by a minute speck of dust (*rajo-lava*) in every respect, they have emerged from "dust"—that is, from the defilements (*kilesa*)—and are thus "dustless" (*niraja*).
They attain, that is, reach, the state of being dustless, the state of being free from defilements (*nirajatta-nam*). Oh, how wonderful!
For while those who are smeared with dust would surely be defiled, you, sir, [bring about] a state of being smeared for people by the very dust of your feet.
He makes [them] stainless; the meaning is: "It is wonderful for you.

Now he provides an illustration with the verse beginning "O lotus-feet," and so forth. O Gotama, those beings whose limbs are smeared with the dust of your lotus-feet—those creatures whose heads, foreheads, and other parts of the body are covered by the pollen of your foot-lotuses—they are, in every respect, freed from the dust and mire known as the defilements (*kilesa*).
Because they are unstained, they go to—that is, they reach—the state of being stainless in every respect, the condition of being free from the dust of the defilements;
oh, how wonderful! The sense is: those who are "dust-stained" would indeed be defiled, yet even when beings are stained by the dust of your feet, you make them stainless.
Here, the supreme excellence of the Blessed One’s qualities is illuminated. His feet themselves are like lotuses (*ambhoja*).
And: "those who are called kings," and "those whose limbs are smeared by them," and "those who have emerged from stains (rajas) which are defilements," and "the state of those"—such is the sentence.
Thus, the pre-eminence of the Victor’s power is seen here.
One possessed of wisdom should contemplate the supreme [state] according to this method.
(144) If it is asked: "What excellence of quality is there here by which the bond becomes well-guarded? He says:
"Thus," and so forth. "Thus" means that the preeminence—the surpassing intensity—of the power of the Conquerors, the majesty of the Fully Enlightened One, is seen, is perceived.
Regarding this bond: therefore, through the power of the Conquerors (*jina*), may the bond be well-supported by excellence in its highest degree.

Extending this method to other instances as well, he says "the wise one" (*paññavā*) and so forth. One who is wise, endowed with wisdom, should by this method—in this manner—reflect upon or contemplate another such as this, of such a kind.
144. Now, with the words beginning "Thus" (*evaṃ*), he demonstrates both the indication of the qualities as previously described and the instruction for disciples.

Here, in this immediately preceding verse, the excellence (*samukkaṃsa*)—that is, the preeminence—is seen, is perceived, of the power of the Conquerors (*jinānubhāva*), the majesty of the Tathāgata, according to the sequence already stated.
Therefore, by means of that quality characterized by excellence, which is designated as the power of the Conquerors...
The bond would become possessed of a protector. One who is wise, endowed with praised knowledge, should by this method and in this sequence contemplate and conceive such another supreme [state].
That too should be understood as sublime.
That which is a praised qualification [is called *viśeṣaṇa*]; for example:
*kīḷāsara*, *līlā*, *hāsa*, *hāsa* (variant *ka.*), *hemaṅgada*, and so forth.

145. To show another noble variety, he says "noble" (*udāra*), and so forth. That which adopts a praiseworthy and commendable qualification should not be understood as "noble" in the manner previously stated.
He provides an illustration with the word "such as" (*yathā*).
"An arrow for the sake of play," "a smile joined with sport," and "an armlet made of gold"—these are compounds; the external meaning is "those things of which these are the first."

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is an inclusion of flower garlands, jeweled girdles, and so forth. However, this [type of ornament] arises from the abandonment of harshness in composition and vulgarity.

(145) By the words "noble" (*udāra*) and so on, he shows another [kind of ornament] as well. That which is a praiseworthy qualification—that is, a qualification worthy of praise—should also be understood as "noble.
He illustrates that with the word "just as" (*yathā*). A "sport-lake" (*kīḷāsara*) is a lake made for sport. A "playful smile" (*līlāhāsa*).

The analysis of the compound is as follows: *līlāya yutto hāso* (a smile joined with playfulness), *hemaṅgadādayo* (golden armlets and so forth)—meaning golden (*hema*) armlets (*aṅgada*) and so on—and *kīḷatthāya saroti ca* (and "it flows for the sake of sport"), *līlāya yutto hāso* (a smile joined with playfulness), *hemaṃ hemamayaṃ aṅgadaṃ* (golden means made of gold, [referring to] an armlet), *līlāhāso ca hemaṅgadañca* (both the playful smile and the golden armlet), and *tāni ādīni yesaṃ kusumadāmamaṇimekhalādīnaṃ* (those which are the beginning of things such as flower garlands, jeweled girdles, and so forth).
This [type of] sublime composition (*udāro bandho*) is accomplished by abandoning faults such as harshness of construction and vulgarity.
Transcending worldly states,
desirable even to all people— this is what is called "Kanti" (Desirability) for one who has thus spoken.
That [meaning] has been stated by way of exclusion, as in "O Lord of Sages" (*muninda*), and so forth.
(146) He explains the desired [meaning] with the words "worldly" (*lokiya*) and so on. That which is known in the world is "worldly" (*lokiya*); that worldly meaning is the object to be expressed.
That which is not surpassed, not exceeded by any poets or other people, and which is beloved and captivating, is called *kānti*.
This quality of sound, moreover, arises from the avoidance of the fault of over-elaboration (*ativutta*).
Therefore, he says: "Of that which is over-elaborated," and so forth. The purpose of the examples has already been stated above.
146. Now, he demonstrates *kānti* (elegance) with the words beginning "worldly" (*lokiya*).
That which does not transcend worldly meanings, nor transcend the meanings of words well-known in the world, and which is beloved and pleasing to all people and to all poets, is called *kānti*.

It has been explained in the section on the avoidance of faults as being stated by way of avoiding the fault of *ativutta* (excessive expression). Precisely because it avoids the fault of *ativutta*, [it is so described].
The intention is that because it is accomplished through beauty (*kānti*), its characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) are indeed those of this [beauty]. The analysis of the compound *loke vidito* is:

"that which is known in the world" (*so ca so attho ceti*). The word "just as" (*yathā*) shows an example of beauty, namely "O Lord of Sages" (*muninda*), and so forth; that has already been explained. Because of the clarity of meaning (*atthabyatta*), the referent (*abhidheyya*)—
That which is to be led by way of the word and by way of the meaning—
this [method] is shown as the "avoidance of the term" for that which is to be led by both.
As in the cases of "a mirage" (*marīci*) and so forth, and "delighting the mind" (*manonurañjana*) and so forth.
(147) It clarifies the manifestation of meaning through the phrase "having a manifestly clear denotation" (*atthabyattābhidheyya*) and so on.

The non-derivability of the connected meaning of the denotation—whether from the word itself, from its literal sense, or from its functional capacity—is the understanding [of that meaning]; otherwise, there would be no other way of reaching it, because there is no alternative mode of access.
For it has been said: "The state of being difficult to understand transcends the power of words. Having repeated that, the clarification of the meaning is now set forth.
That [clarification], moreover, arises from avoiding faults such as being scattered or difficult to lead.

Born from both of those, this lack of being easy to lead (*aneyyatā*) is shown—that is, made manifest—in the exclusion of what is difficult to lead. The meaning of the first and second examples has thus been stated.
147. Now, he demonstrates the clarity of meaning (*atthabyatti*) with the words beginning "clarity of meaning" (*atthabyatti*).
The clarity of meaning is the state of the denoted object not being led away from the word, from its literal sense, or from its functional capacity, because it exists right there;

it is the absence of anything further that must be brought forward or stated regarding either the word or the meaning. This [clarity] arises from both of those two, and thus it is characterized by this state of being unleadable.

The clarity of meaning (*atthabyatti*) is demonstrated and revealed in the section on avoiding faults in what is to be understood (*neyyaparihāre*), specifically regarding the avoidance of defects in what is to be understood.

Since it is stated that "the state of being difficult to reach transcends both the word and its functional capacity," the term *atthapatī* (clarity of meaning) cannot be found otherwise than through the word and its capacity; therefore, it is said here: "from the word and from the meaning. Thus, *atthabyatti* and *patīti* [are explained].

And there is the sentence: "There is no further meaning to be brought forth for that which is denoted," and "the state of being that," and "those two meanings of the word," and "that which has those as its constituent parts," and "the exclusion of what is to be inferred.

Now, with the words beginning "Just as" (*yathā*), he introduces examples for the two modes of clarifying the meaning in their respective order by means of the pair of verses beginning with "Death" (*marī-*).
That has already been explained above.
Furthermore, according to the meaning—as it says:
"O Wise One, the stainlessness of intrinsic nature..."
In vain are those toenails of yours,
since the shadows of the crowns of infinite beings bowing before you do not leave them.
148. Furthermore, in the second verse, *dhīrā* is an address meaning "O wise ones.
That natural purity and innate stainlessness of your toenails is in vain—that is, empty. Why is that?

Because, for this reason, those toenails possess the luster and complexion of the shadows cast by the crowns (*moḷi*) of the bowed and submissive infinite Nāga kings, or else by the infinite crowns of men and gods who have prostrated themselves.
"They do not abandon, they do not relinquish; rather, they shed their skin.

Here, regarding the nails, because the shedding of skin on the toenails is invariably and continuously associated with the *moḷi* (the hair-tuft), it is clearly understood by implication that [the gods] pay homage to the Blessed One’s lotus feet, as well as to the gods and others.
148. “Furthermore, by way of meaning, ‘just as their own nature,’ and so forth: O Wise One, the natural purity and innate stainlessness of your toenails is not in vain—that is, it is not empty.

Why is that? Because those toenails belong to the crown of the infinite Naga King who bows down [in prostration], or rather, they belong to the crests (*moḷi*) of the infinite gods and humans who bow down.”
Their shadows do not abandon or desert their natural luster; rather, having relinquished their ordinary color, they become like the radiance of their crowns.

Therefore, in this context, because there is an absence of any lack of continuous adoration toward such [beings], the continuous adoration paid by the Kṣatriyas and others at the pair of lotus-feet of the Lord of Sages—which occurs when the rays of the fingernails, resembling moonbeams, reach a state where their own natural luster is not suppressed by the rays of the crowns—is [the subject].

It is understood through the force of the context (*sāmatthiya*). [The analysis is as follows: "the state of that" (*tassa bhāvo*); "and by that, they are stainless" (*tena amālā*); "and the state of those two" (*tesaṃ bhāvo*);
in the first alternative, "it is both bent down (*avanato*) and infinite (*ananto*)" (*avanato ca so ananto ca*); "its crest-lock (*moḷī*)" (*tassa moḷī*); "in its shadow" (*tassa chāyāya*).

In the second alternative, "they are both infinite and crest-locks" (*anantā ca te moḷī ca*); "of the infinite-crest-locks that are bent down" (*avanatānaṃ anantamoḷī*); and "their shadow" (*tesaṃ chāyāya*). Such is the sentence.
“Even the wise, though united, imagine that this quality called concentration (samādhi)—which has reached the occasion for its manifestation—is the ‘essence of bondage.

(149) He states the fruit and function of concentration with the words beginning “bondage” (bandhe), etc. “Yaṃ” means that concentration which [is the cause] of the state of being about to arise as a roar of bondage.
"Sāra" means the life-force of all things; because they are dependent upon it, all wise people, even those who are learned and poets, think, consider, and know it.
This quality called "samādhi"—which is synonymous with concentration—has reached its peak in others due to its unsurpassed nature in regard to vision and exposition;
thus it has been presented according to the sequence of the enumeration.
149. Now he explains the *samādhis* with the words beginning "bandhi" and so forth.

Even all wise poets, though united, consider that *samādhi*—which they regard as the very life of *bandha*, consisting of what is called the mixture of *padya* and *gajja*—to be the quality known as *samādhi*.
This quality has now reached the occasion for its demonstration, having arrived at the place of exposition according to the sequence previously indicated.

The analysis is: "it exists," "the essence of bondage," "and they enter into the vision," and "he has attained that. Another phenomenon [arises] elsewhere than from that, in accordance with the boundaries of the world.
"Because it is rightly concentrated (*sammā ādhīyate*), it is defined as 'concentration' (*samādhi*).
(150) To the question, "How is this linguistic usage—that what is bound is called 'concentration'—justified?", he says "of another," and so forth. Of another...
When a quality (*guṇa*) is established as a property (*dhamma*) in relation to its primary substrate (*vatthu*), then— because of that—

by conforming to worldly convention (*lokasīmā*) and following worldly understanding (*lokappatīti*) regarding another, non-primary object, the very conformity to worldly convention is here rightly and properly attributed (*ādhīyate*) or superimposed (*āropyate*) as "goodness" (*sādhutta*);
for this reason, such a property is called "concentration" (*samādhi*).
The meaning is: "It is called *samādhi* here because it is properly (*sammā*) placed (*ādhīyati*)," having thus extracted [the etymology] as "it is spoken of after being led forth.

Regarding the doubt as to how this conventional term "concentration" (*samādhi*) applies to the domain of binding, he first states the etymological derivation (*nibbacana*) in the passage beginning with "of another," etc.
Because another phenomenon is the primary object of concentration, [it is so called].

The quality that is well-established in the primary object is correctly applied and established elsewhere—in a non-primary object—by conforming to worldly convention (*lokavohāra*) and by not contradicting the boundaries of worldly usage (*lokamariyādā*), simply through following worldly understanding.
For this reason, this aforementioned quality is etymologically defined and called "concentration" (*samādhi*). [The phrase] "the property of another" means...
The analysis [of the compound] is: "and," "the boundary of the world," and "conformity to that.
Summary of Concentration:
The Dhamma of living beings is rightly established somewhere in what is not a living being.
In the formless, there is the state of being possessed of form; in the flavorless, there is the state of being possessed of flavor;
and in the non-fluid, there is the state of being possessed of fluidity. Even for that which is not an agent, there is the status of being an agent;
and even for that which is not a body, there is the state of being solid. These are their respective forms.
151–152. He states the subject of concentration with the words beginning “apāṇe,” etc.

In some instances, the quality (guṇa) or property (dhamma) belonging to living beings—that is, to those possessing breath—is correctly applied (ādhīyate) or superimposed (āropyate) upon an object devoid of breath, that is, one lacking life, by following worldly convention;
the same applies to the subsequent cases as appropriate. “Nirūpeti” means [superimposing] upon an object devoid of form; the word “kvaci” (in some instances) recurs throughout all these cases.
In a basis that is bodiless, non-material, and uncomposite, the examples for the hardness and firmness of those aforementioned concentrations are stated in their respective order. 151–152.
By means of the plural term "concentrations" (*samādhayo*) indicated in the summary, he demonstrates the objective domain of those concentrations.

“*Apāṇe*, etc.”: In some place, the quality (*dhamma*) of living beings—those bound by sense faculties—is correctly placed or superimposed upon a thing devoid of life (*apāṇa*), in accordance with worldly convention;
in some cases, the quality of a material thing (*rūpayutta*) possessing form is [superimposed] upon a thing lacking form (*nirūpa*);
and in some cases, the quality of a thing possessing flavor (*sarasa*) is [superimposed] upon a flavorless thing (*nirasa*).
In some cases, the quality (*dhamma*) of a moist substance (*dravavantavatthu*) is correctly applied to that which is not moist and is devoid of moisture;

in some cases, the agency (*kattutā*), which is an agent-quality (*kattuguṇa*), is [applied] even to a non-agent; and in some cases, the quality of a solid and rigid substance (*kaṭhinassa thaddhassa vatthuno dhammo*) is correctly applied even to what is bodiless and devoid of a body.
The form (*rūpa*) of these six concentrations (*samādhi*) is the illustration (*udāharaṇa*) in order: "in one who is breathless" (*apāṇe*).
"Of Pāṇini" means it may be or could be according to the sequence of what has been taught. "There are no living beings (pāṇā) in this" means:

[the word] is derived from *rūpa*, it is connected with *rūpa*, it is derived from *rasa*, it exists together with *rasa*, it is different from *drava*, it is connected with *drava* or the state of being *drava*, it is different from the agent (*kattā*), and it is the state of the agent; [of these], there is none.
The analysis of the compound is: "it has a body" (sarīram assa). This is from the Exposition of Concentration:
"The nature of living beings toward those who are not living."
“O Lord, because of union even by day with your moon-like ūrṇā-hair, the night-lilies, I imagine, rejoice free from sleep. (153) Regarding the verse beginning with “Ūrṇā”:
He addresses the Blessed One as “Lord” (*nātha*) because he is the sole refuge for the three worlds. [The word] “your” (*tava*)...

"Through union—that is, by coming together—with the full moon, which is designated as the hair-tuft (*uṇṇā*) and the bodily elements (*dhātu*), the night-lilies (*kumudinī*), the lilies (*kumudiniyo*), and the beds of lilies (*kumudākara*) rejoice even during the day;
they are 'viniddā,' meaning free from sleep. I imagine that they 'sampamodanti,' meaning they indeed rejoice exceedingly.
Herein, the state of being non-sentient is superimposed upon the sentient phenomenon of the union with the moon-tree, and upon the rejoicing and the freedom from sleep.

When the moon is full of wool-like rays, and the night-lilies have likewise assumed the state of women, this well-known phenomenon is called "concentration" (samādhi) because of its stabilization in accordance with worldly convention.
And the word denoting it, by way of metaphorical application (upacāra), demonstrates a linguistic usage that follows the meaning; the same applies to what follows, as appropriate.
153. Among those, he provides an illustration of the concentration on the breath-object (*pāṇidhamma-samādhi*) with the words beginning "the ūṇā," and so forth.

O Lord, because of the union—the mutual coming together—with your *ūṇā*, that is, the full moon consisting of the circle of hair-tufts, the night-lotuses known as the beds of white water-lilies (*kairava*) are, I think, joyfully blooming even during the day.
"I imagine they are exceedingly satisfied" refers to the joy of Indra (Indusampamoda), which is understood through the word "saha.
Here, three meanings—sexual union known as the act of breathing, the departure of sleep, and the state of being exhilarated—are established as having the nature of living beings (*pāṇidhamma*).

This is achieved by applying them to the three non-living things known as the full moon, the *induka* flower, and the night-lily (*kumudinī*) by means of intellectual superimposition (*āropana*), without overstepping worldly convention (*lokavohāra*). Thus, these three meanings are well-known through their functional characteristics of living beings.

Here, "concentrations" (samādhayo) refers to the states of concentration; the texts that establish them should also be regarded as "concentration" by way of metaphorical designation (*tadupacāra*), because they follow the meaning.

Furthermore, the analysis (*viggaha*) is: "Puṇṇo" (full) and "indū" (the moon), thus "puṇṇindu"; and "those from whom sleep has departed," thus "vigataniddā. [This applies] to that which is joined with form (*rūpayutta*) when formless (*nirūpe*).
People who immerse themselves in the flavors of compassion, as if in the flavor of the Deathless, are happy and free from faults, O Lord, through their bowing at your lotus feet.
(154) “Compassion,” and so forth. O Lord, those people throughout the hollows of the three worlds who bow down at your lotus feet by means of prostration—

Beings [delight] in qualities that are like the taste of compassion and the taste of mercy, as if they were the taste of nectar or the taste of ambrosia. For the *Amarakośa* (3.3.226) states in its glossary:
"In the erotic sentiment it is poison; in energy it is vigor; in a quality it is passion; in a liquid it is flavor.

Here, those who are "sinking" or "submerging"—that is, being overwhelmed—have their faults, such as the bodily humors (wind, etc.), destroyed on the side of the nectar; whereas in other contexts, those whose faults, such as passion and so forth, have been destroyed and lost, [are the ones who attain it].
"Viggaha" means conflict. "Sukhitā" means those who have attained (itā) happiness (sukha)—that is, physical and mental bliss; this is the meaning.
154. Now, he cites an example of concentration on material phenomena (*rūpadhamma-samādhi*) with the words beginning "Dayā.
O Protector, those people—gods and humans—who bow at your lotus-feet (*pādambuja*), [behold you] as if in nectar-essences, like in the waters of ambrosia (*sudhājala*).
Sinking and immersing themselves in the essence of compassion—the quality of mercy that is not shared by others—they have their faults destroyed;
their wind, bile, and other humors are cured, or else their passion and other defects are eradicated. Thus they are happy, having thereby attained the bliss known as agelessness and deathlessness.

Here, the act of sinking, which occurs in water possessed of form, is metaphorically attributed to the formless quality of mercy. Compassion itself is the "essence" (*rasa*) and the "quality" (*guṇa*).

And: *ca*, *amatā eva rasā* (nectar itself is the flavor), *hatā vātādayo rāgādayo vā dosā yesam* (those in whom the winds and so forth, or passion and so forth, have been destroyed), *pādāni eva ambujāni* (feet themselves are lotuses), and *tesu ānatā* (bowed down before them)—this is the analysis (*viggaha*).
In the *Amarakośa* (3.3.226), which states:
*“siṅgārādau viśeṣe vīriye, guṇe rāge drave rasaḥ,”* the word *rasa* here refers to both quality (*guṇa*) and water (*jala*).
O Sage, those who do not find faith in you,
though you possess the quality of sweetness that is free from all dregs—
what kind of mental conduct is theirs, O you whose food has the quality of pungency? (Sī.)
155. “In the sweet,” and so forth. One who moves by means of wisdom is a *dhīra* (wise one).

O wise one, as for those people who do not take delight—that is, do not feel serene confidence—in your sweet and heart-stealing qualities such as compassion, what is the nature of the activity of their minds, the movement of their consciousness? How is it perceived? It is not understood; one cannot say, “It is like this.”
Because they are averse to the realization of such qualities, they are connected with the darkness of delusion. 155.
Now, he cites an example of one whose mind is concentrated on the essence of the Dhamma, beginning with the words "O sweetness," and so forth:
"O steadfast one, even toward those sweet qualities of yours—those naturally beautiful qualities of compassion and wisdom—those people of inferior disposition do not have faith."
What is the nature of the mental activity, the movement of the mind, of those people who possess bitter qualities and non-sweet qualities? How does it develop?

It is analyzed as follows: "It is moved and set in motion by wisdom (*dhiyā īrati pavattati*)," and "How is that [movement] seen? and "Those in whom there are bitter qualities (*ye santi khārā guṇā*).

Herein, what is called "concentration" (*samādhi*) consists of the two qualities of sweetness and bitterness, which are phenomena endowed with a superimposed flavor upon that which is devoid of flavor.
For one who has become fluid through the fluid [remedy],
the small dose of *sabbatthasiddha* to be drunk from the hollowed palm possesses great merit;
it runs in all directions, characterized by the radiant beauty of the *kunda* flower.

156. “The Accomplishment of All Aims,” and so forth. From the small vessel of the Great Sage who has accomplished all aims, the drinkable [nectar]—possessing the characteristic of the splendor of the *kunda* flower, radiant with the beauty of the *kunda* blossom, and bursting forth with great qualities—flows everywhere, in all directions and intermediate points.
156. Now, with the words beginning “Sabbattha,” he indicates an example of concentration associated with fluidity (*dravayutta-samādhi*):

“O Tathāgata, you who have accomplished all things (*sabbattha-siddha*), who have perfected all duties (*sabbakicca-parinipphanna*), or who are endowed with all perfections (*nipphanna-sabbattha-samannāgata*), the beauty of jasmine (*kundasobhā*)—characterized by the splendor of jasmine—that is to be drunk from a small vessel (*cūḷakapuṭa-peyyā*), [is equal] in its characteristics to the splendors of jasmine.”

Or, "great" means that great qualities—either because of their vast number or because of their great power—are like the splendor of a bowl, or else the great qualities such as *arahatta* (worthiness) run everywhere, all around, in the ten directions.
Herein, the state of being a small vessel for drinking, which is a quality consisting of a liquid substance, is superimposed upon a quality devoid of liquid substance;
this is what is called "concentration" (*samādhi*). And all those meanings are "and" (*ca*), and they are established.

The grammatical analysis (*viggaha*) is as follows: *yasseti ca*, *cūḷakameva puṭamiti ca*, *tena peyyāti ca*, *mahantā ca te guṇā ceti ca*, *kundānaṃ sobhāti ca*, and *tāhi samānaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ yesanti ca*.
This is an instance of "agency where there is no agent" (*akattari kattutā*).
The various blunt weapons discharged by the enemy Māra, having been shamed, now bow at your feet under another guise. (157) “Māra,” and so forth.
Māra himself is the enemy (*ari*), thus he is the "enemy Māra" (*mārāri*). By him, through his own power and weaponry... [the rest of the verse continues].
Or, by the power of the army, various and manifold weapons such as *bhindivāla* and so forth— cast away and abandoned facing the enemy, including *kuṇṭha-bheṇḍivāla* and so forth (*ka*)—
having lost their sharpness and having become blunt, feel ashamed because they have reached that state of dullness; feeling ashamed, thinking, "Even for us, whose majesty is world-renowned,
such a thing has occurred," they appear in another guise, [thinking] "How indeed..."
Thinking, "Others might not recognize us," he changed his own weapon-attire for a floral attire;
"Jina" is an address, and "pādānatā" means bowing down at your feet. 157.
Now, he indicates an example of the concentration on the nature of the agent with the words beginning "O enemy of Māra. O Jina, [the one] released from the power of the enemy Māra...
Various weapons— such as bhindivālas, iron arrows, spears, lances, and so forth— of many kinds,
discharged by the enemy Māra with his own spear or released by Māra’s army and cast down before him, became blunt and lost their sharpness; feeling ashamed, as if thinking,
"Why has such a failure occurred even to us, whose power is thus world-renowned?", they appeared under another guise.
Thinking, "How might others not recognize us?", they cast off their armed appearance and, assuming another guise—
that of flower-gatherers— bowed at your feet, falling prostrate near them. Herein, the shame (lajjana), the transformation into another appearance, and the bowing (ānata)—
these meditative absorptions (samādhayaḥ) are attributed to the objects of shame and so forth, which are themselves non-agents (akattubhūteṣu viṣayeṣu).

The analysis [of the compound] is as follows: *māro* (Māra) and *eva* (indeed), *arī* (enemy), and *iti* (thus); *balena* (by force) and *vissaṭṭhā* (dismissed); *mārārinā* (by the enemy of Māra) and *balavissaṭṭhā* (dismissed by force);

*mārārino* (of the enemy of Māra) and *balaṃ* (army) and *senā* (host); *iti* (thus) and *tena* (by that) and *vissaṭṭhā* (dismissed); *nānā* (various) and *anekavidhā* (of many kinds) and *pakārā* (modes) and *yesaṃ* (whose);

*aññesaṃ* (of others) and *veso* (dress/appearance); *añño* (other) and *ca* (and) *so* (that) and *veso* (dress) and *cā* (and); *pādesu* (at the feet) and *ānatā* (bowed) and *iti* (thus). This is the grammatical analysis (*viggaha*).
The sun-like Lord of Sages,
having cast off the body of the Kaṭhina robe,
has risen upon the mountain of enlightenment.
It shines with the radiance of the true Dhamma, utterly dispelling the blinding darkness [of ignorance]. 158.
Regarding the verse beginning with “Muninda”: awakening is like the knowledge of omniscience, or it is that very [awakening] which is the mountain of sunrise, the mountain of emergence.
At that time, at the end of the night, when he had gone forth, the Lord of Sages— arisen and manifest,
like a Lord of Sages, or indeed the Sun himself— shines and glows as he pierces and shatters the blinding darkness,
or delusion, with his rays which are like the True Dhamma, or which are the True Dhamma itself.
158. Now, he cites an example of the formal act (*kaṭhina-dhamma-samādhi*) with the words beginning “O Lord of Sages” (*muninda*).

On the Mountain of the Arising of Enlightenment (*Bodhodaya-acala*), which is like the knowledge of omniscience—or on the Mountain of Arising (*Udayapabbata*) known as the knowledge of omniscience—the Sun of the Lord of Sages, who is like the Lord of Sages or indeed the Lord of Sages himself, arose at the end of the night, having appeared at the time of the defeat of Māra.

The sun shines and glows, piercing and shattering the blinding darkness—the dense darkness of its own nature and the thick darkness of delusion—by means of a ray that is like the True Dhamma, identical to the True Dhamma, or indeed the True Dhamma itself, through its supreme excellence. Herein, "shattering" is a quality belonging to a solid substance;
it is superimposed by the intellect upon darkness, which is not a physical substance, and this is what is called concentration (*samādhi*).

The analysis [of the compound] is as follows: "the Lord of Sages" (*munīnām inda*), "he himself is the sun" (*bhānumā*), "enlightenment itself is the mountain of sunrise" (*udayācala*), and "the True Dharma itself is the ray" (*raṃsī*).
It is that which has emerged from the practice of virtues, having been cast forth by the act of vomiting and spitting [out defilements].
But one may certainly experience village-like desire, thinking it to be exceedingly beautiful.
(159) To show that some quality shines when its primary object is suppressed, but not when it is in its primary object, he says: "Vamana," and so forth.
"Vamana" means vomiting; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), purging and other such acts are included. These aforementioned qualities are subordinate to the principal ones.
The function (*vutti*), which has well-known objects as its domain and is characterized by the apprehension of other objects, takes the form of application (*payoga*);

therefore, that which is not abandoned, not spilled, existing, yet not primary—being exceedingly beautiful and extremely captivating due to its nature as ornamentation—is one thing, whereas the other is said to be "primary" (*mukhya*).
Granted, vulgarity (*gāmmata*) is entirely of an improper nature; however, it is [employed] in composition because it is appropriate for that [specific context].
The meaning is that one finds, acquires, or produces.

Now, among these very phenomena such as the breath and so forth, he says "vomiting, belching," etc., to show that a certain phenomenon is praiseworthy when applied to a secondary object, but blameworthy when applied to its primary object.
This refers to vomiting, belching, and so forth—namely, emesis, eructation, purging, and the like.
That which is free from the discharge of impurities, not employed in a primary sense, uncorrupted, and not being the principal [object], is exceedingly beautiful and very dear to all;

however, another thing—distinct from that and employed in its primary sense, such as vomiting or belching—is indeed entirely vulgar, for it possesses and partakes of the vulgar defect of being naturally unpleasant.
This refers to "vomiting" (*vamana*) and "belching" (*uggirana*).

The grammatical analysis (*viggaha*) is: "and those [qualities] which belong to him" (*yassa etāni*), "the qualities are subordinate to the activity" (*guṇā appadhānā vutti*), and "not separated from that" (*tato apariccuta*).
Under the pretext of vomiting rays of light, the rows of the Sage’s toenails, as if drinking up the splendor of the moon, render it lusterless.

160. He illustrates this with the verse beginning “Of beauty,” and so forth. I imagine that the rows—the series—of the nails on the feet of the Sage, the Perfectly Enlightened One, are drinking, as it were, and taking their fill, because they are spread everywhere;

under the pretext of vomiting—that is, by way of disgorging—their own continuous streams of excellence of beauty, they seem to drink the moonbeams, which possess the luster of the moon, due to being diffused in all directions.
He states the seed of the poetic conceit (*parikappanā-bīja*) with the words "deprived of luster" (*nippabha*), etc., asking, "Of what kind?
They are making that moon devoid of luster, stripped of its radiance, while they are burning [with passion]. For this is the seed of the conceit:

because the moon’s splendor is eclipsed by the beauty of her nails during their embrace, one perceives its lack of luster and conceives the idea that her rows of nails are drinking up the moon’s brilliance.
And the pretext of vomiting beauty.
(160) By the words "of beauty," etc., he indicates an example of the vomiting and spitting out [of beauty] directed toward desirable objects.
The rows of the Sage’s toenails—the series of the Sage’s toenails—are the pretext for vomiting their own beauty, which resembles the splendor of moonbeams.
By the act of vomiting, they render that stainless moon lusterless; because they spread everywhere, as if drinking the splendor of the moon and its rays, they make it lusterless.
Seeing that even the moon, though possessed of radiance, has become lusterless and that the rays of her nails have become predominant because they spread everywhere— *Note:
The provided text fragment appears to be a commentary on a poetic description of a woman’s fingernails (nakharaṃsī) outshining the moon. The translation reflects this interpretation.*

The phrase "they seem to drink the moonlight" refers to the rows of nails; both the drinking of moonlight and the vomiting of one's own luster are not natural occurrences, but are imagined as a poetic conceit (*byāja*) by the poet.

Here, it should be understood that the term "vomiting" (*vamana*), which is applied to a non-primary object—namely, what is designated as "luster" rather than the primary object such as the rice of a meal—is used in a figurative sense (*guṇavutti*). Furthermore, the terms "the conceit of vomiting itself" and "the feet of the Sage" [are examples of this].
The analysis of the compound is as follows: "of those [nails]," "their rows," "the luster of the moon," and "emerging from the radiance.
That which has an inanimate agent, such as "healing" (*rujha*), is a quality-object (*guṇakamma*); that is called a "quality-object-verb" (*guṇakammaka*).
But that which has a sentient agent is the "supreme" quality-object (*guṇakamma*). (Sī.)
161. He concludes what was stated [above] with the words "devoid of mind" (*acitta*), and so forth. Thus, that which has a mindless agent is "mindless-agentive" (*acittakattuka*).

That which has beauty as its object is "beauty-objective" (*guṇakamma*). And that—namely, the vomiting and so forth—becomes pleasing, charming, and delightful because it is appropriate for the connection [of the narrative].
For the rows of nails are the mindless agents, and the splendors are the beauty-objects; thus, the vomiting is exceedingly beautiful. This alone is not [the case].
Rujhati says: “Sacitta,” etc. This [action] such as vomiting and so forth is an action possessing qualities such as having a conscious agent (*sacittakattuka*) and being beneficial (*piyadiguṇa*);
it is supreme and best because it is appropriate for relatives.

161. Furthermore, the excellence of the immediately preceding example lies in the fact that when there is a quality in the object (*kamma*), there is also vomiting and so forth with a conscious agent.
Showing that it is desirable (*iṭṭha*), he says "without a conscious agent" (*acittakattuka*) and so forth.

Thus, in this manner, a subordinate action (*guṇakamma*) possessing an unconscious agent—namely, the nails—which is characterized by the act of scraping, possesses a primary action (*appadhānakamma*) characterized by the luster of the nails;
such an action, like vomiting and so forth, being suitable for composition, produces delight (*ruccana*). This [action], such as vomiting and so forth, even when having a conscious agent...
Even if it possesses consciousness and agency, if the action [of vomiting] is a subordinate action (*guṇakamma*), it is indeed supreme and distinguished;

thus, although there is a genitive case in the sense of a relationship between entities in the word "of desires" (*kantīnam*), the status of the action as the object (*kammatta*) is not exceeded by the act of vomiting.

Furthermore, [the compounds] *acittā* (those who have no mind) and *yassa... kattāro* (whose agents are mindless), as well as *yassa... guṇo kammaṃ* (whose subordinate action is this), are used together.
And the phrase "proceeding by means of the mind" (*cittena vattamāno*). Here, *iti* is a particle used for illustration (*nidassana*) or to indicate a manner (*evaṃ-pakāra*);

or else, it is a collection of particles used at the beginning of a summary or introduction (*nigama-ārambhe*) regarding the words and what is to be expressed, such as "words and what is to be expressed.
The Supreme Victor, as if vomiting forth the essence of his affection for people...
"Who would he not gladden by preaching the sweet Dhamma?

(162). He explains this with the words "as if vomiting," and so forth. That supreme Victor, as if vomiting or disgorging the essence of affection—that is, his own love known as *anurāga*—toward all classes of beings, [preaches] the sweet, most refined Dhamma.

Whom would he not gladden by speaking? He gladdens everyone indeed. Here, the Supreme Victor (*jinavara*) is the agent (*kattā*), consciousness (*sacitta*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*), the essence of affection (*sneharasa*) is the action (*kamma*). 162.
Now, he cites an example under the category of the conscious agent (*sacittaka-kattupakkha*) with the verse beginning "Uggiranto" and so forth. That Supreme Victor...

As if vomiting, as if disgorging, the essence of affection—the passion known as his own love—for all classes of beings, while speaking and teaching the sweet, sublime Dhamma, the True Dhamma, which is excellent in its beginning and so forth, and speaking according to the inclinations of people, what person, of what kind, would he not gladden? He gladdens them all.
Herein, "vomiting" (*uggirana*) refers even to that which possesses the agent characterized by the Supreme Victor’s mind.

It is praised because it is joined with the primary function known as the essence of affection (*sneharasa*). The analysis of the compound is: "affection itself is the essence, which is to say, passion" (*anurāga*).
He who is skilled in the science of grammar, proficient in lexicography, prosody, and poetics, and constantly devoted to their practice;
Thus, even though he was deficient in the art of *kāvya*,
he attained among poets a fame that was truly beyond measure.
Thus [ends the work] composed by the venerable Master Saṅgharakkhita.
The Third Chapter, titled "Understanding the Qualities," in the *Subodhālaṅkāra*. 163.

Even when there is no latent impression (*vāsanā*) derived from other texts, and no corresponding intuition (*paṭibhāna*) following upon it, [one may still succeed] through learning and the power of diligent application.
He instructs that poetry and fame follow from that [knowledge] with the words beginning "he who" (*yo*).
Because there is no fixed rule stating "this alone" regarding any particular word-meaning in grammar (*saddasattha*), he is skilled and clever;
and likewise in lexicography (*nighaṇṭu* or *abhidhānasattha*), in prosody (*chandovicitisattha*) which elucidates the various types of meters and their rules, and in rhetoric (*alaṅkārasattha*).
And he was skilled not only in the science of grammar (*saddasattha*), but moreover,

having applied constant and uninterrupted effort and exertion day and night toward the field of composition, he— though lacking the technical variety of poetic meters (*kavitta*) and devoid of the specific qualities of poetry known as *bandhakaraṇa*—
entered and attained a place among the poets who possess poetic excellence, and acquired no small, indeed very great, fame.
"One who knows" means one who finds or obtains that which is known as having its origin in the characteristic of a composition with pure construction.
Thus, in the *Subodhālaṅkāra-ṭīkā* named *Mahāsāmi*,
within the *Subodhālaṅkāra*.
The third chapter: The Comprehension of Qualities (Guṇāvabodha).

163. Now, having demonstrated the ornaments of sound (*saddālaṅkāra*) according to the order of enumeration, [the author] instructs his students that constant application to this work—which is surrounded by grammar, lexicography, and prosody—is the cause for attaining the great glory of this world and the worlds beyond.

“Whoever is skilled in the science of grammar,” and so forth. Whoever—whether among the elders, the juniors, or those of middle standing—is skilled in the science of grammar, being expert in the analysis and formulation of bases (*pakati*), suffixes (*paccaya*), and so on within the domain of grammatical exposition (*saddānusāsana-byākaraṇa*);
who is also skilled in the Nighaṇṭu, prosody (*chanda*), and the treatises on rhetoric (*alaṅkāra*) as well as the lexicons (*abhidhāna*) and prosody;

who is expert in imparting the understanding of their respective classifications; and who is constantly devoted to the practice through the power of memorization and mental attention (*dhāraṇa-manasikāra*).

He was constantly industrious. Thus, although he was not skilled in poetic composition and lacked the natural qualities of well-crafted verse, he entered the ranks of poets and was counted among the makers of *kāvya*.

Having immersed himself in such ways as composing *kāvya* and writing commentaries on its creation, and having attained that status, he acquired an immense, faultless, and noble reputation characterized by the artistry of a teacher.
One finds or indeed obtains an accumulation of merit or success arising from that [merit].
Application to the aforementioned scriptures is the sole cause of bondage. For it is said: "Natural eloquence..."
“Learning that is very pure,
and unremitting application—
this is the cause of bondage here,” so it is said in the Kāvyādāsā 1.103.
In this context, innate intelligence, wisdom established by its own nature, abundant and stainless learning that is not meager and free from entanglement,
as well as no small application and extensive practice— all of these together constitute the cause and the reason for this bond, for this composition of verses.
[The word *hetu*] is explained here in the sense of "that by which" (*etena*) or "in this matter" (*etasmin*).

Having applied the appropriate suffix and its substitute place, it should be understood as *saddasattha* (grammar). Regarding the phrase "skilled in grammar" (*saddasatthe kusalo*), the analysis (*viggaha*) is:
"lexicon (*nighaṇṭu*) and prosody (*chanda*), and ornamentation (*alaṅkati*) and ornament (*alaṅkāra*). Here, the word *alaṅkati* is neuter in view of the treatise (*sattha*).
It is also [analyzed as]: "one for whom constant application has been made," and "the state of a poet (*kavino bhāvo*)."
Thus, there are two phrases: "it is devoid of conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*) and "that whose intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) is non-dull form.
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Subodhālaṅkāra-nissaya*.

4. Chapter on the Understanding of the Eight Figures of Sense (Atthālaṅkārāvabodhapariccheda) The path of composition, when endowed with the figures of sense (atthālaṅkāra) and possessed of poetic qualities (guṇa), is exceedingly beautiful because it is indeed exceedingly beautiful; therefore, these [figures] shall now be explained.
164. Having thus distinguished the ornaments of sound (*saddālaṅkāra*), he says "the ornaments of meaning" (*atthālaṅkāra*) and so forth, in order to explain the ornaments of meaning.
A "composition" (*bandhapaddhati*) is a poetic construction accompanied by "qualities" (*saguṇā*), that is, endowed with the aforementioned qualities of sound such as clarity (*pasāda*).

They are called "ornaments" (*alaṅkāra*) because the composition is adorned—that is, led to beauty—by them, just as a body is [adorned] by necklaces and the like. By these ornaments of meaning, characterized by *jāti* and so forth...

"Endowed" means joined together; "possessing qualities" means being equipped with virtues such as faithfulness (*patibbatā*) and the like. "Endowed with wealth" means possessed of property, riches, ornaments, and jewelry—just like a beloved woman.
Since she would thus be exceedingly lovely and supremely charming, for that reason those meanings and ornaments which have reached their proper occasion are now being stated and explained.

164. Having thus shown the classification of verbal ornaments (*saddālaṅkāra*), he now begins the composition of figurative ornaments of meaning (*atthālaṅkāra*) which depend upon that very [language], saying:

"The figurative ornaments of meaning," and so forth. A "mode of composition" (*bandhapaddhati*)—meaning a sequence of poetic structures (*racanāvali*) divided into types such as *pajja*, *gajja*, and so on—is "endowed with qualities" (*saguṇā*), being possessed of the aforementioned verbal qualities such as clarity (*pasāda*).

It is "accompanied by figurative ornaments of meaning" (*atthālaṅkārasahitā*), being conjoined with the figurative ornaments of meaning known as both natural expression (*sabhāvavutti*) and indirect expression (*vaṅkavutti*).
The topics (*attha*) are "endowed with qualities" (*saguṇā*), meaning they are like lovely women (*kantā*) possessed of virtues such as faithfulness;
or like women endowed with wealth such as gold, silver, jewels, and pearls, and with ornaments such as necklaces, bracelets, and anklets—being exceedingly lovely because they are most delightful.
Therefore, those ornaments of meaning (*atthālaṅkāra*) will now be explained. They adorn the composition, the body [of the work].

The analysis [of the compound] is as follows: "and by these," "ornaments of meaning," "accompanied by those," "it functions together with qualities," "the path of composition," and "extremely and exceedingly beautiful.
The ornaments (alaṃkriyā) are of two kinds, according to the division of those whose natural course is crooked.
The first [section] therein distinguishes between various types of subjects (vatthu).

He said, "of many kinds," beginning with "intrinsic nature" (sabhāva) and so forth. The distinctions and varieties of these—namely, *sabhāvavutti* (expression of intrinsic nature) and *vaṅkavutti* (crooked expression)—constitute the two-fold ornaments of meaning (*atthālaṅkāra*). Among those, as to what kind of *sabhāvavutti* it is, he said:

“First,” and so forth. Therein, among those [modes], the first is the occurrence of intrinsic nature (*sabhāvavutti*). It is manifold and variegated with respect to the bases—that is, the meanings of words—consisting of the intrinsic natures of genus, quality, action, and substance.
It is not merely one or two states or occasions; it is discerning, manifesting, and intelligible.
Fully disclosing the various modes of the meanings of words such as genus and so on according to their respective intrinsic natures, it makes the intrinsic nature of the word-meanings variegated.

The intended meaning is that "it speaks" refers to what is called *sabhāvavutti* (the function of its own nature). That very [function] is also called *jāti* (genus), because it is the function (*vutti*)—by means of which the form of the word-meaning is presented in its various ways—and because it is given (*dattiya*). (Ka.

To show that there are this many divisions of the excellent ornaments (*pasatthālaṅkāra*), he says "of its own nature" (*sabhāvi*) and so forth. (Ka. "Excellent ornaments" means those beginning with the excellent simile (*pasatthopamā*) and others. (Ka. He states this to demonstrate how many there are according to their classification.
Ornamentation consists of meaning-ornaments (*atthālaṅkāra*). By way of their divisions and sub-divisions, they are twofold, of two kinds.

Among those two, the first—the natural mode of expression (*sabhāvavutti*)—is that which reveals various states and manifests manifold aspects for the meanings of words characterized by genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), and substance (*dabbalakkhaṇa*).
Herein, it is that which manifests the manifold-natured characteristics of the word-meanings such as genus and the rest.

This is called "natural occurrence" (*sabhāvavutti*). This very thing is called "birth" (*jāti*) by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), because it presents the fourfold categories of meaning—such as genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), and so forth—in their own forms through those [conventional] modes.

By setting aside the true nature of the categories of meaning such as genus and the rest, it manifests a distorted nature (*vaṅkasabhāva*) consisting of metaphors, similes, images, and so forth, which are designated as having a form similar to those [original meanings].

"Devious conduct" (*vaṅkavutti*) means: it is a compound of *yabbhāvo* ("the state of being") and *vaṅko* ("crooked"), and of those two, there is the "conduct" (*vutti*); or, "by means of these they adorn [themselves]";
or, "that condition is various and manifold" (*nānā anekā ca sā avatthā*).
For example:
The Bodhisatta-sprout,
beautiful with playful grace,
casting a steady glance toward the quarters, spoke these words:
He uttered a voice that resounded.

(166) "Thus" he illustrates it: on that very day of his birth, the Bodhisatta-sprout—who was fortunate and beautiful through his playful grace, his charm, and his gait consisting of the seven-step stride—possessed a steady and unshakable gaze toward the ten directions.
The Mahābodhisatta shone forth, having attained a state of exceptional loveliness, as he uttered the peerless, fearless words of a bull among men, beginning with “I am the foremost.
This is the natural mode of being (*sabhāvavutti*). In this way, the natural mode of birth, the natural mode of character, and so forth, are also to be understood by analogy. 166.
Now, he provides an illustration of the natural mode of being with the verse beginning, “As—graceful in his playful movement,” and so on: *“Līlāvikantisubhago”*... [and so forth].
With his graceful gait, his seven-step stride, his beautiful steady gaze toward the quarters, and his unshakable look across the ten directions,
the Bodhisatta-sprout— the Great Bodhisatta-sprout— shone and was resplendent while uttering the authoritative words beginning with “I am the foremost,” which are the speech of one who is fearless.
Herein, [the splendor] belongs to the substance designated as the Bodhisatta, consisting of his grace, beauty, steady gaze toward the quarters, and the utterance of speech.
Because it manifests a state of being, it should be understood as the functioning of the intrinsic nature of a substance (*dabbasabhāvavutti*).

This very [functioning] is called "ornament" (*alaṅkāra*) because it adorns the various forms—such as the movement and so forth—belonging to the substance; however, the movement and so forth belonging to the substance are called "the act of adorning" (*alaṃkiriyā*) because they are themselves being adorned.

The functioning of the intrinsic natures of genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*kriyā*) should likewise be viewed in this same way. Furthermore, it is "skillful activity" (*vikanti*) when joined with grace (*līlā*).

The phrases are: "She is fortunate" (*subhagā*); "He whose gaze is steady in all directions" (*disāsu thiraṃ vilokanaṃ yassa*); "A being through the wisdom of enlightenment" (*bodhiyā paññāya satto*);
"That very sprout" (*soyeva aṅkuro*); and "The state of a bull" (*usabhassa bhāvo*). The unshakable stability known as the state of a bull is called *āsabha*;
because it is an unshakable state, the speech associated with it is also called *āsabhī* by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).

"Vutti" refers to the occurrence of the intrinsic nature (sabhāva) of a thing (vatthu), which is the meaning of the word consisting of such forms as birth and so forth. That which is otherwise [than that nature] is "parābhava" (destruction). Because that [destruction] possesses infinite conceptual variations, there is the illustration by means of a seed.
He states the second [verse] with the words beginning with "vutti. In this context, *vatthu* is the referent (padattha) whose intrinsic nature consists of birth and other such characteristics.

In this context, "vutti" (mode of expression) refers to the statement that describes a particular form of a thing as it truly is, by means of its non-alteration—that is, by making that form manifest as it actually exists.
Another mode would be what is called "crooked expression" (*vaṅkavutti*), which occurs when [the description] is otherwise. To the question, "Is it possible to express that in its entirety?
he says: "Of that," and so forth. Because that crooked expression possesses infinite conceptual possibilities, it has an immeasurable variety of divisions, like a seed.
Because it is the cause of the universal form that pervades all individual entities, from which various further ornaments are produced;
its manifestation is a description, since it is impossible for anyone to express [the object] exhaustively. 167.

Now he shows "crooked" function (*vaṅkavutti*) with the words beginning with "function" (*vutti*). Of the intrinsic nature of the subject matter, which is connected to the meanings of words such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth—

In whatever various states a particular nature exists, if there is a mode of being or a way of speaking that abandons the actual manner in which that nature exists and proceeds by means of some other mode—

such as exaggeration, comparison, metaphor, or the like— imagined by a speaker, this is called "crooked speech" (*vaṅkavutti*), distinct from the natural mode of being (*sabhāvavutti*) within the context of defeat. Because such crooked speech possesses infinite variations:

Because it is impossible to complete the exposition due to its immeasurable scope, this presentation of the "seed" (bīja) serves as a mere illustration of the reason for encompassing that infinite category by way of methodological principles (*naya*).

The intention is that even each single instance, according to the distinctions to be explained hereafter, is capable of indicating the knowledge of its own likeness and the inclusion of its infinite variations. [This concerns] the bases (*vatthu*).

The analysis [of the compound] is as follows: "sabhāvo" means "that which has infinite conceptualizations as its nature," and "tassa bhāvo" means "the state of that"; it is also the manifestation of the seed.

This concludes the commentary on the section concerning the ornament of meaning (*atthālaṅkāra*) regarding crooked expression (*vaṅkavutti*). Therein, the "exceedingly hyperbolic simile" (*atisaya-upamā*)—
Metaphor (rūpaka), repetition (āvutti), illuminator (dīpaka), objection (akkhepa), corroboration by another meaning (atthantaranyāsa), contrast (byatireka),
and the manifestation of the unmanifest (vibhāvanā).
The sequence of roots, the more beloved [meaning], the formation of compounds and suppositions;
the composed, the figurative expression, the indirect description,
the distinction, the conventional, and the partiality.
Concealment is *tulyayogitā* (equal pairing);
the illustration is its greatness,
while deception is praise for what has not been done.
The single string (ekāvalī), mutual [relation], co-existence (sahavutti),
opposition (virodhitā), exchange (parivutti), confusion (abbhāma), absence (abhāva), mixture (missa), and the aesthetic flavors (rasī)—
these varieties have been enumerated. Sentiment (bhāva) is said to be their lifeblood.
He nourishes those of crooked conduct, but *śleṣa* (paronomasia) nourishes supreme glory.

(168–172) Desiring to explain [the types of *śleṣa*] according to their enumeration, he states the heading beginning with "Therein" (*tattha*), and so forth. "Therein" (*tattha*) means in that crooked conduct;
it is connected with the phrase "these divisions have been enumerated. "Enumerated" (*samuddiṭṭhā*) means stated by way of summary. [The term] *atisaya*...
Simile, metaphor, repetition, and the illuminator; compound, compound-repetition, and poetic fancy;
distinction, conventional usage, and the figure of life—these are so called because, in their absence, the composition would be like a mere skin and thus fit to be discarded.

As for the figure of "coalescence" (śleṣa), it occurs in cases of crooked expression where, having abandoned the natural mode of expression, there is a conceptualization of things otherwise than their actual nature, such as in hyperboles and the like.
It nourishes, fulfills, and brings about supreme glory and beauty among modes of expression. 168–172.

Since the description of the intrinsic nature of the constituent word-meanings becomes clear through the sequence of enumeration (*uddesa*), he speaks this tetrad of verses beginning with “*Tatthātisaya...
rasī*” while enumerating them by means of the ornaments currently being discussed. Therein, “*tattha*” (therein) refers to—
In this *vaṅkavutti* (crooked mode of expression), these thirty-five varieties have thus been indicated; they are stated in brief.
However, the meaning of these terms will become clear in the *niddesa* (explanation). By this, he demonstrates that both *bhāva* (sentiment) and *sileśa* (poetic embellishment) are highly praised.
*Bhāva*—the ornament of sentiment—is said to be the life-force of composition, its very soul; for [a work] devoid of *bhāva*, [there is no life].
Because it is as unworthy of acceptance as a corpse, *bandha* (bondage) is not to be adopted;

however, *śleṣa* (punning), which is a figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*), nourishes and fulfills the supreme glory and splendor found in crooked expressions, specifically those crooked expressions such as hyperbolic similes (*atisayopamā*).
Commentary on the Exposition.
That which manifests excellence may be an extraordinary mode of activity whose sphere transcends the world.
And that [function] is twofold:
mundane (*lokiya*) and supramundane (*lokuttara*). 173. Therein, pointing out first those functions characterized by excellence (*atisaya*), he says "illuminating" (*pakāsikā*), and so forth.

Having restated that it is "the illuminator of an exceeding degree (*atimatta*) residing in the substrate (*vatthu*)," it is then prescribed that "that function is one of excellence"; [namely,] the excellence of the substrate, its pre-eminence (*ukkaṃsa*).
The practice that is foundational is the superlative practice. Since it is of two kinds, he says "the world," and so forth.
That which has a range or domain transcending the world—that is, transcending worldly convention—is "transcendent in its range" (*lokuttaravisaya*);
and that which exists in the world because it does not transcend the worldly mode of existence is "worldly" (*lokiya*). Thus, the superlative practice is twofold, being of two types.
173. Now, by means of the phrase beginning with "he manifested" (*pakāsi*), he demonstrates the function of excellence (*atisayavutti*) according to the order of the summary.
That function which makes manifest a distinction—that is, a superior quality residing in the referents of terms such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth—is called the function of excellence.

And that function of excellence has a domain that transcends the world (*lokātikkantavisayā*); for it transcends the worldly mode of existence (*lokathiti*) as determined by the intrinsic nature of referents such as genus and so forth. Thus, it is "transcending the world."
They are both "objects" (*visaya*) and "worldly" (*lokiya*). They are thus twofold, of two kinds, because they proceed without transcending the world as previously described.

The analysis of the terms is as follows: *vutti* means "speaking"; *atisayavutti* means "excessive speaking. Furthermore, it is that whose object (*visaya*) has transcended the world, and it exists in the world (*loke bhava*).
By the mention of its well-known quality, it is called "the illuminator of distinction" (*visesassa pakāsikā*), which refers to its excessive function (*atisayavutti*).
The word "siyā" (it may be) establishes a formulation of an extraordinary mode of expression that is otherwise unproven, such as: "He who wears earrings is Devadatta.
The distinction between the subject of the statement (*anuvādaka*) and the object of the statement (*anuvādanīya*) should be understood in exactly the same way hereafter.
These two are [the means] for worldly excellence.
Those distinctions such as birth and so forth are set aside today, for you are now established in a sphere that transcends the world.
174. If it is asked: "Is this twofold *atisayavutti* (hyperbole) distinct from *sabhāvavutti* (natural description) and the others? He says: "The world," and so forth.

Since birth (*jāti*) and the other [categories] express the manifold essential form (*sarūpa*) of the referent (*padattha*), *sabhāvavutti* is also an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) because it conveys that manifold essential form;
however, the subject matter (*vatthu*) is merely the basis for the ornament. Therefore, those distinctions or specificities (*visesa*) such as *sabhāvavutti* and the rest—these [are what is meant].

Due to the distinction of worldly excellence (*lokīyātisaya*): just as that which is innate beauty in the body and its enhancers, such as pearl necklaces and other ornaments, are called "ornaments" (*alaṅkāra*), so too in composition, that quality by which the excellence of the subject matter (*alaṅkāriyavatthu*) is heightened is called "excellence" (*ukkaṃsa*).
And that mode of expression (*vutti*) is expressed by the word "ornament. Furthermore, it is indeed an expression of excellence.
For this very reason it was said: "Birth and the rest are these distinctions of worldly excellence. Since this is so, they must therefore be shown separately as having a supramundane object;
thus he said "the path" (*paṭipadā*), and so forth. The particle *tu* indicates a distinction. The connection is: "But now, at this time, the supramundane domain is to be set forth."
174. Now, in order to show that these two types [of excellence] are not different from the natural course of things (*vutti-sabhāva*) and so forth, he says "in the worldly" (*lokiye*), and so on.

Because they manifest the various forms residing in the categories of genus, quality, and so forth—such as birth and the rest—they are designated by the term "birth and the rest" (*jātyādayo*) through a metaphorical usage based on their support.
These distinctions and specificities, such as the natural course of the genus (*jāti-sabhāva-vutti*) and the natural course of the quality (*guṇa-sabhāva-vutti*), constitute the worldly excellence.

The "parts" (*avayava*) are indeed the varieties of worldly excellence (*lokīyātisayavutti*). In this context, "worldly excellence" refers precisely to the modes of natural disposition (*jātisabhāvavutti*), the modes of the nature of qualities (*guṇasabhāvavutti*), and so forth.
This very [excellence], which brings about various forms, is also called "elevation" (*ukkaṃsa*).

Thus, because the example "graceful in his playful gait" (*līlāvikantisubhago*) is understood through worldly excellence, he acknowledges what is about to be explained with the words beginning "it is brought about" (*paṭipādīyate*). But now, at this time...

Furthermore, the "exceeding of the world" (*lokātikkanta*) refers to a mode of conduct that transcends the ordinary; it is established by way of example and brought to completion through illustration.
The phrase "that which exists in the world" (*loke bhavo*) and its excellence (*atisaya*) or superiority (*ādhikya*) constitute the sentence.
Those who drink the beauty of the body—
With your net-like hollowed palms,
you are not able to slay me, O Conqueror; for even you,
the remover of craving, cannot destroy craving itself.

175. He illustrates this with the verse beginning “They drink,” and so forth. O Conqueror, those people who drink the splendor of your body—the beauty of your form—with the hollow of their hands, that is, with the hollow of their palms formed by their pair of eyes;
for these people, you remove, pursue away, and eliminate their craving, thirst, or even greed.
Even though you are one who removes craving, why do you turn back to kill [them]?
"Not able" means you are incapable. Those called "thirst-removers" indeed dispel thirst itself. Here, even while striking, it dispels [thirst];
having transcended the worldly condition, the quality of being abundant in bodily beauty is stated. 175.
Now, following what was promised, he arranges [the verses] beginning with "they drink," etc. O Victor, your bodily beauty...

Those people who drink the splendors of your body with the hollow of their eyes—the hollow of the hands known as the "eye"—for those virtuous persons, you, the remover of craving (*taṇhā*), are capable of destroying, warding off, or killing even their thirst, greed, or indeed craving itself;
why are you not able? Why are you incompetent? Here, "drinking" means "removing thirst."
"Worldly nature" (*lokasabhāva*) means that it is not capable of destroying craving; thus, its meaning is "having transcended the world.

"Excellence" (*kantīnam*) refers to the quality of being exceedingly dear, and its function is to proceed by taking as its object that which has transcended the world, in the sense that it is not capable of destroying craving.
Furthermore, that [excellence] is incapable of destroying craving regarding the state of being exceedingly dear that one wishes to express.

One who speaks and then illuminates [the meaning] is called "crooked in conduct" (*vaṅkavutti*). Even for similes, metaphors, and so forth that are being spoken, their status as "crooked in conduct" is due precisely to the fact that they reveal the intended meaning by means of another mode of expression.

Just as ornaments such as bracelets, diadems, and necklaces—which exist in the manner of illuminators—become known as "ornaments" because they [enhance] the beauty of fullness and so on that is co-nascent with the body;
even so, in the case of the subject matter to be adorned, which is designated as the "body of composition" (*bandhasarīra*)...

Having illuminated this very state of being exceedingly dear while it exists, the ornament called *vācābhaṅgī* (verbal artifice) consists in adorning [the subject] by saying, "You are a destroyer of craving;
you are not able to destroy the craving of those who drink your beauty. Indeed, the "ornamented" (*alaṅkāriya*) refers to the abundance of that beauty and dearness which is to be adorned.
Furthermore, the distinction between the ornament and the ornamented, as well as the sequence of application, should be joined accordingly in the same manner.

It should be understood as follows: the analysis [of the compound] is "beauty in the body" (*dehe kantī*), "the hollow of the hands is indeed the palms joined in reverence" (*añjalīyeva puṭo*), "the eyes are indeed the hollow of the hands" (*nettāniyeva añjalipuṭo*), and "it carries away craving" (*taṇhaṃ harati*).
When the object of comparison and the subject of comparison possess a common quality, that is "simile" (*upamā*).
And that [simile] is threefold: based on word-meaning, sentence-meaning, and both.
(176) He explains the simile with the words "the standard of comparison" (*upamāna*), etc. That by which something is compared is the *upamāna*—the object such as the lotus and so forth.
The word "lotus" and the like is the designator of the standard of comparison. That which is compared is the *upameyya*—the object such as the face and so forth. The word "face" and the like...

The word "saddo" (sound/word), however, expresses that which is to be compared (*upameyya*). Regarding those objects of comparison (*upamāna*) and things to be compared (*upameyya*), such as the lotus and the face, etc.:

"Possessing a common property" (*sadhammatta*) means that which has a common property (*sadhamma*)—that is, a shared quality such as loveliness (*kantimantatā*); the state of being such is "possessing a common property" (*sadhammatta*). This refers to the connection with a common property that serves as the ground for the application of the word "sadhamma.

When this [connection] is established between the object of comparison and the thing to be compared, it constitutes a simile (*upamā*); it is by means of this that something is compared (*upamīyati*).

This is said by taking it as the aforementioned relationship (*sambandha*). Furthermore, that [relationship] is a mode of expressing the excellence of the embellished phenomenon (*alaṅkāriya-dhamma*).

To the question "In how many ways is it? he says: "Sound," and so forth. Sound and meaning—those which are understood or apprehended through them are "understood through sound and meaning" (*saddatthagamma*).

A sentence (*vākya*) is a collection of words (*pada*). That whose object (*visaya*), domain, or range is the meaning of such a sentence is "having the meaning of a sentence as its object" (*vākyatthavisayā*); and that is simile (*upamā*).
