It is threefold, being directed toward the word, the meaning, and the sense of the sentence.
176. Now he explains the ornament of simile (*upamālaṅkāra*) with the words beginning "the object of comparison" (*upamāna*).

It is the commonality of attributes (*sadharmatva*) between the objects of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subjects of comparison (*upameyya*)—such as sandalwood, blue lotus petals, and so forth, on one hand, and the face, eyes, and so forth, on the other—consisting in a connection with similar qualities such as radiance, fullness, and the like.
What is called *upamā* (simile) is a mode of expressing the excellence of the object to be embellished;
it is threefold—namely, based on words, based on meaning, and based on both—and thus consists of three types according to these three ways.

Herein, the connection between the qualities of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameyya*), such as the moon and the face, characterized by their common properties, consists in their mutual possession of qualities such as beauty, fullness, and so forth.

An object is called a "simile" (upamā) because it is established as a basis for comparison through its state of being present; however, the moon and so forth, which are the supports for that [object], are called a simile by way of metaphorical designation (*vohāra*) based on what they support.
Furthermore, words such as *candimā* (the moon), which convey the meaning of the moon and so forth that serves as the standard of comparison, are also called a simile in the sense of that [meaning].
Moreover, the status of being the object of comparison (*upameyya*) applies not only to the object itself, but also to the support of that object and to the words that convey it.
It should be viewed in this very way. Taking the sense that "it is compared by means of this," the moon and so forth are called the *upamāna* (the standard of comparison);

that which is compared is the *upameyya* (the object of comparison), such as the face and so forth. [The compound] *upamānañca upameyyañca* means "the standard of comparison and the object of comparison. [The term] *samānadhammo* means "that which is a common property. [The term] *tassa bhāvo* means "the state of being that.

[The term] *saddo ca attho ca* means "both the word and the meaning. [The term] *tehi gammo* means "comprehended by those. And [the term] *vākyassa attho* means "the meaning of the sentence. That is the *visaya* (domain/object).
And there is the phrase "of which simile.
Words such as compounds, suffixes, and so forth, are threefold according to their influence:
those understood through a compound, such as "the Lord of Sages with a moon-like face" (*munindo candimānano*).
177. Therein, in order to show that [the compound] may also be understood through words in three ways, he says "compound" (*samāsa*) and so forth.
"Compound," "suffix" (*paccaya*), and "ivādi"—these are what are called "words. The meaning is that by the term "word," it is intended to speak of compounds and the others.

By virtue of those [categories], such as compounds, the understanding through words is threefold: that which is understood through the word "compound," that which is understood through the word "suffix," and that which is understood through the word "ivādi."
In brief, it remains to be said that by the word "compound" (*samāsa*), a simile based on a compound is meant. He provides an example: "The Lord of Sages, moon-faced" (*munindo candimānano*).
One whose face (*ānana*) is as beautiful as the moon (*candima*) is "moon-faced.

In this instance, the moon is the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), the face is the object of comparison (*upameyya*), "loveliness" is the common property (*dhamma*), and the word "like" (*viya*) indicates the connection between the moon and the face through that shared property.

Among these, because the use of the word *viya*—which expresses a common property and indicates a simile—is omitted due to its being expressed through composition itself, the word *viya* here enters into a connection with the word *candimā*, which denotes the standard of comparison (*upamāna*). Thus, it expresses similarity residing in the moon alone;
however, that which resides in the face is understood by implication (*sāmatthiyā*). It should be viewed in this manner.
177. Among those [types of implied meaning] mentioned above, in order to show the threefold nature of that which is reached through words (*saddagamma*), he says:
"In compounds," and so forth. A compound, suffixes, and so on, as well as words such as *iva* (like) and the like, are called "words" (*sadda*).

By way of these—namely, compounds and the rest—the implied meaning is threefold: implied by compound-words, implied by suffix-words, and implied by words such as *iva*. First, by means of a compound...

By the term *samāsa* (compound), the "evident simile" (*gammopamā*) is expressed, as in: “The Lord of Sages (*munindo*), moon-faced (*candimānano*). The Lord of Sages, the Fully Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddho*), is possessed of a moon-like face—a circle of a countenance as charming as the moon.

[The phrase] “the compound (*samāso*) and the suffix (*paccayo*) and ‘like’ (*iva*) and so forth,” as well as “by the word (*saddena*) it is evident (*gammā*),” and “the lord (*indo*) of sages (*munīnaṃ*),” and “a face (*ānanaṃ*) as beautiful as the moon (*candimā viya*)”—[all these constitute the definition].
The analysis of the compound is *yassa mukhaṃ* (“whose face”). Here, “moon” (*candimā*) is the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), and “face” (*ānana*) is the object of comparison (*upameyya*).
Radiance (*ruciratta*) is the common property shared by both the standard and the object of comparison.

The word “like” (*viyā*) illuminates the connection with this common property, showing that the radiance residing in the face exists in the moon, and the radiance residing in the moon exists in the face. In this case:

The words *rucira* (beautiful), which expresses a common quality, and *viya* (like), which indicates a simile consisting of a similar quality, are not employed here because those meanings have been stated by way of a compound (*samāsa*).

In this context, the word *viya*, when joined with the word *candimā* (moon), which denotes the object of comparison (*upamāna*), illuminates the similarity residing in the moon; however, the similarity residing in the face [is understood] by implication (*sāmatthiyā*).

It is understood [in this way]. For instance, when it is said that "the face comes to resemble the moon," since this cannot be otherwise (aññathānupapatti) without the moon possessing a resemblance to the face, this very impossibility of another [explanation] constitutes the power of implication (sāmatthiya).
From those conditions such as water (āya), the face is born from the mud (paṅkaja).
The pair of eyes of the Sage shines like the petals of a blue lotus.

(178) Now, he shows that which is understood through the word *paccaya* (condition/affix) by means of the phrase beginning with "āyādi" (āya, etc.). "Āyādi" refers to the affixes such as *āya*, *īya*, and *ka*;
these affixes are called *paccaya*-words, and the simile is said to be understood through those *paccaya*-words. He provides an example with the verse beginning with "vadana" (the face), etc.
"It acts beautifully like a lotus" means "it becomes a lotus. Here too, the lotus is the standard of comparison (*upamāna*);

the face, acting as the agent of the action of acting beautifully, is the object of comparison (*upameyya*); beauty is the common property (*sadhamma*); and the word *iva* indicates the connection between the common property of the lotus and the face.
In that regard, the prior application of the words "beautiful" and "*iva*" is stated by way of a grammatical suffix; thus it is in all cases.
It is to be understood.
The same applies to what follows. Now, with the words beginning “āyādi,” he demonstrates the simile based on grammatical suffixes (*paccaya*).
The suffixes such as “āya, īya, ka,” and so forth, are called *paccaya-sadda* (suffix-words). By means of these suffix-words, the simile based on suffixes is expressed as: “The face... [is] crushed.”
The face, the mouth, acts like a lotus; it behaves as beautiful as a *paṅkaja* (lotus). The pair of eyes of the Lord of Sages, the two eyes of the Omniscient One, act like the petals of a blue lotus;
they behave as beautiful as the leaves of a blue lotus (*nīluppaladala*). [The compound] "āyo ādi yesaṃ īyādīnaṃ" means those for which "āya" is the beginning, such as "īya" and so forth.
It means that which acts, proceeds, or functions beautifully like a lotus. And [the phrase] "the pair of eyes of the Lord of Sages" [refers to] the blue lotus...

The phrase is both "like a lotus" (*paṅkajam iva*) and "it performs that which is beautiful" (*ruciram ācarati*). Here, "lotus" (*paṅkaja*) and "blue lotus" (*nīluppala*) are the standards of comparison (*upamāna*);

the face and the pair of eyes, acting as the agents of the action of performing, are the objects of comparison (*upameyya*); loveliness (*ruciratta*) is the common property (*sadhamma*) of the standard and the object of comparison;
and the word *iva* indicates the common property shared by the standard and the object of comparison. Of these...
Because they are stated as conditions for non-existence (*atthāna*), their application is not [required]. This should be understood in the same way for other such cases as well.
The suffix *iva* and others: *iva*, *tulya*, *samāna*, *nibha*, *sannibha*;
*yathā*, *saṅkāsa*, *tulita*, *ppakāsa*, *patirūpaka*.
Similarity, correspondence, opposition, resemblance, as if similar;
the adversary, the opponent, the partisan, and the comparison—these are the types of simile.
There are also the reflected image, the concealed form, the likeness, the equal, and the commensurate.
Similarity, appearance, counterpart, common characteristics,
and specific characteristics [are the marks of a reflection]. It conquers, reviles, laughs, roars back,
harms, envies, despises, censures, forgets, and obstructs.
It steals away his good fortune, it plunders his splendor;
it quarrels with him, it mounts upon him as his equal.
It plunges into his very depths, and having followed him, it clings to him.

"He restrains that conduct and imitates him"—this is the connection with the words "these" (*ime*) in [the verse] beginning with "these" (*ivādi*). In the compound *iva... pe... sannibhā*, the terms *iva*, *vā*, *tulya*, *samāna*, *nibha*, and *sannibha* form a *dvanda* (copulative) compound.
Because they depend on the word *sadṛśa* (resembling), they take the masculine gender. The same applies to the subsequent cases.

According to the context. In the phrase "sadhammādī" (common characteristics, etc.), the word "etc. includes common shadows and so forth. In cases such as *jayati* (he conquers), it is the object (*kamma*). 179–184.
In the section on similes understood through words such as *iva*, he first shows that "these are called *iva*-etc. by means of the verse beginning with "ivādi.
The word "imeti" (these) in the sixth verse is connected to the word "padassa" (of the word); and the particle *ca* in the phrase "tassa ca" is to be joined where appropriate.

Having joined [the preceding], *sannibhā*, *cāti*, and so forth should also be joined. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "sadhammādi," common shadows (*sādhāraṇasacchāya*) and others are included.
The word division is *nindati* and *issati*; these two and fifty others are called "ivādi.
Because phrases such as *jayati*, *akkosati*, and *hasati* are imitations of various verbal roots designated as action-words (*kriyāpada*), they constitute a *dvanda* compound.

Regarding the statement “*sandhisamāsā addhassā*,” because it is said that *sandhi* and *samāsa* [apply] to half of that (*tadaddha*), since a *sandhi* or *samāsa* cannot be obtained for the half of a verse (*gāthaddha*) without both halves, the *samāsa* must be formed prior to even two words; otherwise, it should be understood as not being a *samāsa*.
In the case of [expressions such as] *tassa coreti* or *sobhaggam icc-ādi*, this is treated as an imitation of a sentence (*vākyānukaraṇa*).
In this context, it should be understood that there is a compound [in the verse], whereas in the prose sentence there are only individual words.

Since all these terms are synonyms for *iva*, they possess a similar meaning; thus, in every instance, the sense of "state" (*bhāva*) is present, while the sense of "part" (*avayava*) is self-evident.
One should discern the commonality of properties between the object of comparison and the subject of comparison.
“By means of these various types of similes, some are led [to understanding] at once.
(185) Having shown the scope of application for *iva* and the other particles, he undertakes to show the classification of similes with the words “*Upamāna*,” etc.
By the word “some” (*keci*), he indicates that their divisions are limitless; thus he will say later:
“*Pariyanto vikappānan*,” and so forth. They are brought forth and illustrated. 185.
Now, he undertakes to show the simile understood through words such as *iva* and others, by means of the phrase beginning with “*Upamāno*.

The commonality between the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameyya*) is the connection with a shared quality (*samānadhamma*). These meanings are to be known through these words, *iva* and the rest, which are the revealers (*vibhāvīhi pakāsakehi*).
Certain varieties of similes, due to their being limitless, are now brought forth as they find their opportunity and are presented by way of mere examples.
"Like a blossoming lotus"—the face of the Sugata is beautiful;
this is called a simile of phenomena (*dhammopamā*), which demonstrates a common quality.
186. “Vikāsi,” etc. The face of the Sugata, the countenance of the Lord of Sages, is exceedingly beautiful and supremely charming.
Like what? Like a blooming lotus, like a lotus awakening. Thus, this is called a *dhammopamā* (simile by way of quality).
Why? Because it demonstrates the commonality of the qualities, virtues, and characteristics shared between the face and the lotus.
"By way of demonstrating its beauty.

(186) He provides an illustration with the words beginning "blooming," etc. The face of the Sugata—the Blessed One's mouth—is exceedingly beautiful, like a blooming lotus, that is, like a lotus flower opening.
Thus, such similes demonstrate a common quality, [showing] that it is exceedingly beautiful.

The comparison of phenomena (dhammopamā) occurs through the observation of common qualities. Because it illustrates a quality shared by both the lotus and the face, it is called a "similarity" (tulyadhamma), meaning "extremely beautiful.

Here, although the comparison—consisting of the connection with the similarity residing in the lotus—is expressed by the word *iva*, because it is stated as "extremely beautiful," it is [classified] according to the phenomenon (*dhamma*) of the aforementioned comparison.
The intention is that it is called a "simile by way of the dharma" (dhammopamā) because of its logical fitness.
"The Sage’s face-lotus is like [the lotus] devoid of dharma"—this is a "perverse simile" (viparītopamā).
"Your lotus is equal to the lotus in measure"—this is a "simile of equality" (tulyopamā).
187. “The Dhamma,” and so forth. The mouth of the Muni, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is similar to (*sadisaṃ*) a lotus (*ambhojena*), that is, a water-born lily (*paduma*).
Thus, this is called a "deficient simile" (*dhammahīnopamā*) because the quality designated as "beautiful" is not explicitly stated; however, it is understood through the force of the meaning.
For how else would it be appropriate? In this context, the word *sadisa* (similar) is an adjective qualifying the face, which is the object of comparison (*upameyya*).

It is the presence of the lotus itself that is expressed, whereas its presence in the mouth is understood through implication. Such cases are to be known in this way. Regarding the passage beginning with "In the case of the reverse" (*viparīte*):
it is understood from the context that "the Sage" (*muni*) is meant; thus, "O Sage, they compare your face with a lotus"—this is a "reverse simile" (*viparītopamā*).

Even though it lacks the [standard] attributes [of a lotus], it is designated by that very name because it is stated as the opposite of what is commonly established. The same applies to the subsequent examples.

187. “*Dhammahīne*,” etc. “The Sage’s face is like a lotus”—this is a simile (*upamā*). They are called “devoid of Dhamma” (*dhammahīnā*) because they lack the beautiful words that proclaim the Dhamma equally with [the Buddha].
If it is asked: “In the absence of a speaker, how can the equal Dhamma be understood?”—[the answer is:

“The Sage’s face, his countenance, is like a lotus (*ambhoja*), that is, like a water-lily (*paduma*). Here, the similarity of the face to the lotus is [established] by means of the face and the lotus.
If there is no common property (sādhāraṇadhamma), how can it be [said to be] so? It is by the power of the characteristic of "impossibility otherwise" (aññathānupapatti-lakkhaṇa-sāmatthiya).
Since the word *iva* is a synonym for the word *sadisa* and serves as a qualifier of the "mouth," it therefore expresses a similarity residing in the mouth;
however, the similarity residing in the lotus is understood through the power [of the context] alone. "O Sage, your face and the lotus are equal (*tulya*) and identical (*samāna*)."

This is the *viparītopamā* (inverse simile). Because it is stated that "the lotus is equal to the face" by reversing the worldly convention that "the face is equal to the lotus," it is called an inverse simile even though there is a deficiency in the attributes (*dhammahīnatā*).

According to the statement in the *Paribhāsendusekhara* (112), "Between what is heard and what is inferred, the connection with what is heard is stronger," here [the word] "muni" [is understood] even though it is not explicitly present.
In the first half [of the verse], because the word “of the Sage” (*munino*) is heard, the sense of address (*āmantana*)—though implied—is understood through the proximity of the word “your” (*tavo*).
Here, the word “equal” (*tulya*), used as a synonym for “like” (*iva*), expresses a similarity residing in the lotus;

and by the force of implication (*sāmatthiyā*), the common property shared by both the lotus and the face is also understood, such that the similarity residing in the face is likewise conveyed. Thus it is said.
This should be understood according to the method already stated. Even in subsequent instances, the appropriate application should be made to the clear examples.
"Your lotus is like your face; your face is like a lotus;
this is a mutual simile based on mutual comparison."
188. “*Tava*,” etc. “By way of mutual comparison” means by way of comparing each other—the face and the lotus—using those two respectively as the points of comparison.
188. “*Tavānana*,” etc. “The lotus is like your face; your face is like the lotus”—this is the simile (*upamā*).
Because they serve as the point of comparison for one another, it is called a “mutual simile” (*aññamaññopamā*) due to their being mutual points of comparison. It is a comparison of one another.
And the analysis is: “the mutual comparison of each other. In both analyses, there is the elision of the preceding case-ending (*pubbavibhattilopa*).
By the characteristic of reciprocal exchange (*byatihāralakkhaṇa*) pertaining to words such as *sabba*, there is the elision of the subsequent case-ending (*uttaravibhattilopa*).

Because the requirement for another referent (*aññattha*) is established by the characteristic of compound formation (*samāsalakkhaṇa*), that which is other than the face is the lotus in relation to the face, and that which is other than the lotus is the face; these two are respectively called the objects of comparison (*upameyya*).
The lotus is a simile for the face because it looks toward [the beauty of] the lotus, and the face is a simile for the lotus because it looks toward [the beauty of] the face.
If there were some lotus that possessed the playful charm of the eyes and the eyebrows, [it could serve as a simile].
"To preserve the beauty of your face"—this is a marvelous simile (abbhutopamā). 189.
"If," and so forth. That lotus (*ambhoja*) in which there is the playful charm (*vibbhama*) of both eyes and eyebrows—such [a lotus].
If there were anything whatsoever like it—that lotus is capable of bearing the splendor of your face, the radiance of your countenance.
"What wonder is there in such a thing?"—by thus manifesting a marvelous meaning, the face is compared to a lotus;
this should be known as the *abbhutopamā* (the simile of the marvelous).

189. “If,” etc. If there were some lotus possessing the playful grace of your eyes and brows—some marvelous *paduma*—then that lotus would be capable of bearing the splendor of your face, the radiance of your countenance.
Thus, such a simile is an “extraordinary simile” (*abbhutopamā*) because it reveals an extraordinary phenomenon.
[This is] the name. Here, although the connection with the delusive beauty of the lotus-eyes does not actually exist [in the lotus], it is imagined as existing;

this connection is made manifest by the qualifying term "ambhoja" (lotus) through the expression "locanabbhamuvibbhama" (the delusive beauty of the lotus-eyes). Therefore, because the lotus (*ambhoja*) functions as the indicator of the simile consisting of that connection with the delusive beauty of the lotus-eyes, it is a simile by way of dependent designation (*nissitavohāra*);
and since the face is the object of comparison (*upameyya*), the connection with the delusive beauty of the lotus-eyes residing in the face [is likewise established].
If it were not in the mouth, how could it be capable of sustaining such a beauty of the face? This is known through its capacity (*sāmatthiya*).
Furthermore, regarding the common quality (*sādhāraṇadhamma*) designated as the "bewildering charm" (*vibbhamasaṅkhāta*) of the eyes and eyebrows:

by means of a compound with a different substratum (*bhinnādhikaraṇa-aññapadattha-samāsa*) resulting from the analysis (*viggahe*) "the eyes and the eyebrows (*locanāni ca bhamuyo ca*), [and] the charm (*vibbhamo*) of them (*tāsaṃ*) is in that [face]," [it is established].
"Even though it has become a subordinate element (*guṇībhūta*), it is understood because the act of grasping is itself being understood" (Ka.).
"Your face is like a lotus: fragrant, connected with beauty, and opposed to cool rays"—this is considered a simile based on paronomasia (*silesopamā*).
190. “*Sugandhi,*” etc. Your face is the opposite—that is, the adversary—of the cool-rayed moon, just like a lotus;

for the face and the lotus are alike in their beauty, yet the lotus undergoes contraction upon the rising of that [moon]. Both the face and the lotus are connected with splendor (*sobha*), meaning they possess radiance (*kanti*).
Furthermore, both are *sugandhi*, meaning they possess a sweet fragrance (*sugandha*). Thus, through this application of paronomasia (*silesa*).
Because of the application of a simile to the lotus-like face, that which has been described as such is considered a *śleṣopamā* (simile based on double entendre). 190.
“Fragrant,” etc. Your face is like a lotus; it is opposed to the cool-rayed moon because of their equality.
However, the lotus is opposed to the rising moon because of its own closing [at that time].

Furthermore, it is connected with a splendor that belongs to him alone and is not shared by others, and it is endowed with a connection to a radiance residing in his face. A lotus, however, is endowed with a connection to a radiance residing in the lotus itself.

And it is fragrant because it carries the fragrance of the four types of perfumes and because it emits [scent] from its interior; a lotus-born flower, on the other hand, is endowed with the fragrance of the lotus alone. Such is the simile.
The simile of *silesa* (the "cleaving") is so named because it is expressed by way of a *silesa* (cleaving) characterized by both the benefit of a single word and the benefit of both meanings.
It is called *sisira* because its rays (*amsu*)—that is, its radiance—are cool; and it is so called because it is obstructed by character (*sila*).
Furthermore, since two distinct meanings are obtained for each pair [of words] through the power of their respective conditions, another meaning also cleaves (*silissati*) here as an ornament.
The analysis of the compound is: "the similes are stated by way of *silesa* (poetic figuration).

Here, being fragrant, being connected with the ear, and being opposed to the cool-rayed moon—these are the common properties (*tulyadhamma*) of the objects of comparison (*upameyya*), namely the lotus and the face.

Among these, the connection with the property residing in the lotus is called a simile (*upamā*) because of its shared characteristic (*sadhammattā*). That [simile] is indicated by the word *iva*, which is connected with the lotus; as for the property residing in the face...

However, when the suffix *tasi* is applied in the sense of "established in" (*assatthita*), it is understood precisely as having the capacity [to express comparison], because it is expressed by a word of identical form (*sarūpasadda*).
Such is the simile of continuity (*santānopamā*):
"This forest path is like a young girl, beautified by groves of *sāla* trees."
191. “*Sarūpa*,” etc. This garden grove is like a young woman. How so?

Just as a young woman is adorned with *sāla* flowers—meaning she is beautiful because of her particular arrangement of hair (*sāla-kānana*)—so too this garden grove is beautiful because of the forest (*kānana*), the thicket of *sāla* trees, which are a specific kind of tree. Such is its nature; it is of that very sort.

It is described as being like a "chain" (santāna). Why? Because, even though its intrinsic nature consists of a series of phonemes (*silesa*), it is understood to be so called because it is expressed and manifested by a specific, distinguished chain of sounds—such as the phrase “*sālakānanasobhinī*”—which is similar in form.
The word *yathā* is used in the sense of an illustration. 191. Regarding the passage beginning with “*sarūpe*”:
because it is expressed by words of identical form (*sarūpa*), it is a string of statements whose connection is uninterrupted due to their equal phonetic sequence (*tulyasuti*).

Because it is expressed [through a series], that simile is called a "simile by series" (*santānopamā*); the intention is that it is called a "simile by series" because it is expressed through sequences of words formed by compound terms, even though they possess the nature of *silesa* (paronomasia). He provides an example with the word "yathā" (just as):
"This garland of a garden, this row of gardens, beautified by a grove of *sāla* trees, shines with a face accompanied by a hair-arrangement known as 'alaka' curls."
Like young women, she is graced by groves of *sāla* trees; thus, she shines with *sāla* forests. [The analysis of the compound is as follows:
It refers to those words which possess a common form between the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameyya*); these are "similar words" (*sarūpasaddā*).

By means of these, there is (1) the expression of the comparison (*upamā*), (2) the state of that [comparison] (*tassā bhāvo*), (3) a comparison connected by a continuous series (*santānena yuttā upamā*), (4) a garland of gardens (*uyyānānaṃ mālā*), and (5) that which exists together with *alaka* (curling locks of hair).
And: "and that face," and "it shines by virtue of that virtue," and "the grove of sal trees," and "it shines by virtue of that virtue"—this is the sentence.
The moon has decay, the lotus has much dust; compared to those two, your face [is superior].
“Though equal, it is superior”—this is considered a simile of censure (nindopamā). 192. “The waning one,” etc.
The moon is “waning” because its waning (*khaya*)—its passing away—is present; the lotus is “full of dust” because it has many particles of pollen (*parāga*).
Although [the face] is equal to—that is, similar to—the moon and the lotus in such qualities as radiance and so forth...
"Your face is peaceful, surpassing the supreme excellence [of others]," because it is free from the sound of decay (*khaya*) and the fault of passion (*raja*),
and because— by means of a pun on the word *sadda*— there is an absence there of the fault-form of decay and the state of being full of passion.
Thus, this is considered a "simile of censure" (*nindopamā*), since the censured object, such as the moon, is compared to decay.
192. “Waning,” and so forth. The moon wanes; from the first day of the lunar fortnight onwards, it is subject to the nature of diminishing day by day due to its proximity to the sun.
The lotus is full of dust, being possessed of much pollen.
Although your face, your countenance, is equal to those—the moon and the lotus—being similar to them in radiance, fragrance, and other qualities, it surpasses them.
Because even a fault must be expressed by means of the words "khaya-rajas" (dust of decay), such a fault—though implied through a verbal pun—is not actually present in the mouth;

thus, it possesses an exaggerated excellence. Therefore, this simile is called a "simile of censure" (*nindopamā*), because the censured objects—the moon and the lotus—are compared to the mouth by means of a qualification of the mouth using the word *iva* (like/as).
By the word *samāna* (equal), the common property residing in the mouth is illuminated;

likewise, the common property residing in the moon and the lotus—constituting the simile—and the common property shared by the two [the face and the moon], are understood through the force of implication (*sāmatthiya*). Here, the particle *api* serves to include another element to be stated, namely, the phrase "surpassing" (*samukkaṃso*).
"O Conqueror, the moon is unable to roar back at you with its mouth."
“‘Dull-witted and stained’—this may be a simile of prohibition (paṭisedhopamā).

[Verse 193: “‘Incapable,’ and so forth. O Victor, by your mouth he is dull-witted (*jaḷa*), cold, and unskilled; and because he possesses a stain (*kalaṅka*)—the mark characterized by the deer—he is ‘stained’ (*kalaṅkī*).
This is a statement of fault through the deceptive guise of a word (*saddacchalena*). Such a one, namely the moon (*indu*), is unable to roar back in opposition.”
"Unable to dispute, yet his mouth is bright and adorned"—how can he be similar to this [Buddha]? Thus, by way of negation, their shared nature (*sadhammatā*) is understood;
this may be a *paṭisedhopamā* (negation simile). 193. "Unable," etc.
O Victor, he who is dull-witted and cold toward you is unable to roar back or dispute with your mouth.

The statement, "The moon, even if it is spotless (*avisada*), marked with a stain (*kalaṅkin*), or possessed of a blemish (*sadosa*), is incapable [of being compared]," is such an example known as a "prohibitive simile" (*paṭisedhopamā*). The phrase is: "He who has a stain (*kalaṅka*) belongs to him.

Here, by means of two prohibitions, it is shown that the moon—though similar to a face that is cool and spotless (*avisada*)—is incapable of being equal [to it] because it possesses a blemish (*sadosa*). Thus, through these two negations...
The intention is that, because the connection between the common attribute and the objects of comparison—
namely, the moon and its face— is made manifest, there exists what is called a "prohibition simile" (paṭisedhopamā), even though it lacks the status of a "censure simile" (nindopamā).
The phrase "to roar back" (paṭigajjituṃ) illuminates a quality residing in the moon, as it serves as an epithet for the moon.
"Having surpassed the range of the moon and the lotus, [your face] has arisen as its own equal;
thus, this is an incomparable simile (asādhāraṇopamā).
(194) Regarding the verse beginning with "kaccha": having surpassed—that is, having transcended—the range or path of both the moon and the lotus.
Because it is not possible for them [the moon and the lotus] to be equal to you, O ascetic, your face has become equal to them only by its own form;
thus, through the expression of an uncommon quality (*asādhāraṇatā*) that produces a perception of similarity, this is called an "uncommon simile" (*asādhāraṇopamā*). 194.
"The marsh," etc. O Sage, your face is [equal to] the moon and the lotus—the moon and the water-lily—which are honored by the world.
Having transcended the bank, the path, or the stage, it has become "equal" (sama) because there is no object whatsoever equal to itself due to its own incomparability;
such similes are called "unique similes" (*asādhāraṇopamā*) because they reveal a state of incomparable quality.
Here, by means of demonstrating the inferiority of the face through the moon and the lotus which serve as the similes—
Because they are designated as being equal to the moon and the lotus by way of comparison, the moon and the lotus are called "uncommon similes" (*asādhāraṇopamā*).
The word *sama* (equal) illuminates the common quality residing in the face. The rest is easy to understand.
[He is] the essence of the radiance of all food, as if gathered into a single mass somewhere.
"Your face shines"—this is an *abhūtopamā* (unreal simile).

195. "All," etc. In a certain place, [it is said]: "Your face shines like the very luster of all lotuses gathered together in one spot. Such is this *abhūtopamā*. 195. "All," etc. In a certain place, [it is said]:
"Like the very luster of all lotuses gathered together in one spot, [your face shines]. All lotuses—of every lotus...
"Your face shines especially brightly, like a mass of supreme beauty"—such a simile is called an "unreal simile" (*abhūtopamā*) because it compares an object that does not exist;
it is an unreal simile because the object of comparison is non-existent. The analysis of the compound is: *arāsi* means "become a mass.

Here, [the mass] is conceived in the sense of being non-existent, as it is merely a conceptualization arising from the application [of the comparison], since such a mass of radiance does not actually exist.
But in some cases, it is understood through the sense [of the context] due to the inherent power of the word, even without the connection of compounds, suffixes, or words such as *eva*.

(196) The phrase beginning with "is understood" (*patīyate*) and so forth shows an example where the comparison is understood through the sense. That is to say, in certain instances, the comparison is understood through the sense.

In this context, even for words that are not explicitly joined [by a compound], the meaning is understood through the power (*sāmatthiya*) characterized by the impossibility of another [explanation] (*aññathānupapatti*), which is profound due to the specific application of the words and so forth.

Having shown the threefold simile based on what is reached through words (*saddagammopama*), he now shows the simile based on what is reached through meaning (*atthagammopama*) with the words beginning "it is understood" (*patīyate*).
However, in certain instances, an analogy based on what is understood through meaning (*atthagamma*) is perceived through the power of the words themselves—
even without the application of compounds, suffixes, or particles, and even setting aside the explicit connection between those words—
by virtue of the inherent capacity of the words. "The power of the words" (*saddānaṃ sāmatthiyaṃ*) is the analysis [of the compound].
"These are not bees, but these are eyes; this is not a lotus, but this is a face"—because of the similarity of their excellence, this is considered a simile of identity (sā rūpopamā). 197.
He illustrates it with the verse beginning "bhiṅge" and so forth: "These are not bees, but rather these are eyes; this is not a lotus..."

However, they recognize the face itself as being of such a nature; this is considered a simile of identity (*sarūpopamā*) because it illustrates the non-different similarity between the eyes of a bee and [the eyes] of a lotus-faced woman.

Thus he said, "Subyatta," and so forth. By means of the clearly manifest, distinct similarity characterized by flickering, radiance, and other qualities of the well-developed eyes of bees and the lotus-like faces, the possibility of non-difference is distinguished even before [any doubt arises], except in the case of the eyes and so forth [in other contexts].

When the cognition of "bhiṅga" (bees) has arisen, even in the absence of words such as "upamā" (simile) or "jotaka" (indicator), the similarity of the "bhiṅga-locana" (bee-like eyes) and so forth is understood through the power of implication (*sāmatthiya*). The same applies to the subsequent cases as appropriate. 197.
Now he provides an example with the words beginning with "bhiṅgāni": "These bhiṅgas are not bees..."
Furthermore, regarding the eyes: this is not a lotus flower, but rather a face.

Such a simile is called a *sarūpopamā* (simile of identical form) because it clearly demonstrates the similarity between the eyes of a *bhiṅga*-bird and a lotus face through their well-evident likeness.
Herein, even in the absence of compound words, suffixes, or the use of particles such as *eva*, [the meaning is conveyed] by such expressions as "these are the eyes of a *bhiṅga*."
Having refuted the erroneous cognition that perceives "bees and lotuses" in the eyes and faces, one asks:

"In the absence of similarity—such as in the arrangement of the eyes and faces, or in qualities like flickeringness and loveliness—what kind of cognition of 'bees and lotuses' could arise in relation to the eyes and faces?
By the power of the definition of "inexplicability otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*), this establishes the bees and lotuses as the objects of comparison (*upamāna*).
The similarity between the things compared— the eyes and the face— is understood. The phrases "well-known" (*suṭṭhu byattaṃ*) and "manifest" (*pākaṭaṃ*),
as well as "that [quality] and that similarity," and "that simile whose form or nature (*sabhāva*) is common," and "that and that simile"— in these sentences,
there is no boastful exaggeration (*vikatthanā*) such as "the beauty of my own face is like that of the moon."
"Since she exists even in a lotus, this is a *parikappa-upamā* (hypothetical simile).
(198) "In me alone," and so forth. "Indu" means the moon. "The radiance of the face"—the splendor of the mouth—of this Sage is "in me alone, and not elsewhere";
such boasting is a negation, meaning it is enough to praise the excellence of the subject. Why? Because of that reason.

That splendor of the face exists not only in the moon, but even in the lotus; since there is an imaginative conceit (*parikappa*) that it exists even where it does not, the face is compared to the moon—such is this "imaginative simile" (*parikappopamā*). 198.
Regarding the verse beginning with "In me," etc.: O Moon, the splendor of the face—the radiance of the countenance—of this Lord of the World exists in me alone.
Thus, such boasting is sufficient for self-praise and is useless. Why? Because that splendor of the face exists even in the lotus;
therefore, this simile is called a "parikappopamā" (a hypothetical or presumptive simile).

Furthermore, the phrase "since [it] exists" indicates an unspecified reason, yet by showing that it exists in the lotus as well, it simply demonstrates its presence in the *paduma* too. This is due to the act of presumption (*parikappanā*).
The analysis of the compound is: “the similes have been stated” (*vuttā upamā*).

Here, because the moon—which is not present—is imagined as being present despite its absence (through the act of *vikatthana*), even though there are no words expressing a common property (*sadhamma*) between them, the similarity between the moon, which serves as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), and the face, which is the object of comparison (*upameyya*), is understood through this functional power of meaning (*atthasatti*).
[This is so] because one might ask: "How can such an imagination of the subject occur without the similarity between these two? Thus it is understood.
Is it a lotus with bees within,
or is it a face with tremulous eyes? My mind wavers—
This is a simile of doubt. 199. “Or what?
and so forth. Is it a lotus such that within it there are *alī*—bees—or is it such that within it there are *lolāni*—tremulous—eyes?
O Victor, regarding this face of yours, my mind wavers like a swing.
It moves to and fro; thus, by encompassing both sides, the meaning is that it "wavers.
Therefore, this kind of simile, understood through the guise of doubt regarding lotus-faced women, is a "simile of doubt" (saṃsayopamā).
199. “Or what [is there] in the lotus? and so forth. A lotus possessing bees wandering within its interior.
Or else: "What does your face with its restless eyes—your flickering gaze—smell like? My mind wavers;

because it produces agitation toward both [objects], it becomes like a swing (*dolā*). Thus, this kind of simile is called a "simile of doubt" (*saṃsayopamā*), because it is expressed through the doubt regarding the similarity between two things.
[The analysis of the compound is: "that in which there are bees (*ali*) moving within," and "that in which the eyes (*nayana*) are restless (*lolāni*)."
The analysis [of the compound] is: "it behaves like a swing" (*dolā viya ācarati*) and "the similes are stated by way of doubt" (*saṃsayena vuttā upamā*).

Here too, even though there is no other word expressing the common property (*sadhamma*), since the two lotus-faces—distinguished by the two aforementioned qualifications—are not equal in being the cause of doubt, how could doubt arise?
By this very implication (*sāmatthiya*), the connection with a common property is understood.
Because it demonstrates a certain subject matter and designates its own doctrine,
and because there exists a comprehension of its similarity [to other systems].
The simile of the cloth, as follows:

200. “Something,” etc. Having pointed out some desired object such as the Fully Enlightened One (Sambuddha) and so forth, and then expressing another object similar to that first object through the Dharma in some respect, [there is] the similarity between them.

Because there exists the possibility of a conviction and a determination regarding the similarity between two things, this is called a "counter-example" (*paṭivadthu-upamā*) by virtue of its existence.
Through such a counter-example, the equality of the object attained with that [other] object is demonstrated. He provides an illustration with the word "Just as" (*yathā*).
200. "Something," etc. Having first pointed out some desired object—such as the meaning of the words "the Victor" (*jina*) and so forth—...
Because, after having demonstrated [the subject], there is the presence of a comprehension of similarity—

since some object is expressed or spoken of as being similar in some respect to the Dhamma in the sense of its being practiced— and because there exists a thorough knowledge of that which is connected with similarity,
it is a "counter-subject simile" (*pativatthūpamā*), since it clarifies the meaning of the equivalent term for the subject matter, such as the Victor (Jina), which has been presented.
The phrase is "Pativatthūpamā by name. It means: that which has a common property (samāno dhammo) such as the *pārijāta* tree and so forth;

or the state (*bhāvo*) of the comparison and the object compared (*upamānopameyya*), which are similar (*samāna*) or equal (*tulya*); or the understanding (*pati*) of the similarity (*sāmya*); or the existence (*sabbhāva*) of the understanding of similarity (*sāmyappatīti*);
or the comparisons expressed by means of a corresponding object (*pativatthu*). "Yathā" provides an illustration.
While people are being born,
there is not even one who is equal to the Victor; indeed,
a second [such as he] does not exist at all.
The *pārijāta* tree. 201.

“Among people,” and so forth. Among people who are being born, not even a single person exists who possesses virtues equal to the Victor (*jina*), that is, equal to the Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*).

Thus, first, one subject (*vatthu*) has been shown; the second [line], beginning with “and so forth,” is the demonstration of a counter-subject (*pativatthu*) by way of a simile. “Is it not? (*nanu*) is used for assent.

Being the second tree to the *pārijāta*, that specific celestial tree, no other tree exists at all. Just as the *pārijāta* alone is supreme among species of trees, so too is the Victor (the Jina) supreme among beings. 201. "Among beings," and so forth.
Among those beings who are being born, not even one is equal to the Victor, equal to the Fully Awakened One (*sambuddha*), just like the *pārijāta*.
"There is no second tree equal to that tree; indeed, there is no second tree. The word "nanu" is used here as a particle of assent (*anuññāyam*).
By this, he grants that the Omniscient One is incomparable with any other.
Herein, both the superiority of the Pārijāta tree over other trees and the superiority of the Buddha among all beings constitute the pair of the simile and the subject of the simile.

The similarity between two bases is indeed this very similarity; it is illuminated precisely by stating that [the tree] is not equal to the Pārijāta trees which serve as its counterpart by way of corroborating the stated meaning.
It is the meaning of the sentence itself that [clarifies] the meaning of the sentence.
If anything is compared [to something else], because of its being either conjoined or disjoined,
that simile of the meaning of a sentence is of two kinds.

202. He demonstrates the simile based on the meaning of a sentence with the words “By the meaning of a sentence,” and so forth. The meaning of a sentence is a specific relationship between action and its factors (kāraka);

it is by means of that [meaning], and not merely by the meanings of individual words, that some intended meaning characterized as a sentence-meaning is compared—if it is stated to be similar to something else—that is a simile of sentence-meaning (vākyatthopamā).
It is divided into two types. How? As the connected (yuttā) and the disconnected (viyuttā), which together constitute the connected-and-disconnected (yuttaviyuttā).
This is a definition of the meaning [of simile] by way of its function: “The simile is both connected and disconnected; its states and causes are twofold”—this is the addition.
202. Now, he shows the simile whose scope is the meaning of a sentence with the words beginning “In the meaning of a sentence,” etc.

If some intended meaning of a sentence—any meaning of a sentence characterized by the aforementioned definition, consisting of a composite formed by the specific relations between actions and factors (kāraka)—is compared by way of similarity [to another such meaning], [it is a simile].
That which is thus described is called a simile (*upamā*), specifically a simile based on the meaning of a sentence (*vākyatthopamā*).

It is twofold, of two kinds, according to whether it is joined with or devoid of the particle *iva*. Here, because the sense of "like" (*iva*) and so forth is intended by the term *iva*, both the word *iva* itself and its synonyms are included. [End of] *Ivayutta* (joined with *iva*).
This Victor has appeared for the sake of people tormented by defilements,
just as [the moon appears] for those tormented by the heat of the summer season.
Like a cloud in the heat of summer (verse 203). He illustrates this with the words beginning with "the Victor" (*jino*).

This Victor, the Fully Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddho*), has appeared in the world because he has accomplished his task through the attainment of perfect enlightenment, for the sake of those people who have not yet reached the cessation of the burning heat caused by the ten kinds of defilements.
It has appeared. First, there is one sentence serving as the object of comparison (*upameyya*). To the question "Like what?", he says "In the heat," and so forth.

"Like a cloud during the hot season, the time of summer, for people tormented by the heat"—this second sentence serves as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*). This is thus a "simile of sentence-meaning" (*vākyatthopamā*) joined with the particle *iva*.

Here, the relationship between the preceding and succeeding sentence-meanings is that of the qualified (*visesya*) and the qualifier (*visesana*), precisely because they constitute a single sentence-meaning.
It is to be understood. The same applies to what follows.
203. He illustrates this with the words "The Victor" (*jina*) and so forth: This Victor is the Teacher who has conquered the five Māras;

he has appeared for the sake of those people whose very selves are afflicted by the manifold kinds of defilements and the heat of the *saṃkleśas*, and having fulfilled his task through the attainment of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
He is present in the world. If one asks, "Of whom who is distressed by what is he like? [the answer is:

He is like a cloud (*ambuda*) during the summer season, the time of heat, for people tormented by the scorching heat of the summer. Here, because it performs the function of distinguishing, the meaning of the latter clause is the qualifier (*visesana*);
however, because it is that which is to be distinguished, the meaning of the former clause is the qualified (*visesya*). Thus, although there is a division of clauses, the meaning of the sentence—

It should be understood as "even one. The same applies in subsequent instances. In the latter sentence, the word *iva* (like) illustrates the similarity between the qualities (*guṇa*) and the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*) within that very context.

However, in the former sentence, the similarity between the qualities and the possessor of qualities is known through the principle of *anyathānupapatti* (the impossibility of being otherwise), namely, by virtue of the meaning of the latter sentence being identical to that of the former.
Furthermore, [the expressions] "it is hot because of the defilements" and "heat itself is the burning" [should be understood in the same manner].
And thus, the phrases "it is that" and "the Dhamma itself is time" [are established].
The radiance from the face of the Sage of Sages shines forth, uniquely captivating in its splendor.
"O Moon, though you have risen high, what is the use of your display?

(204). He spoke the second [verse] beginning with "O Lord of Sages" (*muninda*). Because there is no other like it, the face of the Lord of Sages shines—meaning it excels in splendor—being uniquely charming due to its grace;
this is first one sentence which serves as the object of comparison (*upameyya*). O Moon!
Even for you who have risen high above the surface of the sky, what is the purpose of your stretching out and your haughty wandering?
None at all, because of the absence of any attainment of splendor equal to that [of the Buddha].
The incomparability of the face of the Lord of Sages—even as it rises higher than that—is merely a display, merely a fondness, for the sake of the production of fruit.

The second sentence serves as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*). Thus, here, by the negation of the rising and blossoming that would be produced through the perception of total similarity, there arises a perception of some common property (*sādharmya*) between the moon-like faces; this is the meaning of the simile in a sentence devoid of the particle *iva*. 204.
Now he illustrates the very same simile in a sentence devoid of *iva* with the words beginning "The eyes of the Lord of Sages," which are "exclusively charming in their grace."
The face of the Lord of Sages, the omniscient one, shines and transcends all else; it is incomparable in its playfulness and thus exceedingly captivating.
Therefore, O Moon, what is the purpose of your display—your vain wandering with pride—even though you have risen high into the upper sky?
Here, the meaning of the subsequent sentence serves as an illustration (*upamā*) for the meaning of the preceding sentence.

It is so called because, for one who conceives the pride of thinking, "I am in every way identical to the moon," both the moon’s ascent into the vault of the sky and its blooming [in the water] serve as points of contrast;

thus, by the negation of these two, the fact that the face and the moon possess a charming gracefulness and a similarity consisting merely of radiance is understood even in the absence of particles such as *iva*.
Therefore, the meaning of the subsequent sentence [serves to clarify] the meaning of the preceding sentence.

It is both a simile (*upamā*) and an adjective (*visesana*). The analysis (*viggaha*) is: "that which is incomparable with grace" (*vilāsena ekamatulyaṃ*) and "that which is captivating" (*tañca taṃ manoharaṃ*).
The particle *api* has the sense of possibility or inclusion.
However, that which possesses different genders and so forth disturbs the wise.
This is sufficient for the refutation of similes (*upamādūsanā*).
In the section on defects (*dosapariccheda*), in order to show the refutation of the simile-ornament (*upamālaṅkāradūsana*) regarding faulty ornamentation, he says: "It agitates," and so forth.

As for that which has different genders (*bhinnaliṅga*) and so on—the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes differences in number (*bhinnavacana*), deficiency, excess, and the like. The particle "tu" (but/however) [is used here].
The meaning is "likewise, it illuminates the sense. It agitates—that is, does not satisfy—the wise and intelligent person;

this [fault], which consists of a discrepancy in gender and so forth, is sufficient and capable of spoiling the simile in some instances, though not in all, for the purpose of contradiction. He provides an example with the words "Just as that.

205. In the section on Faults (*doṣa-pariccheda*), after the enumeration of faults has concluded, regarding the faulty ornament (*duṭṭhālaṅkāra*) that was pointed out, the examples to be shown are as follows:
“That which corrupts an ornament is a ‘corrupt ornament’ (duṭṭhālaṅkaraṇa);
its definition as an ornament will be made manifest in the section on Rūpa.
Following the promise [previously] made, he now says “it agitates,” etc., in order to demonstrate that which possesses different genders and so forth. However...
However, that which will be explained— namely, the discrepancy in gender, number, and so forth— which agitates the wise, the intelligent poet, generating agitation [in him] by making him think,
"It ought to be stated thus," this discrepancy in gender and so on serves for the purpose of corrupting the simile (*upamādūsanā*),
that is, for the sake of destroying the aforementioned simile; it occurs in certain contexts where the intended expression is, for example, "this person goes like a woman" (*itthīvāyaṃ jano yāti*).
"Elsewhere" means sufficient or adequate. "Just as that" he provides as an illustration.
"That which is both broken and dissimilar, and that which is a gender," and "that which begins with dissimilar speech and so forth," and "the refutation by way of simile"—this is the sentence.
"This hare-marked moon is like a swan"—it is broken...
Like lakes within the expanse of the sky,
those who speak of inferior castes are base;
such a person is like a soldier devoted to his lord.
206. “Like a female swan”: this moon, together with its crescent, is like a female swan, similar to a female swan;

this is a simile of different genders (*bhinnaliṅga-bhinnaliṅgopamā*). “Like lakes in the sky”: because these are words denoting different species, it is a simile of dissimilar words (*visadisa-vacanopamā*). “The servant is devoted to his lord, just as that [dog] is devoted to its master”:
this is a low simile (*hīna-hīnopamā*), because a superior being is compared to an inferior one in terms of birth and other qualities, such as the dog.
206. “*Haṃsī*,” etc. This moon, *sasī*, is like a female swan (*haṃsī*), as in “like a female swan.

Such similes where the genders differ from that of the object being compared—due to having a gender different from the object of comparison—are called “similes with differing genders” (*bhinnaliṅgopamā*).

“The sky, the firmament, like lakes”—this is a “simile of different classes” (*vijātivacanopamā*) because the words used are of a different class than the object of comparison, being dissimilar in their verbal expression. [The term] *adhipa* means a lord or master.
"A servant, an attendant, like a dog, a master"—this is called a "low comparison" (*hīnopamā*) because a superior person is compared to an inferior dog.
The grammatical analysis (*viggaha*) is: "its gender is broken," or "it has various kinds and natures," or "its comparison consists of words denoting different species."
"Like the sun-garlanded [Khajjoto] shines"—
this is an excessive simile (adhikopamā);
"the ocean of strength was not touched."
It was agitated like the ocean.
(207) “Like a firefly,” etc.: “The firefly shines like the sun, the garlanded with rays”—this is an *adhikopamā* (excessive simile), because something inferior is compared to something superior.
“The army-ocean, like the ocean, was agitated”—this is an *aphuṭṭhatthopamā* (simile of unimpeded meaning).

In the phrase “an ocean of strength,” because the vastness of the army is understood through the metaphor (*rūpaka*), and because no further specific meaning is touched upon by the subsequent simile (*upamā*) “like the ocean,” [the former is considered a *samādhi-upamā*]. 207.
“The firefly,” etc. “The firefly shines like the sun”: this is an *adhika-upamā*, that is, a simile with an excessive [degree of] comparison.

Because it is already compared [to something else], it is called an "excessive simile" (*adhikopamā*). In the phrase, “The army, like the ocean of strength, like the sea, was agitated,” the greatness of the army—which has not yet been touched upon—is understood through a concealed simile (*tirobhūta-upamā*) by means of the term “ocean of strength”;
therefore, since there is no further object to be touched upon by the subsequent simile “like the sea,” it is called an “untouched-object simile” (*aphuṭṭhattha-upamā*). It is untouched—
The phrase "its meaning" (*attho etissā*) and the phrase "the ocean is indeed strength" (*balaṃ eva ambhodhi*)—
this [verse] is dependent on the simile "a spot on the moon" (*cande kalaṅko bhiṅgo*).
“The moon is like a broken white lotus;
the night-maker is spotted.

(208) Regarding the verse beginning with “In the moon,” etc.: the comparison [of the moon] to a bee is a simile (*upamā*) that requires a further simile, namely, “in the moon which resembles a cluster of flowers.”
Since a bee cannot exist on the moon, whereas it can exist on a flowering tree, this is an "expectant simile" (*upamāpekkhinī*). The phrase "the moon, the maker of night, is spotted,
possesses its characteristic marks, has the form of a white water-lily (*kairava*), and resembles a kumuda lotus" is a "fragmentary simile" (*khaṇḍitopamā*),
because in order to establish that the interior of the *kairava* is yellow, one ought to have said, "having the form of a *kairava* with bees."

208. “In the moon,” and so forth. “In the moon, a spot like a bee”—this is called *upamāpekkhinī* (dependent on a simile) because it depends on things such as flower-clusters that serve as the actual similes for the moon.

The intention is that it is defective because, since there is no occurrence of a bee in the moon, those things such as flower-clusters which are its [the bee’s] objective domain have not been mentioned as being the moon’s simile. It is “with a spot,” meaning accompanied by a spot.
The moon, the maker of night, has the appearance of a *kairava* flower and resembles the *kumuda* lily;
this is called a "fragmented simile" (*khaṇḍitopamā*) because, although one ought to say "having the appearance of a bee and a *kairava*," the comparison to the bee is absent and thus fragmented.

It is so called because it "relies on a simile" (*upamaṃ apekkhati*), or because "the parts have gone" (*khaṇḍaṃ itā gatā*), or because it is "joined with what has gone in fragments" (*khaṇḍena itā yuttā*), or because it is "the appearance of a *kairava*" (*keravassākāro*).
There is the statement, "it exists," and "it proceeds together with a stain.
In such forms as these, the wise become indifferent;
yet they apply their attention only to certain specific applications.

209. It is stated [in the commentary] by way of the words “*iccevaṃ*” and so forth. Regarding forms (*rūpa*) and usages (*payoga*): those for whom respect (*ādara*) and esteem (*sambhāvanā*) have departed or vanished are such [as described].
Is that which has a different gender (*bhinnaliṅga*) and so forth necessarily to be disregarded, or not necessarily?

To the question “Is it *niyamena* (necessarily)?”, he says “*karonti*,” etc., implying that there are indeed cases where it is acceptable to employ [such forms]. However, in certain usages, the wise poets...
"And they show respect. The particle *ca* (and) conjoins a further sense that ought to be stated.
209. "Thus" (*iti*), etc. Regarding the applications (*payoga*) beginning with "thus" that were just indicated, the wise (*dhīra*) become devoid of respect [for them].
Yet these same wise ones do show respect in certain applications where there are differences such as gender and so forth. Thus.
The analysis of the compound is as follows: "those for whom this kind [of thing] is the beginning," and "those which are both those and forms," and "those for whom respect has departed.

The word *ca* (and) serves to connect the various clauses. Therefore, by the sense of "departed respect," it draws in the performance of another act of respect toward the continuity of the discourse that is about to be told.
This person goes like a woman,
yet she speaks like a man;
she is as dear to me as my own life.
"Knowledge is heaped up like wealth.
(210) He illustrates this with the verse beginning "A woman," and so forth. This person moves about like a woman, following after her actions;
yet she speaks like a man, due to her association with such audacity. Herein, there is a difference in gender between the object of comparison and the thing compared.

“This person is desired by me as dear and beloved as my own life; knowledge, grammar, and so forth are honored by me like wealth”—this is the distinction in expression regarding the quality of being a collector (*rāsikatā*).
(210) Now, he shows the scope of application for words of different genders with the phrase “This person, like a woman,” and so on.

This person goes like a woman—that is, like a female (*mahilā*)—due to a lack of clear understanding. This [person], though a man, acts like a woman because of being possessed of such immodesty (*pāgabbhiya*).

"He speaks like a man. In this case, even though there is a difference in gender between the two—the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameyya*)—poets pay close attention [to such usage].
This person is as dear to me as my own life, as my very soul, and as my vital breath.
His knowledge—accumulated through study, including grammar, lexicography, and so forth—is like his wealth. Here, regarding the number of the object of comparison and the subject of comparison...
Even though there is a distinction, it is indeed desirable.
O Protector of the Earth, like the Lord of Beings himself, this King of the Gods shines resplendently;
he is capable of outshining even the region of the sun with his brilliance.

211. He provides an example of the inferior and the superior with the words beginning “*bhavaṃ viya*. The address “O Protector of the Earth” (*mahīpāla*) is used; [the king] shines like the Lord of the Gods (*devarāja*).
Thus, it occurs even by means of the inferior. This shows that in such a suitable subject matter, differences in gender, number, and so forth, do not defile the simile. (Ka.)
211. “*Bhavaṃ*,” etc. O King Mahīpāla, Sakka, the king of the gods, shines like your majesty (*bhavaṃ*).
Here, even though it refers to an inferior state by comparing Sakka to “your majesty,” it is nonetheless intended as a term of praise.

This king is capable—meaning able—to ascend to, or reach, the path of the radiant sun (*aṃsumato sūriyassa kacchaṃ*) by means of his splendor (*tejasā*). In this context, although the sun is superior in splendor, [the comparison is made].

The word *iva* (like) is used as a synonym for *upamābhūto* (being like), as in the phrase "to ascend the bank. Such instances where the gender and other attributes differ do not constitute a flaw in the simile (*upamādūsana*).
[The definition of a simile is:
the perception of non-difference between the object of comparison and the thing compared.
When the simile itself has its distinction obscured, it is called *rūpaka* (metaphor).
[The author] defines *rūpaka* with the words beginning "the object of comparison" (*upamāne*).

Because it defines—that is, because by means of superimposition it represents or demonstrates the non-difference, the absence of distinctness—between the object of comparison and the subject of comparison as previously described, it is called *rūpaka*.

That very simile (*upamā*)—which has its distinction (*bheda*) or diversity (*nānatta*) concealed and unmanifest through the superimposition (*āropa*) of non-difference between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameyya*)—is called "metaphor" (*rūpaka*), according to the definition stated above.
In the expression “*padambujaṃ*,” the foot itself is treated as a lotus because of its resemblance to a lotus;
thus, by means of the superimposition of non-difference between the foot and the lotus, which serve respectively as the object of comparison and the standard of comparison...

Although the distinction between the simile (*upamā*)—defined as the common property residing in both the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameyya*)—is indeed present, it remains concealed.

It is not, however, manifest as something extraordinary, as in the phrase "the foot is like a lotus. And the intention is that such a simile, by attaining a state of non-difference between the object of comparison and the subject of comparison, is called a metaphor (*rūpaka*).
212. Now, in accordance with the order of enumeration, he demonstrates the figure of speech *rūpaka* (metaphor) with the words beginning "the object of comparison" (*upamāna*).

When there is a difference between the object of comparison and the object compared—even though they were just mentioned as being non-different by nature—the discernment of a non-difference imagined by speakers who say "this is that" or "that is this," based upon a concealed similarity, occurs within the word-meanings of the object of comparison and the object compared.
Based on the mental superimposition (*āropaṇa*) whereby the difference [between the object and the standard of comparison] has become latent,
the very metaphor (*upamā*)— in which the distinctness is not manifest as "the foot is like a lotus," but rather the difference is concealed as "the lotus-foot"—

is called a *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification), because it consists of the common property (*sādharmya*) that constitutes the meaning of the term. Relying on the disappearance of similarity, the bases of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object compared (*upameyya*) are apprehended as non-different.
By the very apprehension of their non-difference, even the difference in the simile—which is defined as a distinct common property (sādharmya) occurring in dependence upon them—is concealed.
Thus, the intention is that it is called a *rūpaka* because the simile itself, defined as a common property whose variousness is concealed, illuminates the non-difference of the bases (*vatthu*).
Furthermore, it is so called because its difference is concealed (*tirobhūta-bheda*), and it "fashions" (*rūpayati*) non-difference.
And the phrase "he reveals" [is explained as follows]:
it has as its object the entirety of the subject matter, and it is also a partial exclusion;
that is further twofold each, and by way of compounds and so forth, it is threefold.
213. He explains its classification by means of the passage beginning with "without remainder" (*asesa*). That which has as its object a subject matter that is without remainder is of such a kind;
and that which unfolds (*vivattati*) in a single part or portion is "partial unfolding" (*ekadesavivatti*). Thus, that metaphor (*rūpaka*) is twofold.

Furthermore, each of these is divided separately according to whether the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameyya*) have been compounded or not: namely, compound metaphor (*samāsa-rūpaka*) and non-compound metaphor (*asamāsa-rūpaka*).

It may be threefold by way of being a compound, a non-compound, or a compound-cum-non-compound metaphor (rūpaka). 213. Regarding the phrase beginning with "asesi" (without remainder): that metaphor is twofold—having as its object the entirety of the subject matter (asesavatthuvisaya) and having partial exclusion (ekadesavivatti).

Furthermore, each of these two types is again divided according to whether it is a compound and so forth, resulting in the compound metaphor (samāsarūpaka), the non-compound metaphor (asamāsarūpaka), and the compound-cum-non-compound metaphor (samāsāsamāsarūpaka).

The analysis of these [compounds] is threefold: (1) "the object (*vatthu*) and the scope (*visaya*) of that which possesses no remainder (*asesa*)," (2) "it turns away (*vivattati*) from one part (*ekadese*)," (3) "it understands each one (*ekaṃ ekaṃ patīti*)," (4) "those whose beginning consists of compounds and compound-like forms (*samāso samāsarūpakaṃ ādi yesam*)," (5) "the division (*bheda*) of those according to their nature (*tesaṃ vaso*"), and (6) "in three ways (*tīhi pakārehi*).
This is the grammatical analysis (*viggaha*).
Who would not wear upon their heads the lotus-feet of the Lord of Sages,
which are adorned with fingers as petals and the radiance of the nails as filaments?
214. He provides an illustration with the verse beginning "Aṅguli" (the fingers), etc.
Because it is understood through comparison by means of the fingers themselves, [the feet] are adorned with petals that are glossy and copper-colored; they shine most intensely.

Wherein the rays—the very light—of the nails are like filaments, such a lotus, which is the very foot of the Lord of Sages, who indeed would not wear upon their heads—that is, upon their crowns—as an ornament? All people indeed do so.

“They do not bear [it]”: this is a *samāsa-rūpaka* (compound metaphor) concerning an object that is not incomplete (*asesavatthu*), because it represents the form of all the parts—such as the fingers and so forth—of the whole word (*aṅgin*).
The same applies to what follows, as appropriate. 214.
Now he provides examples, beginning with “fingers” (*aṅguli*) and so on: “shining with leaf-like fingers,” meaning with leaves designated as fingers.
Who does not wear upon their head the lotus-foot of the Lord of Sages, whose filaments are the luster of the nails— the filaments formed by the rays of the toenails?
Because the foot, which is the object qualified (*visesya*), and the toes and the luster of the nails, which are the qualifiers (*visesana*),

are taken as a unity through the metaphorical identification (*abhedakappanā*) with the lotus petals and filaments that serve as the standard of comparison, they are thus indicated by means of a compound (*samāsa*).
This is called the "Metaphor of the Compound Form" (*asesavatthuvisayasamāsarūpaka*). The sentence is:

"The fingers themselves are the petals," "it is beautified by them," "there is luster in the nails," and "they themselves are the filaments. This is the "Non-compound Metaphor of the Entirety of Objects" (*asesavatthuvisaya-asamāsa*).
The jewels are his abundant virtues; compassion is his cool water;
his depth and unfathomability—this Victor is a directly manifest ocean. (215) “‘The jewels,’ etc.:
This Victor, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is a directly manifest ocean for us, not one beyond our sight.”

[Sāgara] means the ocean. How so? Those abundant and manifold qualities of his, such as loving-kindness (*mettā*) and the rest, are "jewels" by virtue of their common characteristic of being incomparable and difficult to behold.
His compassion (*karuṇā*) is "cool water" by virtue of its common characteristic of removing the fever of affliction from all people.

That depth of his—his lack of shallowness regarding gain and the like—is "bottomlessness" by virtue of its common characteristic with the ocean of being unfathomable. This is a compound metaphor (*asamāsa-rūpaka*) whose scope encompasses every single object.
215. “The jewels,” and so forth. This Victor is our very own ocean;

for his abundant qualities—virtue, concentration, and the rest—are indeed jewels, since they share the same characteristics as jewels such as being highly esteemed. His compassion, which is not shared by others, is cool water;
because it shares the characteristic of dispelling the heat of suffering, it is truly cool water. His profundity regarding gain, loss, and so forth...
Uniformity is indeed unfathomability and profundity. This is a compound metaphor (*asamāsarūpaka*) whose object is the entirety of all things.

"Bhūrī" is an indeclinable. O Lord of Sages, those two—the Moonlight (*Candikā*) and the Gentle Laughter (*Mandahāsā*)—are from the moon of your face, which has as its object the entirety of all things.
“This [moonlight] awakens the forest of white water-lilies that is the minds of the virtuous.
(216) “*Candikā*” and so forth. “*Muninda*” is a form of address. “The moon of his face” (*vadaninduno*) is a compound metaphor (*samāsa-rūpaka*).
This gentle smile is the moonlight (*candikā*) of the moon-like face; this is a non-compound metaphor (*asamāsa-rūpaka*). The minds of the virtuous are themselves the white water-lilies (*kumuda*).

*Keravāni* is a compound metaphor (*samāsa-rūpaka*). "Their grove, the forest, awakens [them]"—that is, it causes them to blossom—this is a metaphor that is both a compound and a non-compound (*samāsāsamāsa-rūpaka*).
216. *Candi*-etc. O Lord of Sages, the moonlight (*candikā*) of your moon-like face—the gentle smile (*mandahāsa*) acting as the moonlight of the moon that is your mouth—is radiant.
Here, by using the singular number for the genus (*jātyekavacana*), the "moonlight of the gentle smile" is indicated. Alternatively, [the word *candikā* may be understood as follows:]...
This moon-like face awakens and causes to blossom the forest of the white water-lilies of the minds of the virtuous—the forest of white lotuses known as the hearts of noble persons.
“The moonlight is a gentle smile” is a non-compound metaphor (*asamāsa-rūpaka*). “Of the moon-like face” and “the forest of mind-water-lilies” are compound metaphors (*samāsa-rūpaka*).
Therefore, this is a metaphor consisting of both compounds and non-compounds whose scope encompasses all possible bases. And those smiles are gentle.
The analysis [of the compound] is as follows: "moon" (*indu*) is the very act of speaking (*vadana*); "pleasing to the virtuous" (*sādhūnaṃ manāni*) is the very lotuses (*kumudāni*);
and "their grove" (*tesaṃ kānanaṃ*) is the grove of those [lotuses]. This is the classification of metaphor (*rūpaka*) regarding the domain of all objects.
Regarding the partial metaphor (*ekadesavivatti*), the classification is now being stated.
[The author] concludes with the words beginning “without remainder” (*asesi*). With the words beginning “one,” he promises to state the subdivisions of the second type.

217. “Without remainder,” etc. In metaphors whose scope is an object without remainder, this triad of examples beginning with “glittering with finger-petals” constitutes the subdivision. Now, the specific classification—that is, the distinction—regarding the partial metaphor is being stated.
Who would not find happiness beholding the face of the Sage, with its flower-like playful smile and its lovely bud-like lower lip?
218. “*Vilāsa*,” and so forth. Whose flower is laughter itself, joined with grace (*vilāsa*)? Whose sprout is the lower lip itself, beautiful and charming?
Seeing such a face of the Sage, what people indeed do not find happiness? All of them.
This is a *ekadesavivatti-samāsa-rūpaka* (partial metaphorical compound), because the limbs—laughter and the rest—are personified (*rūpita*), while the face, the possessor of the limbs, is not.
The same applies to the subsequent sections as appropriate.

218. Regarding the verse beginning with "vilāsi": Who indeed among people would not find happiness while beholding the face of the Sage, which is like a flower consisting of playful smiles and graceful laughter, and which has lovely lower lips like tender sprouts?
They find joy and happiness, yet they do not merely experience them; rather, they truly experience them.

Having shown the non-difference between the smile—the qualifier—and the flowers and sprouts—the objects of comparison—by means of the latter, there is an imposition of non-difference (*abhedāropa*) because the face—the subject qualified (*visesya*)—has not been stated as non-different from one of the objects of comparison.
This is therefore a *ekadesavivatti-samāsa-rūpaka* (a metaphorical compound with partial concealment). It is endowed with grace (*vilāsa*).
The phrase "hāso" (a smile), which is itself "kusumaṃ" (a flower); and "ruciro" (beautiful) which is itself "adhara" (the lower lip);
and "pallavo" (a sprout), which is itself that [lip]—this is the sentence. May the pair of feet of the Lord of Munis, containing compounds with partial elision (*ekadesavivatti*), grant you victory!
“Nakharaṃsī paraṃ kantā, yassa pāpajayaddhajā.
(219) “Pāda,” etc. May the pair of feet of the Victorious Lord of Sages grant you victory—the defeat of adversaries.
Of what kind? Whose fingernail-rays are supremely—absolutely—charming and pleasing, and which serve as banners for the conquest of evils such as greed and the rest.
"Victory! The banners and flags are raised! This is an example of a partial metaphor (*ekadesavivatti*) within a compound.

219. Regarding the verse beginning with "On the feet": the pair of feet—the two feet—of that Lord of Sages, for whom the rays from his toenails—the splendor of the nails on his feet—are exceedingly lovely and charming, and which serve as victory banners over evil, like banners raised high in the conquest of wickedness.
"May it grant you victory, that is, the defeat of your adversaries.

By superimposing non-difference through the banners which serve as a simile for the rays of the claws, and because the term "pair of feet" (*pādadvandam*) is not explicitly analyzed [as a compound], this is called a *ekadesavivatti-asamāsa-rūpaka* (a metaphorical compound with partial transformation). The analysis (*viggaha*) is:
"the victory over evils" (*pāpānaṃ jayo*), and "banners in that [victory]" (*tasmiṃ dhajā*).
Upon the moon-like face of the Lord of Munis, whose cheeks are perfectly pure,
