To this it is replied: Where another figure of speech (alaṅkāra) is also perceived, yet a correspondence occurs that conforms to the order of the enumeration, there the figure of speech is designated as "correspondence" alone, because it is that which is intended to be expressed primarily. Where no other figure of speech is understood, there...
It should be understood that this is indeed the ultimate pleasure.
260. He illustrates this with the words beginning with "ālāpi" (addressed).

O Lord of Sages, through your conversations, the playfulness of your smiles, and the playfulness of your sweet voice, together with the playfulness of your gentle laughter, the kokilas, karavīkas, and the kumudas and keravas have attained victory—that is, they have become the cause of your triumph.

And one should consider that they "resort to" the forest and water as if they were making them their support by means of desire. Herein, "with the play of conversation and laughter" is the *uddesa* (enumeration);

"the cuckoos [and] the night-lotuses" is a non-enumeration (*anuddesa*) because it refers back to what was previously stated; and "the forest and the water" is an enumeration because it refers forward to what is yet to be said.
In reality, through such a distinction, there is an absence of any causal basis for the cuckoos and others to resort to the forest and so forth; thus, the word "as if" (*iva*) is employed.
It has been explained. This being so, this [following] supposition does not occur.

Why? Because when a collection of various ornaments exists, whichever ornament is desired by the speaker is primarily designated. Thus, even though there is a conjunction of the ornament of supposition (*parikappanālaṅkāra*), because the non-enumerated (*anuddesa*) shown according to the order of enumeration (*uddesakkama*) is primary, this is called the ornament of sequence (*kamālaṅkāra*). Such is it also.
It should be understood in this very way. The analysis [of the compound] is: "speech and laughter" (ālāpo ca hāso ca), and then "the playfulness of those two" (tesaṃ līlā).
There may indeed be something called "dearer," which is the surpassing presentation of some object of affection.
It is that which constitutes an excess of love for what is already dear.

261. [The author] explains *piyatara* (the more beloved) with the words beginning with "it might be" (*siyā*). That which is the presentation or narration of some object of speech (*abhidheyyasabhāva*) that is exceedingly dear—this is what is called *piyatara*.
261. Now, he demonstrates the figure of speech *piyatarālaṅkāra* with the words beginning with "it might be":
that which is the presentation or statement of some object of speech that is exceedingly dear—this presentation is called *piyatara*.
It is called "the most beloved ornament. The meaning is: "it is exceedingly dear," and the phrase is "the very essence, the form, the intrinsic nature.
"The joy that has arisen within me through the sight of you, O Peaceful One—this joy shall arise again in due time through the sight of you once more."
262. He illustrates this with the words beginning with “pīti. O Peaceful One, Great Sage, O True Person:
the joy that has arisen in me merely by your being within the range of my vision and by hearing your sweet speech—this joy, at such a time, is a bliss belonging to you alone and to no one else;
for who else indeed could be like you? May there be another meeting with you!
262. “Rapture,” and so forth. O peaceful, true person, Tathāgata:

because you have come within the range of my vision through your guidance, this rapture that has arisen in me—this rapture, by such an occasion, will increase further from seeing you alone, since there is no one else like you; for here, the object of experience is exceedingly desirable, serving as the cause for the intensity of the rapture.
By the word *atigedha* (“excessive greed”) in the context of seeing, and by the word *atipīti* (“excessive joy”) in the context of manifestation,
the meaning of the term *atipiya* (“extremely dear”) is made clear. Furthermore, because a joy that arose previously— thinking “this joy will exist”— cannot arise again,
only a joy similar to that [previous state] is intended, just as one says, “that very same spider,” or “those very same medicines.”
"By means of a praised simile, through the description of the intended subject—this is called 'compound usage' (samāsavutti) because it consists of a concise expression of meaning.

(263) He spoke "by means of a praised" and so forth in order to explain compound usage. By means of a "praised" (vaṇṇita), that is, a commended simile, [there is a concise expression] of the intended subject...
This is called *samāsavutti* (compound-usage), characterized by the statement of a meaning that has been kept in mind through the narration of a subject matter.
Why? Because its nature (*rūpa*) or essence (*sabhāva*) consists in the abbreviation—namely, the concise narration—of the intended meaning;

therefore, this technical designation (*anvatthasaññā*) is applied as "abbreviated usage" (*saṅkhepavutti*) or "compound usage" (*samāsavutti*). Why? Because this [meaning] has become subordinate (*guṇībhūtā*).
It establishes a different meaning from its own primary sense, yet it does not have that primary sense as its predominant factor. 263.
Now he explains the function of the compound with the words "by means of what is described" (*vaṇṇitena*), and so forth.

By means of a "described" (*vaṇṇita*)—that is, praised—simile (*upamāna*), which serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*), through the expression (*vutti*) or narration of the intended subject (*adhippetavatthu*), that is, the desired object (*icchitattha*), [the meaning is conveyed] by way of a concise form of the sense (*atthasaṅkheparūpato*).
Because it has the nature of encompassing the meaning intended to be expressed, this is called "compound-function" (*samāsavutti*) according to the definition stated above.

Here, having encompassed and attended to the meaning intended to be expressed, this is called "compound-function" because it elucidates that which has been attended to by means of the description of its state as a simile. In this [function], the inherent meaning denoted by the words is subordinate.

However, the meaning currently being discussed is primary. "That" refers to the intended subject matter, and "and this" refers to the compound (*samāsa*), which is the concise statement (*saṅkhepena vutti*).
"Concise form" (*saṅkhepo yeva rūpaṃ*) means "having that as its form" (*sarūpa*); thus, the analysis (*viggaha*) is "the concise form of the meaning.
This [compound] has a qualifier that is both distinct and non-distinct from the qualified object (*visesya*) by virtue of its mere quality (*visesya-mattena*).
There is indeed another [type], distinguished by being both different and non-different (bhinnābhinna-viśeṣaṇā).
He demonstrates its classification with the words "That which... and so forth.

This compound function (samāsa-vutti) is when any given object, perceived through a general form, is excluded from anything else—on account of some quality or other—with the thought, "This is such and not otherwise."
That which is delimited is the qualified (*visesya*); that very measure [is so called] because it excludes the distinctions of the qualifiers (*visesana*).

Because the property of a part is applied to the whole, they are distinct and unequal. That which possesses a qualifier that is non-distinct and of an identical form is "that which has a non-distinct qualifier" (*abhinnavisesanā*);
this also certainly exists. There is another as well; not only that one. Of what kind? Distinct and...
Those whose qualifiers (*visesana*) are both non-distinct and distinct possess "distinct-and-non-distinct qualifiers. The qualified (*visesya*), however, is distinct.
Now, he demonstrates the divisions of that compound operation (*samāsavutti*) with the words "That this... and so forth.

This compound operation is [performed] when something taken as a standard of comparison (*upamānavatthu*), by means of some instrument consisting of a quality or similar attribute, is brought to mind as a mere qualified object.

"This is the object of comparison (upameyyavatthu) such as this"—thus, there is another [type] which is distinct from the common ground (sāmaññāvattha) by means of a distinguishing attribute (visesya), being separate or dissimilar;

or, it may be undifferentiated by a distinguishing attribute, joined with a similar distinguishing attribute; or it may have both differentiated and undifferentiated distinguishing attributes, joined with both dissimilar and similar distinguishing attributes, and joined with a distinct subject of distinction. Thus, the function of the compound (samāsavutti) is twofold.

It exists. Regarding the phrase "only the distinction is the measure" (*visesyameva mattam*): they are called "distinct" because the differentiation of possibility and nature that exists in the parts also occurs in the whole.

Regarding the analysis (*viggaha*): it is that in which the qualifiers (*visesana*) are non-distinct; and it is that in which [the qualifiers] are both distinct and non-distinct; and it is that in which those qualifiers exist.
The giver of the stream of pure wisdom characterized by non-differentiation,
the praised treasury of jewels.
"And this ocean is deep;
it has been brought about by merit and attained through merit by me. (Sī.

265) He illustrates both [aspects] with the words beginning "purified" (*visuddha*). This ocean, the sea, was brought about by merit—that is, by roots of wholesome action practiced over a long period.
By me, through the cause [of my practice], the attainment (patta) has been reached; what is it like? It is the ocean that bestows the pure nectar of immortality (visuddhāmatasandāyī).

Because it was not mixed with armies during the churning of the gods and asuras, it is "pure" (visuddha); because it bestows the nectar (amata) of immortality. Furthermore, because it is untouched even by a trace of fault (dosa), it is "absolutely stainless" (accantanimmala);
and because it bestows the element of Nibbāna—which is designated as "immortal" (amata) due to the absence of death—by way of being its instructor, it is the ocean.
The True Dharma bestows purified minds. Jewels such as pearls and gems are praised because they are faultless;
their abode, the place where they arise, is the ocean. The jewels consisting of the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment are praised and extolled in many ways by the Buddhas and others;
their abode is the True Dharma. And it is profound because it is bottomless.

It is established that "the ocean" and "the true Dhamma" are brought together here. This is a case where the qualifiers (*visesana*) are not distinct from one another, even though they differ only in their relation to the qualificand (*visesya*).

This is because the intended qualifiers—the true Dhammas—are non-distinct from the qualificand, the ocean, and because the qualifiers—such as "bestowing pure nectar"—are non-distinct in the manner already described.
265. Now he provides an illustration with the words beginning "pure" (*visuddhā*).
It bestows pure nectar because, according to worldly convention, it was not mixed with poison during the churning of the ocean by the gods and asuras; thus, it is the giver of pure elemental nectar.

Furthermore, because it reveals the True Dhamma existing within the intellect through the metaphorical description of the ocean, it bestows pure nectar, being free even from a mere drop of the defects of the bait of sensual pleasures.
Because it is free from impurity, it is exceedingly stainless; because it is devoid of aging and death, it is Nibbāna. By bestowing instruction, he is a donor to those who are to be trained.
In the sense of the ocean, he is a repository for praised jewels, being the place where faultless jewels such as pearls and gems originate.

In the sense of the True Dhamma, however, he is a repository for praised jewels, being the locus of the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma), which are praised by the Buddha and others.

This ocean and this sea are profound by their very nature, being unfathomable even in their ordinary state; they are deep through the fourfold methods beginning with the method of unity (*ekattanaya*).
Furthermore, the True Dharma grasped by the mind has been brought forth and attained by me through merit—that is, through wholesome karma accumulated over other existences.
Because the ocean, which serves as the subject of description, is distinct from the True Dharma, which is intended to be expressed, [the two are compared].
And because qualifiers such as “bestowing pure delight” (*visuddhāmatasandāyī*) are non-different according to the method already stated even with respect to both qualificands,

this operation of compound formation (*samāsavutti*) is one where the qualifiers are non-different while being differentiated merely by their qualificands. This is called *bhinnābhinnavisesana* (differentiated-non-differentiated qualifier).
This tree, which is the foundation for desired goals,
whose essence is its fruit and flowers,
and which is graced by shade, is as if unprecedented.
The wish-fulfilling tree (kapparukkha) has arisen.
266. Regarding the phrase beginning with "icchite": this very same [tree] has arisen as a wish-fulfilling tree because it possesses the aforementioned qualities and its form is marvelous.
Of what sort is it? It is called the "giver of desired objects" (icchitatthapada) because it bestows whatever worldly purpose is desired; such is the wish-fulfilling tree.
The Victor is the "Giver of Desired Aims" (*icchitatthapada*) because he bestows whatever aim is desired, whether mundane or supramundane.
The Victor is the "Essence" (*sāra*), the "Best" (*seṭṭha*), and the "Wish-Fulfilling Tree" (*kapparukkha*). The Wish-Fulfilling Tree is adorned with fruits and flowers;
it exists together with its shade—the shade being that which is contrary in nature to the light of the moon and sun—and thus it is "with shade. But as for the Victor, previously...
"Endowed with shade" (*sacchāyo*) means being possessed of the "shade" (*chāyā*) described as bodily loveliness and so forth.

This is an example of a qualifier that is both distinct and non-distinct from the qualified (*visesya-matta-bhinnā bhinna-abhinna-viśeṣaṇā*). This is because the qualified—the wish-fulfilling tree (*kapparukkha*)—is distinct [from the shade], yet the state of being adorned with fruits and flowers occurs only in the wish-fulfilling tree itself;
and because, due to the essential nature of the word-meaning "desired object," the quality of having shade exists in both meanings according to the method stated.

266. “The one whose purpose is desired,” and so forth. The phrase “whose purpose is desired” refers to the giver of worldly things—such as clothing, ornaments, and the like—which are desired by sentient beings;
it is used here because of the desire to explain the meaning of the Victor’s words established in the mind through the description of the wish-fulfilling tree (*kapparukkha*).

Furthermore, the phrase “whose purpose is desired” refers to those who, in accordance with the capacity of each respective being, [bestow] all purposes—both mundane and supramundane—that are sought after by sentient beings.

It is a giver; it is the heartwood among trees because no such tree exists that is superior to it; it is the heartwood among the worlds of beings, including those with devas, because no such distinguished being exists who is superior to it;
it is adorned with fruits and flowers, being graced by fruits like those of the wish-fulfilling tree (*kappaduma*) and by blossoms;
it possesses shade, having the shade of a tree that can obstruct the light of the moon and sun; it possesses shade through the sixfold nets of rays, such as blue, yellow, and so forth.
"Endowed with this, never before seen and never before arisen, this wish-fulfilling tree (kapparukkha)— this very wish-granting tree (kappapādapa)—

has appeared in the world through the power of the merit of sentient beings. This is because the qualifying terms— defined as "the granting of desired objects," "the essence," and "possessing abundant shade"—

are distinct from the referent of the word *jinapada* (the words of the Conqueror), which is intended to be expressed as the subject of the description, due to the difference between the wish-fulfilling tree and that [referent].

Because it is common to both [the tree and the person], and because it serves as a qualifier for the tree alone due to its being adorned with fruits and flowers, this compound construction (*samāsavutti*) is indeed a "qualifier distinct from the qualified" (*visesya-bhinnā*), characterized by a qualifier that is both distinct and non-distinct. The corresponding analytical sentences (*vākya*) are:
"He desires that object," "and he gives that word," "it is adorned with fruits and flowers," and "it exists together with shade."
The True Dhamma is like the ocean;
the Victor is proclaimed to be like a tree;
all common qualities [are shared].
"Except for the three from before.

(267) He explains both of these with the words "By the state of being an ocean," and so forth. The connection is as follows: the True Dhamma (*saddhamma*), spoken by the Fully Awakened One, is proclaimed "by the state of being an ocean" because it resembles the qualities of an ocean;
that is to say, it is praised. The Victor (*jina*) [is proclaimed] "by the state of being a tree"...
In the manner already described, that [meaning] has arisen for those words such as "ocean" (*ambhodhi*) when they are not examined through their literal function;
however, it arises through comprehension in that way by means of context and so forth. Otherwise, how could words such as "ocean" possess the capacity to reflect phenomena (*dhamma*) and the like?
As for the distinction, all those [words] mentioned previously—such as "bestowing pure nectar"—are included therein.
The common and equal qualities such as *visuddha*, *amata*, *sandāyitta*, and so forth, are qualifiers because they are possible in both cases;
however, apart from those, the pair [of qualities] mentioned immediately before in the phrase "the word for the desired goal" (*icchitatthapada*) and so on,
are both common and uncommon qualifiers according to the method already stated.
267. Now, he clarifies the two meanings expressed by those two compound words with the passage beginning "Sāgara...

and so forth. By way of being the ocean—that is, in the form of the ocean—the True Dhamma (saddhamma), meaning the True Dhamma of the scriptures taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One, has arisen and been proclaimed;
by way of being the tree, the Victor (jina) has arisen. Words such as "ocean" and "kalpa-tree" [refer] to their own denoted objects, namely the ocean and the tree, and so forth.

The intention is that [these terms] function in their primary sense (*mukhyabhāvena*), because even when the meaning occurring in the intellect is understood through the apprehension of a common qualifier, it is only the intended meaning of the words of the Conqueror—the true Dhamma—that can be grasped from the treatise and so forth;
for otherwise, the comprehension of such a meaning would be impossible. For if these [words] did not function in their primary sense, [the result would be as follows].

Regarding the question of how the words "ocean" (*ambhodhi*) and "wish-fulfilling tree" (*kapparukkha*) reveal the meaning of the Victor’s True Dhamma (*saddhamma*), in these two examples, in the former instance— namely,

the previous example beginning with "bestowing pure nectar" (*visuddhāmatasandāyī*)— all phenomena are "bestowers of pure nectar," and thus all qualifying attributes (*visesanadhammā*) are common to both the ocean and the True Dhamma;
however, this is not the case in the latter instance, beginning with "the abode of desired aims" (*icchitatthapado*).
In another example, however, the three qualifiers—"possessing the word for the desired meaning," "essential," and "having shade"—are common [to both].
But the state of being adorned with fruit and flowers is unique to the tree (*rukkhāveṇika*), as are qualifiers such as "unprecedented" (*apubba*).
For in this case, no particular quality belonging to the nature of a tree is being illustrated; thus, the status of being a qualifier is stated only in relation to other things.
Where the mode of existence of a basis (*vatthu*)—whether animate or inanimate—is conceived in a manner other than its actual state, that is "fanciful construction" (*parikappanā*).
(268) He explains "fanciful construction" by means of the verse beginning with "of a basis," and so forth. Of a basis...
A state of being (*vutti*) exists in one form, depending on another form that is intended to be expressed in a different way;
when, within that state of being, it is conceived in a manner other than its actual mode of existence—that is, imagined in a different way—it is called "imagination" (*parikappanā*).
This is because the established state of the object (*vatthuṭṭhiti*) is imagined, meaning it is made otherwise.
268. Now, he demonstrates the act of conceptualizing (parikappana) with the words beginning "of the object" (*vatthuno*).

Of whatever object—whether a sentient or insentient thing—the mode of existence (*vutti*), that is, its occurrence, exists and proceeds in a manner other than the mode in which it could be conceptually imagined; that is, it exists and occurs in a mode that is actually present.
When, in relation to that existence, one conceives of it otherwise—that is, by way of a non-existent mode different from that actual mode of existence—it is [called] conceptualizing.
That is what is called "hypothetical construction" (*parikappanā*). The analysis of the compound is: "that in which the state of affairs is constructed—that is, made otherwise.
I shall now give examples of the various types of hypothetical construction in their proper order, according to their inclusion within similes and by way of actions and so forth.

269. He demonstrates its divisions with the words "The simile," and so forth. That which has a simile within it—its state, and by means of that, as well as by way of action and so on, there are various and manifold conceptualizations;
these I shall now illustrate in sequence. 269. Now he demonstrates its divisions with the words "The simile within," and so forth.
Because of the existence of a simile within—that is, because of its being contained within a simile—and by way of action and so on, the various conceptualizations I shall illustrate in sequence.

The analysis (*viggaha*) is as follows: "upamā" (simile), "abbhantare" (within), "assā" (of it), "parikappanā" (conception), "iti" (thus); and "tassā" (of that), "bhāvo" (the state); and "aneke" (many), "vidhā" (kinds), "pakārā" (modes), "yāsaṃ" (of which).
Thus, the compound is *upamābbhantaraparikappanā*. [She was] sitting, distressed by the failure of her desire, and conceiving various internal similes.
Then, free from agitation and envy,
they seem to lead the wise one under their control through his application to yoga.

270. He provides an illustration with the words beginning "desire" (*icchā*). Due to the frustration of their desire—the destruction of the longing they had formed at the foot of the Bodhi tree, thinking, "We shall bring the Buddha, the Blessed One, under our control"—those goddesses became distressed and pained;
they reached a state of utter immobility and sat down, remaining completely motionless by fixing their eyes intently upon the tip of their noses, resembling female yogīs.

"By Māra’s maidens": the activity of the objects—namely, those possessing the characteristics of being sentient Māra-maidens and the secondary characteristics of Māra-maidens—as they actually exist, is here described;

yet that [activity] is now imagined otherwise. This is because even for celestial maidens, he remained unshaken by the excess of coquettish charm associated with amorous states, however skillfully employed.
"To him, the Blessed One. *Yoga* is the practice of mantras; through application (*abhiyoga*) therein, by means of one who is intent upon it, he brought himself under control.
“They carry [them] as if making them dependent at that time. Here, because of the presence of the word *iva* (as if), one should not entertain doubt regarding the simile.
Since they do not actually bring [the men] under their control, it is merely imagined that the women of Māra are "bringing them under control as if. And there is the verse:
“‘They bring the wise under control as if’—the act of leading is not the object of comparison.”
For there is no relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison between the agent and the action.
Even though this is a metaphorical conceit (*parikappa*), it is a conceit internal to the simile itself, rather than a mere conceit regarding the action;

for it demonstrates the similarity between the women of Māra’s retinue and the application of effort toward entering Mount Acala. And such an act of entering [the mountain] would be possible even for a steadfast person (*dhīra*) of that kind.
"By means of the Blessed One’s final passing" means by way of imagining it.

Now he provides an illustration with the words beginning "desire" (icchā). Afflicted by the failure of their desires, the daughters of Māra—thinking, "We shall entice the Blessed One"—sat at the foot of the Ajapāla banyan tree where the Blessed One was seated; they were tormented by the non-fulfillment of the very desire they themselves had formed.
Having become utterly motionless, they were endowed with a state of vision fixed upon the tip of the nose, being devoid of any other activity.
Seated and meditating, those nymphs were like female practitioners of yoga;

yet even by means of manifold playful charms and seductive gestures performed with amorous intent, they could not shake that Blessed One, who remained steadfast due to his dedication to yoga, [unmoved] by those women of Māra known as Craving, Discontent, and Lust.

"By one engaged in the practice known as the muttering of mantras, they [the Māra-maidens] are thought to bring themselves under his control—that is, to lead him into their power—at that time when he is defeated by them.
Here, by the first half-verse, the existing mode of being of the living entities known as the Māra-maidens is shown;
then, by the latter half-verse, their subjugation through the application of non-existent yogic practices is imagined."

Because the steady sitting of women intoxicated by liquor is similar to the silent recitation of mantras by female yoginīs, the relationship of comparison (upamānopameyyatta) between the women intoxicated by liquor and the female yoginīs is understood through the force of the context;
this is what is called "the internal conceptualization of a simile" (upamābbhantaraparikappanā).

Even when the usage "they lead, as it were" (nenti iva) is employed, there is still no "conceptualization of an action" (kriyāparikappana). Furthermore, because there is a cessation of desire, she is therefore "afflicted" (āturā).
And [the word *niggataṃ* means] "gone out," and "moving" or "shaking from this seat"; and "extremely motionless" is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāvisesana*).
The phrase "application in yoga" (*yoge abhiyogo*) is the sentence.

Regarding the expression "they lead as it were" (*nenti iva*), one should not entertain doubt on the grounds that the presence of the word *iva* here is for the purpose of indicating a simile; for there can be no state of being a simile for a mere action when there is no connection with a specific quality characterized by a common property (*sādhamma*). For it has been said:
"In ‘They lead the wise as if by force,’ there is no status as a simile (upamānatā) according to this method;
for between the agent and the action, there is no relationship of the object of comparison and the standard of comparison.
In the phrase "They lead the wise as if by force," although leading is implied, there is no status as a simile—that is, the state of being a standard of comparison—regarding the act of leading.

Indeed, it is just so; for there is no relationship of subject and action, nor the state of being a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) or the state of being the object of comparison (*upameyya*), between an agent and an action connected to that agent—this is the meaning of the preceding [passage].
This is the metaphorical attribution of action (*kriyāparikappanā*).
Māra has mounted an elephant, exceedingly and excessively lofty for battle;
surely, terrified of the Victor, he seeks a path to flee.
(271) “An elephant,” and so forth. He has mounted an elephant—that is, a *hatthi*—which is exceedingly (*accantaṃ*), meaning to an extreme degree, lofty (*unnataṃ*) or high, for the sake of battle.

"Thinking 'Māra, the wielder of power, will conquer me,' he is surely afraid of the Victor and, seeking some place of concealment or a path—a way to flee—searches for it," such is the construction of the verb.
This is because the act of searching for a path is metaphorically attributed to the act of ascending. 271. "The elephant," and so forth.

For the sake of battle—that is, for the purpose of fighting—it was exceedingly and pre-eminently lofty, endowed with the quality of height corresponding to its one hundred and fifty *yojanas* in length.
Having mounted the elephant Girimekhala, Māra, fearing the Victor (the Buddha), seeks—indeed, surely searches for—a path of escape, a path free from fear.

Because the poet has imagined that his mounting of the elephant was for the purpose of battle while his seeking of the path was for the purpose of escape, this is called *kriyā-parikappa* (poetic conceit regarding action).
Regarding the word *accantaṃ*: although it signifies both the innumerable (*asaṅkhya*) and the numbered (*saṅkhya*), it is [understood here] according to the context.
It applies only to excess.
O Lord of Sages, there is an attribution of qualities to your lotus-like feet, which are as beautiful as lovely royal lotuses.
I imagine that the crimson hue [of your feet] arose from being crushed by evil beings.
O Lord of Sages, both that lovely lotus and that beautiful water-lily possess a crimson quality in their pair of feet;
thus, the characteristic of redness remains as it is in that insentient object.

The etymology has already been stated; it is now being conceived in another way. "Soṇa" means blood (rudhira) produced by the excessive crushing—that is, by the thorough pounding—of the evils that are the enemies of the defilements (kilesa).

[The name] is thought to be "born from that. Thus, there is a figurative attribution of a quality (guṇaparikappanā), because the quality of being red, which resides in the vicinity of the pair of feet, is attributed [to the name] as "by the blood of the evils... and so forth.
272. “O Lord of Sages,” and so forth. O Lord of Sages, on your pair of feet—which are as beautiful as lovely lotuses and as charming as delightful water-lilies—there is a red hue.

I imagine this red color to be blood produced by the crushing of evil; that is, I imagine it to be blood born from the crushing of the evils residing within the mental continuums of both yourself and others.
On the feet of the Omniscient One, this red color has arisen through the power of meritorious deeds accomplished over many existences.
“By the crushing of evils”: because this is a conceptualization, it is called a "conceptualization of qualities" (*guṇaparikappanā*).
The analysis (*viggaha*) is as follows: “It is beautiful and it is a lotus,” “the crushing of evils,” “born from that,” “that and it is red,” and “the state of being red.
[The particle *nūna* is used] with words such as *maññe*, *saṅke*, *dhuvam*, *nūnam*, and *ivam*.
This [meaning] is sometimes expressed explicitly, and sometimes understood through a sentence.
To show the words that indicate a figurative assumption for the sake of conventional usage, he says "I think" (*maññe*), and so forth.
Thus, this collection of words—such as "I conjecture," "I imagine," "I reflect," "as if," and so on—with which it begins, by means of those [words], this [meaning]...

In some instances, as previously stated, the hypothetical assumption (*parikappanā*) is manifested or made explicit; in other cases, however, it is understood from the sentence even in the absence of words such as *maññe* and so forth.
(273) He shows the sounds that manifest a hypothetical assumption for the sake of ease of expression with the words beginning with "I think" (*maññe*). "I think" (*maññe*), "perhaps" (*saṅke*).
By means of words such as *dhuvaṃ*, *nūna*, and *iva*, this type of supposition (*parikappanā*) is manifested or made clear in some instances;

in other instances, it is understood through the sentence—that is, through a collection of words accompanied by the relationship between action and its factors—even in the absence of the use of words like *iva* and so forth, it is known solely by the power of the sentence itself.
The pentad of words beginning with *maññe* is [to be understood] as a copulative compound (*dvanda-samāsa*).

It has been explained. Thus, the analysis (*viggaha*) is: those things beginning with "I think" (*takkemi*), "I imagine" (*parikappemi*), "I reflect" (*cintayāmi*), and "just as" (*yathā*), which have such a collection of words as their beginning.
This is the imagination of a village (*gammaparikappanā*).

274. "O Victor, those bodies of yours, delightful through the flow of compassion and made sweet by the arising of compassion, with their radiance streaming forth from your forms—while delighting the virtuous, they have led them to a state of sweetness.

He illustrates this with the verse beginning "compassion" (*dayā*), and so forth. *Rasa* means affection (*sineha*); that which exists together with it is *sarasa*. [This refers to] the body (*deha*). Through compassion...
The movement of compassion is a continuous flow directed toward suffering beings; therefore, it is "full of essence" (*sarasā*).

From that [compassion], O Victor, rays of light issued forth from your body, gladdening and warming virtuous people, and led them to a state of essentiality—that is, to a state of affection for you alone.
Such radiance, issuing from such a body, gladdens those virtuous people.

In this instance of *gamyamānaparikappanā* (conception of the implied), it is understood that because the bodies [of the virtues] have acquired their essence through contact with the essence of compassion (*dayā*), they themselves, as if possessing that essence, lead even virtuous people to a state of essentiality while serving them. 274.
He illustrates the conception of the implied in a sentence (*vākyagammaparikappana*) with the words beginning "O Compassionate One" (*daye*). O Jina, your movement of compassion...
Due to the continuous flow of compassion directed toward suffering beings within its own domain, rays of light emerged from his body; these rays of six colors, such as blue and others,
issued forth into the ten directions, gladdening virtuous people who have performed meritorious deeds— those most excellent persons—
and led that very same virtuous folk to a state of affection characterized by the essence of the moon’s digits and a heart full of love.
They brought [them] to ruin. In the phrase "they led to the state of being destroyed," it is understood through connection with the word "the virtuous" (*sādhujana*) heard previously.

Because of contact with a body that is gentle due to the moisture of compassion, the rays themselves—being gentle by virtue of their own supporting qualities—take themselves as the object and likewise make the people present soft;
thus, even in the absence of words such as *iva*, there is a figurative construction (*parikappa*) based on the context of the sentence. Herein, the objects of beauty, though insentient...

The phrase "the stability of the basis for inspiring confidence in people" is conceived in various other ways, such as "as if having the essence of the movement of compassion" (*dayāsañcārasarasā iva*).
The sentence can be analyzed as follows: "the movement of compassion" (*dayāsañcāra*) means its repeated occurrence; "possessing essence" (*sarasa*) means existing together with affection (*sneha*);

"having the essence of the movement of compassion" (*dayāsañcārasara*) means possessing that movement; "and those rays have emerged" (*nikkhantā ca tā kantiyo ca*); "and that person is good" (*sādhu ca so jano ca*); and "the state of having essence" (*sarasassa bhāvo*) is the meaning of the word.
When one who has begun whatever task may be undertaken, through the power of merit, attains further means for its accomplishment, that they call *samāhita*.
[The verse] beginning with "ārabhantassa" explains how one brings about *samāhita*: in order to perform some action, such as the breaking of an enemy's forces, etc.

For any person who has begun and is prepared, by virtue of merit, through the power of the wholesome (*kusala*), and by means of the capacity for the wholesome—that which is accomplished or being accomplished—is the "means" (*sādhana*).
From that, or from another internal [cause], there is the attainment;
the meaning is the attainment of another cause. They call that "composed" (*samāhita*); it is composed because of its state of composure (*samādhāna*).
275. Now he demonstrates the ornament of the composed (*samāhitālaṅkāra*) with the words beginning "one who begins" (*ārabham*).
For one who begins to perform any task such as the conquest of enemies, there is the acquisition of another means which assists in the accomplishment of that very effect;
this acquisition of a cause (*kāraṇalābha*), which occurs again by virtue of merit and through the power of skillfulness, is what is called "composed."
They say it is "composed" (*samāhita*) because of the settling and stabilization of that very task; thus the poet speaks. Furthermore, there are phrases such as:
"that by which something is accomplished" (*sādhyate*), "this and that, internal and external," and "the attainment thereof.
[This refers to] the mind of that Teacher, which was directed toward the destruction of the enemy Māra.
"The great earth raised a great roar; this attendant [earth] cried out.

(276) He cites the passage beginning with "Māra" and so forth. It refers to that Teacher whose mind was directed toward—rather than turned away from—the breaking and overcoming of Māra, the enemy and adversary;
it is his attendant, which assisted in the undertaking of the act of breaking Māra.
This great earth let out a mighty roar, a great cry that was difficult for the enemy Māra to endure.

Here, as the crushing of the enemy Māra has begun to be carried out, the characteristic should be applied thus: "By the power of that very merit, the roar of the earth has reached another stage of accomplishment.
276. Regarding the phrase "Mārāri" and so forth: [it refers to one] whose mind is intent on the breaking of the enemy Māra, with a heart directed toward the subduing of the foe known as Māra.

This great earth, acting as an assistant to that Teacher who had commenced the conquest of Māra, made a great roar—like something crushing the very seat of Māra’s heart—which was a loud cry impossible to endure.
Herein, the production of Māra’s defeat is the task undertaken by the Teacher; it is the cause for his success.
"Another reason" means "the great roar. The analysis [of the compound] is as follows: it is Māra who is the enemy (ari-sattu), and there is the destruction of him;
furthermore, it refers to one whose mind is directed toward that [destruction], and it is both "great" (mahantī) and "earthly" (mahī).
Without stating what is intended for him, the accomplishment is shown otherwise.
Those of pure intellect say that this is a figurative mode of expression (pariyāya-vutti).
[The author] establishes this figurative mode by means of the words "without stating," etc.

Without stating some intended object characterized by the giving of wealth and so forth—that is, without directly expressing it through the function of denotation—for the purpose of accomplishing or bringing about that intended object:

The wise and intelligent declare that whatever seeing or speaking occurs in another way—that is, in a different manner—conducive to the production of that [result], is called "figurative usage" (*pariyāyavutti*).
Figurative usage means speaking by way of a figurative expression (*pariyāya*).
Now, he demonstrates figurative usage with the words beginning with "without stating," etc. The intended object is the desired form, such as the giving of wealth and so forth.
Without mentioning any object such as wealth, grain, or the like, and without speaking directly, whatever statement there may be that expresses something else in a manner other than intended—
in order to achieve the accomplishment or fulfillment of that desired object, yet in accordance with another meaning that was actually wished to be expressed—
that they call a "metaphorical expression" (*pariyāyavutti*), O pure-minded ones. By way of metaphor...
And the statement "the description of their livelihood," and the phrase "those whose intellects are pure.
Wealth placed in the open courtyard, devoid of guards—
O you who desire wealth, go as you wish if you so desire.
278. He gives an example with the verse beginning “In the open courtyard,” and so forth. Wealth placed in an open courtyard—meaning a visible spot—is not enclosed by anyone;
furthermore, it is devoid of protection. “O you who desire wealth” (*dhanakāme*) is an address.
Rather than directly stating the desired theft of wealth by saying, “If you wish to go, or for the sake of wealth, go as you please,” [the poet says this].
He speaks under the pretext of that attainment. This is a figurative usage (pariyāyavutti). 278.
He illustrates this with the words “open” (vivaṭa), and so forth. Wealth—such as pearls, gems, and the like—is placed in an open courtyard;

because it is devoid of enclosures such as walls, it is in an unobstructed place where it has been set down by anyone whatsoever, and furthermore, it is without protection. O you who desire wealth! You...
"If you desire wealth or a journey, go as you wish"—
this method of seizing wealth according to one's mental desire is called "indirect speech" (*pariyāyavutti*), because it is stated under such a pretext,

saying "bring the wealth," rather than speaking directly. It is [so called] because it is both open and exposed, because it is deposited therein, because it is devoid of protection, and because it desires wealth.
And there is the statement: "Indeed, without overstepping that craving or the consciousness associated with it.
He offers praise while appearing to criticize, as if providing a commentary on its movement;
for here, even faults appear as virtues when they lead to the accumulation [of merit].
279. He describes the description of a pretext (*byājavaṇṇanā*) with the words "praise" (*thuti*) and so forth.
One who offers praise and speaks of excellence as if censuring or as if pointing out a fault—that is the characteristic of a "pretext-praise," known as *byājavaṇṇanā*.
To the question, "How are virtues understood here?", he says: "faults" (*dosi*) and so forth. In this particular mode of expression, faults appear and manifest as if they were [virtues].
By such speech, qualities such as possessing supernormal powers (*iddhimantatā*) appear as faults; yet they are indeed virtues, and no fault whatsoever remains present or persists.
The word "hi" is used for emphasis; here it indicates that this is merely a description of the *byāja* (the pretext), not a censure.
279. Now he shows the description of the *byāja* with the words beginning "thuti" (praise). As if censuring, as if showing a fault—
One offers praise and provides a description; that act of providing a description is called "description by means of a pretext" (*byājavaṇṇana*).

If it is argued that this is indeed blame because the praise occurs under the guise of blame—here, in this particular mode of expression, what appear to be faults are in fact virtues, such as supernatural power (*iddhimantatā*) and so forth, which, through the employment of such words, constitute a collection of virtues and remain established in their true nature as virtues.
"They go" means "they reach. The phrase "praise by means of a pretext" (*byājena vaṇṇanaṃ*) is a statement meaning that faults appear and manifest as if they were virtues.
"You are capable of shaking the entire world of blue lotuses," O Lord;
what further distinction of your virtues shall we speak of beyond that?

280. He illustrates this with the verse beginning "sañcāletu" and so forth: "O Lord, even though you are fully capable—able to move, that is, to whirl about here and there, the entire *kuvalaya* (the blue water-lily), the *uppala* (the lotus), and the circle of the earth—nevertheless, for that reason alone, why (*kiṃ*) and by what cause (*kena kāraṇena*) do we speak of the excellence, the characteristic of pre-eminence, of your virtues?
Here, it is by way of manifesting the capacity to move the lotus [that the excellence is shown]."

He censures [others], yet this Blessed One is joined with the highest praise because he has fashioned the Greatly Powerful One as the crest-jewel of the world-sphere by causing him to move throughout the entire circle of the earth. Such a description of his speed is exceedingly delightful;
and this, moreover, lives entirely upon poetic ornament (*śleṣa*).
280. Now he provides an illustration with the words beginning “sañcāletuṃ”:

“O Lord, you are fully capable—possessing an exceeding power—to cause the entire *kuvalaya*, that is, the whole grove of blue lotuses (*nīluppalavana*), or even the circle of the earth, to shake or tremble.
To what extent can we speak of, or how can we describe, the preeminent excellence of your virtues? This is because the word *kuvalaya* denotes a specific kind of lotus.

First, regarding the censure: because that very word denotes the circle of the earth (*pathavīmaṇḍala*), the praise of his supreme qualities is thereby established as, "What is this distinction of yours, O possessor of psychic power?
Such figurative descriptions (*byājavaṇṇanā*) are commendable, and they proceed entirely on the basis of punning (*silesa*).
The compound *kuyā pathaviyā valayaṃ maṇḍalam* means "the circle or orb of the earth."
Where there is a demonstration of deficiency in the substance, the action, the genus, or the quality intended as a qualification, that is what is called *viśeṣa* (qualification).
(281) He explains the application of *viśeṣa* with the words "in the case of a qualification" (*visesi’cchāyaṃ*), etc. *Viśeṣa* means excellence, or some particular effect.

In this context, where there is a statement showing the absence of deficiency regarding substances (*dabba*) and so forth, this is called "distinction" (*visesa*), and it would be termed "functioning as a distinction" (*visesavutti*). 281.
Now, he demonstrates the figure of speech "Distinction" (*visesālaṅkāra*) with the words beginning "visesi. In this desire for distinction, it refers to an excellence or a specific effect.

When there is a desire [to express] the deficiency—that is, the statement of non-existence—regarding a specific mode of expression (vuttivisesa) involving substance (*dabba*), action (*kriyā*), genus (*jāti*), or quality (*guṇa*), this specific mode is called "distinction" (*visesa*), and it may be termed "specific function" (*visesavutti*). The phrase is:
"the state of being deficient" (*vikalassa bhāvo*) and "the demonstration thereof" (*tassa dassanaṃ*).
Neither chariots nor elephants, neither horses nor infantry;
the enemy Māra was conquered by the Sage through the application of the necessary requisites. This is a specific instance of the function of the causal factors.

282. He provides the example beginning with “No chariots,” and so forth. This is easily understood. Here, by the absence of the material characteristics of a fourfold army—the equipment for victory—he describes a distinction characterized by the conquest of the enemy Māra, which consists solely in the mobilization of the provisions comprised by the thirty pāramīs.
282. “No chariots,” and so forth. There are no chariots—meaning even three chariots, including their attendants, in the sense of being designated as an “army”—nor are there such three chariots.
Nor are there three elephants in the manner already described, reckoned as an army.
Nor were there three such horses reckoned as a troop;
nor were there four such men, even if they were armed, to be designated as a troop.
Nevertheless, by the Sage’s mental application toward the thirty-two qualities of the perfections (*pāramitā*) through the act of recollection, [he overcame] Māra, the enemy.

Māra, along with his retinue, was conquered and overcome. Herein, by demonstrating the deficiency of materials such as chariot-arrays that exist merely as instruments of victory, and by describing the excellence of the mental application (*āvajjana*) of the requisites whose very nature is the conquest of the enemy, this is called "the operation of specific materials.
A chariot is defined as one surrounded by four men; three such chariots constitute a chariot-array (*rathānīka*).
[This is] the name [of the unit]. An elephant, however, has a retinue of twelve men; three such elephants constitute what is called an "elephant-force" (*hatthānīka*).
A horse has a retinue of three men; three such horses constitute what is called a "horse-force" (*hayānīka*). Four men equipped with weapons constitute what is called a "foot-force" (*padānīka*).
Here, the men who fight by traveling swiftly on foot, as if stationed upon chariots and so forth, [are the foot-force].

They are called "feet" (*pādā*) by virtue of their service as feet. Having shown that the measure of chariots and so forth constitutes an *anīka* (division) in the context of military units, it is understood from the context that even though the measure of men was not explicitly stated, four men at the very least constitute an *anīka*; thus, they are known to be "four.

Otherwise, since the plural form "foot-soldiers" (*padātayo*) occurs for the word *padāti*, which denotes armed men, [the question arises: "Are there no chariots, no elephants, no horses... [and so on].

The connection is: "not [as] foot-soldiers, not [as such]. Regarding the phrase *dabbavisesavutti*: it is called "the expression of a distinction" (*visesakathana*) because a substance (*dabba*) functions by negating another substance, and it is also called "the function of a distinction" (*visesavutti*). The sentence is thus:

"the function of a distinction by means of the negation of one substance by another. The triad beginning with "the function of a distinction of action" (*kriyāvisesavutti*) should be understood in exactly the same way.
"Not bound, as if by a frown; the lip was bitten."
The heroic and supreme Sage himself brought about the destruction of Māra’s host.
This is the specific mode of his activity. (Verse 283):
“Not knit,” and so forth. A frown, which is a contraction of the eyebrows produced by anger, was not knit—that is, it was not formed—nor was the lip [compressed].
Furthermore, his lower lip was neither quivering nor trembling with rage. Nevertheless, the excellent, supreme Hero of Sages—the enemy of Māra himself—inflicted a shattering defeat upon him.
By the absence of actions such as knitting the brows, a distinction characterized by a victory free from outward agitation is shown. (Verse 283) "Not bound," and so forth:
even the knitting of the eyebrows (*bhūkuṭi*), which is a physical manifestation of anger, was not bound—that is, it was not performed.
The lip-covering and the covering of the teeth were neither quivering nor trembling.
Nevertheless, the excellent, supreme Hero of Sages—the Tathāgata endowed with the heroic qualities of a sage—himself brought about the defeat of Māra, the enemy.

Herein, without performing any action such as the knitting of the eyebrows and so forth, there occurred the specific nature of Māra’s defeat characterized by the absence of agitation; thus it is called "the unagitated defeat of Māra" (nibbikāramārabhaṅga). (Ka.)

Because it has been so stated, this is called a "functioning of a specific action. "The hovel of the ruined" and "crookedness," and "Māra himself is the enemy," and "the destruction of those"—this is the sentence.
There is no radiance (*raṃsi*) that is skillful or pervasive in the directions.
Light does not illuminate the world as much as the supreme,
well-spoken word of the virtuous,
which dispels even the blinding darkness.
The conduct of a specific class of beings. 284.
"Ni" and so forth. There is no radiance that has spread throughout the ten directions; there is no light that has pervaded the entire world.
"Tathāpi" (even so) expresses a particular desire, [referring] to the virtuous even in the absence of being of that same nature.

The well-spoken word, known as the True Dhamma, removes the blinding darkness— the darkness of delusion that is the blindness of the eye of wisdom arising from the confusion between the desirable and the undesirable—

and thus it is called "the remover of blinding darkness" (*andhatamahara*). By the phrase "removal of darkness," the specific quality of the well-spoken word’s capacity to dispel darkness through its turning away [from unwholesome states] is demonstrated.
284. “There is no radiance in the quarters,” and so forth. There is not even a ray of light extending through the directions, nor is there any light pervading the world.
Nevertheless, the well-spoken words of the virtuous—the True Dhamma—completely dispel the blinding darkness;

it removes the gloom of delusion and ignorance from the eye of wisdom, which is capable of discerning what is beneficial and what is harmful. Herein, it is that which is capable of destroying darkness.

Having set aside [the comparison with] the sun and other such things, because the specific quality of well-spoken words—namely, their being described as "dispelling darkness"—is stated, this is called a "functioning through a specific quality" (jātiviśeṣavṛtti). Furthermore, the phrases are:

"spread abroad in the world," "blindness is delusion (moha) because it blinds," "it is 'darkness' (tama) itself because it resembles darkness," "it removes that [darkness]," and "well-spoken by the virtuous."
O Lord of Sages, your speech is neither harsh nor rigid;
yet it digs deep and uproots the pride of the people. (This is the function of excellence of qualities.)
285. “It is not harsh,” and so forth. O Sage-Lord, your speech is neither harsh nor rough, nor is it stiff or hard;

indeed, it is not so. Nevertheless, even in the absence of such qualities as harshness and the like, it digs out—root and branch—the deep-seated, firm craving (*taṇhā*) of the populace, that is, of the multitude of people.
This is by way of negating the qualities of harshness and so on that are well-known in the case of an iron spike.
The distinction of the Muninda’s word has been revealed. 285.
“It is not harsh,” and so forth. O Muninda, your word is neither harsh nor rough, nor is it rigid.
Nevertheless, it crushes the pride of the multitude—that swelling conceit arising from birth and other such factors within the mass of people.
"Having made it firm, he digs it up rootless, leaving nothing behind.

This is called a "functioning of a specific quality" (*guṇavisesavutti*), because it excludes qualities such as hardness found in iron spikes and the like—which are capable of digging—and instead expresses the specific characteristic of the Buddha’s word, namely its nature of "digging up pride.
Furthermore, [it may mean] "there is no root for this digging," or [it refers to] people...
The analysis [of the compound] is: *samūheti* and *tāya mādo*. Because it qualifies the action of digging with the words "deeply" and "rootless," the construction is:
"he performs a digging that is deep and rootless.
It is seen as "extremely bright" ... whereas *tirittaṃ* (variant reading *ka*).
Where the wise speak of the quality of heroic courage, such as this,
it is a term used for one whose ego-conceit has been transcended.
286. They speak of *ruḷhāhaṅkāra* (conventional metaphorical expression).
Now, he demonstrates *ruḷhāhaṅkāra* with the words beginning "it is shown" (*dassīyate*).

When the state of being brave and heroic—the nature of being courageous and the nature of being a hero—is shown in an exceedingly brilliant sentence, such speech is [called] *ruḷhāhaṅkāra* by wise poets.

"They say it is 'conventionalized conceit' (ruḷhāhaṅkāra)" means: "A hero and a brave man," "the state of being those two," and "conceit has arisen and gone high here in this particular expression"—this is the sentence.
In the case of Nandopananda at Damaka...
What is the use of seeing my misconduct?
My sons are devoted to their parents;
such as they are, they are already prepared.

287. He illustrates this with the verse beginning with “In the taming,” and so forth. What is the purpose of showing the interference of another or prescribing a remedy for me, even though my fame follows upon immeasurable power and boundless tranquility in the taming—that is, the subduing—of Nandopananda, the nāga king of immeasurable great majesty?
It is none at all; for those who are devoted to my feet, who bow down at my feet, [behave] toward such [a being as that].
"Ready for action, with girdles fastened, existing and indeed present"—thus it should be construed. 287.

Regarding "In taming," etc.: By showing my exertion in the act of taming Nandopananda, the king of nagas, and by the manifestation of such an undertaking on the part of one who possesses majesty operating throughout the three worlds and a multitude of renown, [the purpose is shown].
What is the purpose? It is because I have many sons who are devoted to my feet, who bow at my feet, and who are ready and equipped for such a task;
therefore [I do not fear]. Here, the state of being a hero and a warrior due to mastery over the mind is shown as being exceedingly evident.
And the phrase "the manifestation of activity" refers to the expression "devoted to my feet."
Silence consists of multiple expressions joined by a single word;
it includes non-differentiated words,
sentences, and so forth.

This "śleṣa" (punning conjunction) has been thus defined in three ways. [The author] points out *śleṣa* with the words beginning with "śleṣo" and so forth. That which has multiple distinct objects of denotation is called *anekābhidheyya*.

Having restated that it is a statement (*vacana*) consisting of an expression (*vutti*) joined—that is, endowed—with a single common word (*padena*), namely one that is identical in form (*sarūpena*), that is *śleṣa*.
It is prescribed because, by some form or other, the characteristics of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameyya*) are joined through a pun (*sileśa*).
This *sileśa*, characterized in this way, is declared to be threefold. How so? By virtue of having non-distinct words, sentences, and so forth;

that is, where there is a single non-distinct word consisting of either a form ending in a case-suffix (*syādyanta*) or a form beginning with a particle (*tyādyanta*), that very thing is a sentence because it possesses the characteristics of a sentence. The meaning is: "by virtue of those things of which that [word] is the first."
288. Now he demonstrates the figure of speech *śleṣa* (punning) with the words beginning "śleṣo" and so forth.
That statement which possesses multiple meanings, joined by a single word, and connected by a common form of sound due to its being shared in both senses, is called *śleṣa*.

Furthermore, because it is closely knit (*siliṭṭha*) through some common characteristic (*sādhamma*) between the objects that serve as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object compared (*upameyya*), it [binds] them together mutually.

It is called *silesa* because it stands by having been joined together (*phusitvā*). This *silesa*, possessing the characteristics already stated, is declared to be threefold according to its divisions:
those consisting of unseparated words and phrases, those accompanied by words ending in case-suffixes (*syādi*) or personal endings (*tyādi*), and those endowed with the characteristics of sentences.

Furthermore, it is that which has many things to be expressed (*anekamabhidheyyaṃ yassa*), and it is that which is joined (*tena āyutaṃ*) by being both "one" (*ekaṃ*) and a "word" (*padaṃ*), and they are "unseparated" (*abhinnāni*).

The sentence is as follows: "In that which [there are] words," and "that and that sentence," and "that is the beginning of those [cases of] non-differentiated words and sentences," and "the division is the power of those"—this is the sentence.
"He who destroys the blinding darkness, the one who brings liberation, has ascended to the great exaltation."
This sun-garlanded Blessed One shines, awakening people.
[The verse] has an unbroken structure of words and phrases. 289.
He cites the passage beginning with "blind darkness" (*andhatama*). This Blessed One is both the sun and the Great Sage. Therein, the sun...
The sun is a dispeller of the blinding darkness that naturally brings about gloom; the Great Sage, however, is a remover of the darkness of delusion.

Both the sun and the Great Sage are captivating and beautiful; yet while the sun has ascended the great mountain of sunrise (*mahodaya*), the Great Sage has ascended the great exaltation (*mahodaya*) consisting of the attainment of Perfect Enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*).
*Patto*. One who possesses a garland (*mālā*) of rays (*raṃsi*) is *raṃsimālī*; this refers both to the sun and to the Great Sage (*mahāmuni*).
"Awakening people"—meaning causing them to wake up by means of the departure from sleep, or by means of the departure from the sleep of the defilements (*kilesa*)—he "shines," that is, he radiates.
This is an instance of *abhinnapadavākyasileso*, because, without a formal split (*bhaṅga*), the words are applied to both meanings exactly as they stand.

289. Now he provides an illustration with the words beginning with "blind" (*andha*). He has "ascended" (*samāruḷho*)—that is, mounted upon or reached—the "Great Rise" (*mahodaya*), which is either the great mountain or the great exaltation designated as the state of omniscience.
He is the destroyer of the "thick darkness" (*andhantama-ro*), which is the natural, dense gloom spread within the interior of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*);
or it refers to the delusion called "darkness" because it blinds the eye of wisdom. He is "captivating" (*hārī*) by that very [destruction].
The Blessed One is this sun, lovely and endowed with his own garland of rays;

awakening and causing to awaken sentient beings who are possessed of natural sleep or the sleep of the defilements, he—the Buddha—shines and glows, being endowed with the six qualities of a Blessed One.
This is because the words stand as equal in both respects (the sun and the Buddha).
This is the analysis of the undivided words and phrases: "He is both blind and darkness" (andhaśca sa tamaśca); "he takes that away" (taṃ harati iti);
"it is both great and it is the mountain Udaya" (mahāñca so udayo pabbato ca); "it is both great and it is rising, i.e., exaltation and growth" (mahāñca so udayo abbhudayo abhivuddhi ca);

"it is a garland of rays" (raṃsīnaṃ mālā); "it possesses that" (sā assa atthi iti); "fortune and glory belong to this sun" (bhago sirī assa sūriyassa atthi iti); and "fortune and glory consist of various kinds such as the desire for objects, movement, light, and so forth."

The analysis (*viggaha*) is: "There is [something] belonging to that teacher. *Sileso* (a figure of speech) is defined as a combination of words and sentences that remain inseparable. Furthermore, it is called *sileso* because another meaning is here joined together (*silissati*).
In this same manner, expressions such as "the joining of distinct words and sentences" (*bhinnapadavākyasileso*) should also be understood.
It has the luster of a fresh *āmalaka* fruit, with its gathered [juice] exhausted.
The awakening of the lily pond, the wise one, gladdens the people.

This is the *Bhinnapadavākyasileso* (the breaking up of words and sentences). 290. “In the autumn,” etc. One who possesses nectar (*sudhā*) is *sudhī*; [this refers to] the moon. Beautiful is its form, which is the knowledge of omniscience.

One who possesses wisdom (*buddhi*) is *sudhī*; [this refers to] the Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*). He whose radiance (*ābhā*), which is stainless (*amala*) and pure (*nimmala*), arose during the autumn (*sārada*), that is, in the autumn season—he is the Moon.
He is "autumnal" (*sārada*) because he bestows the essence of Nibbāna upon others; he is the "stainless radiance" (*amalaka-ābhāsa*);
or he is the one for whom there is the awakening of all those to be trained (*ñeyya*), like the radiance of a myrobalan fruit held in the hand (*hatthāmalaka*)—that is the Perfectly Enlightened One.

The moon is that by which the dark fortnight (*kaṇhapakkha*), having been brought to its complete exhaustion (*parikkhaya*) through being led correctly (*saṃ*) by its course, has been brought to its end.

The Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*) is he by whom the destruction (*khaya*) of the enemy that is the defilements (*kilesa-sattu*)—that is, their cessation (*vūpasama*)—has been attained through being brought to completion (*sama*).
The moon is he whose rays are the blossoming of enlightenment (*sambodhi-vikāsa*) for the night-lotus (*kumuda*) of the world.
It is called *kumudākara* because it produces joy and rapture upon the earth (*pathaviyā*). He whose awakening is the realization of the Four Noble Truths is the *Sammāsambuddha*.

He delights the people, that is, the multitude of beings. This is an example of a compound of split words and phrases (*bhinnapadavākyasileso*), because the words are split according to the method already described.

290. Regarding the passage beginning with “Sāra”: *Sārada* means produced during the autumn season; or, it refers to one who bestows the essence (*sāra*) of Nibbāna upon those to be trained. *Amalakābhāsa* means possessing stainless splendor;

or, because he is endowed with a garland of stainless banners, he possesses a corresponding majestic radiance. Alternatively, *sāradāmalakābhāsa* means possessing stainless splendor arisen during the autumn season;
or, it means possessing the stainless splendor that bestows the essence of Nibbāna upon those to be trained. Or else...

Or, it is like the autumn *āmalaka* fruit in its radiance; it is like the *āmalaka* fruit in the hand of one who bestows the essence of *nibbāna*, for it brings about the awakening to what is to be known.
"One whose decline has been brought to an end" refers to the moon that has been properly brought to its waning during the dark fortnight and is now full;

or alternatively, it refers to the decline consisting in the abandonment of the defilements, which has been brought about by the peace of the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata-santi*). "The awakening of the night-lotus grove" means being endowed with the blossoming of the night-lotuses.
Or, he is one endowed with the awakening to the Four Noble Truths that produces joy for people who dwell upon the earth of well-formed conditions (*kusaṅkhāta*).
"Sudhī" refers to the moon, so named because it possesses nectar (*amata*) which is called *sudhā*;

or it refers to the Perfectly Enlightened One (*Sammāsambuddha*), so named because he possesses beautiful wisdom (*paññā*). He "delights the people," meaning the multitude of beings. In both cases, the word is analyzed to reveal its meaning.
This is a section consisting of split words and phrases. *Sārada* means the autumn moon. It is "sārada" because it gives essence (*sāra*).
This term "sārada" serves as an adjective for the word "ābhāsa" (splendor).
It may be understood as: "the splendor of this moon is stainless and pure," or "the splendor upon its peak," or "the stainless splendor belonging to the Teacher."
"Of that Blessed One, the radiance is like an autumnal *āmalaka* fruit," means that the Blessed One’s realization of the knowable is like the radiance of an autumnal *āmalaka*.

"By whom the complete destruction and the reduction of parts have been rightly brought about," means by whom the destruction and diminution of the defilements and of sentient beings have been brought to total pacification. "It causes the blooming of the white water-lilies (*kumuda*)."
And: "He whose awakening (sambodha) is the blossoming (vikāsa) of them" and "he who produces joy (muda), that is, rapture (pīti)," thus he is *mudākara*.

"He who produces joy upon the earth (kuya pathaviyā)" and "he whose awakening is the realization of the Four Truths," thus he is [the one]. "Nectar (*sudhā*), which is the deathless (*amata*), belongs to this moon," thus he is [the one].
And "his wisdom (*dhī*) or intelligence (*buddhi*) is beautiful (*su*)," thus is the analysis (*viggaha*) for the term *Sambuddha*.
The Well-Gone One, the Leader of beings, whose self is concentrated, who has subdued pride without being diminished— may he protect us.
This is the section on the analysis of distinct and non-distinct words and phrases.

291. “Samāhita,” etc. He in whom the self’s discipline (*vinaya*)—that is, its thorough establishment (*saṃ-āhita*) or training—is placed correctly (*sammā*) such that it moves unimpeded everywhere within its own domain, he is Garuḷa.

He in whom discipline exists by way of the activity of body and mind being secluded, and who has tamed [them], he is the Perfectly Enlightened One (*Sammāsambuddha*). Thus, this is a compound word (*abhinnapada*). Of the snakes (*ahīnaṃ*), that is, the serpents (*sappānaṃ*), he is the leader (*inā*, *nāyakā*); of them...
He who crushes the pride of snakes is *ahīnamadamaddano*, the Garuḷa.
He who crushes the pride of even superior beings (*ahīna*) such as the Great Brahmās and others is *ahīnamadamaddano*, the Perfectly Enlightened One (*Sammāsambuddha*).
He whose beautiful movement (*gata*) or gait is capable of rising up immediately from the mass of water after breaking through the ocean is the Garuḷa. Beautiful...
He is the Sugata because his gait possesses the majestic stride of an elephant; he is the Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*).

This is a compound word. He is the leader of the winged birds, the Garuḍa. Because he gives poison (*visaṃ*), he is *visada*; may he protect (*pātu*) the world of beings (*pāṇinaṃ*) in the realm of the Nāgas by way of non-harming.

He is the Leader (*vināyaka*) because he leads those to be trained (*veneyya*); he is the Perfectly Enlightened One. [May he protect] the world of all beings (*sakalasattalokaṃ*), which is full of poison (*visadaṃ*) and not sluggish (*asallīnaṃ*).

May he protect. This is a combination (*silesa*) of both distinct and non-distinct words and phrases, according to the method already stated, because the words possess both types of mixing. 291. “In one who is concentrated,” etc.
One whose mind is disciplined through concentration (*samāhitattavinaya*) is endowed with the movement of the body within its own domain as it has been properly placed and established;
or, he is endowed with the taming of the mind as it has been properly placed and established; he who crushes the pride of those who have not yet subdued their pride.
The Subduer of the pride of the Nāga kings; or, the Subduer of the pride even of the supreme among serpents, such as Bakabrahmā and others.
The Sugata, having split the waters of the ocean in two by the force of the wind from his wings, went to the abode of the Nāgas while those waters remained undisturbed;
because he was capable of seizing the Nāgas and departing, he is "of beautiful gait. He is "of all-auspicious and manifold gait."
Or, may the Leader, the guide of birds, that king of the Garuḍas, protect the world of serpents from poison— the giver of poison due to his terrible venom—
by means of non-injury. Or else, may the Leader, training those to be trained, that Fully Enlightened One,
protect all living beings in the entire world of creatures by making them free from poison— that is, confident— and by removing what is harmful and providing what is beneficial.

"May he protect. This is a collection of both distinct and non-distinct words and phrases, because it is endowed with distinct phrases such as "the subduer of the pride of the serpent-king (Ahi-nāga)" and so forth, and non-distinct phrases such as "the Tathāgata who has a disciplined and concentrated self" and so forth.
Furthermore, it means "the discipline of the self," or "the Tathāgata Garuḷa whose disciplined self is concentrated," or "the leaders of the serpent-kings (Ahīnā) who are not deficient."

And "of the non-deficient nāga-kings" means the pride of those who are not deficient; and "of others who are superior to the deficient" means the pride of those who are more excellent than the inferior;

and "it crushes that" means it subdues that pride. And "the leader of the winged birds" refers to the leader of the *vīna* (birds); and "he guides the people to be guided" is the phrase. In the second alternative, "clearly" (*visadaṃ*) is an adverbial modifier of the action.

The other [type of *śleṣa*] consists of actions that are distinct yet neither contradictory nor non-contradictory, which expresses a restriction, or which, though not contradictory, implies a contradiction.
It includes the nourishment of propriety (*aucitya*) and so forth, as well as the various types of words such as *pada-jāti*. (Note: *padajāti* is also mentioned in the Kaśikā.)
"Form will become manifest in these very examples.
(292–3) To show that there are other ways of breaking the *silesas*, he says "contradictory," and so forth.
Those actions or activities which are contradictory, non-contradictory, and mutually distinct—these are the three *silesas*. "Niyama" means restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) in this context.

"Atthīti" refers to that which possesses a restriction (*niyama*); "paro" means another or different; "silesopi" means even a pun. "Niyamassa akkhepo" means the rejection or negation of a restriction; "yassa taṃ vacanamabhidhānaṃ" means that of which such is the word or expression; "tādisopi" means that too [is such].

"Nāssa virodho atthīti avirodhi" means that which has no contradiction; "sopī" means that too [is such]. "Virodho asaṅgati ettha vijjatīti virodhi" means that wherein contradiction or inconsistency exists;

"sopī" means that too [is such]. "Ocityaṃ samposetīti ocityasamposako" means that which nourishes or enhances propriety; "so ādi yassa alaṅkārantaragocarassa" means that which is the beginning of the domain of other ornaments.
This is *śleṣa* (punning) arising from the word (*padato*). There are also other varieties of *śleṣa* occurring even when another word follows.
The form, nature, and characteristic of these aforementioned examples will become manifest through their very usage in the illustrations provided. 292–3.

To show the specific varieties of *śleṣa* not yet mentioned, he introduces [the section] with "Viruddhā... and so forth: "Those whose actions are both contradictory and non-contradictory, yet not different..."
Furthermore, there are three types of *silesa* (emphasis): that which is endowed with action (*kamma*) that is contradictory, non-contradictory, and non-distinct regarding both meanings;
another, distinct *silesa* joined with a restrictive particle (*niyama*) through a term of limitation (*avadhāraṇa*);
a *silesa* consisting of an expression that negates a restriction even while employing a restrictive particle; and a *silesa* that is non-contradictory, being non-contradictory to both sides.

Furthermore, there is the "simile of contradiction" (*virodhisileso*) which involves a contradiction between two things; and there is the "simile arising from a word," such as that arising from a single word or a sentence, including similes that enhance propriety (*ocityasamposaka*) and so forth.

The form (*rūpa*) or characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) of these similes will become manifest through the very illustrations (*nidassana*)—that is, the examples (*udāharaṇa*)—by means of the examples being illustrated, for it is through the example itself that the characteristic is revealed.

The intention is: "Since it has already been explained, I shall not discuss it separately. And: "Those whose *silesas* (stylistic ornaments) consist of actions that are contradictory, non-contradictory, and yet undivided";
and: "That which possesses a restriction (*niyama*), meaning a limitation (*avadhāraṇa*)";
and: "That which possesses a negation (*akkhepa*) of such restriction"; and: "That *vacana* (statement), that *abhidhāna* (expression), which belongs to such a *sileso*."

The analysis (*viggaha*) is as follows: "and," "there is no contradiction for him," "he cultivates propriety," "that is the beginning of the series of similes and so forth," "born from a word," and "that is the beginning of the sentence.
This is the *viruddhakamma-silesa* (simile of contradictory action).
Bringing the world under his own control, he of the beautiful form and melodious voice—the enemy of Māra—overcomes his foes;
the King of Dhamma unfolds his power. (294) Then, in due course, it is said:
"Bringing [the world] under his own control," and so forth. Bringing the entire world under his own control, the enemy of Māra...
And as for the Dhamma King: "vigraha" means a fit and charming conflict or dispute for the Foe of Māra; or, "vigraha" refers to the perfection of his body for that Dhamma King.
Among these, the Foe of Māra suffers defeat and goes to ruin by virtue of having met with defeat at the Bodhi tree;
whereas the Dhamma King, Samantabhadra, exerts himself by way of the continuous turning of the victory-banner that proclaims triumph throughout the three worlds.
"It becomes equal" refers to this summary of contradictory actions (*viruddhakamma-sileso*), due to the mutual opposition between the manifestations of ruin (*parābhava-vijambhanānaṃ*).
294. Now, he provides an illustration according to the order of the summary: "Under one's own power," and so forth.

"Bringing the entire world under one's own power" means bringing it under one's control by engaging it in what is harmful; otherwise, [it means] bringing the whole world under one's own [control] by engaging it in what is beneficial.

While the enemy of Māra, possessing a beautiful form and a charming voice, utters his cries—if he does not, that is, if he is not endowed with a beautiful physical perfection—he meets with defeat at the foot of the Bodhi tree by virtue of having suffered defeat;
whereas the Dhamma-King, the Tathāgata, exults, exulting by virtue of the resounding cry of victory spread throughout the three worlds. [This concerns] the actions of defeat and exultation.

Because they are mutually contradictory, this is called the *viruddhakamma-sileso* (the figure of speech of contradictory action). The phrase "his own power (*vaso*) and sovereignty (*issariya*)" and the phrase "one whose dispute (*viggho*),
