quarrel (*vivādo*), or body (*deho*) is fit (*kallo*) and agreeable (*manuñño*)" constitute the *aviruddhakamma-sileso* (the figure of speech of non-contradictory action).

People hear the speech of the Sage, which is sweet by its very nature and born from the arising of a particular excellence of merit, and they behold the Deathless. (295) “By its very nature,” and so forth.
Speech that is sweet and dear by its very nature is [called] *madhura*; the Deathless (*amata*) is also sweet. Of the particular excellence of merit...
There is an increase (*udayo*), and from that, an arising (*sambhavo*); or rather, people hear the speech of the Sage, which is designated as the True Dharma (*saddhamma*).
Seeing that this [speech] is the Deathless (*amata*) and its basis is also the Deathless—this is the summary of the non-contradictory action, because hearing and seeing are not contradictory.
295. “Of its own nature,” and so forth. It is “naturally sweet” because it is sweet by its very essence even without the application of effort such as “I shall make my speech sweet”;
otherwise, it would be “naturally excellent” only through the absence of some specific condition that has not arisen.
It arises from the emergence of a particular excellence of merit, belonging to a certain Sage who is the teacher of a particular excellence of merit.
It has arisen through the increase of specific wholesome qualities;

otherwise, if it were not so, those people who are to be trained would hear the Sage’s speech—known as the True Dhamma—which has been attained as the objective support for the increase of specific wholesome qualities performed with the aim of Nibbāna, and those people who are to be trained would see the deathless Nibbāna. This is because the actions of hearing and seeing are mutually exclusive.
This is the analysis of the non-contradictory compound (*aviruddha-kamma-silesa*). The grammatical analysis (*viggaha*) is as follows:

"his own state" (*sassa attano bhāvo*), "sweet by that" (*tena madhurā*), "it is sweet" (*madhuram iti ca*), "merit itself is the excellence" (*puññameva viseso*), "its arising" (*tassodayo*), and "that from which its origin arises" (*tena sambhavo yasseti ca*).
This is the analysis of the inseparable compound (*abhinnakamma-silesa*).
It dispels darkness,
is sweet by its very nature,
and gladdens and refreshes the minds of living beings.
The Victor [delights] by means of his speech and his radiance.
(296) “In darkness,” etc.: He dispels darkness—that is, the darkness known as delusion (*moha*), or natural physical darkness—therefore he is the Dispeller of Darkness.
By means of that, through his natural effulgence and his splendor, the Victor delights the mind and heart of living beings.
This one, whose moral discipline (*sīla*) is unbroken, is endowed with speech and demeanor that are characterized by nourishment through a single unified action.

296. Regarding the passage beginning with “Andhakārā”: for the removal of darkness—meaning for the removal of the darkness of delusion (*moha-andhakāra*) or natural physical darkness—with speech and demeanor that are naturally sweet, naturally pleasant to the ear, or naturally delightful to the eye.
And because the Victor gladdens and satisfies the minds and hearts of beings with the radiance of his body—

since two verbal expressions acting as instruments are joined here with a single action whose nature is to satisfy— this is an *abhinnakamma-sileso* (a compound where the action is not split). Furthermore,
the phrases "he removes darkness" and "sweet by its very nature" [are examples of other types].
Just as there is blackness in the hair and eyes of those possessing self-restraint, crookedness in those who are upright,
and excessive redness in the hands, feet, and lips of the Lord of Sages.
297. “*Kesī*,” and so forth. Blackness belongs only to the hair and eyes, not to the mind; the quality of blackness and wickedness are closely linked.
Crookedness belongs only to the eyebrows, not to the underlying intention (*ajjhāsaya*); crookedness, dishonesty, and deceitfulness are closely linked.
Excessive redness belongs only to the hands, feet, and lips, not to the heart; the quality of excessive redness and passion (*rāga*) adhere together. “Of the Sage-Lord (*muninda*).”

The term “blackness” (*kaṇhatta*) and so forth should be connected to everything [in the following verses]. The use of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) in the phrase “the ornament of fixed order (*niyamavā sileso*) belongs only to the hair and eyes” is as follows:
“Of the hair and eyes,” etc. The blackness of the Lord of Sages (*muninda*) belongs only to his hair and eyes; the unwholesomeness (*akusala*) characterized by blackness does not exist in his mind.
The crookedness belongs only to his eyebrows, not to his intention (*ajjhāsaya*). The extreme redness belongs only to his hands, feet, and lips, not to anything else.

Regarding the phrase "in the bases": because the word of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), which signifies a definite rule, exists in such expressions as "of the hair or the eyes," there is a close connection between blackness and evil, crookedness and deceitfulness, and redness and passion;
thus, this is called a "rule-possessing simile. Furthermore, [the compound] *kesāni ca akkhīni ca* means "hair and eyes," and *kaṇhassa bhāvo* means "the state of being black."

The analysis of the compound is as follows: "crookedness" (*vaṅka*), "the state of being crooked" (*vaṅkassa bhāvo*), "hands, feet, and lower parts," and "the state of being excessively red" (*atirattassa bhāvo*).
Regarding the *silesa* (poetic figure) of "rejection by restriction" (*niyamakkhepa*):
"Only in your hands, feet, and lower parts is passion (*sārāga*) seen."
Or rather, O Lord, this [redness] is seen even in the virtues of the virtuous.
(298) “In the hands,” and so forth. O Lord, in your hands, feet, and lips alone is *sārāga*—that is, a beautiful red color—seen, and not in the mind.
*Sārāga* means both a red color and sensual desire (*chandarāga*); thus [the verse] is well-constructed. This restriction is set aside. Now...
Or how is it restricted, since this passion (*sārāga*) of yours is seen by the virtuous as having the characteristic of dispassion (*virāga*) precisely toward their qualities?
Therefore, the word *sileso* here expresses a restriction that serves to reject [the literal sense], asking:
"How then is it determined? (Verse 298): "O Lord, your passion—beautiful and red in color—is seen only on your hands, feet, and lips."

But greed is not seen in the mind. Alternatively, this "attachment" (sārāga)—which consists of the wholesome desire (kusalacchanda) for the wish to act—is seen even toward the virtues of the virtuous and the qualities such as morality (sīla) of good people.

Because it is accompanied by the phrase "alternatively" (atha vā), which negates the restriction shown by the word "only" (eva), greed is closely connected with attachment in the sense of a red color.
And this is the essence of a statement that subverts a restrictive rule (*niyamakkhepavacanasileso*). The analysis (*viggaha*) is: "Saṃ" means beautiful, and "rāga" means passion.
This is an example of a non-contradictory essence (*avirodhisileso*): "He is exceedingly fortunate, possessing a distinctive mark."
Radiant, destined for rising,
the Lord of the World who has conquered all defilements—
the Master of Recluses shines forth.
299. “Salakkhaṇo,” etc. One who exists together with his marks—that is, with his own form, or with the thirty-two marks of a superior man—is “salakkhaṇo”;
this refers to both the moon and the Lord of Sages (the Buddha). He is exceedingly beautiful. The sun is “tejassī” because it is endowed with a distinction of radiance;
it is “niyatodayo” because its daily rising is certain, characterized by light; the sun is “niyato” in the sense of being stable.
Udaya is the Perfectly Enlightened One; he whose nature is that of enlightenment is Niyatodaya. Muninda is the Lord of the World and Brahmā.

He is Muninda because he has conquered the afflictions through his delight in meditation, thereby overcoming physical and mental ailments. He is Brahmā because he has conquered the tenfold defilements by attaining the knowledge of the supreme path.
He is the lord of jewels—the peerless jewel, the most excellent gem—and among ascetics...

It should be construed thus: "The Lord of Sages shines as the Sovereign. This is an *avirodhi-silesa* (non-contradictory pun), because both meanings—those of *lakkhaṇa*, *subhaga*, and so forth—are unimpeded in both senses.
299. Regarding the passage beginning with "Salakkhaṇo": *Salakkhaṇo* means endowed with characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*); *atisubhago* means possessed of an exceedingly beautiful consort (*lakkhī*).
Alternatively, if not [in that sense], it means endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpurisalakkhaṇa*) and joined with extreme splendor and the like.
Possessed of the great majesty that dispels darkness through its brilliance, with its rising assured as it invariably ascends the sky at the time of dawn every day;
otherwise, endowed with the continuous radiance of the Buddha’s splendor, possessed of the growth known as the firm state of omniscience,
the Lord of the World who has become like Brahmā, having conquered the defilements and overcome the distress of body and mind through the rapture of meditative absorption.

If not, then he who has become the lord of the three worlds, whose eightfold defilements have been destroyed by the knowledge of the fourth path—that supreme jewel, the Lord of Recluses, shines and glows; if not, then the Lord of Recluses does not shine or appear.
Furthermore, because there is no contradiction between the two phrases beginning with "Salakkhaṇo subhago," the moon is [implied] in the first quarter and the sun in the second.
Because it is well-connected with the meaning of "omniscience" (sabbaññu) through the Brahmin in the third [line] and the jewel in the fourth,

this is called *avirodhisileso* (non-contradictory metaphor). It is so called because it functions together with its defining characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), and because he possesses an exceedingly beautiful portion or glory (*siri*)—
such as the exertion for the sake of glory— or because he possesses splendor (*tejas*), or because his arising (*udaya*) is certain, or because he is the ruler (*iso*) of the world.
And [the phrases] "one by whom defilement is conquered" and "lord of jewels or of recluses" constitute the sentence. This is the *virodhi-silesa* (contradictory paronomasia):
"Though unequal, he is equal in the world."
Though he is the supreme among men in the world,
he is ever compassionate toward the wicked;
such is the mind of the Sage.
300. “*Asamo*,” etc. One who has no equal (*asama*) in terms of royal qualities and so forth is *asama*; such a king or other person is called *asama*.

Here, the Sage (*muni*) is [called] *asama* because he is the unique crest-jewel of the world. In that context, when [the term] refers to a king or the like, it is a contradiction for him to be called *sama* (equal) in the world, due to his inequality (*asamattā*).
The word *api* indicates this contradiction. However, in the alternative sense [referring to the Sage], there is no contradiction, as in the case of Devadatta and others in the world.
Because it applies equally to beings who are antagonistic, such as Rāhula and others, and to beings who are non-antagonistic, this very [term] is indeed a contradiction [only] in appearance;
it is actually a true contradiction. Brahmā, Lokese, and Muni: therein, the statement "Brahmā is the supreme among men" is contradictory because his birth is divine (*dibbayoni*);
however, in another sense, there is no conflict because he is the most excellent of men. *Daya* means giving (*dāna*); one who possesses *daya* is *sadaya*.

"A certain man. One who acts with compassion is "compassionate," namely, the Sage (muni). In this context, the term "man" contradicts [the idea that he is] a donor toward sinful people, as he is "without compassion";
the Sage contradicts [the idea that he is] "without compassion" toward sin such as lust and so forth. Therefore, this aforementioned state, activity, or mental disposition of the Sage is marvelous;
thus, this figure of speech based on contradiction (*virodhisileso*) has been illustrated according to the method described.
300. “Asamo,” and so forth. Although he is peerless (*asama*) and incomparable (*atulya*), there is no one in the world—such as a king or the like—who is his equal;
rather, being devoid of any person who resembles him, he is equal to the entire world, including Rāhula-bhadra and Devadatta, by virtue of the absence of both attachment and aversion.

Even in the world, although he has become Brahmā, he is the supreme among men (*naruttama*) and the best of men (*naravara*); otherwise, he would be the supreme among men only by being the lord of the entire world. Furthermore, he is compassionate toward those who beg.
Even one endowed with generosity known as "compassion" (dayā) may be cruel toward the most wicked evildoers and devoid of giving;

yet, if not so, one who possesses compassion is indeed merciless toward unwholesome states. This is the movement and activity of the Sage’s mind—varied and manifold—and his state of unequaled equality toward kings and others alike;
it is his becoming Brahmā while remaining in the form of a supreme human being, and his state of being devoid of giving toward any person who is otherwise possessed of giving.
And it is contradictory. Therefore, because of the smoothness [of the meaning] between the king and the royal officers and the Sage, this is called "contradictory alliteration" (*virodhisileso*).
In the successive preceding positions, the contradiction is resolved by the subsequent positions. In the preceding position, the word *api* indicates contradiction;
in the subsequent position, it indicates restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). And as for the phrase "one to whom there is no equal," he is both a man and the supreme one.
The analysis [of the compound] is as follows: "cetī" means "one who exists together with compassion" or "for the sake of compassion"; and "adayo" means "one who has no compassion.
The people, who have been struck by the suffering of saṃsāra, find their refuge in you, who nourish them through your words that possess the elegance of propriety.
One finds the desired, ultimate happiness, which bestows the deathless.
(301) He explains with the verse beginning "In saṃsāra," and so forth. *Saṃsāra* is simply the uninterrupted succession of aggregates (*khandha*) as they proceed;
it is suffering by way of its nature as suffering and so on. By that [suffering], the multitude of people is afflicted and struck down. *Amata* refers to happiness, or alternatively, to Nibbāna.

"Amatandadāti" means "he gives the deathless"; it is an address of invocation. [The phrase] "tvayi avanatā" means that, through prostration, one attains and acquires the ultimate physical and mental happiness born from the removal of suffering—whatever is desired and longed for.
Here, "the deathless" (*amata*) refers to both nectar (*sudhā*) and Nibbāna.

Because he who gives the deathless (*amatandada*) brings happiness to those afflicted by suffering, he is worthy; thus, the phrase "he gives the deathless" is applied to the object [of praise] already attained.

“*Ocityasamposako*” means that which nourishes propriety; this is a fragment of a simile (*upamāsileso*). By the word “etc. (*ādi*), fragments of similes such as “connected with fragrance and beauty” are included.

301. Regarding “*Saṃsāra*,” etc.: “*janatā upahatā*”—the people afflicted by the suffering of *saṃsāra*, meaning afflicted by the suffering known as the continuous occurrence of the aggregates (*khandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*).
“*Amatandada he*”—O giver of the Deathless, O giver of nectar, O Tathāgata, giver of *nibbāna*. If [you do not grant it]...

"Bowing down to you"—meaning prostrating with humility—one finds and enjoys (*vindati sevati*) the desired and cherished happiness, that is, physical and mental bliss, in an absolute and supreme manner.
Regarding the phrase "givers of the deathless (*amata-dāyakā*) who bring happiness to the suffering," this is indeed entirely appropriate;
for the term "giver of the deathless" (*amataṃ dadāti*), which expresses both [meanings], refers to the bestowing of happiness upon such a person.
"He nourishes propriety" (*ocityaṃ poseti*)—this is the core of the phrase "one who thoroughly nourishes propriety. The sentences are:
"Samsara itself is suffering," "they are afflicted by it," and "it bestows the deathless, the ambrosia, which is Nibbana.
Having made [the subject] equal to objects endowed with qualities belonging to someone;
That which constitutes a collective mention is considered *tulyayogitā* (Equal Pairing).
He illustrates *tulyayogitā* with the words beginning "guṇe" and so forth. A quality (*guṇa*) is a property, whether good or bad;
having made things equal by means of objects associated with that quality—even though there is no actual equality in their substance—one superimposes such a state upon some person or other.
That praise or narrative intended for the purpose of eulogy or censure which possesses equal characteristics is considered *tulyayogitā* (Equal Pairing).
Because it establishes an equal connection (*tulyayogitā*) among such things by means of a quality intended to be expressed, *tulyayogitā* thus functions in two ways for that purpose.

302. Now, he demonstrates the ornament of *tulyayogitā* with the words beginning "by those endowed with qualities" (*guṇayuttehi*). [By] those endowed with qualities, whether beautiful or unbeautiful...
When, having made things equal by means of whatever qualities they may possess— even though they are not actually equal— and having established a perception of equality through that act,

one engages in a description consisting of praise or blame directed toward a person or other subject, such as the recounting of their virtues or faults, that is considered *tulyayogitā* (Equal Pairing).
This is because it involves being "joined with qualities" (*guṇehi yuttā*) and because it is a "joining together with a common quality" (*tulyena guṇena saha yoga*).
The analysis (*viggaha*) is: "There exists [the quality] of these, such as the Blessed One garlanded with rays (*raṃsimālī*), etc.

and "the state of theirs is a connection with equal qualities (*tulyaguṇa*). Here, since the connection with those qualities among the referents (*padattha*) associated with equal qualities constitutes the state of *tulyayogitā*, that particular expression which conveys it should be known as *tulyayogitā* by means of the suffix *-tad-atthiya*.
The world has attained intoxication,
it has attained the attainment of light;
and by both [of these], the sun-garlanded one [shines].
And the Blessed One is the dispeller of darkness (*tamonudo*).
He utters [the verse] beginning with "When [the sun] has arrived," and so forth. It is called "dispeller of darkness" because he dispels darkness.

Both the sun, which is garlanded with rays, and the Fully Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*)—by means of these two, acting as instruments or as causes—the world, that is, the world of sentient beings, has arrived.
"Sammada" means rapture (*pīti*) by which one is of such a nature; "sampatti" means the attainment of light by which one is likewise of such a nature.

Here, the definition should be applied as follows: it is the praising and extolling of the Blessed One by way of hymns of praise, comparing him to the sun-garlanded one who is endowed with qualities such as the giving of rapture.

303. Now he provides an illustration with the words beginning “sampatti. By means of both—the dispeller of darkness (tamonudo) who strikes away the gloom, and the one garlanded with rays (raṃsimālī), namely the Blessed One—acting as instruments or causes, the world (loko), that is, the world of sentient beings, becomes possessed of the joy of attainment (sampattasammado), having obtained rapture (pītiko), and possesses the perfection of light (sampattālokasampadā).
Here, by means of the sun, which is endowed with the qualities consisting of the giving of rapture and the making of light;
By making [the subject] equal [to the example], there is a statement of qualities by way of praising the Blessed One.
There are such phrases as "by whom perfection of rapture and joy is attained," "perfection of light," and "by whom the perfection of light is attained," as well as "he dispels darkness.
Even when no example is explicitly shown, a censure directed at someone by comparing them to some object endowed with the qualities of the unworthy should be understood in the same way.
When establishing a different meaning, that which is shown—whether it be non-existent or existent—as some fruit similar to it, is an illustration (nidassana).

(304) The term "illustration" (nidassana) is explained by the verse beginning with "establishing a different meaning" (atthantaraṃ), etc. It is called an "illustration" in view of that which is to be illustrated.
When someone, by means of some suitable action to be accomplished, demonstrates or establishes— on account of that very thing acting as a cause—
a certain result that is either non-existent or undesirable, or existent and desirable, which is similar or equal to that other matter,
such a thing characterized in this way may be an *nidassana* (illustration).
304. Now he illustrates the ornament of illustration (*nidassanālaṅkāra*) with the words beginning "another matter" (*atthantara*).
An "other matter" (*atthantara*) is a different thing from that which is to be illustrated—a mere measure consisting of a customary action or a customary duty...
by means of some object that accomplishes it, [there arises] some fruit that is similar to it, equal to that other matter; whether it be non-existent or undesired, or existent or desired.
That which is shown by means of examples and established is such a fruit called an "illustration" (*nidassana*).
The analysis (*viggaha*) is: "it is both that meaning and another internal one," and "similar to that other internal meaning," and "it is illustrated.
[This refers to] the illustration of a non-existent fruit.
