"They go to destruction" means they perish. This indicates a result similar to the intermediate state of perishing through evil, which is preceded by arising.
What are they doing? "The King of Dhamma," "the King who has not fallen away from Dhamma," and "the Lord of Sages"—this is the elegant phrasing.
[It refers to] those opposed to him; the state of that whose end or conclusion (*anta*) is corrupted and hostile—that state. That...
This indicates that this non-existent fruit is caused by opposition to the Dhamma King; it is an illustration of ruin because of its undesirable nature.

305. Now he provides an example with the words beginning "From the arising," etc. From the arising—that is, the manifestation in the world—of the Lord of Ascetics, the Lord of Sages, evil things such as greed and so forth [disappear] due to kings who possess the royal virtues opposed to those contrary to the Dhamma King, and by the Sovereign of Dhamma.

"By the Lord of Sages" means that they reach, arrive at, and undergo ruin and decline, indicating and making manifest the state of being wretched and having an undesirable end for those who oppose him.
Here, by the first half [of the verse], another meaning—namely, the ruin and decline consisting of evil—is shown as preceding the arising;
by the second half, the unreal fruit characterized as "wretchedness," which is caused by a similar opposition, is shown.
[The text] shows this: because it is undesirable, this is an unreal fruit caused by opposition to the King of Dhamma.

The phrase "of those hostile to the Lord of Ascetics" (*samaṇānaminda*) means either "a king endowed with Dhamma" or "one who rules over [the teachings of] Dhamma"; and "hostile to him" (*tena viruddha*);
and "those whose internal end is corrupt and deformed" (*duṭṭho virūpo anto pariyosānaṃ yesam*); and "the state of being such" (*tesaṃ bhāvo*)—this is the construction of the sentence.
This is the display of the fruits of peace for those who have placed their feet upon the lotuses of the Arahants.
The Victor makes known his own state of supreme wonder in the world. 306.
"The head," etc. [He said this] so that the earth might receive the two lotus-feet of the Blessed One, which are themselves wonderful.
The feet of that Conqueror were placed upon the very tops—the heads—of the lotuses that had burst open and risen up, endowed with marvelous qualities.
By means of this secondary meaning (atthantara) regarding the characteristic of placing his feet upon the lotuses, he demonstrates a corresponding fruit;
he makes known his own state of supreme excellence. This peaceful fruit is the illustration for the desired quality of revealing the wonderful attributes of the Conqueror.

306. “Siro,” etc. This Conqueror, having placed his feet upon the heads of those lotuses—worthy of being seized by the fingers of goddesses—which had emerged from the earth after it was split open for the sake of receiving his own wondrous feet, makes known and awakens the world—the world of beings—to his own supreme wonder, his exceedingly marvelous quality. Herein:

It signifies supreme wonder by means of another meaning—the act of placing his feet upon the heads of wondrous lotuses; for this [verse] is desirable as it illustrates the marvelous qualities of the Victor through a corresponding and excellent fruit.
Furthermore, it refers to one by whom the feet have been placed upon the head (*sirasī*), and to those who deserve a clap of the hands (*accharaṃ accharā-saṅghātaṃ arahanti*);
thus, it is the most excellent and supreme marvel (*paramo uttamo abbhuto*).
The analysis [of the compound] is either “this is its quality” (*guṇo assa*) or “the state of that” (*tassa bhāvo*).
It may refer to the greatness of manifestation or to the intention;
that which has reached the highest excellence is what is called “greatness” (*mahantatta*).
307. He demonstrates "greatness" (mahantatta) by means of the passage beginning with "by way of manifestation" (vibhūtiyā).

That which has reached or attained the state of supreme excellence, the highest distinction, of either manifestation (vibhūti), success (sampatti), intention (adhippāya), or aspiration (ajjhāsaya), is called and described as "greatness."
307. Now, he shows the ornament of greatness with the words beginning “vibhūti.

That greatness which has reached the state of being the highest excellence (*paramukkaṃsataṃ*), that is, the state of exceeding excellence (*atyukkaṃsabhāvaṃ*)—whether by way of manifestation (*vibhūti*), success (*sampatti*), intention (*adhippāya*), or disposition (*ajjhāsaya*)—that is what is called “greatness.
It is also [defined as] “the state of the great,” or “that which has the supreme excellence as its pre-eminence (*atisaya*).”
And the phrase "the state of that" [is used]. Regarding the greatness of his majesty:
he has a sunshade through which the heat is filtered, intermingled with the radiance of the jewels of his crown.
Long ago, before his Great Renunciation, the Bodhisatta attained supreme glory.

He uttered [the verse] beginning with “Kirīṭe,” etc. Long ago, in the past, the Bodhisatta—the son of Queen Māyā—attained and obtained supreme, most excellent glory and splendor, such as was not shared by others. Of what kind? [He was adorned] with a kirīṭa, that is, a crown.
"Pervaded and sprinkled by the shadows and splendors of jewels" refers to the white parasol (*setacchatta*) belonging to one such as he;
thus, the "greatness of his majesty" is expressed by the phrase "the parasol, pervaded by the shadows of jewels.
(308) Now, he provides an illustration with the words beginning "kirīṭa" and so forth. In his final birth, the Bodhisattva, the Great Being, [went forth... abhinikkhamā.

Prior to his Great Departure, it is said that he experienced and enjoyed supreme glory and magnificence, with a sunshade whose rays were interwoven with the luster of the crest-jewel, and a white parasol colored by the radiance of the diadem-jewel.
Herein, by describing how the rays of the diadem-jewel interpenetrated the white parasol, the vastness of his magnificence is established. "Jewels in the diadem" means...

And [the compound] "ca, tesaṃ chāyāyoti ca" means "and their shadow"; and the phrase "tāhi anuviddho churito ātapavāraṇo yasseti ca" means "he whose sunshade is pierced and sprinkled by those [shadows].
Because of the greatness of his intention, he is called "Satta" (the Being) in relation to enlightenment (*sambodhi*). "Bodhi-" [is used as a prefix].
That being, for the sake of the welfare of beings,
abandoned even Rāhula’s mother,
though she was bound to him by the essence of affection.
309. “A being,” etc. Having abandoned—even Bimbādevī, the mother of Rāhula—who was bound by the attachment born of affection, by the state of being dear, and by the passion of desire;

how much more so any other young woman—having left her behind without regard and remaining unattached, the Bodhisatta Siddhattha, for the welfare of beings and for their mundane and supramundane progress, [struggled] for enlightenment, that is, for omniscience itself.
“Attached, clinging, stuck right there”—this is the intended meaning. His greatness is characterized by the supreme excellence of such noble qualities as his compassion for various virtuous people.

309. Regarding the passage beginning with “The Bodhisatta”: that Bodhisatta, even having abandoned Rāhulamātā—Bimbādevī—who was bound by the essence of affection and fettered by the passion known as endearment, [set out] for the welfare of beings, for the sake of the worldly and supramundane goals of beings toward Perfect Enlightenment.

"He is attached only to the knowledge of omniscience. By stating that he was not attached even to such a woman-jewel (*itthiratana*), the greatness of the Bodhisatta’s sublime aspiration (*ukkhaṭṭhajjhāsaya*) is expressed.
Regarding the analysis (*viggaha*): it is called *bodhi* because one awakens rightly by means of it;

*satto* because he is attached to awakening; *hitam* because it is for the welfare of beings; *rāgo* because it is a "flavor" (*raso*) born of affection and endearment; and *tena ābaddhā* because they are bound by that [flavor].
Whatever further excellence is shown after having concealed what is already praiseworthy— whether it be unequal or equal to that [concealed excellence]— is not truly superior.
If that is considered deception:
310. He speaks of deception by means of the words "having concealed," and so forth;

if, having concealed or set aside some object worthy of description, one were to show something else—something unequal, uneven, dissimilar, or different—that is not the same as the object worthy of description.
Having described it through a poetical conceit (*kavi*), that [concealment] is prescribed as *vañcanā* (deception).
310. Now he demonstrates the ornament of *vañcanā* with the words beginning “gopetvā.
If, having concealed some object intended for description, one describes another object—whether similar or equal to that object intended for description, or dissimilar or unequal—then...
That which is shown by the poet is considered to be *vañcanā* (deception). The sentence is: "By means of this function (*vutti*), one deceives (*vañceti*) that which is to be described.
*Asamavañcanā*:
"Not among thousands in front," [etc.]
And for such a one among the five,
Māra has no power over others;
he [faces] ten thousand multiplied by ten.

311. He provides an illustration with the words beginning "In front" (*purato*). Māra is Kāma; because he is not "such-like" (*tādina*) regarding greed and other defilements, he does not exist "in front," that is, face-to-face, before the Sage.
Furthermore, he does not possess a thousand arrows, nor does he possess five arrows—thus it should be explained that Māra is here concealed [by these negations].
He who is the conqueror of his three worlds over others, that is, over other beings...
Among those full of passion who desire [gain], ten increased by ten—that is, a thousand multiplied by ten—is the number;
otherwise, how could he conquer the three worlds? Thus, by concealing Māra and showing him a cloth marked with ten thousand, there is no deception in this matter. 311.
Now he provides an illustration with the words beginning "In front," etc. Māra [approached] the Tathāgata, who is unchanging amidst gain, loss, and so forth.
In front, directly facing him, there was not even a thousand arrows among thousands;
having placed five such arrows among five, there were no more than those five arrows.

Even when others, in the presence of the Sugata, [encountered] such other defilements as these, for that Māra—the Conqueror of the Three Worlds—there was a thousand of these arrows, increased tenfold by way of tenfold calculation.

"It becomes ten thousand. This is called "the deception of inequality" (*asamavañcanā*), because after excluding the Māra to be described, another substantial entity consisting of a numerical calculation is shown by way of the number ten thousand. The sentence is:
"He possesses a thousand arrows," and "He possesses five arrows," and "It is increased by ten."
Deceiving themselves by engaging in disputes, [they are eclipsed] by the moon-like face of the Lord of Sages.
“This is not the full moon;
this is the parasol of the Mind-Born One.

(312) Regarding the verse beginning with “Dispute,” etc.: “of the Mind-Born One” means of Kāma. This is a deceptive comparison (*samavañcanā*), because the parasol is presented by setting aside the full moon.
312. “A dispute,” and so forth. This full moon visible before us, which engages in a dispute with the moon of the Sage’s face—the moon of the Omniscient One’s mouth—is not truly the moon.
Rather, this lunar orb is the raised white parasol for the manifestation of the Mind-Born (Manobhū), the Bodiless One (Anaṅga). Setting aside the lunar orb that is being described, beyond that—
Because another parasol resembling the moon has been shown, this usage is called *samavañcanā* (a deceptive similarity). The analysis (*viggaha*) is as follows: "Indu" refers to the Moon;
"Munīnaṃ indu" means the Moon of the Sages; "tassa vadanaṃ" means his face; thus, "indū" is the face of the Moon of the Sages, which resembles the [actual] Moon.
Furthermore, it is analyzed as "puṇṇo samantato" (full on all sides) and "manasi bhūto" (become manifest in the mind).

That which is performed here as weariness with the world through following others and so forth, yet is expressed in praise for what has been done only slightly, is "Praise for What Has Been Done Slightly" (Appakatatthuti).
(313) It explains "Praise for What Has Been Done Slightly" by means of the word "pari" and so on. Following others—meaning service to anyone whatsoever—is...

When, by those who are weary of and disenchanted with that [world] from its very beginning, praise is performed here toward some object within the range of the intellect—which is uncreated and non-existent—that praise or gratification is what constitutes "praise of the uncreated" (appakatathuti). 313.
Now, he demonstrates the praise of the uncreated with the words beginning "parānu... (for others...). By means of conforming to others and so forth, for another person...

When there is praise— counted as "conciliatory" (*saṃrādhanā*)— offered here in some matter whatsoever, directed toward a limited and unattained sphere of wisdom by one who has become weary through following others and so forth, and who has reached a state of agitation (*ubbega*),
that is what is called "praise of the limited. And "following others" (*anuvattana*) is the first among those [factors] such as causing harm to others.
And [the word] "not artificial" (*appakatena*): the letter *r* is a euphonic junction (*sandhija*). The sentence is: "Praise is offered for what is not artificial.
"The deer live happily in the forests, serving no one else, with water, grass, sprouts, and so forth, obtained without effort."
314. He provides an illustration with the words "Happiness," and so forth. By "waters" is meant *dabba* sprouts—that is, the growth of *dabba* grass.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), tree shoots and the like are included. Of what kind are they? They are "attainable" (*upalābhya*), meaning they are to be obtained without effort, that is, without the distress of service and the like.
They are called "non-servants" (*aparasevino*) because they do not serve anything else by means of their virtue. Like deer in the forests, they are averse to the calamity of pleasing others.
“They live happily and undisturbed. Here, the life of a deer, characterized by detachment from the distress of following a king, is praised.

Now he provides an illustration with the words beginning with “happily”: “By means of a livelihood that does not depend on others—deer living as deer who do not serve others, and which is obtained without effort because there is no ownership by others, they are free from the toil of serving others and obtain what is needed without difficulty.”
They live happily, leading a life of ease, in the forests—be they desired or otherwise—by means of water, grass, sprouts, trees, creepers, shoots, and so forth.
Herein, even the "deer-life," though not attained by someone who has fallen into the calamity of serving a king, is praised.
Furthermore, it is because they do not serve others due to their virtue (*sīla*), and because there is an absence of exhaustion; for this reason...

The grammatical analysis (*viggaha*) is as follows: "to be perceived" (*upalabhitabba*), "shoots of grass" (*dabbānaṃ aṅkurāni*), "water and shoots of grass" (*jalañca dabbāṅkurāni ca*), and "those which have these [water and shoots] as their beginning" (*tāni ādi yesaṃ pallavādīnam*).
Where there is a successive sequence, each preceding term is a qualifier for what follows.
This *ekāvalī* may be twofold, according to affirmation (*vidhi*) and negation (*niṣedha*).

[The author] explains the *ekāvalī* by means of the word "uttara" and so forth. Wherein, in a composition, each successive answer (*uttara*), each subsequent position, serves as a qualifier for each preceding one—whether by way of affirmation or negation—that is what is called *ekāvalī*. This is the *ekāvalī*.
It is twofold by way of affirmation and negation—that is, by way of affirmation and by way of negation.
(315) Now, he demonstrates the *ekāvalī* (single-string ornament) with the words beginning "uttaram.

Wherein each successive term (*uttara*), occurring one after another, serves as a qualifier for each preceding term, acting as a qualification for the preceding word by way of affirmation or negation.
That [ornament] may be called *ekāvalī*. This *ekāvalī* is twofold by way of affirmation and negation, and by way of affirmation-negation.
"The subsequent" (*uttaraṃ*) refers to the word that has become the locus (*ṭhānībhūta*) through the metaphorical extension (*ṭhānūpacāra*) from the locus itself.

And [it is so called] because it is a qualifier for each preceding [word], and because words are strung together (*saṃvaliyanti*) as a single garland (*āvalī*) by means of it; furthermore, there is affirmation (*vidhi*) and its application (*vidhāna*), as well as negation (*nisedha*) and prohibition (*paṭisedha*).

And this is the statement. Here, the etymological derivation (*nibbacana*) occurs according to the desire for analysis through the quality of qualifier and qualified (*visesanavisesyaguṇa*) in sequence—namely, "the latter of the latter" and "the former of the former"—where the quality of the qualified is understood even though not explicitly stated.
This is the *vidhiekāvalī* (single-string necklace of positive injunction).
The feet are beautiful with rows of nails;
the rows of nails are radiant with rays of light;
the rays are the sole destroyers of darkness... the sole strikers.
The qualities of the Teacher shine forth.

(316) He provides an example beginning with the words “the feet,” and so on. This is easily understood. Here, because the feet and other subjects are qualified by the qualifiers—such as being beautiful with rows of nails—it is a *vidhiekāvalī* (a string of positive descriptions).
(316) Now he provides an example with the words “the feet,” and so on: “The feet of the Teacher are beautiful with rows of nails; they are lovely with their lines of nails.”

The rows of nails (*nakhālī*), shining with rays, being illuminated by those rays, and possessing the beauty of rays whose sole function is the dispelling of darkness, shine forth as they become peerless in their task of destroying the gloom.

Here, because the preceding terms such as "feet" (*pāda*) are qualified by successive adjectives that specify their beautiful rows of nails and so forth, this is called a *vidhiekāvalī* (a single-stringed necklace of specifications). Furthermore, *nakhānam āli* means a row or series of nails.

The analysis (*viggaha*) is as follows: "exceedingly beautiful" (*rucirāti*) by means of the claws (*nakhālīhi*), and "resplendent" (*bhāsurāti*) by means of rays (*raṃsīhi*); and "the removal" (*apahāro*) is the taking away (*apaharaṇa*) of darkness (*tamaso*).
Furthermore, "that single flavor" (*so eko raso*) is the function (*kiccaṃ*) of these rays (*etāsaṃ raṃsīnam*).
This is the *Nisedha-ekāvalī*.
The ascetic who is not content is not truly contented, nor is he one who is unassailed by attachment;
for he who is attached to living beings is not free from attachment.
It does not bring endless calamity. 317.
"One who is discontented," and so forth. There should be no one at all called a "wandering ascetic" (*yati*) who is not content with the four requisites.
Furthermore, that which is struck by *ālaya*—that is, by craving—is not what is called contentment. [This applies] to those beings, to living creatures...

It does not bring about endless calamities; thus, it is not what is called "attachment" (*ālaya*). This is a "single-string necklace of negations" (*nisedha-ekāvalī*) consisting in the occurrence of qualifiers that negate discontent and the like, by way of establishing contentment and so forth. 317.
"One who is discontented," etc. One who is discontented with regard to the four requisites, such as robes, [lacks] the twelve kinds of contentment shown therein.
A wanderer who is dissatisfied with anything whatsoever is indeed not called a bhikkhu. Contentment does not exist for one struck by attachment (*ālaya*) and wounded by craving (*taṇhā*).
That which brings endless calamity to living beings and which does not inflict boundless affliction upon creatures—that is not "attachment" (*ālaya*).
These adjectives—beginning with "dissatisfied"—serve to negate the state of being a wanderer and so forth.
Because it proceeds [in this manner], this is called the "Single-String Prohibition" (nisedhaekāvali).
The term *asantuṭṭha* stands as a common property for the entire collection of beings together with the ascetics (*yati*).

Since there is no ascetic [who is not so], by establishing [the term] upon the other members included in the category of all beings—other than the ascetic—the word "unsatisfied" (*asantuṭṭho*) is the substantive (*visesya*), while "to the ascetics" (*yati ne*) is the qualifier (*visesana*). This same relationship of qualifier and substantive applies to the remaining [terms] as well.
It should be applied as appropriate according to the stated rule. The sentences are:
"not being content," "struck down by attachment," "there is no end to these," "and those various calamities," and "it brings those about.
Where there is the state of being adorned or not adorned, it refers to the mutual relationship of the bases.
318. That which is a mutual adornment even without similarity is called *aññamañña* (reciprocal).

By the words "yahiṃ" and so forth, he explains it: when there is a state of being mutually adorned between the bases—that is, the meanings of the words—even without similarity, that is the ornament known as *aññamañña*.
Now, he demonstrates the *aññamañña* ornament with the words "yahiṃ" and so forth. In this ornament, without similarity...

Thus, the mutual relationship between things as that which is adorned and that which adorns constitutes the state of being the ornamented and the ornament; this is what is called "mutual adornment" (*aññamaññavibhūsana*).
The analysis of the compound is as follows: *bhūsiya* (the thing to be adorned) and *bhūsā* (the adornment), their state (*bhāva*), and [the repetition] "this and that" (*aññañca aññañca*).
In the term *aññamañña*, the indeclinable (*abyaya*) is used without a numeral (*asaṅkhya*), whereas when accompanied by a numeral, it is expressed as *bhūsiyabhūsatta*.

Having made this distinction, it should be stated as follows: that which is the ornamented object (*alaṅkāriyavatthu*) in relation to the ornament (*alaṅkāra*), and that which is the ornament in relation to it, are mutually [designated].
Even an ornament that illuminates that [object] receives its name from that purpose.
By means of that circle of rays extending a fathom, by that Sage, the Kinsman of the World...
He too, by that very [act], finds great splendor such as that. 319.
He illustrates this with the verse beginning “Byāmaṃsu,” etc. This is easy to understand. 319.
Now he illustrates it with the verse beginning “Byāmaṃsu,” etc. “Byāmaṃsumaṇḍalaṃ” means a circle of fathom-wide radiance [emanated] by the Kinsman of the World.
By means of that [halo], which serves as the instrument, he finds and enjoys great, vast, and venerable radiance and splendor;
yet that sage also finds such radiance by means of that very fathom-wide orb of light.
Thus, between these two distinct things—the fathom-wide orb of light and the one designated as the "sage"—the fathom-wide orb of light is the ornament in the first sentence.
It exists; it is an ornament for the meaning of the Sage’s words. In the subsequent sentence, these two become ornaments through the figure of *vipallāsa* (inversion).

The analysis (*viggaha*) is as follows: "a circle of rays" (*aṃsūnaṃ maṇḍalam*), and "a fathom-long circle of rays" (*byāmaṃ eva aṃsumaṇḍalam*), and "the world is his kinsman" (*loko bandhu assa*), and "she appears as if she were that" (*sā viya dissati*).
The mention of coexistence, of action, and of quality should be understood as "co-occurrence" (sahavutti); an example of this is as follows.
(320) He explains co-occurrence with the words "the mention," etc. This is easily understood.

320. Now, he demonstrates co-occurrence (*sahavutti*) with the words beginning "the mention" (*kathana*). It should be understood that co-occurrence is the mention of the simultaneous existence or concomitance of two things—namely, an action (*kriyā*) and a quality (*guṇa*).
Its illustration is to be viewed according to the method that will be explained, just as its example is [already given].
Furthermore, it is the state of being together (*saha-saddhiṃ-bhavana*), which is the mention of the occurrence of concomitance (*sahabhāva-vutti*).
And the analysis [of the compound] is "the illustration of that. Coexistence (*sahabhāva*) refers to the meanings of the words such as "moon," "rays," and "nails.

Even though this is so, since their coexistence occurs in relation to an action or a quality within which it exists, and considering that coexistence belongs to both the action and the quality, it is stated: "The statement of coexistence, and of the action and the quality."
The Teacher’s rays from his fingernails shine together with the rays of the moon,
and the moonlight of his face expands in harmony with the moon.

321. “They shine,” and so forth. *Samam* means together; [together] with that Teacher’s moon-like face. The rest is easily understood. Here, because the coexistence of the two actions—shining and expanding—which are common to both [the rays and the face] is established, this is called *kriyāsahavutti* (co-occurrence of action).

321. Now, he shows the example as promised by means of the verse beginning with “they shine. The Teacher’s splendor of nails—the rays from his fingernails—shine together with the rays of the moon, and his moon-like face expands together with the moon.

Here, because the coexistence of the common natural actions of water and waves is stated for both word-meanings, this is called "co-occurrence of action" (kriyāsahavutti). The phrases "the rays of the moon," "the shoulders of the nails," "the face of that Teacher," and "the moon itself, because of its resemblance to the moon" constitute the sentences.
*Samaṃ* is a particle synonymous with *saha* (together).
Stained by the mind of the wicked along with the rise of the Jina’s virtues,
the directions became utterly pure along with the mind of the virtuous.

322. “By the arising of the Conqueror,” and so forth. By means of the arising of the Conqueror—acting either as an instrument (*karaṇa*) or as a cause (*hetu*)—the ten directions become utterly stainless, supremely pure, and beautifully adorned with garlands of extremely pure rays, because the minds of the virtuous are free from evil.
Herein, [there is a contrast between] the stained nature and the stainless nature.
The coexistence of things related by way of logic has been stated;
this is "co-occurrence with a quality" (guṇasahavutti). 322. Regarding the verse beginning with “Jino”:

through the appearance of the Blessed One, who has conquered Māra by his victory, acting as the instrument or the cause, evil—namely, the phenomena of greed and so forth—becomes stained and defiled together with the wicked mind, the mind of the ignoble.
By this very arising of the Victor, the ten directions, together with the minds of the virtuous, became utterly stainless;
for, through the departure of evils from the continuum of the virtuous minds, the garlands of fame spread throughout the three worlds, making them exceedingly pure.
This [verse] expresses the coexistence of the quality characterized by both the state of being stained and the state of being perfectly stainless, which is common to both referents.

The term *guṇasahavutti* means: "the arising of the Conqueror," "the mind of the wicked," "that from which impurity has departed," "extremely stainless (*su-vimala*"), and "those people who are virtuous.
The phrase "of them" (*tesaṃ ceto*) refers to their minds. Where there is a demonstration of the association of contradictory word-meanings, [that is the figure of speech known as *virodha*].
This opposition is considered to be for the purpose of expressing excellence (samukkaṃsa).
It clarifies the contradiction in the passage beginning with "of the contradictory" (virodhīnaṃ), etc.
Where there is seen the proximity of the conjunction of actions and so forth that are mutually contradictory—what is the purpose? It is for the sake of excellence, that is, pre-eminence (atisaya).
"For the purpose of expression" means for the purpose of stating; this aforementioned contradiction is considered "the contradictory" (*virodhī*).
Now, he demonstrates the figure of speech *virodhālaṅkāra* with the words "of the contradictories," and so forth.

Wherein, for the purpose of expressing excellence through a particular mode of expression—that is, for the sake of describing the superior qualities inherent in the subject under discussion—there exist word-meanings such as actions, qualities, and so on, which are mutually contradictory.
It is a demonstration of association, a demonstration of determination, and a demonstration of connection; this is considered the "utti" [explanatory particle] meaning "is opposed.

Furthermore, there are the following statements: "these qualities and so forth possess opposition (*virodha*)," "it is the demonstration of the association and connection," "it is the designation of excellence or superiority (*samukkaṃsa*)," and "the state of being opposed is not included."
The *Virodhitādīpaka* commentary is named after its subject matter.
Even the virtues, which are sweet by nature, when cultivated by those who associate with the wicked,
defile the mind— yes, they utterly defile it— even though [the virtues] belong to the Sole Kinsman of the World.
324. He provides an illustration with the verse beginning "The virtues," and so forth.

Although the virtues—such as Arhatship and the like—of the World-Teacher, the Sole Kinsman of the World, are inherently sweet and uniquely skilled at delighting virtuous people, when they are cultivated by those who serve evil, they utterly corrupt the minds of those evildoers, revealing them by way of producing defilements through hatred, [thinking], "Such an excellence of virtue belongs to him. Herein, regarding the virtues that are inherently sweet:

It should be understood that there is a contradiction between the excellence [of virtue] and its defilement by those who are capable of producing a particular kind of joy. 324. He illustrates this with the verse beginning "The virtues," and so forth:

although the virtues—such as Arahantship and the rest—of the Buddha, the sole kinsman of the world, are sweet by their very nature and naturally sweet, when they are cultivated by those who cultivate evil, they utterly defile the minds of those evil-doers.
"Exceedingly provoking. Thus, the excellence of his virtues is such that it cannot be endured by those of inferior disposition.
Now, would not a virtue naturally sweet fail to cause provocation without joy? And would even provocation not occur without such a naturally sweet virtue?

Therefore, this is for the purpose of demonstrating the quality of their union—the conjunction of these mutually contradictory factors: the act of sweetness and the act of provocation—by means of the superiority of their combined qualities.
It should be construed according to its grammatical characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*). The particle *api* is used here in the sense of contradiction.
The sentences are: "sweet by nature," "he alone is that kinsman," "the sole kinsman of the world," and "they practice evil by their very character.
[This applies] to whatever gift, and to whatever object.
The taking of something superior is considered *parivutti* (exchange).

(325) He explains *parivutti* by means of the words beginning with "of whatever," etc. "Of whatever" indicates the recipient. "The taking of something superior" is the grammatical connection. The rest is easily understood.
(325) Now he demonstrates *parivutti* with the words beginning with "of whatever," etc. "Of whatever object"—that is, even a small object—
Whatever taking or grasping there is of an excellent, superior object by means of a gift given to any recipient acting as the cause—that is considered "exchange" (*parivutti*).
It is called exchange because it consists of giving and receiving through a gift.
Having first given to others something pleasing, such as the eyes and so forth...
The glory of omniscience has now been attained by the Sage; indeed, the glory of omniscience has now been attained by the Lord of Sages.

326. He illustrates this with the verse beginning “purā,” etc. This is easily understood. Here, the taking up of the glory of omniscience through the gift of his eyes and so forth constitutes the *parivutti* (exchange).
326. Now he illustrates it with the words beginning “purā. Formerly, in the past, [the Sage gave] to others his pleasing eyes and so forth.
"Having given, he has now attained the glory of omniscience—the glory designated as 'omniscience' which is not shared by any other.

Here, because the word *parivutti* (exchange) is conventionally established in the sense of taking from that very place to which something was given, there is the "taking" of the glory of omniscience through the "giving" of the eyes and so forth;
and because there would be no taking in the absence of giving, [the exchange holds] even though a recipient person is not present.

The phrase "omnipresence" (*sabbaññutā*) undergoes a transformation by being conceptualized through its state of existence (*vijjamānattena*). For that very reason, in the *Daṇḍiyam*, it is said in the poetic work *Kāvyādāsa* (2.356):

"Having bestowed the weapon of the sword upon your arm, O King, the fame of those [enemies], pale as white water-lilies, has long been carried by their funeral pyres."* *Note: This verse illustrates how the concept of "omnipresence" is applied through a metaphorical shift.*
In this example, having dealt a blow with a weapon from his enemies, their fame—which had long been heaped up by those kings—is brought forth by your arm, as pure as a *kera* flower.
By showing that the taking [of the fame] occurs precisely through the application of action (*kamma*), the reciprocity is made manifest.
The sentence is: "He whose supreme limbs and so forth are eyes," and "he who knows everything," and "his state of being."
Having perceived something and understood it,
the wise person acts accordingly toward that object, which is now free from doubt.
Where this delusion (bhamo) is considered to exist:

by means of the phrase "something" and so forth, one conceives of a delusion. Having seen something—such as a flickering light or the like—a cognizing person perceives another object similar to that thing previously seen, which is free from doubt.
Having set aside non-proximity, one proceeds and knows that specific distinction; this is considered *bhrama* (delusion/confusion).

327. Now he demonstrates the ornament of *bhrama* with the words beginning "something," etc. Wherein, having perceived a certain particular expression that causes understanding—such as a glance toward a direction—and having seen another object equal to that currently being seen, [one mistakes it for the former].
One who practices having removed doubt from the subject matter and made it free from uncertainty knows; this is the analysis:

*alaṅkārabhamo* means "the wandering [of doubt] as an ornament," *tena tassa vā samanti* (it is equal to that, or for that), and *saṃsayo apagato etasmā* (doubt has departed from this), as well as *bhamanaṃ anavaṭṭhānaṃ vatthūnaṃ* (the wandering, the instability, of the subject matters). *Saṃsayāpagataṃ* is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāvisesana*).

In all directions that shine brightly, people whose minds are as clear as the moonlight rejoice, beholding [the radiance] from the rays of the Victor’s toenails. (328) He recites the verse beginning with "samaṃ" and so forth.
From the rays of the Victor’s toenails on his feet, [the light shines] equally and simultaneously in all directions.
"Those people who, seeing those brilliant directions filled with flames, perceive them as the light of the moon, are such [as described].
They rejoice and are satisfied.
(328) Now he provides an illustration with the words beginning "sama," etc.: by means of the rays from the nails of the Victor’s feet, acting as the instrument, throughout the ten directions...
When people, at the same moment, see those blazing directions as blazing, their minds proceed with the thought "it is moonlight," and they rejoice.
Because one applies the cognition of "moonlight" to what is actually a shimmering mirage (*marīci*) by failing to recognize its true nature, it is called a delusion (*bhamo*).
"Equal" (*samaṃ*) means immeasurable. The phrase is: "those whose minds [proceed] with the thought 'it is moonlight'."
That which is called "name" and so forth,
by whatever description it may be, serves as the poets' means for awakening the intended meaning.
This is called *bhāva* (the state of being).
It is so termed by such expressions as "he cultivates the state" (*bhāvaṃ bhāveti*). The *bhāva* of poets is their intention;

that which makes this known is *bhāvabodhana*, which refers to names and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), qualifying phrases are included. By whatever form of negation it may take— [End of fragment]
"It is called this: 'bhāva' (state of being) is said to be an emotion.
Now, he demonstrates the figure of speech *bhāvālaṅkāra* with the words "It is called," and so forth.

That which makes known the state of being (*bhāva*)—the intention or purpose—of poets and speakers, whether it be a noun, a particular noun, an adjective, or any other word, by whatever quality or mode [it is expressed].
Whether or not it is stated by way of excluding other meanings such as "the ocean" (*sāgara*), that which is expressed as "this is called *bhāva*" is what is meant.

Furthermore, there is the statement: "That whose beginning is 'name' (*nāma*) consists of two qualifying phrases," and "it makes known the *bhāva*. A particular expression that reveals the *bhāva*, which is the intention (*adhippāya*) of poets, is called *bhāva* in its own sense;
and the series of words beginning with "name," which serves as its support, is [called *bhāva*] here through metaphorical transfer (*upacāra*) based on that which is supported.
"Existence," it is said, refers to these very things:
the oceans, not the mountain ranges.
"Even their own boundaries they do not abandon, even during the dissolution of the world.

He illustrates this with "Is it not," and so forth. "Even their own" means even slightly. "Boundaries" refers to the limits of their own conduct; "even during the dissolution of the world" (saṃvaṭṭe).

Even at the time of dissolution (*palaya*). The rest is easily understood. Herein, these oceans and so forth are not "oceans" and so forth like those which, at the time of dissolution, abandon their boundary—consisting in the non-transgression of their own shores and their immovability. What then?
These oceans and so forth are indeed such that even if they were to overflow at the time of dissolution, they would still [maintain] their own...

They do not abandon their boundaries. The meaning is this: by way of negating others, it is stated that "someone who has met with misfortune awakens to his own unsurpassed steadfastness," which makes known the aforementioned nature of the poet. 330.
Now he provides an example with the words beginning "Is it not," etc. At the time of the world's dissolution (*saṃvaṭṭakāla*), the oceans overflow their coastal boundaries.

The natural oceans do not become seas [of destruction]. The seven noble mountain ranges, which are called "noble mountains" (*kulācala*) because they do not overstep their boundary—their status as immovable even at such a time—do not cease to be noble mountains.

What then are the seas and so forth? They are the virtuous ones who, even during the *saṃvarta*—the time of the destruction of all things and the destruction of the world-cycle—do not overstep even slightly their own boundary, that is, their boundary of conduct.
They do not abandon [their nature]. Are not those very ones, such as the ocean and so forth, indeed tranquil?

When someone who has met with misfortune manifests their own steadfastness (*dhīratva*), which is not shared by others, then—by means of the ocean and so forth shown here in the form of a negation of other meanings—the intention of the subject (*vattun*) to remain unshaken is made known;
this is what is called the figure of speech "State" (*bhāvālaṅkāra*). *Mana* is a term denoting a short period of time, meaning "innumerable. *Api* is used in the sense of possibility or probability.
When there is a relationship of part and whole (*aṅga-aṅgībhāva*) and a state of equal strength (*sadisa-balabhāva*) in their connection, that conjunction of ornaments is called "Mixed" (*missa*).
(331) He shows the mixed [ornament] with the words beginning "part" (*aṅga*), etc. "Part" (*aṅga*) is that which assists; "whole" (*aṅgī*) is that which is assisted. The state of these two...
The relationship of part and whole (*aṅga-aṅgibhāva*) consists in the state of being the means and the end; and from that [relationship]. Those whose strength is equal or similar—such is their state;
their existence as non-primary, without the relationship of part and whole, and from that cause.
Regarding the subject of binding, the association of those who are adorned—their coming together in one place—that is called "mixture" (*missa*).
331. Now he demonstrates the mixed ornament (*missālaṅkāra*) with the words "aṅgaṅgī," etc.

When there is a relationship of part and whole—by way of the cause consisting in the nature of the facilitator and the facilitated, which is to say, the state of being the means of expression and that which is to be expressed—and when there is a state of equal strength due to the absence of a superior and subordinate relationship, as well as a state of possessing equal power within the context of a composition such as a *pajja* (verse), that conjunction or co-presence of ornaments is [the mixed ornament].

The sentence is as follows: "It is called *missanti* (they mix). [The analysis is: "That which possesses a constituent (*aṅga*)—that is, a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*)—for the sake of that which is to be accomplished (*sādhiya*";

and "the state of both the constituent (*aṅga*) and the possessor of the constituent (*aṅgī*)"; and "the relationship (*sambandha*) consisting of the means of accomplishment and that which is to be accomplished"; and "those ornaments which possess a similar strength (*sadisa-bala*)"; and "the state of those [ornaments], which is mutual independence (*aññamañña-nirapekkhatā*)"; and "mixing (*missana*), which is the act of becoming mixed (*missībhavana*). This is the sentence.
The great river of light from the rays of the Sage’s toenails, mingled with the relationship of part and whole, is praised; oh,
how it brings happiness even to those people who are deeply submerged within it!

332. He provides an illustration with the verse beginning, “The Sage is praised,” and so forth. The rays from the nails on the feet of the Sage are like a great river because of their similarity to one;

that [river] is praised because it has attained a state of wonder, for even when people are deeply and utterly submerged in it, it brings them only happiness—oh, what a marvel, since it surpasses all other rivers! “This [river], even when those submerged deeply within it...”

Regarding the phrase “it brings happiness,” here the metaphor “the great river of rays from the toenails” is established as a constituent part by way of being the means of accomplishment (*sādhanattena*), while “even when submerged” is established as a constituent part by way of being the excellence of concentration (*samādhino sādhiyattena*). Thus, this is a mixed ornament (*missam alaṅkaraṇam*). 332.
Now he provides an example with the words beginning “praised” (*pasatthā*): “Praised” means worthy of praise because of the wonder of the Sage.

The great river of the rays from the toenails—that is, the great Gaṅgā consisting of the radiance of the rays from the toenails—brings happiness indeed to those virtuous and noble persons even when they are deeply submerged, that is, excessively immersed. Oh, how wonderful!

This behavior of this [river] is contrary to that of other rivers. Here, by way of being the thing to be established (*sādhanīyabhāvena*), the subject (*aṅgin*) of the poetic figure of resolution (*samādhi-alaṅkāra*) is "submerged."

The poetic figure *rūpakālaṅkāra* (metaphorical identification) is mixed with these other figures through the relationship of primary and secondary elements (*aṅga-aṅgibhāva*), by taking it as a constituent part in its capacity as a means (*sādhanabhāvena*).
The analysis of the compound is as follows: "nails on the feet" (*pādesu nakhā*), "the rays of those [nails]" (*tesaṃ raṃsī*), and "that which is great and a river" (*mahatī ca sā nadī ca*).
Thus, the sentence is: "The rays from the toenails are themselves a great river, like a great river. Regarding the word *gāḷhaṃ*:

It is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). The construction is: "those who performed a deep immersion, they too. The sentence is: "people possessing happiness [act] toward one who is happy, making him happy.
It is mixed with a state of similar strength.
The Sage’s appearance is sweet by its very nature, his form is an elixir for the eyes, and his speech is like honey;
who would he not delight? (333) The verse beginning with “Veso” is easy to understand.
This, however, is an instance of a simile that combines the qualities of concentration and physical beauty. It is a simile based on similarity of power.

333. “The appearance,” and so forth. The Sage’s appearance—sweet by its very nature, sweet by its inherent character, the unique mark of a Conqueror, and the form of a Buddha—and his physical form, endowed with the primary and secondary characteristics (*lakṣaṇa* and *anuvyañjana*), as well as his speech, which is like honey in its sweetness or equal to honey, who among people does it not delight?
“Sweet by its very nature” is a figure of speech (*samādhialaṅkāra*).

Furthermore, there is the figure of speech *rūpakālaṅkāra* in the phrase “an elixir for the eyes,” and the figure of speech *upamālaṅkāra* in the phrase “like honey. These three [qualities]—in their capacity to nourish—are of equal strength because they are independent of one another;
thus, there is a combination (*missatta*) of these figures. [The term *rasāyana* is explained as follows: It is sweet by its very nature (*sabhāvena madhuro*).

And it is called *rasa* because it is tasted or relished (*rasīyati assādīyati*). An *āyana* is that which is a source, a course, or a mode of proceeding; thus, *rasāyana* means that which has *rasa* as its source—that is, the basis of flavor.
"Rasāyana" refers to beauty as an elixir, and there is also the statement that it is an elixir for the eyes.
The word "āsī" would mean a wish,
just like the wishing for something desired.
May the Lord, the sole refuge of the three worlds, protect the world from the states of woe.
(334) By the words beginning with “āsi,” he indicates that [the Buddha] was [already] present. Having restated that the aspiration for a desired or cherished object is a longing (*patthanā*),...
The word *āsī* (was) is prescribed [by the rule] *siyā*. The word *yathā* (just as) provides an illustration.

May the Protector (*nātha*), who has become the sole refuge and the peerless resort for the people of the three worlds—that is, those dwelling within the triple world—protect (*pātu*) the world, that is, the realm of sentient beings, from the states of misery (*apāya*).
Here, the sense intended is protection (*pālana*) that is exceedingly firm (*atilasita*).
334. Now he demonstrates the *āsī* ornament with the words beginning "Āsī.
An *āsī* is defined as a wish or aspiration for a desired object—that is, for a thing one longs for. An example of this is as follows:

"May the Lord of the World, the sole refuge for the three worlds, the peerless protector of the three realms of existence, protect the world—the realm of sentient beings—from the states of woe. This is what is called *āsī*.
The *patthanā* (aspiration), its illuminator (*taddīpikā*), and its name are indeed identical. In this example, “The sole refuge in the three worlds,” protection is what is intended.
The phrase is: “the combination of the three worlds,” and “the one and only goal and resort,” and “the sole refuge for the three worlds.”
That ornament which produces a relish of flavor should be known as "flavorful" (rasavant), because it is fashioned according to the requirements of flavor.
He illustrates what is flavorful with the words beginning with "rasa": that ornament or decoration consisting of the semblance of flavor and so forth... [335] ...is flavorful.

That which produces comprehension and brings about understanding arises; that ornament, by way of its being composed of or produced from "flavour" (*rasa*), should be understood as "rasavantam" (possessing flavour), just as a word that produces the comprehension of a meaning is called "atthavā" (meaningful). 335.

In the enumeration, the term "rasī" indicates the figure of speech already mentioned, "Rasa," by means of the words "rasa" and so forth. That ornament which exists among the ornaments previously described...
Any ornament whatsoever that, by producing the apprehension of one of the nine flavors (rasa) such as the erotic (siṅgāra),
or even of a semblance of that flavor (rasābhāsa), brings about its realization, is to be known as "possessing rasa" (rasī) because it is an embellishment produced from that which possesses rasa,
and because it manifests its own state of being accompanied by rasa— just like that which produces the apprehension of meaning (attha).

The word *attha* (meaning) is so called because it conveys a sense; likewise, an ornament that produces the appreciation of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) is called "possessing flavor" (*rasavat*) or "flavorful" (*rasin*).

Furthermore, the term *vākya* (sentence) refers to the appreciation of flavor, that which generates such appreciation, that which possesses flavor, the state of being flavorful, or the composition and accomplishment thereof.
The earth, with feet bound by excessive passion for the face of the Teacher of the Three Worlds— which is a wondrous lotus blooming from the lake of lust—
held him firmly with a hand that was eternally moist.
They constantly kiss with an intense passion for what is beneficial. 336.
He illustrates this with the verse beginning with "rāga" and so forth. The face is bent down by passion (rāga) for the earth (dharā), who is like a woman.
The lotus (saroja) is bent down and lowered by its red color (rāga). In the first case, the face is [compared] to a marvelous lotus; therefore—
"Samānādhikaraṇa" (co-locative) refers to a compound with "rāgānata" (inclined by passion). In the second [case], however, it is "rāgānata-abbhuta-saroja-mukha":

that wonderful lotus which arose from the earth after it had split open for the purpose of receiving the glorious feet [of the Buddha], and which was like a lotus of non-greed; and because its face resembles that [lotus], it is called "mukha" (face)—thus, "the face of the wonderful lotus inclined by passion.
These are the feet of the Teacher of the Three Worlds, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Of what sort are they?
Those whose passion (*rāga*) or attachment (*anurāga*) is excessive, or who are of a red complexion (*rattavaṇṇa*), are such [beings].

Having firmly grasped or seized with their hand (*kara*)—which is full of sap (*sarasa*) or possessed of rays (*raṃsi*)—or by means of a ray, they constantly and perpetually display an intense agitation (*ādāna*), that is, earnestness (*ādara*), or an orientation toward that [object];
with this, they kiss or deposit [it]. Herein, there is a combination of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and *rūpaka* (metaphor).

An appearance of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) in its aspect of enjoyment (*sambhoga*) is produced. The erotic sentiment is of two kinds: the deceived (*vipralambha*) and the enjoyed (*sambhoga*).
Of these, only the deceived is captivating because it serves as the basis for the description of union; such is not the case with enjoyment.

Regarding the appearance of enjoyment, however, there is nothing at all to be said. Nevertheless, this example of the appearance of enjoyment has been presented here for the purpose of instructing the ignorant.

We shall consider a certain point here. In this context, the feet’s state of being a lover and the earth’s state of being a beloved woman are understood through the power of the sentence (*vākya-sāmatthiya*).
What is already expressed by the word might be stated again. Here, that [meaning] of the feet is to be understood;
for if the poet had not intended to convey the excellence of their passion (*raty-ukkaṃsa*), then this verse would be inconsistent. It is precisely from such words [that this is known].
It is understood that the feet possess the semblance of the *vibhāva* of love (*rati*). The semblance of the objective *vibhāva* (*ālambana-vibhāva*) of love is the woman who desires [the hero];

the semblance of the excitant *vibhāva* (*uddīpana-vibhāva*) consists of the delightful places and so forth, which are understood through the hearing of the word "wondrous lotus"—for such a lotus does not appear in the absence of specific delightful locations;
and the semblance of the ensuant states (*anubhāva*) consists of the poet’s words that indicate the semblances of the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*). Likewise...

For, by the statement "having grasped firmly with a hand whose essence is constant," the qualities such as *harisā* (joy) are implied through the description of the hand’s essential nature and its firm grasping.
By the phrase "with a constant, well-placed eagerness," qualities such as *ussukkattā* (eagerness) are excluded.

Thus, the "mode of connection" (*bandhavutti*) refers to the appearance of bliss that arises in the mind through the manifestation of the meanings of the words of connection; this appearance of bliss is called the appearance of the *sambhoga-rasa* (the flavor of enjoyment).

336. Now, in order to provide an illustration, and in accordance with the enumeration of sentiments such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), the marvelous (*adbhuta*), the compassionate (*karuṇa*), and so forth, which are yet to be demonstrated, he presents an example specifically endowed with the erotic sentiment by means of the verse beginning with "From passion" (*rāgā*).

If not [otherwise], then from passion—that is, from love—the face of the maiden of the earth, which is like a lotus possessed of wondrous qualities, would be turned toward and bent down by passion; that is, her face would be directed forward and inclined due to her affection. If it were not so...

If the feet of the Perfectly Enlightened One— the Teacher of the Three Worlds, the Instructor of the Three Realms, whose face is formed of wondrous lotuses, and who is inclined toward the color red— were not possessed of an exceeding attachment (rāga) and an exceeding affection (anurāga),
then they would not possess this exceedingly red color produced by past karma; for they are complete in every respect, being held by a hand that is ever-red and endowed with constant affection.
If they do not grasp it firmly— having taken hold of it tightly with rays accompanied by constant excellence—
and if they do not kiss it— kissing it with constant, devoted ardor and continuous attentiveness—
then they merely touch it as the means for accomplishing the act of standing.
It is bent (*ānata*) by passion (*rāga*), that is, made to face [it]; and it is both wonderful (*abbhuta*) and a lotus (*saroja*).
Because of its similarity to that, it is a wonderful lotus; and because it is both that [face] and a mouth (*mukha*), it is a wonderful lotus-mouth.
It is bent—that is, inclined—by passion, which is red in color; and it is both that and a wonderful lotus. That very same...
The analysis of the compound is as follows: it is called "face" (*mukha*) because it resembles such a face; it is called "the teacher of the three worlds" (*tilokassa guru*);
it is "composed having made [it] superior," or "produced by one's own prior karma"; it refers to those whose passion (*rāga*), attachment (*anurāga*), or red color (*rattavaṇṇa*) is present;

it means "existing together with essence (*rasa*), attachment (*anurāga*), or prosperity (*sampatti*"); and it refers to that confusion (*sambhama*), diligence (*ādara*), or state of being directed toward that which has been placed (*āhita*) or ordained (*vihita*).

Here, by means of the poetic ornament of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) in the phrase beginning with “the state of passion,” and by means of the poetic ornament of *rūpaka* (metaphor) in the phrase “the face, a marvelous lotus,” there arises the semblance (*ābhāsa*) of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) in its aspect of enjoyment (*sambhoga*).

This should be understood as a “semblance of sentiment” because such [enjoyment] exists only in the form of an imagined union between men and women, lacking actual physical union. The erotic sentiment is categorized according to application (*āyoga*), separation (*viprayoga*), and enjoyment (*sambhoga*).

In all three types [of commentary], there are two aspects: connection (*āyoga*) and disconnection (*vippayoga*). Because it deceives, it is called "deception" (*vippalambha*); and there is also "enjoyment" (*sambhoga*), making two kinds.
Among these, only deception is charming due to its being the ground for a description that lacks nothing. Enjoyment, however, is not like that; even what appears as enjoyment is inferior.
This being so, because of the suitability of the description produced by one who has applied effort, [the following occurs].

In this context, within the example of an ornament that has become "savorful" (*rasibhūta*) through the manifestation of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) of enjoyment (*sambhoga*) already attained, the manifestation of the savor (*rasābhāsa*) is to be understood as follows.

Even though the state of being a lover is not explicitly stated by a denotative word for the feet, nor is the state of being a beloved woman explicitly stated by a denotative word for the earth, it is nevertheless known from the remaining words that reveal the hands and the qualities [of the speaker], namely: "The feet of the Teacher of the Three Worlds [are upon] the earth."
The appearance of mutual delight between two people is described by these [terms]: "those with excessive, bound passion" and "those leaning toward passion.

This appearance of delight here is the state of stability (*ṭhāyībhāva*), because it serves as the objective support (*ālambana*) for the man’s delight in the woman and the woman’s delight in the man;

thus, the two—the foot-lover and the passionate woman—are appearances of the manifestation of the objective support for one another. [This occurs] without the need for specific delightful places and so forth, as in the case of the arising of a marvelous lotus.

Because the mention of the word *abbhuta-sarasa* (extraordinary lake) implies delightful places and so forth—which, by their very existence, intensify passion—they are called the manifestations of the excitants (*uddīpana-vibhāva*).
By the phrase "having grasped firmly with a hand that is ever-lively," both the quality of the hand being lively and its firm grasping are expressed;
thus, joy and other such states are understood. By the phrase "with constant agitation and haste,"...
Exertion (*ussāha*) and so forth are known [as transitory states]. Among these, joy, exertion, and the like are called "appearances of transitory states" (*byabhicārībhāvābhāsa*).

Those poetic expressions (*vibhāvanā*) mentioned above, which manifest those appearances of transitory states, are called "appearances of consequent states" (*anubhāvābhāsa*). Thus, for the wise who achieve comprehension of the meaning through the permanent states (*sthāyībhāva*), the transitory states (*vyabhicārībhāva*), the determinants (*vibhāva*), and the consequent states (*anubhāva*) as they appear in a literary composition, that appearance of aesthetic flavor (*rasābhāsa*) which arises—designated as an "appearance of satisfaction" (*santosābhāsa*)—[is what constitutes the rasa].
It exists, and it is here described as the manifestation of the flavor of enjoyment (*sambhogarasa*). The states of abiding and so forth will be revealed later on.
Thus, following the power of the former teachers, this [treatise] has been briefly proclaimed for those who are unadorned [by pride].
Who indeed is truly able to see the end of those [metaphors],
which have been conceptualized by poets one after another?
Thus, in the work composed by the venerable Great Master Saṅgharakkhita...
In the *Subodhālaṅkāra*,
the fourth chapter, titled "The Comprehension of the Figures of Sense."
337. Having thus concluded, in accordance with the order of the headings, that which was promised, he now says "Iti" and so forth in order to demonstrate their great number preceded by a conclusion.

"Iti"—by this aforementioned manner, having followed and traced the power of the former teachers such as Daṇḍin and others, as well as the characteristics of composition, this division of the ornaments (alaṅkāra) for those who are adorned is stated in brief.
It has been declared; that is, it has been spoken of in brief. To the question "Why?", he says: "Successively," and so forth.

Indeed, who among people is truly capable—able to see—the end or limit of those ornaments, which have been fashioned by poets one after another over a long period of time, and which continue to be differentiated at every successive stage?
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Subodhālaṅkāra-ṭīkā*, titled the *Mahāsāmi*. 337.
Having thus concluded the ornaments of meaning as promised according to the order of enumeration, [the author] now proceeds by way of a conclusion.
By the words "thus following," etc., he demonstrates the great number of these meaning-ornaments (atthālaṅkāra).

Thus, in the manner already stated, having followed the power of the former teachers—the power of those such as Daṇḍin, Bhartṛhari, and others belonging to earlier times, which is reckoned as the science of ornaments—this division of ornaments has been briefly declared by me; that is, it has been spoken and compiled. Why? [Because...]

Who indeed is the person capable, by himself alone, of seeing the end— the limit— of these ornaments, which have been fashioned in manifold ways by poets from the most ancient times down to the present day,
and which are being individually crafted and embellished? No one at all is able, unless they rely upon a compendium.
The intended meaning is that it is not possible to reach the limit [of this]. The phrase "pure bhavā" means both "those former teachers" and "their power";
thus, the sentence is "it is permissible," specifically because it is unmixed.
Thus, in the *Subodhālaṅkāra-nissaya*.
The Fourth Chapter.
5. The Chapter on the Comprehension of Existence (Bhāvāvabodha).
By one who possesses eloquence and does not follow worldly convention;
Then, the poet, possessing extraordinary brilliance, having further explained that very classification of ornaments as it was promised,
now— on the occasion of discussing ornaments possessed of aesthetic flavor (rasa)— [addresses] those whose minds are satiated by the immersion into the tradition of the True Dharma,
which is purified by the singular essence of the flavor of liberation, the sole cause for escaping all the suffering of saṃsāra.

For those who possess supreme faith, even though they have not attained [this state] themselves, in order to point out just a little for the sake of grasping a mere measure of skill in worldly convention by means of its characteristic alone, he did not speak of it in its entirety, but said "possessing ingenuity" (*paṭibhānavatā*) and so forth.

Ingenuity (*paṭibhāna*) is wisdom (*paññā*) that functions in accordance with each particular occasion; for it is extremely helpful for the composition of a work, and therefore a poem is called "ingenuity."
Therefore he said, "by one who possesses ingenuity. The poet must follow worldly convention;
for he who does not conform to the entirety of worldly convention is not a poet at all. Therefore he said, "by one who follows worldly convention.

Since what is called "propriety" is the supreme secret of poets, and it is only one who knows what is appropriate even within worldly convention that is praised, [the poet] should proceed solely by following appropriate worldly convention.
Furthermore, a composition arranged according to the sequence to be explained results in the enjoyment of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) for sentient beings;

therefore, it is necessary to construct a composition that is clearly radiant with the manifestation of propriety (*aucitya*). Consequently, the poet must be one who perceives the full manifestation of extreme propriety.
Thus he said: "But [the composition] by one who perceives the full manifestation of propriety. And all this refers to "by the poet."
Here, the qualification "by the poet" refers to the agent not explicitly mentioned in the word "composition.

338. Thus, on the occasion of demonstrating the ornaments as they were promised, and in connection with the ornaments possessing aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), [the author speaks] of that which has become a single flavor through the flavor of liberation—which is incapable of providing escape from all the suffering of *saṃsāra*—and which is exceedingly refined.

Desiring now to show in brief—so that those who are greedy only for the nectar of the True Dhamma, yet possess abundant faith and pure self-restraint, may remain undeluded in worldly conventions by means of a thorough understanding of mere characteristics even when [the Dhamma] is turned away from them—the author says: "Possession of ready wit," and so forth.
This refers to one who possesses a specific excellence of wisdom suited to the station of being extremely helpful through spontaneous composition, and who follows worldly convention.
Since, in all the world, one must not— following what is appropriate for conventional usage— allow propriety (*ocitya*) to be excluded from the heart,
nor should it be separated from the bond as if it were a secret; therefore, by one who possesses an extraordinary sensitivity for the manifestation of propriety,
there is the manifestation of a desired object in a manner corresponding to the evocation of the intended meaning through its state of being appropriate.
The connection is: "it is composed by a poet who knows beauty and is a creator of bonds. *Paṭibhā* and *paṭibhāna* are names for wisdom (*paññā*);
since even that which is born [of it] is called "inspired" (*paṭibhāti*), this particular excellence of wisdom should be understood as being of extreme benefit to composition.
Furthermore, because one possesses such inspiration (*paṭibhāna*) and follows the conventional usage of the world, [one is so called].
The analysis of the compound is as follows: "by virtue" (*sīlena*) means "by way of propriety," and "exaltation" (*samullāsa*) means "that which is known through virtue.

The states and manifestations belonging to the *ṭhāyī* (the permanent emotional substratum), accompanied by their respective intensities (*anubhāva*), become connected for the sake of the aesthetic relish (*rasassāda*) of the virtuous.
339. “*Ṭhāyi*,” etc. *Ṭhāyino* (stable) refers to the emotions such as love (*rati*) which are about to be described;

they are called *ṭhāyīsambandhino* because they possess a connection with those [transitory states] through their association with the *vibhāvas* (determinants) and so forth, since love and the other [stable emotions] are being brought to a state of acceptance. Together with the *anubhāvas* (consequents), whose characteristics will be described, they are called *sānubhāvakā*.
*Bhāva* (emotional state) and *vibhāva* (determinant) are mentioned; furthermore, the appearance of an emotion (*bhāvābhāsa*) will also be described by means of the term *bhāva*.
This very [section] is included; the connection is that they "come about for the sake of relishing the aesthetic flavor" (*rasassādāya sampajjanti*).

339. Regarding the passage beginning with “*Ṭhāyi*” and so forth: those connected with the *sthāyin* (the permanent emotion) are, by means of the word *sthāyin*, or by means of its expressed meanings such as joy, laughter, and so on, associated with power (*sānubhāvakā*);
they proceed together with the *anubhāvas* (consequents) to be mentioned, namely the *bhāvas* (transitory emotions) and *vibhāvas* (determinants) to be mentioned.

The compositions (*nibandhā*) bound by a poet endowed with the aforementioned qualities, having been brought together in one place, serve—that is, they function—for the enjoyment of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of virtuous people, who are free from faults such as envy;
that is, for the sake of savoring the erotic (*siṅgāra*) and other flavors to be described hereafter.

By means of this verse, these are presented: the stable state (*ṭhāyībhāva*), the transitory state (*vyabhicārībhāva*), the absolute state (*kevalabhāva*), the determinants (*vibhāva*), the consequents (*anubhāva*), and the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
They are thus designated; how so? The term "of the permanent and the related" (*ṭhāyīsambandhino*) serves as a qualification for "states" (*bhāva*).
Therefore, because it is connected with the word "permanent" (*ṭhāyī*), there is the "permanent state" (*ṭhāyībhāvo*), meaning that which is both permanent and a state.

Furthermore, since there exists a state that is transitory (*byabhicārībhāvo*), the expression "permanent state" (*ṭhāyībhāvo*) functions as its differentiator; thus, it is precisely this term "permanent state" [that provides the distinction].
Furthermore, there is the state of being deviant (byabhicārībhāva) as understood through the power of the mode of expression (payogasāmatthiya);
and again, because the word *bhāva* is heard separately after being compounded with the word *ṭhāyī*, there is a state distinct from both the permanent state (*ṭhāyībhāva*) and the deviant state;

likewise, because the two functions of manifestation (*uppatti*) and indication (*uddīpana*) regarding the meaning denoted by the word *ṭhāyī*—such as joy (*rati*), laughter (*hāsa*), and so forth—have been made clear and prepared, [the meaning is conveyed] by means of those.
The various *vibhāvas*—comprising the objective (*ālambana*) and the excitant (*uddīpana*)—which are connected with meanings such as love (*rati*), laughter (*hāsa*), and so forth;
likewise, the *anubhāvas* shown through their association with the term "possessing the *anubhāvas*";

and the *rasa* indicated by the phrase "for the enjoyment of the *rasa*"—thus these, beginning with the *sthāyibhāva*, are enumerated. Furthermore, there is the connection with the *sthāyin*, and the sense that "this [rasa] belongs to them."

The phrase "and emotion (bhāva) and its manifestation (vibhāva)" means that they occur together with the consequent emotions (anubhāvas). And the phrase "the tasting of the aesthetic flavor (rasa)" is a sentence [meaning the experience of rasa].
However, because specific modifications of mental activity (cittavṛttiviśeṣa) intend toward emotion (bhāva) and thus bring forth the aesthetic flavor (rase bhāvayanti), [they are called emotions].
Rati and the others are thus designated by the term *bhāva*.

Now, among the *bhāva*, *vibhāva*, *anubhāva*, and *sāttvika* as they were previously enumerated, the author first analyzes the term *bhāva* in order to clarify its meaning, beginning with the words "the activities of the mind" (*cittassa vuttiyo*).
These are the movements of the mind, its modes of occurrence such as delighting, laughing, and so forth.

"Distinctions" (*visesa*) refers to specific modes of mental activity, which are the particular natures of the [emotions]. "Rati" and the others are the *sthāyibhāvas*, *vyabhicāribhāvas*, and *sāttvikabhāvas*.

The particle "tu" (but/however) indicates a distinction. Because they bring about—that is, produce—the *rasas* such as the *śṛṅgāra* and so forth, they are designated by the term "bhāva" and described by Bharata and others.
For here, the verbal root *bhū* with the suffix *ṇi* functions in the sense of "producing. And this [term] does not refer merely to...
It functions not only in the act of making, but also in the expanding and the establishing; therefore, they develop and expand his inspired thought (*paṭibhānacitta*).

Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood as follows: they develop and establish the poet’s intention, which is characterized by knowledge of the world’s condition (*lokatthitijñānalakṣaṇa*); thus it is called "bhāva."

340. Now, in order to show that among the states such as "one who stands" (*ṭhāyī*) mentioned above, there is a common nature shared by these three—namely, "one who stands," and so forth—he demonstrates this according to their literal meaning with the words beginning "mind" (*citta*).

However, the specific modes of mental activity (*cittavutti*) are distinguished from the mind by the laughing, sorrowing, and so forth regarding future objects that will be explained later, as well as by penetration (*nibbedha*), stiffness (*thambha*), and the like.

Furthermore, the specific distinctions—consisting of the modes of occurrence, the mutual non-confusion of forms, and the stable, invariable, and emotional elements—bring about, produce, and effect these [distinctions] within the *rasa*, such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and other *rasas*.
Otherwise, they would not bring about—that is, they would not pervade—the minds of the wise regarding the *rasa* as their object, namely the domain of the erotic and other *rasas*.
Otherwise, [they would not affect] the poet’s mind regarding that very same domain of *rasa*.
Taking the world as their object, they cultivate the intention characterized by the knowledge that has arisen; they thus perform the practice.

Then, because the word *bhāva* is derived in the sense of the causal agent (*hetukattar*), the states such as love (*rati*) and so forth—namely, love, laughter, and the rest—are described and spoken of by Bharata and others.
In the phrase "love and so forth" (*ratyādayo*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes laughter and the rest, as well as the stable emotions (*sthāyibhāva*).

It should be understood that the states such as penetration (nibbedha) and so forth, as well as the transitory states (byabhicārībhāva), and the physical states (sāttikabhāva) such as rigidity (thambha) and paralysis (palaya), are included [in this context].

The phrase "the activity of the mind" (cittassa vuttiyo), "those very same [activities] as specific qualities" (tā eva visesā), and "the word 'state' (bhāva)" constitute the sentence. This is intended in the sense of a state of abiding (ṭhāyībhāva).
That state which is not concealed by a contrary or different state stands firm through its own nature.
This is what is meant by "it stands through virtue."

The term *ṭhāyībhāva* (the abiding state) is so called because it remains stable. 341. Regarding the three types of states beginning with the abiding state (*ṭhāyī*), he speaks in sequence with the words "by the opposing," and so forth.

That state, such as joy (*rati*) and the like, which is not obscured or concealed by another opposing state such as disgust (*jigucchā*) and so on—this very state, because it is not being cut off, [is called the abiding state].
“One who stands by virtue” (*tiṭṭhati sīlena*); since the state itself is that which stands, it is explained as being designated by the term *ṭhāyībhāva*.

That which has been brought and led to enjoyment by means of the *bhāva*s and so forth is called *rasa* because it is enjoyed by the members of the assembly. For he will say: “With its *vibhāva*s,” and so on. 341.
Now, he defines the three kinds of *bhāva*s, beginning with the *ṭhāyī*, in sequence with the words “the opposing,” and so forth. By the opposing...
When a state such as joy or laughter is not concealed or obstructed by another state—such as disgust—which is contrary (*viruddha*) to it, that state of joy or laughter remains by its own nature;
because it exists in this sense of "remaining" (*ṭhāyī*), it is designated by the term *ṭhāyībhāva*.
This is stated with reference to that which [remains] through its excitants (*vibhāva*), ensuants (*anubhāva*), and so forth.
That which has been rendered palatable by the worthy ones is called "flavor" (*rasa*) because of its palatability; that is said to be "enduring" (*ṭhāyī*). The analysis (*viggaha*) is:
"that state (*bhāva*) which is another and which is consciousness (*ceti*), and which is to be made transcendent (*tiro kayirittha*); it is both enduring and a state.
This is the enumeration of the classifications of the enduring state.
Delight and laughter, sorrow, anger,
impatience, and fear; as well as disgust and wonder—
"And there are nine equal abiders.
(342) Since the state of being an abider is possible for each of the nine beginning with "delight" (*rati*), he says "delight," and so forth.
The construction is: "And there are nine who abide thus. These nine alone should be connected individually by their respective manifestations and powers, even when taken separately.

If there were a state of mind [arising] from that, then the *sthāyibhāva* (permanent emotion) would attain the status of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgārarasa*) when it is relished by the audience through the performance of an actor or the hearing of a beautiful composition.
In this way, one should apply the same logic to the attainment of the comic sentiment (*hāsyarasa*) and other such states by the *sthāyibhāvas* of laughter and so forth, as appropriate.
To show that the *sthāyibhāvas* consist of exactly nine—namely, love (*rati*) and the rest—he says, "Love, laughter," and so on. And love and laughter...
Sorrow, anger, fear, disgust, wonder, equanimity, and the quality of peace—thus there are nine [mental states] when they are present.

The explanation of the specific nature of these nine, beginning with delight (rati) and so forth, is clear in the subsequent commentary (*niddesa*) on the summary verse (*uddesagāthā*) that begins with "Elegance, humor, and compassion" (*siṅgāra-hāsa-karuṇā*). [The pairs are: delight and humor, and anger and effort (*ussāha*).
The phrase "fear and so forth" (*ca bhayañceti ca*), and the phrase "disgust and wonder" (*jigucchā ca vimhayā ceti ca*).

These nine, as well as the transitory states (*vyabhicāribhāva*) and the sattvic states (*sāttvikabhāva*), should each be composed by the poet after having manifested them through their respective appropriate determinants (*vibhāva*) and consequents (*anubhāva*);
