they must also be grasped and displayed by the actor. Among these three types of states, this *rati* [is characterized] by all the qualities of both men and women.

This delight is produced by men and women joined together; it is kindled by the excitants such as the moon and so forth; it is sustained by the power of physical and vocal exertion consisting of gestures that manifest enthusiasm and the like;
and it is made variegated by various transitory states (vyabhicāribhāva) understood through their respective powers and capacities.

Such is this delight, which constitutes the quality of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgārarasa) and others, being enjoyed by the audience through the actor’s performance and the hearing of the praised composition.

It should be understood that [the term] "attains" (*pāpuṇāti*) refers to this. The logical justification for laughter and the other [emotions] attaining the states of the remaining *sthāyībhāvas*—namely, the states of the rasa of laughter and so forth—should be understood accordingly as appropriate.
This is the intention regarding the state of deviation (*vyabhicārībhāva*).
Those who move about with virtue, manifesting through specific modes such as concealment, non-manifestation, and so forth, in a manner directed toward [the goal];

These are variable. (343) He says they are variable by means of the words beginning with “disappearance” (*tirobhāva*). Disappearance is the non-duration for even a single existing state that is otherwise stable, such as penetration;
and manifestation is its becoming evident. Because it has various tastes as its basis, these are its "beginnings" (*ādi*); by the word "beginning," [the others are included].
The apprehension of a persisting phenomenon (*ṭhāyīdhamma*) in the form of pleasure, pain, and so forth—that itself is the distinction; by that [means].

The apprehension of a persisting phenomenon in the form of pleasure and pain, and the directing toward the superimposition of one's own phenomenon in the form of pleasure and pain upon that which persists.
For thus, in joy (*rati*), there is a tranquility permeated by pleasure; in sorrow (*soka*), it is permeated by pain. Even though joy has the nature of pleasure...
Sickness and the like are deviant states that merely superimpose this suffering upon one's own karma.
Therefore, because of that state of being directed toward [the object], those phenomena which move and proceed by means of virtue (sīla) are themselves deviant.
343. Now, in accordance with the order of the summary, he demonstrates the characteristic of the state of being deviant by means of the passage beginning with "tirobhāvā" (from disappearance).
Because the transitory mental states (*vyabhicāribhāva*) proceed by depending on their own manifold underlying emotions (*sthāyibhāva*) through distinctions such as concealment (*tirobhāva*),
non-manifestation (*avibhāva*), and so forth; and because people have diverse tastes, there is, in one instance, the submergence of the quality of the transitory state within the underlying emotion,
while in another instance, that very same quality becomes manifest— through such distinctions, [the transitory states] relate directly to the underlying emotions.
When one's own forms of pleasure and pain are placed within oneself,

and when those states that move by way of virtue— meaning they proceed according to their own nature— are brought face-to-face through the act of transferring one's own forms of pleasure and pain onto other beings,

those states are called "deviant" (*byabhicārī*). In this very same way, such affliction (*pīḷā*) is, in its own form, a single state of deviance comprised within the category of the assembly (*parisama*).
In *rati* (delight), being merged with its own quality (*saguṇa*), it proceeds permeated by pleasure; in *śoka* (sorrow), being manifest with its own quality, it proceeds permeated by pain.

In the same way, because illness and other such states—which are deviations from the nature of pleasure—impose their own inherent form of suffering upon it, they proceed in a manifest manner through specific variations such as concealment (*tirobhāva*) and manifestation (*vibhāva*).
Regarding "concealment" (*tirobhavana*): [it is the state when the essence of pleasure is obscured].
The analysis [of the compound] is as follows: *ca* (and), *āvibhavanaṃ* (manifestation), *tirobhāvo* (disappearance), and *āvibhāvo* (appearance);

these and others which exist among the states of stability (*ṭhāyībhāvesu*)—namely, the attribution to oneself of the natures of pleasure and pain (*sukhadukkhasabhāvānaṃ*), that very distinction (*soyeva viseso*), and the state of being directed toward (*abhimukhānaṃ bhāvo*).
In the word *byabhicārī*, the prefix *vi-* functions in the sense of distinction (*visesa-atthe*), and the prefix *abhi-* functions in the sense of being directed toward (*abhimukha-bhāve*).
The varieties of states such as infidelity,
despair, doubt, suspicion, mental dullness born of equanimity,
dejection, and the state of being a wretched, outcaste creature;
Fear, terror, illness, envy, joy,
mindfulness, dejection, and arrogance;
anxiety, pregnancy, intoxication, resentment, and pride.
The intoxication of the final stage of delusion,
awakening from the force of sleep, death with its accompanying agitation,
and illness— these are the thirty-three [types].
344. He shows these [defilements] with the words beginning “despair” (*nibbeda*). “Dīnatuggālasatta” means wretchedness (*dīnatā*), loftiness (*uggata*), and sluggishness (*ālasatta*);
“ussuka” means one who strives (*ussukati*). “Capala” means fickleness (*cāpalla*); together with fickleness it is “sacapala.

That, along with disease (*byādhi*) and death (*maraṇa*), constitutes the compound “sacapalabyādhi,” formed by a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*). And because that exists together with “biḷa,” it is “sabīḷa”; these [are the defilements].
Thus, there are thirty-three transitory states (byabhicārī-bhāva) as previously described. For one possessed of enthusiasm, the heroic sentiment (vīra-rasa) is relished through that very state;
for one who is timid, however, it is relished through the fearful sentiment (bhayānaka-rasa).

Because the nature of the world is manifold, these transitory states must be described extensively for each individual sentiment, since through the medium of such descriptions, everyone among them may find some degree of relish.

In this regard, because the sight of an enemy who has come to kill is itself a cause for fear in one of timid nature at that very moment— since it is already broken according to its own natural tendency— it may, however, serve as a stimulus for exertion in one who delights in battle. Likewise,
a grotesque ornament worn by an actor is a cause for laughter in those of low character who abide in such behavior, but it is a transitory cause for those of profound character.
Therefore, when a poet describes a *bhāva* (emotional state), those states should be described in such a way that there is a full development of propriety (*aucitya*).
Any breach of propriety, however, must be avoided with great effort.

Among these, *nirveda* (disgust or world-weariness) consists of self-contempt. Its *vibhāva* (causes) are women and the poverty of low-born people; for yogis, however, the realization of truth (*tattvasaṃvedana*) is the *vibhāva*. Here, the shedding of tears, brooding, and so forth are the *anubhāvas* (consequent effects).
*Takka* (reasoning) is the act of deliberating. Its *vibhāva* (manifestation) is doubt; its *anubhāva* (consequent effect) is the shaking of the head and so forth.
*Saṅkā* (suspicion) is acting contrary [to what is expected]; its *vibhāva* is suspicion itself; its *anubhāva* is trembling and so forth. *Sama* (fatigue) is exhaustion.
In that regard, its *vibhāva* is the act of walking and so forth; its *anubhāva* is perspiration and so forth.
Fortitude (*dhiti*) has contentment as its manifestation (*vibhāva*), and freedom from greed for enjoyments as its functional expression (*anubhāva*).

Stolidity (*jaḷatā*) is the failure to act; its manifestation is the lack of perception regarding what is desirable or undesirable, and its functional expression is the fixed gaze of unblinking eyes and so forth.
Dejection (*dīnatā*) is the lack of luster in the mind; its manifestation is wretchedness and the like, and its functional expression is wearing soiled clothing and so forth.
*Uggaṭā* (arrogance) is the state of harshness. Its manifestation (*vibhāva*) consists of powerful offenses and the like; its effect (*anubhāva*) consists of threatening others and the like.
*Ālasatta* (laziness) has indolence and the like as its manifestation, and crookedness and the like as its effect.
*Sutta* (sleeping) has sleepiness as its manifestation, and drooping of the limbs and the like as its effect.
*Tāsa* is agitation of the mind. Its *vibhāva* (causal condition) is thundering and the like; its *anubhāva* (consequent effect) is trembling and the like.
*Āyāsa* (exhaustion) and thirst and the like are the *vibhāva* of *gilāniya* (sickness); its *anubhāva* is discoloration and the like.
*Ussuka* (eagerness) is the capacity for endurance regarding time. Its *vibhāva* is the desire to see pleasant sights and the like; its *anubhāva* is haste and the like.

Clarity of mind (*cetopasāda*) is the proximate cause (*harita*). In that context, festivals and the like are its manifestation (*vibhāva*), while weeping, sweating, and so forth are its functional consequence (*anubhāva*).
Seeing what is similar and so forth is the manifestation of mindfulness (*sati*), while the knitting of eyebrows, frowning, and so forth are its functional consequence.

Envy (*issā*) is the inability to endure the excellence of others. Its manifestations include wickedness, pregnancy, and so forth; its functional consequences include speaking ill of others and disregarding them.

Despair (*visāda*) is exhaustion. Its *vibhāva* (causal factors) are the failure to accomplish an undertaking that has been begun, and so forth; its *anubhāva* (consequent effects) are distress, heat, and so forth.
Dejection (*abahitthā*) is the concealment of the body. Its *vibhāva* is shame, and so forth; its *anubhāva* is the transformation of other [faculties].
Anxiety (*cintā*) arises from not obtaining what is desired, and so forth; its *anubhāva* is the closing of the eyes, and so forth.
*Gabbha* is self-conceit (*abhimāna*). Its manifesting cause (*vibhāva*) is power and so forth; its effect (*anubhāva*) is contempt and so forth.

*Apamāra* [is pride arising from] houses, trees, and so forth, or falling from houses, trees, and so forth; here, earthquakes and such are the effects (*anubhāva*). *Amarisa* is intolerance (*akkhamatā*).
Its manifesting cause (*vibhāva*) is being treated with disrespect and so forth; its effects (*anubhāva*) are shaking the head, threatening, and so forth.

Delusion (*mada*) is characterized by negligence (*pamāda*). Its manifest state (*vibhāva*) is intoxication; its consequent manifestations (*anubhāva*) are the swaying of limbs, faltering speech, laughter, and so forth.
Wisdom (*mati*) is the cutting off of doubt. Its manifest state consists of instruction and the like;

its consequent manifestations here are the expansion of the face and so forth. Insanity (*ummāda*) is acting without due consideration. Its manifest state is the onset of a derangement of the humors (*sannipāta*) and the like; its consequent manifestations are weeping, singing, and laughing out of place.
Delusion [is known] through fear and so forth; its manifestation is stiffness, trembling, and so on.
Bad conduct and so forth are the cause; looking downward and so on are the manifestations.
Death is well-established by both its cause and its manifestations.
Fickleness (*capalatā*) consists of acting according to one’s own will due to lust, hatred, and so forth; its manifestation is evident. As for the diseases, they are manifest.
Furthermore, there exist other subtle distinctions among the specific modes of mental activity indicated here;

some of these are included within what has already been stated. For just as all desires, which are by nature characterized by longing, are included within sensual pleasure (*rati*), so too [is this the case].

The various types of *dosa* (hatred) are included within anger (*kodha*), resentment (*amarisa*), and so forth; those of the nature of suffering (*dukkha-sabhāva*) are included within sorrow (*soka*), anxiety (*samaviggha*), illness (*gilāni*), despondency (*visāda*), and so forth.

It should be understood that joy (*pīti*) and the rest are of the nature of happiness (*sukha-sabhāva*). Among these, fear (*bhaya*) is distinct from terror (*tāsa*); likewise, suspicion (*saṅkā*) is distinct from resentment (*amarisa*).

Therefore, envy (*issā*) is distinct [from jealousy]; likewise, sickness (*gilānita*) is distinct from distress (*sama*); sleep (*niddā*) is distinct from dreaming (*sutta*); longing (*ussukā*) is distinct from agitation (*capalatā*); and likewise, delusion (*moha*) is distinct from ruin (*palaya*).
It should be understood that "another" will be explained later.
Now, he demonstrates their state of deviation in its true form with the words beginning with "despondency" (*nibbeda*). Despondency consists of self-reproach and doubt based on reasoning;

mental dullness (*jaḷatā*) is the exhaustion resulting from concentration; fortitude (*dhiti*) is characterized by contentment and mental dullness; and wretchedness (*dīnatuggāla*) is a state of being possessed by [such] dejection.
The state of being wretched, the state of being cruel, and the state of being sluggish; sleep and lying down; terror and mental agitation;

the state of being afflicted by illness and exhaustion; eagerness, joy, fear, dejection, and arrogance; exertion, rapture, mindfulness, envy, weariness, and the concealment of one's outward appearance;
anxiety; pregnancy and conceit; negligence; and anger, intoxication, pride, delusion, intolerance, heedlessness, and self-reproach.
Doubt, perplexity, and delusion; awakening and wakefulness; the onset of sleep and sleep itself;
agitation—which is reckoned as flurry—and excitement; shame accompanied by modesty; death and instability, which are death and instability accompanied by fickleness; and illness.
These are the thirty-three so-called transitory mental states (*vyabhicāribhāva*). Furthermore, reasoning and suspicion, equanimity and fortitude.

And "stupidity" (*jaḷatā*) and so forth; and "wretchedness" (*dīnatā*), "arrogance" (*ugga*), and "laziness" (*alasatta*) and so forth; and "eagerness" (*ussuka*), "joy" (*harisa*), "mindfulness" (*sati*), "envy" (*issā*), "despair" (*visāda*), and "lack of composure" (*abahitthā*) and so forth;
and "resentment" (*amarisa*), "pride" (*mada*), "intellect" (*mati*), "insanity" (*ummāda*), and "delusion" (*moha*) and so forth;

and "sleep" (*niddā*) and "agitation" (*āvega*) and so forth; and that which proceeds together with "shamelessness" (*biḷā*); and that which proceeds together with "restlessness" (*capala*) and "fickleness" (*cāpalya*).

And: "disease together with agitation" (*saca-palo*) and "death" (*maraṇaṃ*); thus the phrase is "death together with agitation and disease" (*maranañ-ca sacapala-vyādhi ceti*). "Death, agitation, and disease" (*maraṇa-sacapalā-byādhī*) is a collective compound (*samāhāra-dvanda*).
Therefore, the word "with poison" (*sa-bilaṃ*) serves as its qualifier.
Because the nature of the world is manifold, only the single heroic sentiment (*vīra-rasa*), when possessed of exertion, is to be relished in the form of the heroic sentiment.
It exists, and it is precisely that which is relished by the timid in its aspect of fear. Therefore, these many variations of each individual flavor must be described.
This being so, the world, with its manifold intentions, relishes something among them.
This being so, the composition becomes dear to all people. In this description of the emotional states (*bhāva*), because those who come seeking to kill...
The mere sight of the flour balls, at that very moment, diverges according to the disposition of the people:
it becomes a cause of fear for men who are naturally timid, yet a cause of encouragement for one who is eager for battle.

Likewise, the ornaments and the performance enacted by the actor for the sake of laughter become a cause of a smile of reserve for men of open nature, but a cause of a spontaneous laugh for those of deep nature.

And it would not be a cause [of beauty]. Therefore, a poet describing an emotion (*bhāva*) should describe those words that express the emotion along with its *vibhāvas* (determinants) and *anubhāvas* (consequents), having carefully prepared the appropriate propriety (*aucitya*) without violating it.
Here, because the *vibhāvas* and other factors that awaken the emotion must be known, they should be understood in this way in connection with their respective emotions.
Among those states, disenchantment (*nibbeda*) has the characteristic of self-depreciation regarding those things.

If it arises in relation to women, or to those who are lowly and of low conduct, its objective manifestation (*ālambana-vibhāva*) is called poverty; if it arises in yogis, its objective manifestation is the realization [of the truth] in that manner.
In this context, the shedding of tears, reflection, and so forth are called its functional manifestations (*anubhāva*).
In the case of *vitakka* (reflection), doubt is called the "exciting factor" (*uddīpana-vibhāva*), while shaking the head and so forth are called the "consequent effect" (*anubhāva*).

In the case of suspicion (*saṅkā*), the occurrence of contradictory states is the exciting factor, and trembling and so forth are the consequent effect. Regarding the term "factor" (*vibhāva*) mentioned above, whichever is appropriate between the two—namely, the objective basis (*ālambana*) or the exciting factor (*uddīpana*)—should be understood.
In the case of equanimity (*sāma*) characterized by exhaustion, walking and so forth are the factor, while perspiration and so forth are the consequent effect.

The manifestation (*vibhāva*) of fortitude, which has contentment as its characteristic, consists of the discernment of knowledge and so forth; its manifestation (*anubhāva*) consists of non-longing for enjoyments and so forth.

The manifestation of dullness, which has unfitness as its characteristic, consists of not knowing what is desirable and undesirable and so forth; its manifestation consists of looking directly at things with wide-open eyes and so forth.

The manifestation of dejection, which has mental distress as its characteristic, consists of being in a state of misery and so forth; its manifestation consists of wearing soiled clothes and so forth.
The manifestation (*vibhāva*) of ferocity (*dāruṇatā*) is its fierce nature, such as excessive transgression; its consequence (*anubhāva*) is intimidation and so forth.
The manifestation of indolence (*alasatta*) is its failure to attend to what ought to be done and so forth;

its consequence is a crooked state of being. The manifestation of sleep (*sutta*), which is synonymous with lying down, is drowsiness and so forth; its consequence is gratification and so forth. Herein, "gratification" refers to the pleasure of reclining, the pleasure of lying on one's side, and so on.

The manifestation (*vibhāva*) of fear (*tāsa*), which is defined as the agitation of the mind, consists of thundering and the like; "thundering" refers to speech that produces terror. Its consequence (*anubhāva*) is trembling due to anger.
The manifestation of illness (*gilāna*), which is defined as affliction, consists of exhaustion, thirst, and the like; its consequence is disfigurement and so forth.
The manifestation of longing (*ussukka*), which is the failure to look toward a suitable time, consists of the desire to see pleasant objects and the like; its consequence is haste and so forth.
The manifestation (*vibhāva*) of joy, characterized by mental serenity, consists of festive games and the like; its consequence (*anubhāva*) consists of expressions of contentment and so forth.
The manifestation of mindfulness, characterized by the act of remembering, consists of seeing signs and the like; its consequence consists of knitting the eyebrows and so forth.
The manifestation of envy, characterized by intolerance of another’s success, consists of frowning and the like; its consequence consists of speaking with malice, showing contempt, and so forth.

The *vibhāva* (determinants) of dejection (*kheda*) are the failure to accomplish what has been undertaken, the ruin of one’s purpose, and so forth; its *anubhāva* (consequents) are mental anguish and the like.

The *vibhāva* of dissimulation (*abahittha*), characterized by the concealment of outward appearance or the concealment of one's true nature and disposition, consists of shame and the like; its *anubhāva* are the performance of other actions, looking downward, scratching the ground with the feet, and so forth.
The *vibhāva* of anxiety (*cintā*) are the non-attainment of a desired object and the like; its *anubhāva* are such things as knitted eyebrows or downcast eyes.
The manifestation (*vibhāva*) of envy (*issā*) is the desire for mastery over another's domain and so forth; its consequence (*anubhāva*) is contemptuous disregard and so forth.
The manifestation of spite (*makkha*) is affliction by malevolent spirits (*yakkha*) and so forth; its consequence is falling to the ground and so forth.
The manifestation of resentment (*paḷāsa*), characterized by intolerance, is the feeling of being insulted and so forth; its consequence is shaking the head and threatening others and so forth.

The manifestation (*vibhāva*) of intoxication (*mada*), which has the characteristic of being overwhelmed by negligence, is the drinking of liquor; its consequence (*anubhāva*) is the shaking of hands, feet, speech, gait, laughter, and so forth.
The manifestation of intelligence (*mati*), which has the characteristic of cutting through doubt, is instruction and the like; its consequence is the satisfaction of the face and so forth.

The manifestation of madness (*ummāda*), which has the characteristic of acting without reflection, is the presence of a derangement of the humors (*sannipāta*), fever, demons (*yakkha*), and so forth; its consequence is weeping and laughing without cause, and so forth.

The manifestation (*vibhāva*) of delusion (*moha*), which has the characteristic of mental confusion, consists of excessive fear and so forth; its functional consequence (*anubhāva*) consists of the failure to comprehend the true nature of things and so forth.

The manifestation of awakening (*vibodha*), which is synonymous with the departure from sleep, consists of the passage of time and so forth, or the seeking of light and so forth; its functional consequence consists of rubbing the eyes and so forth.

The manifestation of sleep (*niddā*), which has the characteristic of pressing upon the mind, consists of not thinking or acting regarding certain things; its functional consequence consists of closing the eyes and so forth.

The manifestation (*vibhāva*) of fear (*bhaya*), which has the characteristic of the onset of terror, consists of seeing an enemy and so forth; its consequence (*anubhāva*) consists of trembling from alarm and so forth.
The manifestation of shame (*biḷā*), which has the characteristic of modesty, consists of misconduct and so forth; its consequence consists of looking downward and so forth.
The manifestation of death consists of being struck by a weapon, disease, and so forth; its consequence consists of the distortion of facial features and so forth.
The manifestation (*vibhāva*) of fickleness consists of lust, hatred, and so forth; its power (*anubhāva*) consists of acting according to one's own whims and the like.
The manifestation of disease consists of the predominance of wind, bile, and so forth; its power consists of groaning and the like.
In this *Subodhālaṅkāra*, there are other specific modes of mental activity whose subtle distinctions have not been shown; among these, those whose nature is desire—
It should be understood that all types of attachment are included within sensual delight; all forms of hatred are included within anger, enmity, and resentment;
all things of the nature of suffering are included within sorrow, distress, disease, illness, and despondency; and joy and the like are included within gladness.
Thus, even though there is a grouping of similar states, fear is distinct from terror, enmity from resentment, jealousy from enmity, and depression from illness. Sleep— [is distinct from the others].

It should be understood that these are shown separately and differently due to the distinct characteristics of the *sutta*, the *ussukkata* (eagerness), the *capalatā* (fickleness), and the *moha* (delusion) of the *palaya* (protector) to be described hereafter.
This is the intention regarding the *sāttika-bhāva* (emotional states).
345. "The sattvikas are produced from that which originates in a concentrated mind;
they are also [produced] from emotional intensity (anubhāva), yet they become distinct states.
Regarding the sattvikas, he says "concentrated" and so forth. "Concentrated" means having achieved composure by bringing about one-pointedness of mind.

The mind itself is the self (*attā*); whatever has arisen originating from that is called a "being" (*satta*). Pillars and so forth, which are produced and brought into existence by that being, are called "sentient" (*sāttika*).
Furthermore, these are also "experiences" (*anubhāva*), because they are material forms characterized by modifications of nature that indicate the state of being a pillar and so on.
And he will explain this later with the words, "because of the particularity of the mind's activity," and so forth. Therefore, he says, "even in the sense of being experiences. This being so:
Those *sāttika* expressions are distinct and separate states of being because, according to the method already stated, they differ from the nature of mental states (*cittabhāva*).

(345) Now, following the order of the summary, he demonstrates the state of *sāttika*—which is designated as the "total state" (*kevalabhāva*)—with the words beginning with "concentrated" (*samāhita*).
It is a state of being produced from a mind that has achieved concentration by means of inducing one-pointedness, originating from a concentrated mind.
It is called *nāma*. By means of that cause which consists in the state of being uniform toward gain, loss, and so forth, pillars and other such things are rendered firm and brought to completion;

these are what are called *sāttikas*. Although those *sāttikas* exist as the power (*anubhāva*) [of the mind], they exist as distinct entities even while possessing their own power, because they share the same nature as the modifications that manifest the pillars and so forth—which are designated as the modes of the mind—as it was stated: "The specific movements of the mind, however, bring about the *bhāvas*..."

By the passage beginning with "since in the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*)," it is shown that there are indeed what are called "emotional states" (*bhāva*). These are twofold, by way of the "states of being" (*sāttika-bhāva*) and the "consequent manifestations" (*anubhāva*).

The grammatical analysis of the term is as follows: 1. "That which originates from him who is composed (*samāhita*) and who is the self (*attā*). 2. "Those which come into being from the self (*attā*) who is peaceful (*santa*) and tranquil (*upasanta*).

3. "They come into being (*bhavanti*) from the sentient being (*satta*). 4. "They are produced (*uppādita*) by the sentient being (*satta*). 5. "They are the states (*bhāva*) of the consequent manifestations (*anubhāva*). Such is the construction of the sentence.
*Api* is a particle used in the sense of inclusion.
The varieties of the sattvic emotional states (*sāttikabhāva*) are stiffness, perspiration, and horripilation.
Likewise, perspiration, trembling,
change of color, and loss of voice—
these are the eight emotional expressions (bhāva) that accompany the state of emotion (sāttvika).

346. He shows these by means of the passage beginning with "stiffness" (*thambho*). Here, "stiffness" (*thambho*) is the state of body and mind being unrelaxed. "Languor" (*palayo*) is the condition of sleepiness arising from drowsiness, where only the mere breath-in and breath-out remain; it is the state of being as if asleep. The remaining [characteristics] have well-defined characteristics. 346.
Now he shows the internal (*sāttika*) [reactions] by means of the passage beginning with "stiffness" (*thambho*). Stiffness is defined as the lack of relaxation in body and mind;
languor is the state of sleepiness arising from drowsiness, which consists of nothing more than the mere breath-in and breath-out, and the emergence of perspiration and so forth.

The eight *sāttika* (involuntary) states are as follows: horripilation (*romuggama*), perspiration (*sedo*), trembling (*vepathu*), feverish heat arising from fear and the like (*dāho*), tears arising from contentment and the like (*assu*), shaking (*kampā*), change of color (*vevaṇṇiyaṃ*), deformity (*virūpatā*), and loss of voice (*vissaratā*), which is the state of having a distorted sound.
Furthermore, "the rising up (*añco uggamo*) of the body hairs" is called *romañco*, and it is also called *palayo*.

The phrases "trembling" and "quivering," "sweat, tears, and trembling," "his complexion is disfigured," and "the state of that [disfigurement]," as well as "his voice is disfigured" and "the state of that [disfigurement]"—
these are the sentences. When these states such as *rati* (joy) and so forth [arise],...
If they do not possess stability,
then all those entities become subject to deviation.

347. It is not only the previously mentioned [transitory states] that are transitory; the emotions such as *rati* (love) and so forth are also transitory. Thus he says, “When,” and so on. “They become transitory” means that they become transitory according to their respective application and connection. The rest is easily understood. 347.

Now, by means of the passage beginning with “When,” he demonstrates that just like *nirveda* (disgust) and the others, even *rati*, *hāsa*, and the other emotions may also be transitory at certain times.
When the nine emotions beginning with *rati*—namely, *rati*, *hāsa*, and the rest—are not of a stable nature (*ṭhitisīla*), they do not constitute permanent emotional states (*ṭhāyībhāva*).

If, because they are separated from those various opposing states, these [emotions] do not exist in their own nature—that is, if they do not possess the nature of stability—then all those states such as *rati* (love) and the rest become transitory (*vyabhicārī*).
They become transitory states according to their respective connection with the *vibhāvas* (determinants) and *anubhāvas* (consequents) that correspond to their particular transitoriness.
And [the phrase] "of those [such as] *hāsa* (laughter) and so forth, for whom *rati* and the rest [are the dominant emotions]" means: those whose nature is stability.
The analysis of the compound is "of love and so forth.
Among those, the *vibhāva* (determinant) is the cause for their arising as well as for their intensification.
That which would be their indicator is called "the ensuants" (anubhāva).
Now, he shows the determinants (vibhāva) and the ensuants with the words beginning "the determinant," etc. For the arising of those states (bhāva), such as love and so forth—

Likewise, regarding the cause of intensification (*uddīpana*), the so-called "excitant" (*vibhāva*) is twofold, according to the distinction between the object of perception (*ālambana-uddīpana*) and the intensifying factor itself.

Among these, the excitant as the object of perception consists of the beloved one and so forth, while the excitant as the intensifying factor consists of the moon and so forth. The physical and verbal activity that makes these known and indicates them is called "consequent emotion" (*anubhāva*). It has been thus described.
348. Now, he demonstrates the *vibhāva* (the excitant) and the *anubhāva* (the ensuant) with the words beginning "The *vibhāva*... and so forth.

The cause for the arising of those three—namely, the *sthāyibhāva* (the permanent emotion) and the others—and likewise for their kindling (*uddīpana*) and for the manifestation of those already arisen, is twofold according to the basis (*ālambana*) and the kindler (*uddīpana*);
this is called the *vibhāva*. That which may be bodily or vocal and serves as the indicator (*bodhaka*) of those *sthāyibhāvas* and so forth belongs to actors and poets.

There is an activity; this is called "manifestation" (*īrita*), which is to say "experience" (*anubhāva*). It is called "determinant" (*vibhāva*) because it specifically cultivates or increases [the emotion].

It is called "experience" (*anubhāva*) because it makes manifest or awakens [the emotion]. Herein, what is called "determinant" (*vibhāva*) is twofold: the objective determinant (*ālambana-vibhāva*), which consists of the mutual relationship between man and woman within the sphere of love, and the excitatory determinant (*uddīpana-vibhāva*), such as the moon, beautiful places, and so forth.
The determinants for laughter and the other emotions should likewise be understood as twofold, as appropriate.

It should be applied. "Anubhāva" (manifestation) is twofold: the vocal activity consisting of the expression of various states such as standing still and so forth, and the bodily activity consisting of the dramatic gestures of actors that represent the specific forms of those respective states.
[This is] in order to manifest the manifold causes and the particularities of mental activity.
The *bhāva*, *vibhāva*, and *anubhāva* are clearly explained in the section on *vaṇṇanā* (description) and *bandhana* (bonding). 349.
Through this very description of *vibhāva* and the others, there may be an understanding of the specific distinctions of *bhāva*;

otherwise, when it is said, "Devadatta’s pair of eyes became tearful," who indeed would be able to determine the cause—whether it be grief, joy, or illness—and [to understand] the specific state of the mind?
To show that no one— whether a poet, an actor, or a judge— is able to describe, enact, or understand the *vibhāva* and *anubhāva* without the *bhāva*,
he says "nekahetuṃ" and so forth. To manifest or reveal the *bhāva*— which has many causes (*nekahetu*), many conditions (*bahuhetu*), and specific modes of mental expression—
the *vibhāvas* and *anubhāvas* (defined by the characteristics already stated) are clearly to be described in the composition through words that define their essential nature (*sabhāva*).
Just as by means of the form of a manifestation (*vibhāva*) and so forth, something unspoken is also understood:
when it is said, "Devadatta’s eyes are filled with tears," one does not know [the cause] without a statement of the reason for the tears—whether it be through grief, joy, or disease;
in the same way, joy, laughter, and so forth, which consist of the activity of the mind, [are understood]. 349.

Those states (*bhāva*) cannot be described by poets, displayed by actors, or relished by connoisseurs (*sabhya*) unless they are explained through their respective manifestations (*vibhāva*) and consequent effects (*anubhāva*).
Therefore, one must describe the *sthāyī* (permanent emotion) and the others. Now, instructing [the reader] on this point, he says "nekahetuṃ" and so forth:
"nekahetuṃ" means possessing many causes, such as the various *ālambana-vibhāva* (objective determinants) and other factors, for the arising and so forth of those respective states.

In order to discern and reveal both the specific mode of mental expression and the state of the mind—which is designated as a specific mode of cognitive occurrence—the poet’s descriptions (*vaṇṇiyā*) become worthy of praise when they clearly manifest the power and influence (*vibhāvānubhāvā*) just mentioned, making the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and emotional state (*bhāva*) evident within the context of the bond (*bandhana*).
Thus, [the compound *manovutti* is analyzed as]: "not one" (*na eko*), "that which has this as its cause" (*so hetu assa iti*), and "the expression of the mind" (*manaso vutti*).
And the phrases "and by that," "the distinction thereof," and "both the manifestation and the consequence. Together with the manifestations and consequences,
those various emotions (bhāvas) should be described as appropriate to each,
according to propriety, following the conventions of the world.
350. Now, since these states are to be described by means of their manifestations (*vibhāva*) and so forth, without transcending the nature of the world, he says:
"With manifestations" (*savibhāve*), etc. "With manifestations" means together with manifestations (*saha vibhāvehi*); and those are the "manifestations" (*anubhāvā*). By means of those.
"As appropriate" (*yathārahaṃ*) means they are to be described as appropriate according to their respective relations.

350. Now, instructing that those states which are to be described by relying on the *vibhāva* (the cause) and the *anubhāva* (the effect) must be treated without overstepping the natural order of the world, he said:

"Together with the *vibhāva*," and so forth. By one who conforms to worldly forms and follows worldly convention, those respective states—the three beginning with the state of the stationary (*ṭhāyībhāva*)—should be [described] as appropriate, in accordance with what is fitting, together with their *vibhāva* and *anubhāva*, that is, accompanied by the causes.

By means of the *anubhāvas* (powers) acting as instruments, they are to be described—according to their fitness—in accordance with the various states (*bhāvas*) such as the *vibhāvas* (excitants) and so forth, which are related to them;
that is, they must be described appropriately. Furthermore, [the term *anurūpa* implies] those things which exist together with the *vibhāvas*, and those very *anubhāvas*;
and [it implies] that which is worthy of not being transgressed, and that which is worthy of not being transgressed in terms of propriety; this is the nature (*rūpa*) of the world.
The analysis [of the compound] is: "having the same form" (*sarūpa*) and "it follows that [form] by way of its nature" (*sīlena*).

Because of the specific modes of mental activity, it is described through the influence of external perspiration and so forth, arising from the mental factors (*mānasa*) and the physical constituents (*sāttika-aṅga*).

351. To the question, "How are the *sāttika* [emotions] to be described? he says, "In the mind," and so forth. The state of those things which possess specific modes of activity of the mind is [the *sāttika*].

Therefore, the *sāttika* are mental—that is, they exist in the mind—and they are to be described by means of the *anubhāvas* (consequent manifestations) such as perspiration, which have issued forth and emerged from the limbs, that is, from the body.
However, the intended meaning is that the *bhāva* (the underlying emotion) is not merely the water of perspiration itself.

351. Having thus shown the sequence for describing the general nature of the *bhāvas*, he now shows that the description of the specific *sāttika* (innate) *bhāvas* is as follows, by means of the passage beginning with "mind" (*citta*).
Because they are specific modes of the mind—that is, specific functions of the mind—the *sāttika* *bhāvas* exist within the mind (*mānasa-citte*).
They are [manifested] through external effects such as perspiration, which have issued forth from the body (*aṅgato sarīrato*) as perspiration and so on.
The meaning is that they are "to be described" (*vaṇṇiyā*) by means of the "manifestations" (*anubhāvehi*) acting as instruments;

for, apart from the manifestations of the states such as sweat—which are distinguished by their specific qualities—they emerge outside the [eight] factors, and thus sweat and so forth, when mentioned alone, do not constitute "states" (*bhāva*) and the like.
Furthermore, "the activity of the mind" (*cittassa vutti*) is precisely that which constitutes the distinction of those *sāttika* [emotions].

And the phrase "the state of those" (*tesaṃ bhāvo*), and "that which exists in the mind" (*manasi bhavati*), and "sweat, etc., of which saliva and so forth are the beginning" (*sedo ādi yesaṃ kheḷādīnam*),

and "those sweat and so forth which have issued forth and emerged" (*nissaṭā niggatā ca te sedādayo*), and "those very things are the manifestations" (*te eva anubhāvā*)— this is the sentence. [This is] the intended meaning of the *rasa*.
The joy of those who have attained composure, which is experienced by those who know it as such while following the path to bondage—
this is what is called "flavor" (rasa) by the experts.

(352) Now, because it was stated [in the previous verse], "for the sake of the enjoyment of flavor (rasassādāya)," he speaks the words beginning with "of those who have attained composure" (sāmajjikānaṃ) in order to define that flavor.
The meaning of *bandha* (bond) is that which they recollect by way of mental cultivation; thus, they are called "followers of the meaning of the bond.

The joy (*ānanda*) that arises in the minds of those female companions (*sāmajjikā*) and friends is what is termed the "erotic flavor" (*siṅgāra-rasa*) and so forth within the bond, as described by those who know it and perceive flavors, like the sweet and other tastes of the world.
How so? He says: "It is relished" (*rasīyati*), meaning it is tasted. And what is it? Just as...
Just as men of good mind, while eating food prepared with various seasonings, relish the flavors and attain contentment,
so too do those of good mind and discernment relish the dramatic states (ṭhāyībhāva) which are manifested through various gestures and endowed with the science of vocal expression;
therefore, these are called "drama" (nāṭya).

352. Now, having stated "for the sake of the enjoyment of flavors (rasassādāya) by the virtuous," he demonstrates the flavor that has arrived according to the sequence of the enumeration with the words beginning "Sāma.

That joy and satisfaction which exists in the minds of the virtuous (sāmajjika)—those who follow the meaning of the bond (bandha), that is, those whose intellects proceed in accordance with the meaning of the bond—is what constitutes sweet and other such flavors in the world.
"It is called *rasa* because it is said by those who know its definition—that it is *rasa* by way of this verbal meaning ‘it is tasted (*rasīyati*)’ in the sense of being relished (*assādanīya*).
The phrases ‘engaged in a festival (*samajja*)’, ‘the meaning of a bond (*bandha*)’, ‘recalling that’, and ‘knowing that’ [are used].
Just as those consuming food prepared with various condiments..."
Just as beings would relish various tastes such as salty or sour and would thereby become satisfied, even so,

those endowed with wisdom and free from envy relish the *sthāyibhāvas* (enduring emotional states) when they are joined with appropriate *sāttvika* expressions that serve as the limbs for the description manifested through various types of dramatic acting (*abhinaya*).
Therefore, because these *sthāyibhāvas* are manifested through the acting of actors, they constitute the "taste" (*rasa*) defined as the satisfaction of the audience.
And because they are causes, they are also called "actors" (naṭa) and "flavors" (rasa).
[This is] through their distinctions of flavor, their manifestations, and their powers.
That which is brought to a state of being tasted by means of the sattvic transitory states is indeed rasa.

353. By the words beginning with “*savibhāvo*,” he explains the attainment of the state of being a *rasa* by those very *sthāyins*. The meaning is: “He is that very thing”; that aforementioned *rasa* is nothing other than the state of being a *sthāyin*.

353. Now, by the words beginning with “*savibhāvā*,” he clarifies how the nature of the *rasa* reaches the state of being a *sthāyin*, [stating] that this *rasa* just described—through its various *vibhāvas* and *anubhāvas* accompanied by the respective *vibhāvas* corresponding to each of those *sthāyins*—[attains that state].
Furthermore, when the *sthāyibhāva* (the stable emotion) is brought to a state of relish by means of the *anubhāvas*,
the *sāttvika-bhāvas*, and the *vyabhicāribhāvas*— which serve as instruments conducive to that very *sthāyibhāva*— and is thus attained through the power of the poet,
that very *sthāyibhāva* should be understood as "rasa" by way of metaphorical designation (*kāriyopacāra*). And because they function together with the *bhāvas*, they are called *savibhāvā*.

The phrase "and those [emotions] which are the manifestations (*anubhāva*s), and those which are the involuntary (*sāttvika*) ones, and those which are the transitory (*vyabhicārin*) ones" refers to the state of one who relishes (*assādiya*). The aesthetic flavors (*rasa*s) follow the sequence of the permanent moods (*sthāyin*):
the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), the comic (*hāsya*), and the pathetic (*karuṇa*); the furious (*raudra*), the heroic (*vīra*), and the terrifying (*bhayānaka*);
the loathsome (*bībhatsa*) and the marvelous (*adbhuta*), as well as the peaceful (*śānta*).

354. He explains their classification by way of their names with the words beginning “erotic” (*siṅgāra*). “In the sequence of the permanent moods” (*ṭhāyinam-anukkamā*) means in the order or succession of the permanent moods (*ṭhāyibhāva*) stated as “joy, laughter, sorrow,” and so forth.

354. With the words beginning “erotic,” he now shows the alternative names for the permanent moods—joy, laughter, and so on—which are the states of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and the attainment of the situation (*avatthāsampatti*), according to their sequence.
“In the sequence of the permanent moods” refers to the order of the permanent moods of joy, laughter, and so forth, mentioned previously.

The nine so-called *rasas* (aesthetic flavors) are: the erotic (*siṅgāra*), the comic (*hassa*), and the pathetic (*karuṇā*)—namely, the erotic, the comic, and the pathetic; the furious (*rudda*), the heroic (*vīra*), and the terrifying (*bhayānaka*)—namely, the furious, the heroic, and the terrifying;
and the loathsome (*bībhaccha*), the marvelous (*abbhuta*), and the peaceful (*santa*)—namely, the loathsome, the marvelous, and the peaceful.
The word *rasa* should be applied individually to each, as in "the erotic flavor," "the comic flavor," and so forth. [The phrase] "the erotic, the comic, and the pathetic" is thus explained.

Conflict (*viggaha*). In the remaining cases as well, these are the same gender-compounds (*liṅgasamāsa*). Since these [states] are not different from joy (*rati*) and so forth in the case of the *siṅgāra* (erotic) and other rasas, they should be understood precisely within the subsequent explanation of joy and the rest.
This is a bliss (*ānanda*) in the form of suffering (*dukkha*).
How indeed could there be joy for the listeners regarding [his] compassion and other virtues,
when there was sorrow for Vessantara?
355. To the question, "How can compassion (karuṇā) and the like, which take the form of sorrow and so forth, be an aesthetic flavor (rasa)? he says, "In suffering," and so on.
The intended meaning here is that for Vessantara, the separation from his children and wife was indeed suffering in the form of compassion and sorrow;

however, for the present-day listeners and beings, it is nothing but joy. 355. The flavor mentioned below is contentment alone; how could compassion, anger, and the like—characterized by sorrow and so forth—be a flavor?
Anticipating the doubt that [compassion] might not exist, he says, "In the form of suffering," and so forth. If it is asked:

"How could this Ānanda—referred to by such terms as 'the joy of the female monkeys' (sāmajjikānam-ānando)—exist in the form of suffering, characterized by pain, or in objects such as compassion and its derivatives?"—this is not a fault;
for even in the case of the Bodhisatta Vessantara, there was sorrow born from the separation from his children and wife.
Now, for those virtuous people who hear [this], there may be joy (*ānanda*);
because it is the cause of joy, by way of metaphorical designation (*kāriyopacāra*), it is called "satisfaction" (*santosa*).

The intention is that, through the power of the subject matter, even sorrow and other forms of suffering—which are manifested after having been brought to the state of the flavor of compassion (*karuṇārasa*) and so forth—arouse rapture (*pīti*) in those who hear it, as they exist in the form of suffering. Suffering (*dukkha*).

The phrase "whose nature is compassion and so forth" means that form (*rūpa*) is its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*); and the phrase "of which compassion is the beginning" means that Rudra and others are its beginning.
This is the description of the state of abiding in delight (*rati-ṭhāyi-bhāva-niddesa*). The state of abiding in delight.
The enjoyment and delight of young people who are mutually in love, consisting of the consumption of delightful places, arts, seasons, and so forth, is what is meant by *pamoda* (pleasure).

(356) In order to show the divisions of the erotic (*siṅgāra*) and other [rasas], he says "in delightful places" (*ramme*) and so on. Therein, by the phrase "delightful places" (*rammadeśa*) and so forth, the excitants (*uddīpana-vibhāva*) are indicated.

It has been shown. By the term “youthful,” the manifestation of the object (*ālambanavibhāva*) is indicated; for a woman is the object-manifestation for a man, and a man is the object-manifestation for a woman.
“Delight” (*pamoda*) means having the nature of joy through mutual enjoyment. 356.

Now, he explains in sequence the three types of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) beginning with the erotic (*siṅgāra*), starting with the words “delightful” (*ramma*) and so forth. [This involves] the cultivation of delightful places, times, seasons, dress, and so on.
A delightful, unobstructed, clean, pure, and excellent dwelling place; the arts such as charming songs and the like;
a season conducive to pleasure such as spring; activities adorned with garlands, perfumes, and so forth; a pleasing appearance;

and by the word "etcetera," speech, music, and the like—by means of wisdom, rather than merely regarding these as seen, heard, or sensed objects, one repeatedly experiences them in their various respective modes.

The delight, the satisfaction, the joy, and the pleasure of young men and women who are mutually attached—due to their mutual signs, secondary characteristics, and intentions—arising from excessive attachment, is called "rati" because it is desired (*ruccati*) due to its desirability (*ruccanato*).
In this analysis, the letter *ra* is a euphonic insertion (*sandhija*). Furthermore, those things of which place, art, time, and dress are the first are [the factors of amorous enjoyment].
And: "those delightful regions... [and so on]... and Vesālī and the like," and "the repeated resorting to them," and "one after another," and "attached to them"—such is the sentence.
Their power and majesty are established by reasoning.
The bonds nourish it; and that [bond] is threefold,
according to its power over conjunction,
disjunction, and enjoyment.

357. “By *yutti*,” and so forth. Those aforementioned *bhāvas* and *anubhāvas*, when joined—excluding indolence (*ālasiya*), arrogance (*uggata*), and disgust (*jigucchā*)—with those *bhāvas* such as apprehension (*saṅkā*) and zeal (*ussukka*) which are their manifestors (*tadbyañjaka*) and corresponding *anubhāvas*, and when they are applied appropriately to the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) rasa characterized by non-union (*ayoga*) and so on, it is through being composed with such a joining (*yutti*) that they nourish that *rati* (pleasure);
and thus, being nourished in this very way, [it reaches its full development].
The aesthetic flavor (rasa) known as the erotic (siṅgāra) arises. That too is threefold—this is the connection [of the sentence].

Therein, "union" (ayoga) is the non-union of women and men who, having previously been unconnected, desire union through passion. "Separation" (vippayoga) is the absence of contact between both parties whose love has grown to an extraordinary degree.
"Enjoyment" (sambhoga) is the mutual engagement in looking at one another and so forth by lovers who are distinguished by the intense influence of desire.
357. Now, by means of the passage beginning with “by way of logic” (*yuttiyā*), he demonstrates the cause for the arising of love (*rati*) and the application [of its expression].

Those two—the emotional state (*bhāva*) corresponding to love among the indicated transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*), and the consequential emotion (*anubhāva*) that manifests it—act as the logical reason (*hetu*) by virtue of being conducive to the three types of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), namely: union (*ayoga*), separation (*viprayoga*), and enjoyment (*sambhoga*).

Because it is opposed to pleasure (*rati*), having avoided laziness, excessive greed, loathing, and so forth, and by means of factors conducive to pleasure such as apprehension (*saṅkā*) and eagerness (*ussukka*), the compositions (*bandha*) fashioned by poets nourish that pleasure according to their respective requirements;

just as they fulfill and adorn it through its manifestation, so too does the flavor known as the erotic (*rati-śṛṅgāra*) become fully adorned. And this, though described generally as the erotic flavor (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*), [is further distinguished].
Erotic sentiment (*siṅgāra*) is threefold according to the distinction between union, separation, and enjoyment.
Among these, "union" (*ayoga*) refers to the non-union of a woman and a man who, having previously been devoid of mutual association, long for union through the power of fresh passion.
"Separation" (*vippayoga*) refers to the mutual longing of a woman and a man whose love has grown intense through the excellence of their union.
"Sambhoga" (enjoyment) refers to the gratification derived from mutual seeing and so forth by those possessed of lustful desire and craving for sensual pleasures.
The phrase consists of "bhāva" (being), "anubhāva" (manifestation), "ayoga" (conjunction), "vippayoga" (disjunction), and "sambhoga" (enjoyment).

Furthermore, by the venerable teacher Saṅgharakkhita Mahāsāmi, who composed this ornament [of poetry], [it was intended] for those whose mental continuums are pure and not greedy for the most sweet nectar of the True Dhamma.
Although there is no purpose for those rich in asceticism (tapodhana) in the comprehension of other aesthetic flavors (rasa),

because only the mere definitions of the ninefold rasas— such as the erotic (siṅgāra) and so forth— are presented for the sake of non-confusion regarding various worldly conventions, and because the comprehension of a definition is not easily achieved in the absence of grasping the corresponding defined objects,
[the author] provides the explanation of each respective definition immediately after stating them, for the purpose of comprehending those stated definitions.
Only a mere indication of each respective characteristic (lakkhiya) needs to be shown.
Since the eight types of aesthetic semblances— namely, the semblance of laughter (*hasābhāsa*) and so forth— are to be understood through the very semblance of the erotic sentiment (*siṅgārarasa*),

which was previously defined by the passage beginning with "the face of a lotus, wondrously bent by passion, upon the earth," etc., the characteristic of the erotic sentiment should be understood as follows.
Drawing me along with the melody of her song,
as if binding my gaze with the rays of her eyes, she led me—
rendered helpless by her hand-grasp— to perform such a difficult task.
Today, by means of this method, I have attained Serandadī.
Because she was fond of the singing of elephants, the master of songs—rich in song—drew her near, having pulled her close to himself;
he bound her with the cord known as the "eye-ray" (the tethering rope), and with a grasp of the trunk, he took hold of her hand.
Having captivated him with the melody of her song— like a hand that seizes by the trunk, rendering one helpless, devoid of self-will,
and subject to another's power— and having drawn him near to herself,
she bound him with the bond of the rays of her eyes, which were the radiance of her own gaze; thus, he was rendered helpless, stripped of his resolve, and bewildered by her grasp of his hands.

"She who was dear to me has today, by means of destiny and fortune, been attained and won by me— this young Naga maiden named Irandati, Irandati— who has directed me toward such a difficult task. Here,
the excitant cause (*uddīpana-vibhāva*) is shown by these lines of verse, which consist of the melody, the glance, and the grasping of the hand.
Since both woman and man, as well as man and woman, serve as objects for one another, the manifestation of the object is shown by the phrase, "She was plucked by me.
By the phrases, "Having dragged her near, he bound her helpless," the delight characterized by a state of being inflamed by desire is shown.
And by the phrases, "Even such a one he employed in difficult tasks," the exertion and so forth [attained] through the prescribed method are shown.
By these [terms], such transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*) as joy (*harisa*) and so forth are shown.

Having excluded transitory emotions opposed to *rati* (such as world-weariness, indolence, intense disgust, etc.), those poetic compositions that manifest the aforementioned determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth—being employed in a manner suitable for the arousal of *rati*, such as "with the melody of song" and so on—are here called *anubhāvas*.
In the dramatic and other treatises on the arts of representation, this is known as *abhinaya* (acting).

The *anubhāva* (consequent effect) consists of such things as delightful dress, ornaments, and attire; because pleasure does not arise in their absence, they are understood through their functional capacity (*sāmatthiya*).
Thus, the apprehension of the characterized (*lakkhiya*) by means of the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) should be applied in all cases.

Since this bond is the cause of the pleasure that arises from the words which convey the understanding of the meaning of the connection (*satibandha*), it is called "flavour" (*rasa*) by way of metaphorical designation (*kāriyopacāra*). The same applies to what follows.
Through states such as hatred,
agitation, and transformation,
whether directed toward oneself or another;
Laughter, through its attendant emotions such as sleep,
lassitude, fainting, and so forth,
may reach its full development.

"Furthermore, there are others such as ‘pabhuti’ [etc. (358). Regarding the phrase ‘In modification,’ etc.: modification (*vikāra*) refers to a change in form, such as the binding of hair and so forth, which is the opposite of one’s usual state in place, age, and so on;

it is the first among those [factors] such as other actions and dancing. Through these *vibhāvas* (causes of manifestation), laughter is an expansion of the mind; that too is either connected to oneself..."
Now, regarding that which pertains to another: therein, that which attains manifestation solely through the power of its own destruction (vibhāva) is "for one's own sake" (attaṭṭha).

However, that laughter which, though arisen from the perception of destruction, is concealed by the depth and other qualities of a man and is manifested only when another man laughs, is "for the sake of another" (paraṭṭha).
That laughter belongs exclusively to the category of the transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāva), such as sleepiness and the like, within the group of the consequent emotions (anubhāva).
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), eye-twitching and so forth are included. When there is nourishment (*pariposa*), there may be what is called the comic flavor (*hāsya-rasa*).
The connection is that this comic flavor occurs especially among women and the like. Here, by the word "the like" (*pabhuti*), low-natured persons are comprised. 358.

Now, in order to show the manner in which the comic flavor is nourished, he says "transformation" (*vikāra*) and so forth. [The comic flavor arises] through transformations of shape and so forth, [as well as] place, age, and gender.
Laughter—characterized by the expansion of the mind—is that which arises, either in oneself or in another, due to two kinds of causes consisting of specific forms:
those involving the binding, movement, or posture of the hair, and those such as dancing and singing.

It is accompanied by the transitory states (vyabhicārin) of sleep, lethargy, and intoxication, and by the consequent effects (anubhāva) of sleep, lethargy, intoxication, the twitching of the eyes, and so forth; thus, through its connection with these very transitory states known as sleep, lethargy, and intoxication, it is associated with them.
When there is nourishment by means of the instruments [of sense], there may be a flavor called laughter;
that laughter occurs especially among women and the like, as well as among those of low character.

And "that which has change and form as its beginning," and "those which have sleep, lethargy, laziness, and fainting as their beginning"—these are the powers such as the twinkling of the eyes and so forth. And these...
And "ca" means "and," as in the phrase "women and so forth whose nature is base.
Here, "Hassappabheda" refers to eyes that are wide open with joy.
Whatever being may laugh, that is *hasita*;
laughing with a sweet voice is *vihasita*;
and laughing while shaking the head is *upahasita*.
Laughing with eyes that sparkle and talk,
with limbs tossed about, is "laughter with loud laughter";
if these two types of laughter are mentioned as pairs, [they are so designated].
[These occur] respectively in the superior, the middling, and the inferior [types of laughter].
(359–360) He explains the distinction regarding laughter with the words beginning “*sita*” and so forth. Here, that in which the eyes expand is *sita* (smiling);
that in which some teeth are slightly visible is *hasita* (laughing); and that in which there is a sweet tone or sound is *vihasita* (mirthful laughing).
A smile accompanied by the shaking of the shoulders and head is the "upahasita" (smile). That which is accompanied by tears and water in the eyes is the "apahasita" (laugh).
That which has limbs scattered and extended here and there is called the "atihasita" (loud laugh).
Among these [four], starting from the beginning, two types of laughter each are, in their respective order, the eldest.
The connection is that [these] are said to be [found] in the middling and the inferior as well.
This is understood from the word "by the ancients" (*purātanehi*). Now, he shows the classification of laughter with the words beginning with "smile" (*sita*):

here, in this context of laughter, the opening of the eyes—the expansion of the eyes—is called a "smile. That which involves some manifestation of the teeth, however, is "laughter" (*hasita*), wherein some of the teeth are visible.
[The first] is called *vihasita* (a smile). That which is accompanied by the shaking of the shoulders and head is called *upahasita* (a laugh).
That which is accompanied by tearful eyes and weeping is called *apahasita* (a roar of laughter).
That which has disordered limbs—possessing such members as hands and feet that are extended inappropriately—is called *atihasita* (excessive laughter). Of these six...
"In due order and by stages, two each— regarding the superior, the middling, and the inferior objects—

were spoken by the ancients as they were uttered. "His eyes are expanding," "having observed something slightly," "his voice is sweet," "shoulder and head," "trembling of the shoulder and head," "that which exists together with that," and "together."
The phrase "whose eyes are rolling with water" involves the addition of the anusvāra [to form *jalena*]. The sentence "whose limbs are tossed about" is likewise.

The pair consisting of *sita* (smiling) and *hasita* (laughing) occurs in the highest [degree]; the pair consisting of *vihasita* (mirthful laughter) and *upahasita* (derisive laughter) in the middle;

and the pair consisting of *apahasita* (loud laughter) and *atihasita* (excessive laughter) in the lowest. The intention is that these aesthetic flavors (*rasas*), when employed with their corresponding *vibhāvas* (determinants) and so forth, reach their respective states.
The example of one who speaks with hatred should be understood thus: "Even he who,
full of faith, formerly honored the Dhamma with his neck-jewel,
may now, being afflicted, destroy its peerless sweetness."
"Even by the word of a low-caste woman,
the Naga King showed devotion to me, though I am harsh.
He who was formerly faithful to the Dhamma when that discourse on the Dhamma was being preached— even with his own priceless throat-jewel— gave it away.

He honored him; yet that Nāga king, at the word of a woman—even one who was concealing her own true nature and intention—placed his devotion in me, who am harsh and fierce, though I am unequal to her, devoid of her qualities, and a ruinous fool, for the sake of killing and destroying [the other].
Here, in this very instance, there is the Nāga king’s perverse conduct, such as the destruction of his own confidence.
The objective factor (*ālambanavibhāva*) consists of: the Bodhisatta’s state of being worshipped with priceless and beloved objects at the very beginning;
his incomparable nature; his acceptance of the woman’s words; his lack of awareness regarding her intention; and Puṇṇaka’s ferocity.
Through all these statements, the excitant factor (*uddīpanavibhāva*) is demonstrated. By means of these, that which is designated as the state of the stable substratum (*ṭhāyībhāva*)—

Laughter (*hāsa*) is indicated by the power of implication (*sāmatthiyā*); it is manifested through the concomitant emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*) such as lassitude, contentment, and trembling, while excluding those incompatible with laughter such as despair (*nirveda*), as well as the sattvic emotions (*sāttvikabhāva*). Thus, it is illuminated by implication.

The *anubhāvas* (consequent manifestations) are the aforementioned verbal expressions that reveal the corresponding determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth. These should also be described in relation to a person of middle age, according to the classification of laughter.
These two, the smile and the laughter, are to be seen.
But compassion, which takes the form of sorrow,
is the state of one who stands in the place of compassion.
From the standpoint of their completion, cessation,
and disappearance; therein, through their power,
[arise] weeping, fleeing, paralysis, and so forth.
Despondency, indolence, death, anxiety, and so forth are the transitory emotions (*vyabhicārin*). 361.
“In sorrow,” and so on. This refers to the attainment of the undesirable—such as separation from a son—and the attainment of the desirable—such as being led away from one’s country.
The loss of Dhamma or of wealth and so forth, arising from those things that have become non-existent, is of the nature of sorrow (*soka*) and has sorrow as its essence;

this is what is called the "flavour of compassion" (*karuṇa-rasa*). In this regard, the sorrow of superior persons arises from the occurrence of undesirable events such as the separation from a child, and from the loss of desirable things such as Dhamma.

However, for inferior persons, it arises from the occurrence of undesirable events such as being expelled from their country, and from the loss of desirable things such as wealth, as well as [from the suffering] of others.

However, regarding the loss of wealth and so forth, it is only for the supreme [Buddha] that this occurs because of his great compassion; the rest is easily understood. Furthermore, the power (*anubhāva*) herein should be examined according to what is appropriate.
Now, he shows the sequence for nourishing the aesthetic flavor of compassion (*karuṇā-rasa*) with the words beginning "Sorrow" (*soka*).
From the occurrence of the undesirable—such as the separation from a child or the like—or from the loss of the desirable, such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth, or wealth and so forth...

Through these manifestations of the object—namely, the destruction of a beloved being and so forth—which function as its instruments, that which arises in the form of sorrow is called "compassion" (*karuṇa*).

However, compassion itself has the essential nature of sorrow and the flavor of compassion (*karuṇā-rasa*). In that context, within the flavor of compassion, there are the "consequents" (*anubhāva*), such as weeping, fleeing, and paralysis;
that is, weeping, fleeing, paralysis, and so forth. The specific nature of paralysis and the others was explained below.
It has already been stated. Transient emotions such as despondency, indolence, and thoughts of death occur as variations within that very [state].
Here, sorrow arises for the noble through the attainment of undesirable things such as separation from a son, and through the loss of desirable things such as virtue and Dhamma;

it arises for the lowly through the attainment of undesirable things such as the departure from one’s country, and through the loss of desirable things such as wealth. For others, it arises through the loss of wealth and so forth.
However, because it arises only in one who possesses supreme great compassion, that sorrow does not arise in others regarding that same object.
Therefore, the application should be made accordingly. Furthermore, the nature of sorrow is form;
it is the attainment of the undesired, the loss of the desired, both the attainment of the undesired and the loss of the desired, as well as weeping, ruin, and paralysis.

The grammatical construction is as follows: "ceti ca" (and also), "te ādi yesam" (those which have these as their beginning), "visādo ca ālasyañca maraṇañca cintā ceti ca" (despair, laziness, death, and anxiety, and also), and "tā ādi yesam" (those which have these as their beginning).
The characteristic of this flavor of compassion (*karuṇā-rasa*) should be seen in this way:
"He who, seated in front of the hundred kings drawn forth..."
Like the Conqueror, he used to grace his seat with righteousness;
now that this ornament of the world has been led away by a yakkha,
hanging by his horse’s tail, what can one man do?
He who, honored by one hundred and one kings and surrounded by a retinue of one hundred and one monarchs— like a Conqueror, like a Buddha—
adorns and prepares the Dharma-seat with the Dharma through his sweet discourse on the Dharma;
that Vidhura Paṇḍita, the ornament of the world and the crowning jewel of the world’s affection, having been dragged away by the yakkha Puṇṇaka...
"Having been led away, now that he has clung to his horse’s tail, what can he do all alone?
Here, the phrase "led away" (*ihānīto*) demonstrates the state of the objective basis (*ālambana-vibhāva*) for sorrow, namely the separation from a beloved object.

By the entire sentence beginning with "When the hundred-and-one kings were dragged away," the excitant cause (*uddīpana-vibhāva*) is shown, as well as the dominant state (*thāyībhāva*) consisting of excited sorrow, and the transitory states (*byabhicārībhāva*) such as despondency, lethargy, and anxiety.

The determinants (vibhāva) such as weeping, fleeing, and paralysis, along with the consequents (anubhāva) that reveal them, are illuminated by the power of the sentence. Anger arises from states such as envy and so forth,
while pride arises in a person from states such as arrogance and so forth.
The rasa known as the Furious (Raudra) arises from such factors as the reddening of the eyes and so forth.
(362) The passage beginning with “Anger” is easy to understand. Here, by the first word “and so forth” (ādi), the determinants (vibhāva) such as lack of composure and derision are included;

by the second, the transitory states (vyabhicārin) such as ferocity and agitation; and by the third, the consequents (anubhāva) such as the knitting of the brows, the pursing of the lips, and the pressing of the lips together.

362. Now, he shows the sequence for nourishing the rasa of wrath (*krodha*) with the words beginning "wrath" (*kodho*). Wrath [is nourished] by causes such as envy (*macchariya*), non-discernment (*avikkhepa*), derision (*upahāsa*), and so forth;

by determinants (*ālambana*) and other manifesting factors (*vibhāva*); by transitory mental states (*vyabhicāribhāva*) such as self-conceit (*tāsamada*), arrogance (*uggata*), and agitation (*sambhama*);
and by external effects (*anubhāva*) such as reddening of the eyes (*nayanāruṇatā*), redness of the eyes (*nettaratta*), breaking of the limbs (*subhaṅga*), and biting of the lips (*oṭṭhapīḷana*).

When there is a person (*posa*) by means of the manifestations (*anubhāva*) acting as instruments, the flavor (*rasa*) called "obstructed" (*ruddha*) arises. The grammatical analysis of the compound is as follows: *macchariya-ādi* means "those for which stinginess is the first";
*tāsa-ca-mada-ce-ti* means "those for which fear and pride are the first"; *nayanāni ca tāni aruṇāni ca* means "those eyes which are red"; and *tesaṃ bhāvo* means "the state of those";
finally, *sā ādi yesaṃ* means "that [state] is the first of which"—such is the construction of the sentence.
The example of the *ruddarasa* (the taste of blood) should be seen as follows:
"O you who are preyed upon by humans, you have been captured by a *yakkha*;
do not clutch at his hair, but look toward the city!"
"With all his limbs pulverized by the mouth of the Vairaṃbhavat wind, how can a mortal see the world of the living again?
"O you who are preyed upon by humans, you have been overtaken and seized by a *yakkha*; hold onto the horse's tail! "The tail-hair!"
"Having taken [this], look now at the city; behold your own town!
For just so, how can a mortal man—his entire body pulverized by the face of the Veramba wind—once again see the world of the living, the realm of beings?
Here, by the power of the sentence, both the manifestation of stinginess and the state of persistence characterized by anger are implied.
They are illuminated; by their failure, the transitory states such as intoxication, pride, and haughtiness are manifested.
By the totality [of these], the secondary emotions (anubhāvas) such as the reddening of the eyes and so forth are indicated. The state of being a hero (vīrasthāyibhāva).
The term *vīra* (hero) is known to signify the manifestation of majesty, prowess, and so forth.
Due to its association with valor (*raṇa*), generosity (*dāna*), and compassion (*dayā*), this hero may be of three kinds.
Furthermore, these qualities—fortitude, intelligence, and the rest—are transitory emotional states (*vyabhicāribhāva*).
363. “Patāpa,” and so forth. *Patāpa* is the fiery energy that causes distress to enemies; *vikkama* is the advancing through the circles of adversaries.

These, along with others such as strength (*bala*) and intrepidity (*avikkhepa*), are the manifestations found in those who oppose him. The enthusiasm born from these, having attained the state of a *rasa*, is designated as the heroic *rasa* (*vīra-rasa*).
This hero is threefold due to his engagement in battle, giving, and compassion: namely, the warrior-hero (*yuddha-vīra*), the donor-hero (*dāna-vīra*), and [the compassionate hero].

Regarding "the hero of compassion" (*dayāvīra*), the heroic powers (*anubhāva*) in that case consist precisely of such acts as engaging in battle; while qualities such as fortitude (*dhiti*), courage (*mati*), and loftiness (*uggata*) are the transitory emotions (*vyabhicārin*). 363.
Now, he shows the divisions of the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*) and the sequence of its nourishment with the words beginning "splendor" (*patāpa*). By means of splendor, valor, and so forth...

The heat produced by the power of punishment belonging to other kings, as well as their valor—consisting of the march against their own circle of vassals—and the resulting destruction of their fruits, and so forth;
the enthusiasm arising from these is called "heroism" (*vīra*) by poets and is known as the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*).

This heroic sentiment is threefold, based on the causes of battle, generosity, and compassion, through their association with combat, giving, and mercy. These are indeed battle, generosity, and mercy.

Thus, these are called the "manifestations" (anubhāva). States such as fortitude (dhitimat) and so forth, or those such as fortitude, pregnancy, and so forth, are the "transitory emotions" (byabhicārī-bhāva).
The heroic sentiment (vīra-rasa) is threefold, according to the heroism of battle, the heroism of giving, and the heroism of compassion.
[The compound is analyzed as follows: "patāpa" and "vikkama," and those which have these as their beginning; and "raṇa," "dāna," and "dayā," and the conjunction with them.
The phrase is to be analyzed as follows: "those which have three kinds of assistance," and "those which have both fortitude and intelligence.
An example of the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*) should be seen as follows:
"Having entreated Kuvera... [and so forth].
And even if he were to defeat the entire army of the Kumbhaṇḍas,
seize that most excellent jewel-treasure,
and stake it in gambling;
Having conquered the Kaurava king and the hundred kings by the power of my excellent minister,
I shall bring this jewel of a beautiful young woman here.
"Who here has a burden for me?
Having thus addressed and awakened the Great King Vessavaṇa, who is Kuvera, he alone terrified and struck fear into even that vast, immense army of Kumbhaṇḍas;
and having taken the excellent jewel-treasure, he played with it in a game of dice.

"Having set up the stake and placed it there, and having defeated King Koravya, I shall extract the jewel of the counselor and the jewel of the minister from among the hundred kings by means of a hundred royal relatives;
then, having brought them here, I shall take—seize—the jewel of the beautiful young woman, the jewel of the lovely lady.
In this matter, what burden do I have among those already mentioned? Herein, 'what [burden] is there for me here'..."
By the word "burden" (*bhāra*), the state of persistence characterized as effort is revealed.

Furthermore, in the context of the origin and the elucidation of this [burden], the manifestation of the heat, stride, and other qualities of the Nāga king who undertook the taking up of the female jewel (*itthiratana*)—which served as the cause—and the power (*anubhāva*) consisting of the poetic expressions that illuminate its various forms, are to be demonstrated through the force of the sentence beginning with "having made known" (*viññāpetvā*). [The text continues: "Even a vast army of *kumbhaṇḍas*..."

By the phrases "one" and "from a hundred kings, the treasure of the minister [was taken] due to restlessness," states such as fortitude (*dhiti*), loftiness (*uggata*), and pride (*gabbha*) are manifested;
