and by the phrases "having entreated Kuvera," "having terrified King Koravya," and "having brought him here," etc., states such as intelligence (*mati*) and so forth are manifested as transitory mental states (*vibhāvī-bhāva*). Through these manifested (*vibhāva*), dominant (*anubhāva*), and transitory (*vibhāvī*) states...
It should be understood that the heroic sentiment of battle (*yuddhavīrarasa*) is nourished. By this same method, the heroic sentiments of generosity (*dānavīra*) and so forth are to be understood.
[This concerns] the state of being a source of fear, changeability, and the nature of sentient beings, etc.
Bhayuṅkasa is terrifying; here,
perspiration and so forth are the [physical] manifestations (anubhāva), while fear and so forth are the transitory emotions (vyabhicārin).
364. “*Vikāri*,” etc. *Vikāri* refers to that which proceeds from an unnatural state, being contrary to one’s own nature (*sana*).

These—along with others such as empty forests and so forth—are the sources of fear arising from the inherent natures of women, low-born persons, and the like; or they are the causes of fear arising from eminent persons such as teachers and the like.

The excellence of the fear born from these, or of the terror itself, is called the *bhayānaka* (terrifying) rasa. In this context, there are manifestations such as perspiration, trembling, and the movement of the feet.

The *anubhāvas* (consequents) are [the physical effects], while the *vyabhicāribhāvas* (transitory states) are [such as] despair and so forth. 364. Now, he shows the sequence for developing the *bhayānaka-rasa* (the terrible sentiment) with the words beginning "vikāri" and so on.

The intensification of fear toward things that undergo transformation—such as lightning—is produced by sounds like the roar of lightning, which are contrary to one's nature because they possess transformation, or by beings such as *rākṣasas*.

The "exalted" (*ukkaṃsa*) fear-based sentiment (*bhayānakarasa*), which arises from its causal factors—whether natural (*sābhāvika*) or artificial (*kittima*)—is what is called the "fearful sentiment.

In this context, regarding the domain of the fearful sentiment, the "consequents" (*anubhāva*) such as perspiration and so forth, as well as burning of the body, trembling, and so forth, are the consequents consisting of physical and vocal applications.
The "transitory states" (*byabhicārībhāva*) such as terror (*tāsa*) and apprehension (*saṅkā*) are the transitory mental states here. *Sano*.

And "ca" means both "and" and "also"; "ca" [in *vikāra-va-tā*] means "those which possess a modification"; "vikārino" means "those which undergo modification," and "te" means "they"; "sanasa-ttā" means "beings together with their essence," and "ca" means "and";

"te ādayo yesaṃ suññāraññādīnaṃ" means "those which are the beginning of such things as empty forests and so forth"; "bhayaṃ" means "fear produced by those [forests]"; there is an elision of a word in the middle; "ukkaṃso" means "the excellence thereof";

"sedo ādi yesaṃ kampanādīnaṃ" means "sweat is the beginning of such things as trembling and so forth"; "tāso ādi yesaṃ saṅkādīnaṃ" means "terror is the beginning of such things as apprehension and so forth."
The statement: For women and those of low character, it is caused by fear, such as the movement of a snake or similar things; for superior persons, it is caused by teachers and the like.
Herein, the characteristic should be understood thus:
"That which, quivering at the falling of the sword of [wrong] view..."
The army of Kumbhaṇḍa rākṣasas was sent out in all directions;
like a city that has reached the very edge of the Cakkavāḷa mountains,
Puṇṇaka gazed upon the Lord again and again.

The host of *kumbhaṇḍa* rākṣasas, their army— trembling and quivering from the falling of the sword of wrong views and the piercing of the arrow of wrong views— was driven away as far as the Cakkavāḷa mountain range, reaching all around the entire horizon;
that army which had come upon you, O venerable sirs, was like a city being carried away upon the back of a horse.
"He saw [him] again and again, moment by moment"—that is, he saw him repeatedly at every instant—"I am that yakkha named Puṇṇaka.

Here, by the phrase "by the falling of the sword of his vision" (meaning by the raising of the sword of his view) and by the statement "I am that Puṇṇaka," the *vibhāva*—consisting of the hostile being who is the cause for generating fear—is indicated; and [this is shown] by the phrase "he saw [him] again and again."
The stable state (*ṭhāyibhāva*) consisting of the excellence of the hero’s essence, wealth, courage, and power is manifested;

meanwhile, the transitory states (*vyabhicāribhāva*), such as terror and apprehension, are illuminated by the phrase, “The armies of *kumbhaṇḍas* and *rakkhasas* were sent away on all sides as far as the Cakkavāḷa mountains.
By the word “quivering” (*paripphurantī*), the consequent states (*anubhāva*), such as perspiration and trembling, are shown.
The state of being a source of disgust:
disgust arises from blood and so forth,
and from the loathsomeness of putrefaction and so forth.
The loathsome, the agitation, the surge, the gradual [contemplation], and that endowed with compassion; by means of the nose,
the wrinkling of the nose, and so forth.
His nourishment consists of excrement and so forth. 365. Regarding the passage beginning with “Disgust” (*jigucchā*):

because it is repulsive due to its being filled with putrid worms and the like—such as blood and entrails—it becomes, in sequence, loathsome (*bībhaccha*), agitating, uplifting, and imbued with compassion, through such acts as wrinkling the nose and covering the mouth.
Its nourishment occurs through its manifestations (*anubhāva*), such as suspicion, agitation, and so forth, as well as through its transitory states (*byabhicārī*).
Now, he shows the sequence for nourishing the *bībhatsa* (the loathsome) rasa with the words beginning "disgust" (*jigucchā*).

It is nourished by blood and so forth, by qualities such as redness and so forth, by putrefaction and so forth, by things such as maggots in rotting matter, and by means of detachment—that is, by the state of being dispassionate. 365. Thus, by these [means]...

The loathing that arises through the three modes of contemplation (*vibhāva*) acting as its causes, occurring successively with respect to the three objects of contemplation—blood and so forth—is called the "frightful" (*bībhatsa*) sentiment (*rasa*).
It is characterized by agitation, instability, lack of composure, and trembling; it is accompanied by an upsurge of compassion and conjoined with the form of sorrow.
[This is manifested] through such acts as the contraction of the nose and the closing of the mouth.

The nourishment of this *bībhaccha* (disgusting) rasa occurs through its *anubhāvas* (consequents), such as trembling and the like; its *vyabhicāribhāvas* (transitory emotions), such as apprehension and agitation and the like;

and through these acting as its instruments (*karaṇa*). Because the three locations beginning with blood and the three beginning with agitation are implied, the word "and" (*ca*), though not explicitly stated, should be supplied;
therefore, the *bībhaccha* rasa is indeed associated with the three beginning with agitation.
It should be understood as follows: the phrase "blood, etc. refers to those things beginning with the entrails; "putrid, etc. refers to those things beginning with worms;
"it has agitation" refers to that which is loathsome; "joined with compassion"; "distortion of the nose" means its contraction; "that, etc.
refers to those things beginning with covering the mouth; and "suspicion, etc. refers to those things beginning with trepidation—such are the syntactical connections.
The illustration of this loathsome [meditation] should be understood as follows:
"Those yakkhas fashioned by Puṇṇaka, who wear human skulls and bones,
and who bear hand-buds made of pearls and carry snakes as their necklaces;"
"Anointed with vermilion and red saffron, drinking fat and liquor from human skull-bowls— these rogues of old were seen by me.
Created by the yakkha Puṇṇaka, they wear garlands of human skeletons and bear ornaments made of human bones.
They wore sprout-like hands as ear-ornaments; they bore sprout-like palms fashioned into garlands upon their heads;
they were adorned with serpent-like necklaces of pearl strings; they were accompanied by serpents known as human beings in the form of pearl necklaces;
they were smeared with red saffron known as blood in the form of saffron paste; and they [drank] fat-liquor known as fat from leaden skull-bowls known as leaden cups.

As for those *yakkhas* who might be drinking in the Pure Abhimukha [Heaven], these *yakkhas* were looked upon with indifference by the wise Vidhura, just as one would look upon rogues in a city or drunkards and gamblers.

Here, by the phrases "smeared with red saffron," "bearing hands like sprouts used as ear-ornaments," and "having serpents for their necklaces," there is the manifestation of blood and other such things which cause agitation of the mind; and by the phrase "the man who is a skeleton among corpses... [the text continues].
And by the phrases “drinking fat and liquor from skull-bowls made of lead,” both the manifestation of putridity and so forth— which serves as the cause for the nature of agitation—
and the manifestation of revulsion which serves as the cause for the nature associated with compassion, as well as the consequential manifestations such as the contraction of the nose,
the transitory states such as apprehension and agitation, and the stable state designated as the "fearful" (bībhaccha), are all to be understood as being implied by the power of the sentence.
The state of being a ground for wonder through supermundane matters is this wonderful flavor, the marvelous.
Through its power, there may arise perspiration,
words of praise and the like,
as well as agitation, distress, and wisdom.
“Shame on those who are wayward! (366).

“Excessive,” and so forth. This wonder (*vimhaya*)—a state of stability consisting of a transformation of the mind—arising from things that exceed the world, such as the objects of the words *māyā* (illusion), *vaga* (deception), *ārāma* (pleasure grove), and so on, is called the marvelous flavor (*abbhuta-rasa*). [Its physical concomitants include] perspiration, tears, expressions of praise, horripilation, and so forth.
Through its power, [emotions] such as *tāsa* (fear) may become transitory (*byabhicārī*).
Now, with the words beginning "Ati," he shows the sequence for nourishing the sentiment of wonder (*vimhaya-rasa*).

This wonder arises from causes consisting of word-meanings such as *māyā*, *iddhibhāva*, *ārāma*, and *vimāna*, which function by transcending the established order of the world through word-meanings that exceed the limits of the world (*atilo-kapadattha*).
The state of remaining [in composure] known as the mind’s freedom from ill-will would be a marvelous essence, called a "marvelous essence" (*abbhutaraso*).

Sweat, shouts of "well done," and so forth, would be the manifestations of that marvelous essence. In this context of the marvelous essence, agitation, distress, and wisdom are states that are variable (*byabhicārino bhāvā*).
Furthermore, "transcending the world" (*atikkantā lokaṃ*) refers to those very word-meanings (*padatthā*); thus, it is "well" (*sādhūti*).
"Vāda" means praise; "seda," tears, and "sādhuvāda," acclaim—these are the beginning of those [reactions] such as horripilation and so forth;
and the phrase "tāsa, āvega, dhiti, and paññā" is the statement.
This example of a marvelous flavor (rasa) should be understood in this way.
Though shaken by Puṇṇaka with many terrifying things,
she remained perfectly motionless like a mountain; then,
by him, she was struck down upon the edge of the precipice.
"He is not terrified; he stands firm in his view.

Thus Vidhura the Wise remained perfectly unshakable by that yakkha Puṇṇaka, amidst the many terrors brought forth—like a dancer displaying various transformations—as though they were the many kinds of horrors presented by a theatrical performance.

When Puṇṇaka hurled the Acala mountain—sixty *yojanas* high—from the summit of Mount Kāḷagiri, and while it was falling headlong with its peak downward, he remained entirely unafraid even though there was no foothold; he measured that mountain with his steadfastness of view, exclaiming, "Oh, how marvelous!
Herein, although the cause of fear was present, there was an absence of fear because of his thorough understanding of that situation.
Furthermore, by describing the state of one who has transcended the world— having overcome worldly nature, being unafraid when fear is induced,
and remaining unmoved even when mountains are shaken— the *vibhāva* (the transcendence of worldly objects) is clarified by the phrase,
"Unafraid, he shook it with the strength of his view. Through the word "Aho" and its implied power, [joyful] exclamations, perspiration, tears, and so forth [are indicated].

The determinants (*vibhāva*) have been manifested. Through the power of the combined sentence, the transitory mental states (*vyabhicāribhāva*) such as agitation, fear, and so forth, as well as the dominant mental state (*sthāyībhāva*) known as wonder (*vismaya*), are illuminated. This constitutes the dominant mental state (*samasthāyībhāva*).
The state of being established is equanimity, from which arise loving-kindness,
compassion, sympathetic joy, and so forth; through these states and others, there is the preeminence of that [equanimity].
"Venerated by the noble and the holy.
Thus [ends] the *Subodhālaṅkāra* composed by the venerable Great Master Saṅgharakkhita.
The fifth chapter, titled "Understanding of Rasa and Bhāva," is concluded.
The *Subodhālaṅkāra* is finished. 367.

Regarding the verse beginning with “Ṭhāyi”: The arising of loving-kindness (*mettā*) and other such qualities is the stable state (*ṭhāyībhāva*) termed tranquility (*upasama*). That which possesses an excellence through the corresponding emotional intensifications (*bhāvānubhāva*) is the rasa known as the Peaceful (*santa*). And that [rasa] is cultivated by those who are peaceful.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, "The Comprehension of Flavors and Emotions," in the commentary named Mahāsāmi on the Subodhālaṅkāra. 367.

Now, he demonstrates the sequence for nourishing the flavor of tranquility (*santasa-rasa*) with the words beginning "ṭhāyi": "The arising of loving-kindness (*mettā*) and so forth, and of joy (*āmoda*) and so forth..."

That which arises from the manifestations of loving-kindness (*mettā*), compassion (*karuṇā*), joy (*pīti*), and so forth, is the balanced tranquility of body and mind known as the "abiding state" (*ṭhāyībhāva*).

This occurs through the instrumental factors of the transitory states (*byabhicārībhāva*) such as manifestation and the like; moreover, through the power of those transitory states appropriate to that balance, its excellence is attained.

That which is conjoined with the excellence of this abiding state is "peaceful" (*santa*), meaning it is cultivated by the peaceful and practiced by the virtuous; thus it is "peaceful" and possesses the flavor of peace (*santarasa*).

The phrase "it is called" (*nāma hoti*) is explained as follows: it refers to those for whom loving-kindness (*mettā*), compassion (*dayā*), sympathetic joy (*modo*), and equanimity (*ca*) are the primary qualities (*ādayo*); it refers to that from which their arising (*sambhavo*) occurs;
it refers to that which is the excellence (*ukkaṃso*) of his peace (*santassa*); and it refers to that which is practiced by the virtuous (*sataṃ nisevito*).
This is how the example of its peaceful flavor (*santarasas-sa*) should be understood.
Then even the lionesses entwined him,
as a bamboo thicket surrounds a mountain-elephant in rut;
yet he did not waver even slightly, shaking the yakkhas.
"Even when in distress, he remains peaceful; even sweet things become [unpleasant] to him.

Even when lionesses and male lions approach in a terrifying manner, even when they come near, even when they coil themselves around the elephant, and even when the elephants coil their bodies around him—the singular number is used with reference to the species—he shakes them off like a bamboo thicket shaken by a rutting elephant.
While Puṇṇaka was causing the Kāḷāgiri mountain to shake— as if the yakṣas were shaking it like an elephant with rut flowing from its temples—
the wise Vidhura, having attained peace, remained as if he had reached Nibbāna; he was as if he had entered the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti) by making it his support,
or else he had entered the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), which is termed "Nibbāna in this very life" (diṭṭhadhamma-nibbāna).
The intention is that even slightly or minimally sweet states did not waver from their sweet nature, let alone from their place of sitting.

Here, although the arrival of lions and so forth—which act as causes for running, weeping, trembling, and so on—as well as the coiling of snakes and the shaking of mountains, were occurring, he had attained peace by being free from any such agitation. Thus it is said.

When the ninth state, the "steadfast" (ṭhāyībhāva), is shown in the description that constitutes the natural basis of serenity, its originating causes—the qualities of loving-kindness (mettā), compassion (dayā), and gladness (amodā)—are shown by implication as the causes for its arising and manifestation.

Furthermore, such concomitant states as fortitude (dhiti), intelligence (mati), and mindfulness (sati), as well as their corresponding expressions (anubhāva), are indicated by the phrase: "It winds itself around those who enter and moves them about."
And it should be understood that [the aesthetic flavor] is manifested by the power of the entire sentence.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Comprehension of Flavor and Aesthetic State," in the *Subodhālaṅkāra-nissaya*.
The Commentary on the Subodhālaṅkāra is completed.
